(Understand) a) The pupils are silent for most of the lesson b) The pupils are engaged in intellectually demanding work for most of the lesson c) The teacher gives instructions only once d) No pupil ever breaches a rule In a two-column observation record, the sentence "the teacher used proximity to redirect the talking pupils" belongs in: (Apply) a) the left column, because it records what was seen b) the right column, because it is an inference about what the action meant c) either column, because it is both an observation and an inference d) neither column, because it is a judgement A teacher arranges desks in clusters for a discussion lesson, then is frustrated that the class is noisy. The most likely design failure is: (Apply) a) choosing clusters for a task that needs rows b) not establishing a norm of listening to disagreement before the discussion c) using constructivism when behaviourism was needed d) placing the display wall on the wrong side of the room Wong and Wong (1998) argue that a teacher with a consistent management plan spends the first weeks of term: (Remember) a) establishing consequences for every rule b) teaching the plan, then teaching the curriculum c) letting pupils discover the routines themselves d) focusing on relationship-building before any routines Which pair correctly matches a learning theory with the kind of learning target it serves best? (Understand) a) Behaviourism - interpreting a poem b) Cognitivism - building a new scientific concept from scratch c) Constructivism - practising letter formation until it is automatic d) Behaviourism - drilling a routine until it is automatic A teacher in a low-resource government school cannot move the benches. According to Topic 1.4, what can she still change this week? (Apply) a) Nothing, because the physical environment is fixed b) Only the social environment, because the physical one is fixed c) How the room is used, how the walls are read, how pupils orient, and how they treat each other d) Only the displays, because seating is fixed "Withitness" refers to a teacher's: (Remember) a) ability to teach three theories in one week b) accurate awareness of what is happening across the whole room and willingness to act early c) skill at designing displays from scrap materials d) habit of separating observation from inference A trainee observes a lesson and writes only conclusions in her notebook, with no record of the evidence they are based on. Which observation skill has she not yet developed? (Apply) a) Choosing a focus b) Separating observation from inference c) Using the four lenses d) Completing the five-step cycle

In no more than 80 words, distinguish what behaviourism says learning is from what constructivism says learning is, and give one classroom example that belongs to the first and not the second. (Understand) Explain why a silent classroom is not necessarily a well-managed one, using this unit's definition of classroom management. (Understand) Name the three features of the social environment that carry management weight, and give one concrete indicator a observer could record for each. (Understand) Explain the difference between classroom management and classroom discipline, and give one example of each from a classroom you have observed or experienced. (Understand) A teacher always uses rows. Using this unit's account of seating, explain what kind of learning the row arrangement serves well and what it costs. (Apply) Analyze why a teacher who relies almost entirely on discipline is likely to spend more time reacting than a teacher who invests in management. Refer to the proactive/reactive distinction. (Analyze) A trainee writes in the left column of her observation record: "the teacher praised the pupils who answered correctly and moved on when a pupil gave a wrong answer." Rewrite this as a defensible inference for the right column, and explain why the inference might be wrong. (Analyze) Explain what a resource audit is, and argue why it is a more useful first design step than buying new materials for a low-resource government school. (Apply) A teacher says, "I don't have a philosophy of teaching, I just teach." Using Topic 1.2, explain what that claim overlooks and what the cost is for their management. (Analyze) Describe the five-step observation cycle from Topic 1.3, and explain why the step "separate observation from inference" matters for a trainee's professional development. (Understand)

A teacher believes that "learning is the teacher transferring knowledge to the pupil". Analyze how that belief would shape their management of routines, seating and responses to error, and argue which of the three learning theories it draws on most heavily. (Analyze) Take the Class 4 classroom described in Topic 1.3 (44 pupils, benches for 30, one textbook per four pupils, back benches in shadow, no pupil speaks unless asked). Analyze that room against two features of the physical environment and two features of the social environment, and propose one change to each. Justify each change by reference to a specific learning goal. (Analyze) Using Ertmer and Newby's (1993) continuum, explain why a skilled teacher moves between the three learning theories across a single week rather than choosing one. Illustrate with one concrete week-plan for a lower-primary topic of your choice, showing at least one lesson move drawn from each theory. (Create) Evaluate the claim that "classroom management is just discipline with a nicer name". Use the management/discipline distinction from Topic 1.2, the research findings of Marzano, Marzano and Pickering (2003), and at least one concrete classroom example of your own. (Evaluate) Integrative. You are placed in a low-resource government primary school. The headteacher asks you to improve learning in a Class 5 room with fixed benches, one cracked blackboard, no budget, and a teacher who currently manages mainly through reprimand. Design a management plan for that room that does all three of the following: draws on at least two of the three learning theories, includes at least one change to the physical and one to the social environment, and explains how your plan shifts the teacher's balance from reactive discipline toward proactive management. Justify each choice. (Create)

c - behaviourism defines learning as a change in observable behaviour shaped by reinforcement; (a) is cognitivism, (b) is constructivism. b - activating prior knowledge is a cognitivist move, organising new information against existing mental structures. b - a well-managed classroom is defined by the quality of pupil engagement, not by the absence of noise or breaches. b - the sentence interprets the teacher's action; it is an inference, not a verifiable observation. b - clusters serve discussion, but without a norm of listening to disagreement the noise is unmanaged rather than a sign of learning. b - Wong and Wong's management-plan approach invests the first weeks in teaching the plan, then frees the teacher to teach the curriculum. d - behaviourism best explains the drilling of a routine until it is automatic; (a), (b) and (c) each pair a theory with a target it serves poorly. c - Topic 1.4 argues that even a fixed-bench, no-budget room leaves the teacher multiple levers: use, displays, pupil orientation and social norms. b - withitness is Marzano, Marzano and Pickering's term for accurate whole-room awareness and early action. b - recording conclusions without evidence is the failure to separate observation from inference, which is the core discipline of the two-column protocol.

1. (4 marks) Behaviourism says learning is a change in observable behaviour shaped by reinforcement (1); constructivism says learning is the active construction of personal meaning by the learner (1); the example belongs to behaviourism rather than constructivism (1); the example is a genuine practised response, not a meaning-building task (1). 2. (4 marks) States the unit's definition of management as maximising student learning (1); explains that silence is a behavioural state, not a learning state (1); gives an example of a silent class that is not learning (e.g. copying without understanding) (1); concludes that management is judged by the quality of engagement, not the level of noise (1). 3. (6 marks) One mark per feature correctly named from: participation patterns, norms of help, responses to error, belonging (any three). One mark per indicator that is concrete and recordable (e.g. for participation: "the same six hands went up in a 20-minute lesson"). 4. (4 marks) Management is proactive and acts on the learning environment (1); discipline is reactive and acts on a pupil's breach (1); the management example is genuinely proactive (1); the discipline example is genuinely reactive (1). 5. (4 marks) Rows serve whole-class instruction well because every pupil can see the board and the teacher can see every pupil (1); the cost is that group work is awkward and the pupils nearest the teacher get more attention (1); the explanation is grounded in the Topic 1.4 account of seating (1); the example is concrete (1). 6. (5 marks) Names the proactive/reactive distinction (1); explains that a reactive teacher responds after each breach rather than preventing the conditions for breach (1); links this to the finding that management investment in the first weeks reduces later disruption (1); argues that the reactive teacher spends more time on discipline and less on teaching (1); the reasoning is coherent (1). 7. (5 marks) The inference is a plausible interpretation of the observed action, not a restatement of it (1); it uses language like "the teacher may have been" or "this suggests" rather than stating it as fact (1); names at least one alternative inference the same evidence could support (e.g. the teacher did not hear the wrong answer, or chose not to embarrass the pupil) (1); explains that without asking the observer cannot know which is correct (1); the reasoning is coherent (1). 8. (4 marks) A resource audit is a list of everything in the room that could support learning, marked by whether pupils can actually use it (1); argues that buying new materials is often impossible in a low-resource government school and does not address the use of what is already there (1); links the audit to the Topic 1.4 principle that the design question is "what is already here that I am not using?" (1); the argument is coherent (1). 9. (5 marks) Explains that every teacher has a philosophy, whether examined or not, and that an unexamined philosophy is shaped by how they were taught (1); argues that a teacher without a conscious philosophy manages by habit (1); links this to the cost: the management serves the teacher's default assumptions rather than the current pupils' needs (1); the explanation draws on Topic 1.2 (1); the reasoning is coherent (1). 10. (4 marks) Names the five steps in order: decide what to look for, record what you saw, separate observation from inference, ask why it might be happening, plan one change (1); explains that without the separation step the observer confuses what they saw with what they hope it means (1); links this to professional development: a trainee who cannot keep the two apart will not learn from observation (1); the explanation is coherent (1).

The unit is built to be taught in order, and the dependency is real: Topic 1.2's definition of classroom management draws on the three theories from Topic 1.1; Topic 1.3's observation protocol assumes that definition; and Topic 1.4's design work applies everything that came before. A workable division for the twelve hours is three hours per topic, with the six hours of classroom observation the guide asks for in Week 2 folded into Topic 1.3 as a practicum task. If the block is compressed, compress Topic 1.4 rather than Topic 1.1. The three theories are the foundation everything else rests on, and a trainee who has not grasped them will treat the rest of the course as a set of tips rather than a system. Topic 1.1 is the load-bearing topic of the unit. If only one topic is taught well, it should be that one, because the management/discipline distinction in Topic 1.2 and the observation protocol in Topic 1.3 both assume the trainee can move between the three theoretical lenses.
documents.s: Sequencing across the four-week, twelve-hour block

documents.t: Four come up almost every cohort. Each is named inside the topic that corrects it, but they are worth anticipating. "Behaviourism was disproved and constructivism replaced it." This is the most persistent one, and it matters because a trainee who believes it will skip the hard work of building routines. The strongest counter is not an argument but the Mr Karim vignette in Topic 1.1: the same teacher, the same content, three different lessons, each drawing on a different theory, none of them wrong. Let the class reach the conclusion that the three describe different parts of one process rather than asserting it. "Classroom management means keeping children quiet." Trainees who have been schooled in tightly-controlled classrooms hold this firmly. The two-column observation activity in Topic 1.3 is designed for this moment: when a trainee records a silent copying lesson and then asks "what was the intellectual demand?", the gap between order and learning becomes visible. "Discipline and management are the same thing." This one resurfaces whenever a trainee describes a well-run classroom as one where "the teacher is strict". The sorting activity in Topic 1.2 is the place to correct it. The failure mode is that the group settles each item by majority and moves on; the value is entirely in the disagreement, so intervene if that happens. "I cannot design my classroom because the benches are fixed and I have no budget." Topic 1.4 is built to answer this. Have the class complete the audit table for a real local classroom they know. The list of things they can change this week is almost always longer than they expected, and the exercise does more to build a design mindset than any amount of theory.
documents.s: The misconceptions that recur, and how to handle them

documents.t: Two of the activities ask trainees to work with real classrooms. Two cautions. The observation task assumes access to a live classroom, and not every trainee has one. The topic provides a described classroom as an alternative, but a trainee who can observe a real lesson will learn more. Coordinate with the practicum placement early in the block, and have a recorded lesson ready as a second alternative. A trainee watching a recording should still use the two-column protocol; the discipline of separating observation from inference matters more than the source of the evidence. The audit task in Topic 1.4 can surface frustration. Trainees who teach in the most under-resourced schools may find the gap between the design ideals in the text and the reality of their placement demoralising rather than empowering. Name this explicitly: the point of the audit is not to complain about what cannot change, but to find the one thing that can, and to do it this week.

The Topic 1.1 "one lesson, three ways" activity produces a common failure: the group produces three lesson versions that are identical in practice but labelled with different theory names. This defeats the purpose. The three versions should differ in what the teacher does first, what the pupils do, and what success looks like. If a group's versions are the same, ask them to return to the vignette and identify one thing Mr Karim did on Monday that he did not do on Friday, and one thing he did on Friday that he did not do on Monday. That usually unlocks the distinction.
documents.s: The activity that most often goes wrong

documents.t: Observation task (Week 2). The Topic 1.3 practicum task is the unit's most reliable piece of evidence that a trainee can read a classroom. Collect the two-column records and, if the cohort is willing, read a selection of left-column evidence aloud without naming the school or the teacher. Trainees often discount the protocol when they do it; they accept it when they hear three peers describe the same feature of the same room differently. Theory journal (Weeks 1 to 4). Ask trainees to keep a brief weekly note: one classroom moment they observed or experienced that week, the theory it is best read through, and why. Collect it once, at the end of Week 4. The purpose is to make the habit of reading classroom moments through a theoretical lens, not to test the journal's content. Resource audit (Week 4). The Topic 1.4 audit is the transfer task that matters most for the rest of the course, because Units 2 to 4 all assume a trainee who can look at a classroom and ask "what is working here, and what is working against the learning?" Set it early enough in the week that trainees can carry it out in their practicum school before the block ends.

The bank is on the unit assessment page with model answers and analytic rubrics. Two notes. The RRQ mark schemes are point-by-point and total more than a typical examination would carry; select from them rather than setting all ten. For the ERQs, the rubric caps a response that does not reach "Adequate" on the analysis criterion at 10 out of 20, whatever its other merits. This is deliberate. A fluent, well organised answer that never analyses anything is the most common strong-looking weak response at this level, and the cap is what stops it scoring like a good one.

Unit 1 gave you a definition of classroom management centred on learning and the three theories that explain how learning happens. This unit moves from theory to the teacher's daily planning work. It asks: once you know what learning is, how do you build a teaching plan that is consistent with your philosophy, and how do you make that plan work for every pupil in the room - including when the room holds two grades, or sixty children?

By the end of this unit you should be able to: Explain how curriculum decisions - what to teach, in what order, at what pace - function as management acts that reduce disruption before it starts. Describe the plan, motivate, teach, assess cycle and name the management decision at each stage. Build a teaching plan that is consistent with a stated philosophy of teaching. Differentiate instruction by pupil need, interest and level, and distinguish genuine differentiation from simply making some pupils do easier work. Propose workable management tactics for multigrade and overcrowded classrooms, given the constraints each reality imposes. Take a single curriculum objective and plan it three ways: for a well-resourced single-grade class, for a multigrade class, and for a class of sixty.

Unit 1, in particular the definition of classroom management as maximising learning, the three learning theories, and the management/discipline distinction. This unit assumes you have met those ideas and applies them to planning; it does not re-teach Unit 1.

Topic 2.1 - Curriculum as a management tool - how the curriculum itself does management work; building a teaching plan consistent with your philosophy. Topic 2.2 - Plan, motivate, teach, assess - the four-stage cycle and the management decision at each stage; motivation strategies and what they cost. Topic 2.3 - Differentiation, multigrade and overcrowding - differentiating by need, interest and level; managing multigrade and overcrowded classrooms.

The three topics follow the logic of a single plan. Topic 2.1 asks what your plan is anchored in; Topic 2.2 walks through the cycle that carries it out; Topic 2.3 asks how to adapt it when the pupils or the room make one-size-fits-all impossible. Each topic is one complete learning cycle. The question bank at the end of the unit covers all three topics together. Its answers and mark schemes are in a clearly marked section at the foot of that page; try each item before you read them.

textbook.com.pk Two teachers in the same school in Lahore teach the same Class 4 English lesson from the same textbook. One spends the period managing disruption; the other does not. The difference is not personality. It is that the second teacher made, before the lesson, a set of curriculum decisions - what to emphasise, in what order, at what pace - that removed the frictions the first teacher met unprepared. This topic is about those decisions.

The guide treats curriculum not as a body of content to be delivered but as a set of management decisions that shape the classroom before the lesson begins. Get them right and the room runs more smoothly. Get them wrong and you spend the lesson reacting.

Curriculum, in this course, is the teacher's answer to four questions: what to teach (content selection), in what order (sequencing), at what pace (pacing), and for whom (grouping). Each of these is a management act, because each one determines how much of the lesson's time is spent learning and how much is spent handling the friction that comes from a poor fit between the plan and the pupils. Choosing content is the first management decision. A teacher who tries to cover everything in the chapter sets the class up for rushed explanations, confused pupils, and the disruptions that follow confusion. A teacher who decides what the essential idea is and lets the rest go has created the conditions for depth, and depth is easier to manage than superficial coverage. Sequencing determines whether the lesson builds or stalls. Put the hard idea before the foundation and the class loses the thread; put practice before the explanation and the practice becomes guesswork. A well-sequenced lesson manages attention because each step follows naturally from the last. Pacing is the most common management failure. A pace that leaves the strong pupils bored creates one kind of disruption; a pace that leaves the struggling pupils behind creates another. Evertson and Emmer (2009) treat pacing as a core management skill: the teacher who reads the room and adjusts the speed of the lesson is managing in real time. Grouping decides whether pupils work as a whole class, in pairs, or in small groups, and the management demand of each is different. Whole-class work is the easiest to direct but the hardest to differentiate; group work serves differentiation but requires clear routines. The curriculum decision is not just what pupils learn, but how they are arranged to learn it. The figure above maps these four decisions and the management pressure each one relieves or creates. The point is that curriculum planning is not separate from classroom management. It is the first and most powerful management act a teacher takes.

Topic 1.2 asked how a personal philosophy of teaching shapes management beliefs. This topic takes that a step further: it asks you to build a plan that is consistent with your philosophy, because a plan that contradicts the teacher's own beliefs produces a classroom that feels incoherent to everyone in it. textbook.com.pk The figure above traces two short teaching plans back to two philosophies. The first plan assumes that learning is the transfer of knowledge from teacher to pupil: the teacher explains, the pupils practise, the teacher checks. The second plan assumes that learning is the pupil's active construction: the teacher poses a problem, pupils investigate in groups, the teacher draws out the insight. Both are defensible. What is not defensible is a teacher who holds the second philosophy but teaches the first plan, because the pupils experience the contradiction and the management suffers for it. Wong and Wong (1998) put it as a practical test: a well-managed classroom has a consistent plan that the pupils can learn to rely on. The plan does not have to be elaborate. It has to be yours, and it has to be consistent. Building such a plan starts with three questions: What do I believe learning is? (Unit 1's three theories are your options.) What does that belief imply I should do first, second, third in a lesson? What does it imply I should look like - at the board, moving among groups, listening? The answers are your plan's spine. Everything else - the activity, the timing, the materials - hangs off it.
documents.s: Creating a teaching and learning plan consistent with your philosophy

documents.t: Work in groups of three. Take the following curriculum objective: Class 3 mathematics: pupils will be able to add two-digit numbers with carrying. Now plan this objective three ways: for a well-resourced single-grade class, for a multigrade class (Classes 2 to 4 in one room), and for a class of sixty. For each version, decide: what you would do first, what the pupils would do, and what you would need. Allow 25 minutes. Then present your three plans and identify one decision that changed because of the room, not because of the mathematics.

Name the four curriculum decisions this topic identifies as management acts, and give one example of each. (Remember) A teacher says, "I just follow the textbook, so I don't make curriculum decisions." Using this topic's account, explain what that claim overlooks. (Analyze) Explain why a fast pace can be a management failure even when the content is correct. (Understand) A friend's lesson plan has pupils investigating in groups, but she believes learning is the teacher transferring knowledge. Identify the inconsistency and explain what it costs in management terms. (Analyze) For the objective in the Activity, state one way your plan for a multigrade class would differ from your plan for a single-grade class, and explain why. (Apply)

Curriculum decisions - what to teach, in what order, at what pace, for whom - are management acts that shape the classroom before the lesson begins. A teaching plan that is consistent with the teacher's philosophy produces a coherent, manageable classroom; a plan that contradicts the teacher's beliefs produces friction the teacher will spend the lesson resolving.

I can name the four curriculum decisions that function as management acts and give an example of each. I can explain why curriculum planning is not separate from classroom management. I can build a short teaching plan that is consistent with a stated philosophy. I can identify the inconsistency between a described teacher's philosophy and their lesson plan. I can plan one objective for three different classroom realities.

Over one week, keep a brief note after each lesson: one curriculum decision you made (content, sequence, pace, or grouping) and what happened as a result. At the end of the week, write half a page on which decision made the most difference to how the lesson ran, and why. Do not name the school or the teacher in your write-up.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: Write 350 to 400 words on the following. A teacher in your practicum school says: "I don't have time to plan for every child. I just teach the lesson and manage the class." Write a reply that takes the claim seriously, uses this topic's account of curriculum as a management act, and argues which single curriculum decision would most improve the management of a described lesson. Justify the choice by reference to the pupils or the setting. Mini-rubric Criterion What a strong response does Grasp of curriculum-as-management (Understand) Names at least two curriculum decisions and explains how each functions as a management act Use of example (Apply) The example is concrete and drawn from a described classroom, not generic Argument for the single decision (Analyze) Argues for one decision using a specific feature of the described pupils or setting, not a generic planning tip Register and clarity Writes for a colleague, defines any technical term used, stays within the word count

Evertson, C. M., & Emmer, E. T. (2009). Classroom management for elementary teachers (8th ed.). Pearson. Chapter 4 covers lesson planning as a management act, including pacing and sequencing. Wong, H. K., & Wong, R. T. (1998). The first days of school: How to be an effective teacher (rev. ed.). Harry K. Wong Publications. Chapter 4 describes the philosophy-consistent plan and its role in a manageable classroom.

textbook.com.pk Miss Saira teaches Class 5 science in a government school in Quetta. Her lessons follow the same four moves every time: she decides what the pupils will learn and what they will do, she opens with a question that makes them want to find out, she teaches the content through a mix of explanation and activity, and she checks before the bell whether they have got it. Her pupils know what to expect, and the room runs on that predictability. This topic names the four moves and the management decision each one depends on.

The guide describes a four-stage cycle that carries a teaching plan from intention to evidence: plan, motivate, teach, assess. The cycle is not a list of tips. It is a sequence in which each stage creates the condition for the next, and the management decision at each stage is the thing that determines whether the lesson stays on track or drifts.

Planning is the stage in which the teacher decides the learning target, the activities, the materials, and the time each part of the lesson will take. The management decision here is clarity of target: a teacher who can state in one sentence what the pupils will be able to do by the end of the lesson has a compass for every later decision; a teacher who cannot will spend the lesson improvising, and improvisation is the enemy of a well-managed classroom. Marzano, Marzano and Pickering (2003) found that the clarity of the learning target was one of the strongest predictors of pupil learning, because it lets the teacher cut anything that does not serve the target and keep the lesson focused. A focused lesson is easier to manage than a wandering one. The plan also decides the routines the lesson will rely on: how pupils will get materials, what they will do when they finish early, how transitions between activities will be handled. These are management decisions, and Topic 1.3's observation protocol is the tool for checking whether the routines you planned are the routines that actually happen.

Motivation is the stage in which the teacher creates the want to learn before the teaching begins. The management decision here is relevance: pupils who can see why the lesson matters to them are easier to teach than pupils who cannot. textbook.com.pk The figure above maps four common motivation strategies against what each one costs in time and materials. A well-chosen hook question costs almost nothing and takes two minutes. A hands-on investigation costs materials and time but produces deeper engagement. A competition is fast but can produce winners and losers, which is a management cost of its own. A pupil choice is motivating but needs clear boundaries or it becomes noise. There is no universally best strategy. The management question is: given this class, this content, and the time I have, which strategy gives me the most engagement for the least management cost? Wong and Wong (1998) argue that the first minutes of a lesson determine its management tone for the whole period, so the motivation stage is where the teacher earns or loses the room.

Teaching is the stage in which the teacher delivers the content, and the management decision here is pacing and participation. A teacher who talks for thirty minutes manages attention by force of personality; a teacher who mixes explanation with activity manages it by design. The guide's preferred pattern is short explanation followed by pupil activity, repeated in cycles: tell them what they are going to learn, show them how, let them try, check, move on. Each cycle is a small management unit with a beginning, a middle, and an end, and pupils learn to move with the rhythm. Evertson and Emmer (2009) stress the transition points between activities as the moments most likely to produce disruption. A teacher who signals the transition clearly, gives a time bound, and checks that every pupil has started the new task is managing the room; a teacher who moves on while half the class is still finishing the last thing is not.

Assessment is the stage in which the teacher checks whether the learning target has been met. The management decision here is evidence: a teacher who ends the lesson without checking does not know whether to move on or reteach, and a teacher who does not know is managing on hope. Assessment does not have to be a test. A show of hands, an exit ticket, a pair share, a question to a pupil who looked uncertain - each is a quick check that tells the teacher what to do next. Marzano, Marzano and Pickering (2003) treat feedback as one of the most powerful management tools available, because it tells the teacher whether the plan worked and what to adjust. The figure at the start of this topic shows a return arrow from "assess" back to "plan". That arrow is the point: assessment is not the end of the cycle. It is the information the teacher uses to plan the next lesson, and the management habit of closing that loop is what separates a teacher who improves from a teacher who repeats.

Work in pairs. Take a lesson you have observed during practicum (or one from your own schooling). Trace it through the four stages: what was the plan, how did the teacher motivate, how did the teacher teach, and how did the teacher assess? For each stage, name the management decision the teacher made. Allow 20 minutes. Then compare with another pair and identify one stage where a different management decision would have changed the lesson.

The plan-motivate-teach-assess cycle carries a teaching plan from intention to evidence. The management decisions are: a clear target at the planning stage, relevance at the motivation stage, pacing and participation at the teaching stage, and evidence at the assessment stage. The return arrow from assess to plan closes the loop and is what makes the cycle a habit rather than a formula.

textbook.com.pk Mr Hassan teaches Class 4 mathematics in a government school in Sukkur. In his class of fifteen, five pupils can multiply confidently, six are still building the skill, and four are not yet secure with addition. One worksheet for all three groups is not differentiation; it is a recipe for boredom at the top and confusion at the bottom. This topic is about what genuine differentiation looks like, and about the realities - multigrade rooms and classes of sixty - that make it both harder and more necessary.

Differentiation is the teacher's response to the fact that pupils in the same room are not at the same point. The guide treats it as a management act because undifferentiated instruction produces the disruptions that come from pupils who are either lost or bored.

Differentiation means adjusting the content, the process, or the product of a lesson so that every pupil is working at the edge of their current ability. It does not mean making some children do easier work. That is the single most common misconception about differentiation, and it matters because easier work produces lower expectations, and lower expectations produce less learning. The figure above shows one objective differentiated three ways. The core task is the same for all: every pupil works on two-digit addition. The scaffolded version gives the pupils who need support a number line and a worked example. The extended version asks the pupils who are ready to apply the skill to a word problem with extra information. The learning target is the same; the route and the degree of structure differ. Evertson and Emmer (2009) describe three axes of differentiation: By need - adjusting the scaffolding a pupil requires to reach the same target. By interest - offering a choice of context or material that engages the pupil. By level - adjusting the complexity of the task while keeping the learning target constant. A well-differentiated lesson manages the room because every pupil has a task they can actually do, and a task they can actually do is the best defence against disruption. Common misconception. "Differentiation means making some children do easier work." It does not. It means adjusting the support, the context, or the complexity so that every pupil reaches the same target. Easier work lowers the target; differentiation keeps the target and changes the route.
documents.s: Differentiation of instruction by need, interest and level

documents.t: A multigrade classroom is one in which a single teacher is responsible for pupils of two or more grade levels at the same time, in the same room. It is common in rural and low-enrolment schools across Pakistan, and it requires management tactics that a single-grade classroom does not. textbook.com.pk The figure above maps the tactics this topic describes. The core management idea is the anchor activity: a task that one grade can do independently while the teacher works with another grade. A good anchor activity is self-checking, connected to the current topic, and familiar enough that pupils do not need the teacher to start it. Without an anchor, a multigrade teacher spends the lesson managing transitions between grades rather than teaching. Peer tutoring is the second tactic: a pupil who has mastered an explanation teaches it to a peer. The management weight is that peer tutoring must be structured - the tutor needs a clear role, the tutee needs a clear task, and the teacher needs to check that the explanation is correct. Unstructured peer tutoring becomes one pupil doing the work while the other watches. Vincent (The Multigrade Classroom: Book 3) stresses that the multigrade teacher's most important management investment is a small set of practised routines: how to signal a grade change, how to start an anchor activity, how to end a peer-tutoring pair. The routines do not eliminate the complexity of two grades, but they make it manageable.

An overcrowded classroom is one in which the number of pupils far exceeds the room's designed capacity - a reality in many urban Pakistani government schools, where classes of sixty or more are common. The management problem is not just space; it is the impossibility of individual attention at that scale. The figure above maps the tactics. Whole-class anchors - a question, a problem, a shared text - give the teacher a single point of focus for the whole room, which is easier to manage than sixty individual tasks. Structured routines - how to hand in work, how to ask for help, how to move between activities - prevent the chaos that comes from sixty pupils improvising the same transition. Activity corners are the third tactic: designated areas of the room where a group works on a self-checking task while the teacher works with another group. In an overcrowded room, corners are harder to set up, but the principle is the same as in a multigrade classroom: the teacher cannot be in two places at once, so part of the room must be able to run itself for stretches of time. Common misconception. "An overcrowded class cannot be managed, only survived." It cannot be managed the way a class of twenty can, but the tactics above - whole-class anchors, structured routines, activity corners - make a class of sixty workable. The survival mindset is the real management failure, because it stops the teacher from investing in the routines that make the room run.

Work in groups of three. Take the following objective: Class 2 Urdu: pupils will be able to write a sentence using a given word. Now plan this objective for a mixed-ability class in which some pupils can write independently, some need a sentence frame, and some are still forming letters. Produce three versions of the task that share the same target. Allow 20 minutes. Then present and identify one moment where a pupil might slip from "scaffolded" to "easier", and explain how your plan prevents it.

Assess whether this counts as differentiation in the sense this topic uses the term. (Analyze) Name the three axes of differentiation the topic describes, and give one example of each. (Remember) Explain why an anchor activity is the core management tactic in a multigrade classroom. (Understand) A teacher in a class of sixty says, "I cannot differentiate; there are too many children." Using one idea from this topic, propose a workable first step. (Apply)

Differentiation adjusts the support, context, or complexity of a task so that every pupil reaches the same target - it does not lower the target. Multigrade and overcrowded classrooms require specific management tactics: anchor activities, peer tutoring, structured routines, and activity corners. In each case the principle is the same: the teacher cannot be everywhere, so parts of the room must be able to run on practised routines.

Curriculum decisions are management acts. What a teacher chooses to teach, in what order, at what pace, and for whom shapes the classroom before the lesson begins: a well-chosen, well-sequenced, well-paced plan reduces the friction that produces disruption, while a plan that ignores the pupils in the room creates the conditions a teacher then has to manage reactively. A teaching plan that is consistent with the teacher's own philosophy of learning produces a coherent, manageable classroom. The plan-motivate-teach-assess cycle then carries that plan from intention to evidence: the teacher sets a clear target, creates the want to learn, delivers the content through paced cycles of explanation and activity, and checks whether the target was met - then uses that information to plan the next lesson. When one-size-fits-all is impossible, the teacher differentiates. Genuine differentiation adjusts the support, the context, or the complexity of a task so that every pupil reaches the same target; it does not lower the target. Multigrade and overcrowded classrooms impose specific constraints, and the tactics that work within those constraints - anchor activities, peer tutoring, structured routines, activity corners, whole-class anchors - all share one principle: the teacher cannot be everywhere, so parts of the room must be able to run on practised routines.

In this unit's account, "curriculum" refers to the teacher's answer to four questions. Which of the following is one of them? (Remember) a) How will I mark the homework? b) At what pace will I teach? c) Which textbook will I use? d) How many rules will I set? A teacher sequences a lesson so that the foundation is taught before the hard idea that depends on it. This decision is a management act because it: (Understand) a) ensures the lesson is easier than the pupils expect b) reduces the disruption that comes from pupils losing the thread c) guarantees every pupil will understand the content d) removes the need for assessment at the end of the lesson Wong and Wong (1998) argue that a well-managed classroom has a plan that is: (Remember) a) elaborate and detailed b) approved by the headteacher c) consistent and the teacher's own d) different every day to maintain interest A teacher opens every lesson with a question that makes the pupils want to find out. In the four-stage cycle, this is the: (Understand) a) planning stage b) motivation stage c) teaching stage d) assessment stage A teacher ends a lesson by asking three pupils to explain what they learned. This is an assessment move because it: (Apply) a) gives the teacher evidence about whether the target was met b) keeps the pupils quiet until the bell c) replaces the need for planning the next lesson d) counts those three pupils as the only ones who matter Differentiation by "level" means: (Remember) a) giving struggling pupils easier work and strong pupils harder work b) adjusting the complexity of the task while keeping the learning target constant c) teaching the strong pupils first and the struggling pupils later d) grouping pupils by test score for the whole year An anchor activity in a multigrade classroom is one that: (Understand) a) the teacher leads for the whole room at the same time b) one grade can do independently while the teacher works with another grade c) requires the teacher to explain it again for each grade d) only the strongest pupils in the room can complete A teacher in a class of sixty decides to use a shared text as the single point of focus for the whole room. This is an example of: (Apply) a) an anchor activity for a multigrade room b) whole-class anchoring for an overcrowded room c) differentiation by interest d) the motivation stage of the cycle Which statement best captures the relationship between a teacher's philosophy and their management, as Topic 2.1 presents it? (Understand) a) Philosophy matters only for experienced teachers b) A plan that contradicts the teacher's philosophy produces friction the teacher must then manage c) Philosophy is a private belief and has no effect on the classroom d) The textbook determines the philosophy, not the teacher A teacher who says "an overcrowded class cannot be managed, only survived" is overlooking the argument that: (Apply) a) overcrowded classes should be split regardless of the cost b) survival is the only realistic goal in a large class c) specific tactics such as structured routines and whole-class anchors make a large class workable d) management is only possible with fewer than thirty pupils

The three topics follow the logic of a single plan. Topic 2.1 (curriculum as a management tool) asks trainees to see that management begins before the lesson, in the decisions a teacher makes about content, sequence, pace and grouping. Topic 2.2 (plan, motivate, teach, assess) walks through the cycle that carries that plan from intention to evidence. Topic 2.3 (differentiation, multigrade and overcrowding) asks how to adapt the plan when the pupils or the room make one-size-fits-all impossible. A useful session order is to teach the topics in numerical order across the four weeks the guide allows (Weeks 5 to 8), using the first session of the unit to surface trainees' own planning habits and the last to rehearse the integrative assessment. The unit is designed so that a tutor who needs to compress it can merge the activity time of Topics 2.1 and 2.2 into a single planning workshop without losing the conceptual spine.

These are the misconceptions the unit names explicitly. Surface them early and return to them; trainees often assent to the correct version in a discussion and then revert to the misconception when they plan. "Differentiation means making some children do easier work." This is the most persistent one. Probe it by asking: "If the target is the same but the support is different, is that easier?" Trainees who have taught or been taught in tracked systems will find this counter-intuitive. The figure in Topic 2.3 (one objective, three versions) is designed to make the distinction visible; use it as a poster or handout. "Multigrade teaching is just teaching two lessons at once." Probe it by asking: "If the teacher is working with Grade 3, what is Grade 4 doing?" The anchor activity is the answer, and the question "what is the other grade doing?" is the management question every multigrade teacher must be able to answer. "An overcrowded class cannot be managed, only survived." Probe it by asking: "What is one routine that works better with sixty pupils than with twenty?" Whole-class anchors and structured routines are the answer. The survival mindset is the real enemy, because it stops the teacher from investing in the routines that make the room run. "I just follow the textbook, so I don't make curriculum decisions." This one belongs to Topic 2.1. Probe it by asking: "Did you skip anything in the chapter? Did you spend more time on one idea than another? Did you put pupils in pairs or rows?" Every yes is a curriculum decision the teacher made without naming it.

Topic 2.1 - One objective, three plans (25 minutes). Give trainees the objective on a slide or handout before they form groups. The key teaching move is the debrief question: "What changed because of the room, not because of the mathematics?" If trainees answer "the content," push them back: the objective is the same; what changed is the route. Collect one example per group on the board and sort them by the constraint they respond to. Topic 2.2 - Trace a lesson through the cycle (20 minutes). Pairs work better than groups of three here because the task is a structured trace, not a design. Ask each pair to choose a lesson every trainee in the room has seen - a shared school memory works well - so the debrief can surface disagreement about which stage a given move belonged to. The disagreement is the teaching point: the stages are not always cleanly separated in real lessons, and the management decision at each stage is often invisible to the pupils. Topic 2.3 - Differentiate one objective (20 minutes). This is the most cognitively demanding activity. The trap is that trainees produce three versions that differ in target rather than in route. The debrief question - "identify one moment where a pupil might slip from scaffolded to easier, and explain how your plan prevents it" - is designed to catch this. If trainees cannot answer it, they have made work easier, not differentiated.

Each topic carries a "Try this at your practicum school" task. The unit works best when the tutor sets these up explicitly before trainees leave for practicum and debriefs them when trainees return. Topic 2.1 practicum task (one week of curriculum-decision notes) produces a short reflection. Use it to open Topic 2.2: ask trainees which of their four decisions made the most difference, and use their examples to motivate the four-stage cycle. Topic 2.2 practicum task (a time tally across three lessons) produces a simple data set. Use it to make the point that most teachers underestimate how little time they spend on assessment, and that the return arrow from assess to plan is the loop least often closed. Topic 2.3 practicum task (observe a multigrade or overcrowded classroom) produces the evidence trainees need for ERQ 2 or ERQ 5. If the practicum school has neither a multigrade nor an overcrowded room, ask trainees to observe a single-grade room and note the tactics the teacher uses that would stop working if the class doubled in size.

The unit carries six figures: two concept-map or diagram figures that make a conceptual structure visible (fig-U2-1, fig-U2-3), one flowchart that sequences a cycle (fig-U2-2), and three tables that compare options against a criterion (fig-U2-4, fig-U2-5, fig-U2-6). The tables are the ones trainees most often try to read as prose. Before you project any of them, ask trainees to read the column headers first and say what the table is comparing. That habit transfers to the textbook tables they will use in their own teaching.

The 10/10/5 bank is designed to be used in two passes: the MCQs and RRQs as formative checks at the end of Topics 2.2 and 2.3, and the ERQs as a summative task at the end of the unit. ERQ 5 (the integrative item) is the one that most reliably separates trainees who have understood the unit from those who have memorised its definitions. If you use only one ERQ, use that one.

Unit 2 asked how curriculum decisions function as management acts. This unit moves from planning to the daily machinery that carries a plan through a lesson and across a week. It asks: what are routines and structures, how do they buy instructional time, and how do you design them for the rooms you actually teach in - including rooms with two grades, or with pupils who need different kinds of support?

By the end of this unit you should be able to: Distinguish routines, structures, procedures and rules, and explain how each buys instructional time. Explain why a routine that works in a single-grade class may need to be redesigned for a multigrade or mixed-need classroom. Describe subject-specific routines for mathematics, science and literacy, and explain what each one protects. Design a set of routines that build co-operation and collaborative learning, and distinguish the two. Take a described classroom and propose a routine set that fits its constraints.

Units 1 and 2, in particular the definition of classroom management as maximising learning, the plan-motivate-teach-assess cycle, and the management tactics for multigrade and overcrowded classrooms. This unit assumes you have met those ideas and applies them to the design of routines; it does not re-teach the earlier units.

Topic 3.1 - What routines are, and the time they buy - routines, structures, procedures and rules distinguished; how routines recover instructional time. Topic 3.2 - Routines in multigrade and mixed-need classes - redesigning routines for multigrade rooms and for pupils who need different kinds of support. Topic 3.3 - Subject-specific routines - one routine per subject for mathematics, science and literacy. Topic 3.4 - Routines for co-operation and collaboration - routines that build co-operative and collaborative learning; the difference between the two.

The four topics follow the logic of a single week. Topic 3.1 asks what routines are and why they matter; Topic 3.2 asks how to adapt them when the room makes one-size-fits-all impossible; Topic 3.3 asks what subject-specific routines look like in practice; Topic 3.4 asks how to design routines that build the social skills a well-managed classroom runs on. Each topic is one complete learning cycle. The question bank at the end of the unit covers all four topics together. Its answers and mark schemes are in a clearly marked section at the foot of that page; try each item before you read them.

textbook.com.pk Miss Tahira teaches Class 3 in a government school in Hyderabad. Her lessons run on time. Her pupils know what to do when they enter the room, how to get their books out, what to do when they finish early, and how to hand in work. None of this is accidental. It is the result of a small set of practised routines that Miss Tahira taught in the first week of term and reinforced until they became automatic. This topic is about what those routines are, how they differ from rules and procedures, and why they are one of the most powerful time-management tools a teacher has.

The guide treats routines not as a list of tips but as a management system that buys instructional time. A classroom without routines spends the day negotiating every transition: how to start, how to move between activities, how to finish. A classroom with practised routines spends that time on learning instead.

The figure above maps four terms that are often used interchangeably but mean different things. Confusing them produces confusion about what to teach and what to enforce. A routine is a repeated way of doing something that pupils learn to do without being told each time. "When the bell rings, we put our books away and stand quietly" is a routine once it is practised. A structure is the framework that holds routines. The timetable is a structure; the seating arrangement is a structure; the way the room is organised for group work is a structure. A procedure is a step-by-step sequence for a specific task. How to sharpen a pencil, how to line up for the canteen, how to hand in homework - each is a procedure. A rule is a statement of what is allowed or expected. "We raise our hands before speaking" is a rule. Wong and Wong (1998) argue that the first weeks of term are the time to teach routines, procedures and rules - in that order, because routines make the room run, procedures make specific tasks manageable, and rules set the boundaries. A teacher who starts with rules and never teaches the routines behind them spends the term enforcing compliance instead of teaching.
documents.s: Routines, structures, procedures and rules distinguished

documents.t: textbook.com.pk The figure above shows the arithmetic of a routine. The guide's worked example asks you to time one transition before and after a routine is introduced, and count the minutes recovered across a week. The numbers are striking even for a single transition. Consider the transition between activities. Without a routine, the teacher gives instructions, waits for the noise to settle, repeats the instructions to the pupils who were not listening, deals with the two pupils who have started the wrong task, and finally begins. The same transition with a practised routine takes half the time: the teacher gives a signal, pupils move, the new activity starts. Marzano, Marzano and Pickering (2003) found that the average classroom loses significant instructional time to poorly managed transitions, and that a small set of practised routines recovers more time than almost any other management investment. The key word is practised. A routine that has been announced but not rehearsed is just a rule. A routine that has been practised until it is automatic is a time machine. Common misconception. "Routines make a classroom rigid." They do the opposite. A routine removes the need to negotiate every transition, which frees the teacher to be flexible about content, pacing and response. Rigidity is what happens when there are no routines and the teacher has to control every move by force.

Evertson and Emmer (2009) identify the transition between activities as the moment most likely to produce disruption. A well-managed transition has three parts: a clear signal that the current activity is ending, a bounded time for the move, and a prompt that starts the next activity before the pupils have time to drift. A poorly managed transition has none of these, and the teacher spends the first minutes of the next activity re-establishing order instead of teaching.
documents.s: The transition as the critical moment

documents.t: Over two lessons taught by the same teacher, pick one transition (moving between activities, handing out materials, settling at the start). Time it in seconds on two occasions. Then work with the teacher to introduce a simple routine for that transition, and time it again on the next two occasions. Calculate the minutes recovered across a typical five-day week and write one paragraph on where that time would otherwise have gone.

State the difference between a routine and a rule, and give one example of each. (Remember) A teacher says, "I have told my pupils the routine, so now they know it." Using this topic's account, explain what that claim overlooks. (Analyze) Explain why the transition between activities is the moment most likely to produce disruption. (Understand) A teacher always uses the same routine for settling at the start of a lesson. A colleague says, "That is too rigid; you should vary it to keep the pupils engaged." Evaluate the colleague's claim. (Evaluate) For a described classroom that loses time at the start of every lesson, propose one specific routine and explain how it would recover time. (Apply)

Routines, structures, procedures and rules are distinct management tools. Routines are repeated ways of doing things that pupils learn to do automatically; structures hold them; procedures guide specific tasks; rules set boundaries. Practised routines recover instructional time, especially at transition points, and are the foundation on which a well-managed classroom runs.

I can distinguish a routine, a structure, a procedure and a rule, and give an example of each. I can explain how a practised routine recovers instructional time. I can explain why transitions are the moments most likely to leak time. I can time a transition before and after a routine is introduced and calculate the minutes recovered. I can propose a routine for a described time-loss problem.

Over one week, keep a tally of the time lost to one transition across five lessons. Then work with the teacher to design a routine for that transition and tally the time again the following week. Write half a page on the difference and what it tells you about the relationship between routines and instructional time. Do not name the school or the teacher in your write-up.

documents.t: Write 350 to 400 words on the following. A teacher in your practicum school says, "I do not need routines; I just manage as I go." Using this topic's account of what routines are and how they buy instructional time, argue which single routine would most improve the management of a described lesson, and justify the choice by reference to the time it would recover. Wong, H. K., & Wong, R. T. (1998). The first days of school: How to be an effective teacher (rev. edn.). Harry K. Wong Publications. Chapter 6 describes teaching routines in the first weeks of term and the time they recover. Marzano, R. J., Marzano, J. S., & Pickering, D. J. (2003). Classroom management that works: Research-based strategies for every teacher. ASCD. Chapter 3 covers routines and transitions as time-management tools. Evertson, C. M., & Emmer, E. T. (2009). Classroom management for elementary teachers (8th edn.). Pearson. Chapter 5 covers managing transitions and the routines that carry them.

textbook.com.pk Mr Karim teaches Classes 2 and 4 in one room in a government school in Sanghar. He has one blackboard, forty-two pupils, and no assistant. When he works with Class 4 mathematics, Class 2 must be able to work without him. When he moves to Class 2, Class 4 must not sit idle. This topic is about the routines that make that possible.

Topic 3.1 described routines as time-recovery tools. This topic asks what happens when the room makes a one-routine-fits-all approach impossible: two grades in the same room, or pupils with different needs in the same class. The answer is not to abandon routines but to redesign them for the constraint.

textbook.com.pk The figure above maps the routines this topic describes. The two workhorses of a multigrade classroom are the anchor routine and the independent-work routine. The anchor routine is the task one grade does while the teacher works with the other. Topic 2.3 introduced the anchor activity; this topic adds the routine that makes it work: how pupils start the anchor without being told, what they do when they are stuck, how they check their own work, and what they do when they finish. A good anchor routine is self-checking, connected to the current topic, and familiar enough that the teacher is not interrupted to explain it. Without the routine, the anchor activity is just a task sheet; with the routine, it is a management system that runs itself. The independent-work routine governs what pupils do when they are working alone: how to get materials, how to ask for help without calling out, what to do when finished. Evertson and Emmer (2009) stress that the independent-work routine is the one most multigrade teachers neglect, because it is easier to keep the pupils busy than to teach them to work independently. But a busy pupil who is not learning is just a quiet disruption, and the teacher's time is still being spent on management rather than teaching. Vincent (The Multigrade Classroom: Book 3) describes the multigrade teacher's routine set as a small, practised collection: how to signal a grade change, how to start an anchor, how to end a peer-tutoring pair, how to close the lesson so both grades stop at the same time. The routines are few, but they must be taught and rehearsed as deliberately as in a single-grade classroom.

The figure above also maps routines matched to specific special needs. The guide treats these as routine adaptations, not as separate management systems, because the underlying principle is the same: the pupil who needs something different needs a routine that provides it without requiring the teacher's constant attention. A pupil who needs extra time needs a routine for what to do when the rest of the class moves on: a continuation task, a self-checking extension, a way to signal "I am not finished yet" without disruption. A pupil who is easily distracted needs a routine for where to sit, how to use a timer, how to break a task into smaller steps - the routine provides the structure that the pupil cannot yet provide alone. A pupil who finishes early needs a routine for what to do next: a reading corner, a peer-tutoring role, a self-checking extension. Without this routine, the early finisher becomes the source of disruption. A pupil who needs help but will not ask needs a routine for how to signal for assistance: a coloured card on the desk, a place in the question queue, a check-in point with the teacher at a predictable moment. Common misconception. "Routines are for young children only." They are for every age. The content of the routine changes - older pupils do not need a routine for how to line up - but the principle does not. A well-designed routine frees the teacher to teach, and that is as valuable in a lower-secondary classroom as in a primary one.
documents.s: Routines for special needs and situations

documents.t: Work in groups of three. Take the following scenario: Class 2 and Class 4 share one room. The teacher is working with Class 4 on two-digit addition. Class 2 is working independently on a reading task. Now design the anchor routine: how Class 2 starts the task, what they do when they are stuck, how they check their work, and what they do when they finish. Allow 25 minutes. Then present your routine and identify one moment where a pupil might drift from "working" to "just busy", and explain how your routine prevents it.

State the difference between an anchor routine and an independent-work routine, and explain the management purpose of each. (Remember) A multigrade teacher says, "I just give the other grade a worksheet while I teach." Using this topic's account, explain what that approach costs in management terms. (Analyze) Name the two workhorse routines of a multigrade classroom and describe one feature each must have. (Remember) A pupil finishes every task early and then disrupts the class. Propose a routine that addresses the problem and explain why it is realistic in a class of sixty. (Apply) Assess whether a routine designed for a single-grade class can be used unchanged in a multigrade classroom. Refer to the anchor routine in your answer. (Analyze)

Multigrade and mixed-need classrooms require routines that are deliberately redesigned for the constraint. The anchor routine and the independent-work routine are the two workhorses of a multigrade room; routines for special needs provide the structure that allows a pupil to work without constant teacher attention. In each case the principle is the same: the routine removes the need for the teacher to manage every moment.

I can explain why a routine that works in a single-grade class may need to be redesigned for a multigrade room. I can describe the anchor routine and the independent-work routine and the purpose of each. I can design an anchor routine that is self-checking, connected to the topic, and familiar. I can propose a routine for at least two different special needs. I can explain why routines are not only for young children.

Identify one multigrade classroom. Over two lessons, note the routines the teacher uses when one group is working independently, and write half a page on which routine makes the most difference to the teacher's ability to teach the other group. Do not name the school or the teacher in your write-up.

Using this topic's account of anchor routines and independent-work routines, argue which single routine would most improve the management of the described room, and justify the choice by reference to the constraint a multigrade room imposes. The core text on multigrade routines including anchor activities and independent work. Evertson, C. M., & Emmer, E. T. (2009). Classroom management for elementary teachers (8th edn.). Pearson. textbook.com.pk Miss Nasreen teaches Class 5 in a government school in Lahore. On Monday morning she teaches mathematics, then science, then Urdu literacy, each in a different part of the room. The pupils know what to expect in each session: how to set out their mathematics materials, how to handle science equipment, how to come to the reading corner. The routines are different for each subject, and that is the point. This topic is about why subject-specific routines matter and what they protect.

Topic 3.1 described routines as time-recovery tools. This topic adds a layer: different subjects make different management demands, and a routine that works for one may not work for another. The guide treats subject-specific routines as protections - each one guards against the particular friction that subject creates.

textbook.com.pk The figure above maps the routines this topic describes. Mathematics teaching carries two management risks: materials (pencils, rulers, textbooks, exercise books) that take time to distribute and collect, and checking (is my answer right?) that can produce a queue of pupils waiting for the teacher while everyone else sits idle. The materials routine governs how mathematics materials are distributed, used and packed away. A well-designed materials routine uses a materials monitor, a predictable sequence (textbook first, then exercise book, then pencil), and a time bound. Without it, the first five minutes of a mathematics lesson are spent handing out books. The checking routine governs how pupils get feedback without queuing. Self-checking (answers on the board), peer-checking (swap books with a partner), and traffic-light cards (green = I am confident, yellow = I am unsure, red = I need help) are all checking routines. Marzano, Marzano and Pickering (2003) treat feedback as one of the most powerful management tools available, and a checking routine is the mechanism that makes feedback happen at scale.

Science teaching carries two different risks: safety and cleanup. The safety routine governs how equipment is handled, what pupils do before and after an investigation, and what happens when something goes wrong. The cleanup routine governs how materials are returned, how the room is restored, and how the transition out of science is managed. Evertson and Emmer (2009) stress that the cleanup routine is the one most teachers of practical subjects neglect, and that a science lesson without a cleanup routine ends with the teacher tidying up while the next lesson waits.

The figure above shows a literacy-block layout: a reading corner, a shared-text area, a writing area and a response area, with the flow between them. The layout is the structure; the routines are what move the pupils through it. The reading routine governs how pupils come to the reading corner, how they select a text, how they read (silently, in pairs, aloud to a partner), and how they record their reading. The response routine governs how pupils respond to a text: a written response, a pair share, a drawing, a discussion. Wong and Wong (1998) argue that the literacy block is the part of the day where routines matter most, because reading and writing require sustained concentration and the routines protect that concentration from interruption. Common misconception. "Group work and collaborative learning are the same thing." They are not. Group work is pupils sitting together; collaborative learning is pupils working together toward a shared goal with individual accountability. A routine for group work manages seating and noise; a routine for collaborative learning manages roles, task structure and closure. Topic 3.4 takes this further.

Work in pairs. Take the routine "how pupils get help when they are stuck." Now redesign it three ways: for a mathematics lesson, for a science investigation, and for a literacy session. For each, decide: how the pupil signals, how the teacher responds, and what the pupil does while waiting. Allow 25 minutes. Then present and identify one feature that changed because of the subject, not because of the pupils.

Name the two management risks that a mathematics routine set typically addresses, and give one routine for each. (Remember) A teacher says, "I do not need a cleanup routine; the pupils can just tidy up at the end." Using this topic's account, explain what that approach costs. (Analyze) Describe the difference between a reading routine and a response routine in a literacy block. (Understand) A science lesson ends with the teacher spending ten minutes cleaning up while the next class waits. Propose a routine that addresses the problem and explain why it is realistic in a low-resource classroom. (Apply) Assess whether a checking routine designed for mathematics can be used unchanged in a literacy lesson. Refer to the kind of feedback each subject requires. (Analyze)

Subject-specific routines protect against the particular friction each subject creates: materials and checking in mathematics, safety and cleanup in science, reading and response in literacy. The routines are different because the subjects are different, but the principle is the same: a practised routine removes the need for the teacher to manage every moment.

I can name the management risks that routines for mathematics, science and literacy each address. I can describe a materials routine, a checking routine, a safety routine, a cleanup routine, a reading routine and a response routine. I can explain why a routine that works for one subject may not work for another. I can redesign a routine for three different subjects. I can distinguish group work from collaborative learning.

Over one week, observe one teacher across two different subjects. Note the routines the teacher uses in each, and write half a page on which routines are the same across subjects and which are different, and why. Do not name the school or the teacher in your write-up.

textbook.com.pk Mr Sajid teaches Class 4 social studies in a government school in Quetta. His pupils work in groups of four. Each group has a reader, a writer, a reporter and a timekeeper. The pupils know what each role does, how to begin the task, how to check that everyone is contributing, and how to close the activity with a share. This topic is about the routines that make group work into collaborative learning, and about the difference between the two.

Topic 3.3 ended with a distinction: group work is pupils sitting together; collaborative learning is pupils working together toward a shared goal with individual accountability. This topic takes that distinction seriously and asks what routines are needed to make it real.

textbook.com.pk The figure above maps the structures this topic describes. The distinction matters because the routines for each are different. Co-operation means pupils work in the same space, toward a shared task, helping each other as needed. The routine manages seating, noise and mutual help. Think-pair-share, round-robin and numbered heads are co-operative structures. Collaborative learning adds individual accountability: every pupil has a role, every role is necessary, and the group cannot succeed unless every member contributes. The routine manages roles, task structure, participation checking and closure. The jigsaw method is a collaborative structure. Common misconception. "Group work and collaborative learning are the same thing." They are not. Group work without individual accountability produces one pupil doing the work while the others watch. Collaborative learning requires a routine that makes every role necessary and every contribution visible.

The figure above shows the three phases of a collaborative task. Each phase has its own routine. The set-up routine assigns roles, states the task, checks that every pupil understands their role, and sets a time bound. A strong set-up routine uses a roles card (reader, writer, reporter, timekeeper) and a quick check: "Readers, point to your text. Writers, show your clipboard." Without this routine, the first five minutes of group work are spent negotiating who does what. The run routine governs how the group works: how to take turns, how to check that everyone is contributing, what to do when the group is stuck. The teacher's role during the run phase is to monitor participation, not to teach content - a group that is off task needs a management response, not a content explanation. Evertson and Emmer (2009) stress that the run phase is where most collaborative learning fails, because the teacher confuses "pupils are talking" with "pupils are learning" and does not check that every role is being filled. The close routine governs how the activity ends: a whole-class share, a reflection on how the group worked, a pack-away sequence. A strong close routine includes a reflection question: "What did your group do well? What would you change next time?" Without it, the learning stays in the group and does not transfer to the whole class.
documents.s: The collaborative routine: set up, run, close

documents.t: The figure above maps four co-operative structures against the group size and noise cost each one carries. Think-pair-share is quiet and works in any size of class; the jigsaw is louder and needs groups of four to six; round-robin is structured and works when the task has a clear sequence. The management question is: given this class, this content, and the noise I can afford, which structure gives me the most collaboration for the least management cost? Marzano, Marzano and Pickering (2003) found that the effectiveness of group work depends less on the structure chosen and more on the routines that carry it. A think-pair-share with a practised routine produces more learning than a jigsaw with a routine that has not been taught.
documents.s: Matching structure to group size and noise cost

documents.t: Work in groups of four. Take the following task: Class 5 science: pupils will investigate which material conducts electricity, in groups of four. Now design the full routine: the set-up (roles, task statement, time bound), the run (how to check participation, what to do when stuck), and the close (share, reflection, pack-away). Allow 25 minutes. Then present your routine and identify one moment where a group might slip from "collaborative" to "one person doing the work", and explain how your routine prevents it.

State the difference between co-operation and collaborative learning, and give one example of each. (Remember) A teacher puts pupils in groups and gives them a task, but one pupil does all the work while the others watch. Using this topic's account, explain what routine is missing. (Analyze) Name the three phases of a collaborative task and the routine each one requires. (Remember) A teacher says, "I cannot do group work; there are sixty pupils." Using one idea from this topic, propose a workable first step. (Apply) Evaluate the claim that "think-pair-share is the best group-work structure." Refer to the match between structure and group size in your answer. (Evaluate)

Co-operation and collaborative learning are different, and the routines for each are different. A collaborative task has three phases - set up, run and close - and each phase needs its own routine. The effectiveness of group work depends less on the structure chosen and more on the routines that carry it.

I can distinguish co-operation from collaborative learning and give an example of each. I can describe the set-up, run and close routines for a collaborative task. I can explain why individual accountability is what makes group work into collaborative learning. I can match a co-operative structure to a described group size and noise constraint. I can design a collaborative routine for a described lesson.

Over two lessons that use group work, keep a tally of the time spent on each phase: set up, run and close. At the end, calculate the proportion and write half a page on which phase dominates and whether that dominance fitted the task. Do not name the school or the teacher in your write-up.
