documents.t: Write 400 to 450 words on the following. A teacher in a multigrade classroom (Classes 3 and 4 in one room) wants to use collaborative learning but says, "I do not have time to teach routines for group work." Using this topic's account of the set-up, run and close routines, argue which single routine would most improve the quality of group work in the described room, and justify the choice by reference to the constraint a multigrade room imposes. Routines are repeated ways of doing things that pupils learn to do automatically; structures hold them; procedures guide specific tasks; rules set boundaries. Together they are the management system that buys instructional time, especially at transition points where classrooms most often leak it. Multigrade and mixed-need classrooms require routines that are deliberately redesigned for the constraint. The anchor routine and the independent-work routine are the two workhorses of a multigrade room; routines for special needs provide the structure that allows a pupil to work without constant teacher attention. Subject-specific routines protect against the friction each subject creates: materials and checking in mathematics, safety and cleanup in science, reading and response in literacy. Routines for co-operation and collaborative learning build the social skills a well-managed classroom runs on, and the difference between the two - individual accountability - is what makes group work into learning.

In this unit's account, a "routine" is best described as: (Remember) a) a statement of what is allowed in the classroom b) a repeated way of doing something that pupils learn to do without being told each time c) a step-by-step sequence for a specific task d) the framework that holds classroom procedures A teacher has pupils line up, then walk quietly to the canteen. This is an example of a: (Understand) a) rule b) routine c) procedure d) structure Wong and Wong (1998) argue that the first weeks of term should be spent teaching: (Remember) a) rules, then procedures, then routines b) routines, then procedures, then rules c) the curriculum, then routines, then rules d) consequences, then routines, then procedures A teacher signals the end of an activity, gives a time bound, and prompts the start of the next task. This is a management move that addresses: (Understand) a) the transition between activities b) the set-up of a collaborative task c) the independent-work routine d) the checking routine In a multigrade classroom, the anchor routine is the one that: (Remember) a) the teacher uses to begin the lesson b) one grade follows while the teacher works with the other grade c) governs how pupils line up for the canteen d) the teacher uses to end the lesson A pupil finishes every task early and then disrupts the class. The most appropriate routine response is: (Apply) a) a rule that forbids finishing early b) a procedure for what to do when finished c) a structure that keeps the pupil seated d) a routine that removes the early-finishing pupil from the room Which pair correctly matches a subject with the management risk its routine set addresses? (Understand) a) Mathematics - safety and cleanup b) Science - materials and checking c) Literacy - reading and response d) Mathematics - reading and response A teacher says, "I put my pupils in groups every lesson, so I use collaborative learning." This claim overlooks the importance of: (Apply) a) individual accountability within each group b) the number of pupils in each group c) the subject being taught d) the time of day The three phases of a collaborative task are: (Remember) a) plan, teach, assess b) set up, run, close c) explain, practise, test d) open, work, hand in Marzano, Marzano and Pickering (2003) found that the effectiveness of group work depends most on: (Apply) a) the structure chosen b) the size of the group c) the routines that carry the structure d) the subject being taught

The four topics follow the logic of a single week. Topic 3.1 asks what routines are and why they buy time; Topic 3.2 asks how to adapt them when the room makes one-size-fits-all impossible; Topic 3.3 asks what subject-specific routines look like; Topic 3.4 asks how to design routines that build co-operation and collaborative learning. A useful session order is to teach the topics in numerical order across the three weeks the guide allows (Weeks 9 to 11), using the first session of the unit to time a real transition and the last to rehearse the integrative assessment. The unit is designed so that a tutor who needs to compress it can merge the activity time of Topics 3.1 and 3.2 into a single routine-design workshop without losing the conceptual spine.

These are the misconceptions the unit names explicitly. Surface them early and return to them; trainees often assent to the correct version in a discussion and then revert when they plan. "Routines make a classroom rigid." This is the most persistent one. Probe it by asking: "If the routine removes the need to negotiate every transition, what does the teacher gain?" Trainees who equate flexibility with absence of structure will find this counter-intuitive. The figure in Topic 3.1 (routine, structure, procedure, rule distinguished) is designed to make the distinction visible; use it as a poster or handout. "Routines are for young children only." Probe it by asking: "What routine do you use every morning before you come to university?" The content of the routine changes with age; the principle does not. "Group work and collaborative learning are the same thing." This one belongs to Topic 3.4. Probe it by asking: "If four pupils sit together and one does all the work, is that collaboration?" The answer is no, and the reason is the absence of individual accountability.

Topic 3.1 - Time one transition (practicum-based). The key teaching move is the arithmetic: ask trainees to bring their timed data and calculate the minutes recovered across a week. The number is the argument. If trainees cannot produce data, use the worked example in the figure (a week's recovered minutes, transition by transition) and ask them to verify the calculation. Topic 3.2 - Design an anchor routine (25 minutes). The trap is that trainees produce a task description rather than a routine. The difference: a task description says what pupils do; a routine says how they start, what they do when stuck, how they check, and what they do when finished. The debrief question - "identify one moment where a pupil might drift from working to just busy" - is designed to catch this. Topic 3.3 - One routine, three subjects (25 minutes). Pairs work well here because the task is a structured redesign, not a design from scratch. The key teaching move is the debrief: "What changed because of the subject, not because of the pupils?" If trainees answer "the difficulty", push them back: the routine protects against a management risk, not a cognitive one. Topic 3.4 - Design a collaborative routine (25 minutes). This is the most cognitively demanding activity. The trap is that trainees produce roles without accountability. The debrief question - "identify one moment where a group might slip from collaborative to one person doing the work" - is designed to catch this. If trainees cannot answer it, they have assigned roles but not made them necessary.

Each topic carries a "Try this at your practicum school" task. The unit works best when the tutor sets these up explicitly before trainees leave for practicum and debriefs them when trainees return. Topic 3.1 practicum task (timing a transition) produces a simple data set. Use it to open Topic 3.2: ask trainees which transition lost the most time, and use their examples to motivate the anchor routine. Topic 3.2 practicum task (observe a multigrade room) produces the evidence trainees need for ERQ 3. If the practicum school has no multigrade room, ask trainees to observe a single-grade room and note the routines that would stop working if a second grade were added. Topic 3.3 practicum task (observe one teacher across two subjects) produces a comparison. Use it to make the point that subject-specific routines are not arbitrary: they protect against the friction each subject creates. Topic 3.4 practicum task (tally the time across the three phases) produces a simple data set. Use it to make the point that most group work spends too long on set-up and too little on closure, and that the close routine is where the learning transfers to the whole class.

The unit carries eight figures: two concept-map figures that make a conceptual structure visible (fig-U3-1, fig-U3-7), two flowchart figures that sequence a process (fig-U3-4, and the collaboration cycle), and four tables that compare options against a criterion (fig-U3-3, fig-U3-5, fig-U3-6, fig-U3-8). The tables are the ones trainees most often try to read as prose. Before you project any of them, ask trainees to read the column headers first and say what the table is comparing.

The 10/10/5 bank is designed to be used in two passes: the MCQs and RRQs as formative checks at the end of Topics 3.2 and 3.4, and the ERQs as a summative task at the end of the unit. ERQ 5 (the integrative item) is the one that most reliably separates trainees who have understood the unit from those who have memorised its definitions. If you use only one ERQ, use that one.

Unit 3 asked how routines buy instructional time. This unit asks a different question: what kind of community makes a classroom worth learning in? It moves from the management of time to the management of relationships - between teacher and pupils, among pupils, and between the school and the world outside its walls.

By the end of this unit you should be able to: Explain what community means inside and outside a school, and distinguish participation from involvement. Describe the typical practices of community participation, and explain how they differ in multigrade settings. Explain what an ethic of care is, and argue why it is not the same as never correcting a child. Analyse how a caring classroom builds personal accountability and responsible action. Evaluate a described response to a behaviour breakdown, using the distinction between a punitive response and a caring, accountable one.

Units 1 to 3, in particular the definition of classroom management as maximising learning, the management/discipline distinction, and the routines that carry a well-managed classroom through a day. This unit assumes you have met those ideas and applies them to the relational side of management; it does not re-teach the earlier units.

Topic 4.1 - What community means for a school - community inside and outside the school; participation and involvement; typical practices. Topic 4.2 - Bringing the community in - involving the community in your classroom; routines for community involvement; multigrade differences. Topic 4.3 - An ethic of care - creating an ethic of care; diverse classrooms as caring communities; respectful relations. Topic 4.4 - Accountability, and when things break down - building responsible action and personal accountability; what happens when behaviour breaks down; dealing with the unexpected.

The four topics follow the logic of an expanding circle. Topic 4.1 asks what community means; Topic 4.2 asks how to bring it into the classroom; Topic 4.3 asks what kind of relationships a caring classroom is built on; Topic 4.4 asks what happens when those relationships are tested. Each topic is one complete learning cycle. The question bank at the end of the unit covers all four topics together. Its answers and mark schemes are in a clearly marked section at the foot of that page; try each item before you read them.

textbook.com.pk Miss Farzana teaches Class 3 in a government school in Ghotki. Her classroom does not end at the door. Parents visit once a term. A local shopkeeper lends materials for science lessons. The imam at the nearby mosque talks to the class about respect. This topic is about what community means for a school, and about the difference between asking the community to help and genuinely involving it.

The guide treats community not as a vague aspiration but as a set of relationships that a school can build, neglect or damage. The management question is: who is part of the community that supports learning, and how does the school relate to them?

textbook.com.pk The figure above maps the circles of community around one classroom. The innermost circle is the classroom itself - the relationships between teacher and pupils and among pupils. The next circle is the school - the headteacher, other teachers, the support staff. The next is the parents and families. The outermost is the local community - neighbours, local leaders, businesses, places of worship. Each circle has a different relationship with the classroom, and the management demand of each is different. The classroom circle is managed directly; the school circle through collaboration with colleagues; the parent circle through communication and invitation; the community circle through partnership and reciprocity. Wong and Wong (1998) argue that a well-managed classroom is one where all four circles are deliberately tended, not just the innermost one.

The figure above maps the distinction this topic makes. The terms are often used interchangeably, but they mean different things, and the difference matters for management. Participation means being present: attending a school event, signing a form, contributing money, showing up. A parent who attends a parent-teacher meeting is participating. Involvement means having a voice in what happens: helping to decide the agenda, contributing to a classroom activity, being asked for advice and acting on it. A parent who helps plan the meeting is involved. Marzano, Marzano and Pickering (2003) found that the quality of a school's relationship with its community depends less on how many people participate and more on how many are genuinely involved. A school with fifty parents at a meeting but no voice in what happens has participation without involvement. A school with ten parents who help make decisions has involvement, and involvement is what changes the classroom. Common misconception. "Community involvement means asking parents for money." It does not. Asking for money is a transaction; involvement is a relationship. A parent who raises funds is participating; a parent who helps decide how the funds are spent is involved.

The guide describes several typical practices, and the management demand of each: Parent-teacher meetings - the most common practice, and the one most likely to become participation without involvement if the agenda is set entirely by the school. Home visits - the teacher visits the family, which builds a relationship that no meeting can replace. The management demand is time and cultural sensitivity. Community events - the school hosts an event and the community attends. The management demand is planning, and the risk is that the event becomes a performance rather than a partnership. Community members in the classroom - a parent or local professional contributes to a lesson. The management demand is preparation: the visitor needs to know what to do, and the pupils need to know why they are there.

Work in pairs. Read the following five scenarios and classify each as participation or involvement. For each, explain your reasoning in one sentence. A parent attends a parent-teacher meeting where the teacher reports on pupil progress. A parent helps design the science fair and judges the entries. The school asks each family to contribute towards a new water tap. A local farmer talks to the class about how crops grow, at the teacher's invitation. A parent sits on the school management committee and votes on the budget. Allow 15 minutes. Then compare with another pair and identify one scenario where the boundary is unclear, and explain why.

Name the four circles of community around a classroom, starting from the innermost. (Remember) A teacher says, "We had a great community event; two hundred parents came." Using this topic's account, explain what that claim might overlook. (Analyze) State the difference between participation and involvement, and give one example of each. (Remember) A headteacher says, "We do not need community involvement; we need the parents to pay their fees." Evaluate that claim using this topic's account of what involvement achieves. (Evaluate) For a described school that wants to move from participation to involvement, propose one specific first step and explain why it is realistic. (Apply)

Community is not a single thing but a set of circles around a classroom, each with a different relationship to the school. Participation is being present; involvement is having a voice. The quality of a school's community relationships depends less on how many people participate and more on how many are genuinely involved.

I can name the four circles of community around a classroom. I can distinguish participation from involvement and give an example of each. I can explain why involvement matters more than participation for learning. I can classify a described practice as participation or involvement. I can propose a realistic first step towards greater community involvement.

Over one week, note every interaction between the school and the community (parents, local leaders, visitors). Classify each as participation or involvement, and write half a page on which dominates and what the cost is for the school's relationship with its community. Do not name the school or the teacher in your write-up.

textbook.com.pk Mr Hassan teaches Class 5 in a government school in Sukkur. A local nurse visits his class every month to talk about hygiene. A parent who is a carpenter helps with the science fair. The imam comes during the Islamiat unit. None of this is accidental. Each visit follows a routine: the teacher plans with the visitor beforehand, the pupils prepare questions, and the visit ends with a thank-you and a follow-up activity. This topic is about the routines that make community involvement work, and about how those routines differ in a multigrade classroom.

Topic 4.1 distinguished participation from involvement. This topic asks how to move from one to the other: what routines and structures turn a visitor into a genuine contributor, and what changes when the room holds two grades.

textbook.com.pk The figure above maps the process. The guide treats community involvement as a routine with six phases, not a one-off event. Identify a need. The starting point is the curriculum, not the visitor. A teacher who asks, "Who could help with this topic?" before "Who do I know?" is more likely to produce a visit that serves the learning. Find a community member. The figure above maps community roles to what each can realistically contribute. A health worker can teach hygiene; a carpenter can support design and measurement; a farmer can talk about crops. The match between the person and the topic is what makes the visit work. Make first contact. The invitation is specific: what the class is learning, what the visitor would do, how long it would take, what the pupils will have prepared. A vague invitation produces a vague visit. Plan the visit together. The teacher and visitor plan the session: what the visitor will do, what the pupils will do, what materials are needed. Evertson and Emmer (2009) stress that a visitor who is left to "just talk" is a visitor who will talk for too long and lose the class. Host the visit. The teacher introduces the visitor, sets the expectations, and stays in the room. A teacher who leaves the room during a visitor's session is not hosting; the pupils will read the absence as a signal that the visit does not matter. Follow up. A thank-you note, a follow-up activity, a reflection in the next lesson. Without follow-up, the visit is an event; with follow-up, it becomes part of the learning.
documents.s: Inviting a community member into a lesson

documents.t: The figure above maps the community roles. Community involvement in a multigrade classroom is both harder and more valuable. It is harder because the teacher is already managing two grades; adding a visitor adds complexity. It is more valuable because a community member can work with one grade while the teacher works with the other, effectively doubling the adult presence in the room. Vincent (The Multigrade Classroom: Book 3) describes the community member as a potential anchor: a parent or local professional who can run a session with one grade while the teacher teaches the other. The management demand is the same as for any anchor: the community member needs a clear role, a prepared task, and a practised routine for starting and finishing. Common misconception. "An ethic of care means never correcting a child." It does not. An ethic of care means correcting a child in a way that preserves dignity and builds accountability. Topic 4.3 takes this further.

Work in groups of three. Take the following scenario: Class 4 science: pupils will learn about the water cycle. You want to invite a community member to contribute to the lesson. Now plan the full process: the need, the community member you would invite, the first-contact message, the plan for the visit, how you would host it, and the follow-up. Allow 25 minutes. Then present your plan and identify one moment where the visit could become a performance rather than a learning experience, and explain how your plan prevents it.

Name the six phases of a community visit, in order. (Remember) A teacher says, "I have asked a parent to come and talk to the class." Using this topic's account, explain what that invitation is likely to cost in learning terms. (Analyze) Explain why community involvement is both harder and more valuable in a multigrade classroom. (Understand) A teacher in a class of sixty says, "I cannot host a visitor; there are too many children." Using one idea from this topic, propose a workable first step. (Apply) Assess whether a community visit planned around the visitor's availability is likely to serve the curriculum. Refer to the six-phase model in your answer. (Analyze)

Community involvement is a routine with six phases: identify a need, find a community member, make first contact, plan the visit, host it, and follow up. In a multigrade classroom, a community member can serve as an anchor, working with one grade while the teacher teaches the other. The match between the person and the topic is what makes the visit work.

I can name the six phases of a community visit and describe what each requires. I can match a community role to a realistic curricular contribution. textbook.com.pk Miss Sobia teaches Class 4 in a government school in Multan. In her class, a pupil who gives a wrong answer is not laughed at. A pupil who is struggling is helped, not shamed. When two pupils argue, the class has a routine for resolving it that does not involve punishment. This is not because Miss Sobia is especially warm. It is because she built, deliberately, an ethic of care. This topic is about what that ethic is built from, and about why it is not the same as being permissive.

The guide treats an ethic of care not as a personality trait but as a set of practices that a teacher can build, teach and reinforce. The management question is: what makes a classroom feel safe enough for learning, and what routines produce that feeling reliably?

textbook.com.pk The figure above maps the four components this topic describes. An ethic of care is built from: Attentiveness - the teacher notices what is happening in the room: who is confused, who is being left out, who is about to give up. Withitness (Topic 1.2) is the management version of attentiveness; an ethic of care is the relational version. Responsiveness - the teacher acts on what they notice. A pupil who is confused gets help; a pupil who is being excluded gets included; a pupil who is struggling gets support before they fail. Competence - the teacher's care is effective, not just well-meaning. A caring teacher who cannot manage the room is not yet a competent caregiver; the care must be paired with the skills to make it real. Mutual respect - the care flows in both directions. The teacher respects the pupils; the pupils learn to respect the teacher and each other. Henley (2009) argues that mutual respect is the foundation of a proactive classroom, because it replaces compliance based on fear with cooperation based on relationship.
documents.s: What an ethic of care is built from

documents.t: The figure above maps the respectful-relations moves and the message each sends. A caring classroom is not a quiet classroom; it is a classroom where disagreement is handled with respect, where mistakes are treated as learning, and where every pupil has a voice. The guide treats diversity not as a problem to be managed but as a resource for a caring community. A classroom with pupils of different abilities, backgrounds and needs is a classroom where care is necessary, and where the practice of care is visible every day. A pupil who sees a classmate being supported learns that support is normal; a pupil who sees a disagreement resolved respectfully learns that conflict does not require aggression. Common misconception. "A caring classroom has no consequences." It does. A caring classroom has consequences that are restorative, not punitive: the pupil who disrupts the group repairs the disruption; the pupil who hurts a classmate makes it right. The difference is that the consequence is designed to rebuild the relationship, not to punish the person.
documents.s: Diverse classrooms as caring, democratic communities

documents.t: The figure above maps the specific moves. The guide treats these as routines, not as one-off gestures, because a single respectful act is an incident; a practised respectful routine is a culture. Using a pupil's name - sends the message "you matter as a person, not as a seat number." Listening without interrupting - sends the message "your thinking matters, even when it is unfinished." Correcting privately - sends the message "your dignity matters more than the correction." Acknowledging effort, not just success - sends the message "the attempt matters, not just the outcome." Giving choices - sends the message "you have a voice in what happens here."
documents.s: Respectful relations: the moves that build them

documents.t: Work in pairs. Read the following incident: During group work, Ali knocks over Sara's pencil case. Sara shouts. The class goes quiet. Now trace this incident twice. First, trace it as it might be handled punitively: what the teacher does, what the consequence is, what the message to the class is. Then trace it as it might be handled inside a caring, accountable culture: what the teacher does, what the consequence is, what the message to the class is. Allow 20 minutes. Then present both traces and identify the moment where the two approaches diverge.

Name the four components an ethic of care is built from. (Remember) A teacher says, "I care about my pupils, so I do not need routines." Using this topic's account, explain what that claim overlooks. (Analyze) Explain the difference between a punitive consequence and a restorative one, and give one example of each. (Understand) A pupil gives a wrong answer and the class laughs. Propose a teacher response that is caring but not permissive, and explain what message it sends. (Apply) Evaluate the claim that "a caring classroom is a soft classroom." Use the four components of an ethic of care in your answer. (Evaluate)

An ethic of care is built from attentiveness, responsiveness, competence and mutual respect. It is not the same as being permissive: a caring classroom has consequences, but they are restorative rather than punitive. Respectful relations are built from practised routines - using names, listening, correcting privately, acknowledging effort, and giving choices - not from one-off gestures.

I can name the four components an ethic of care is built from. I can explain why an ethic of care is not the same as being permissive. I can distinguish a punitive consequence from a restorative one. I can describe at least three respectful-relations moves and the message each sends. I can trace a described incident through both a punitive and a caring response.

Over two lessons, note every teacher move that could be described as caring: using a pupil's name, listening, correcting privately, acknowledging effort, giving choices. Write half a page on which move is most common and what it tells you about the classroom's culture. Do not name the school or the teacher in your write-up.

textbook.com.pk Mr Tariq teaches Class 5 in a government school in Hyderabad. During group work, Bilal hits Hamid. The class stops. Mr Tariq does not shout. He stops the behaviour, checks that Hamid is all right, hears both boys, and asks Bilal, "What will you do to make this right?" Bilal apologises and helps Hamid with the task. The lesson continues. This topic is about what makes that response work, and about what happens when the unexpected disrupts even the best-managed classroom.

Topic 4.3 described an ethic of care. This topic asks what happens when that ethic is tested: when behaviour breaks down, when the unexpected happens, when a teacher is alone in a room with a problem and no script. The management question is: how do you respond in a way that is both caring and accountable?

textbook.com.pk The figure above maps the decision aid this topic describes. The guide treats personal accountability not as a trait but as a skill that a caring classroom builds through routine. Responsible action is the habit of acting with awareness of the consequences for others. A pupil who has learned to act responsibly does not need to be told to help a classmate; the routine of the classroom has made helping normal. Henley (2009) argues that responsible action is built through three moves: giving pupils real responsibility (not just tasks), making the consequences of action visible, and reflecting on what happened afterwards. Personal accountability is the willingness to own the consequences of your actions. A pupil who has learned accountability does not blame others, make excuses, or wait to be caught; they say, "I did that, and I will make it right." The guide treats accountability as the internalised version of discipline: discipline is external (the teacher enforces), accountability is internal (the pupil owns). The figure above shows how a caring classroom builds accountability: through routines that make expectations clear, through consequences that are restorative rather than punitive, and through reflection that connects the action to its impact on others.
documents.s: Building responsible action and personal accountability

documents.t: The figure above maps the response. The guide treats a behaviour breakdown as a moment that tests the classroom's culture, not just the teacher's authority. A punitive response stops the behaviour but damages the relationship; a caring, accountable response stops the behaviour and rebuilds it. The flowchart in the figure shows the six steps: Stop the behaviour calmly. A teacher who shouts stops the behaviour but models the loss of control. A teacher who stops calmly models the self-regulation they are teaching. Check for harm. The first question is not "who started it" but "is anyone hurt." This sends the message that safety matters more than blame. Hear both sides. Each pupil gets to tell their version without interruption. This sends the message that every voice matters, even when the behaviour was wrong. Agree a repair. The pupil who caused the harm helps decide how to make it right. This is the accountability step: the pupil owns the consequence. Follow up. The teacher checks later that the repair happened and the relationship is restored. Without follow-up, the repair is a transaction; with follow-up, it is a learning. Restore the relationship. The teacher makes sure the two pupils are not left in conflict. A classroom where unresolved conflict lingers is a classroom where learning suffers.
documents.s: What happens when behaviour breaks down

documents.t: The figure above maps the decision aid. The unexpected is, by definition, not covered by a routine: a pupil who becomes ill, a visitor who arrives unannounced, a power cut, a fight in the corridor. The guide treats the unexpected as a moment when the teacher's management system is most visible, because there is no script to follow. The decision aid has three branches, in priority order: Safety first. Is anyone in danger? If yes, act immediately and calmly. The management principle is: a safe classroom is the precondition for everything else. Learning second. Can the lesson continue? If yes, adapt and continue. If not, switch to a backup activity. The management principle is: a disrupted lesson is not a failed lesson if the teacher adapts. Relationship third. What does this incident tell you about the classroom's culture? A pupil who becomes ill and is cared for by classmates is a classroom where care is real. A power cut that produces panic is a classroom where routines are not yet automatic. Common misconception. "An ethic of care means never correcting a child." It does not. An ethic of care means correcting a child in a way that preserves dignity and builds accountability. The figure above shows the difference: a punitive response says "you are bad"; a caring, accountable response says "what you did was not acceptable, and you can make it right."

Work in groups of three. Read the following two responses to the same incident. Then evaluate each using the six-step model, and write a verdict on which is more effective and why. Incident: During a group task, Ali refuses to do his share of the work and pushes the task away. The group stops working. Response A: The teacher says, "Ali, go and stand outside the classroom until you are ready to behave." Ali leaves. The group continues. Response B: The teacher stops the class briefly, asks Ali to step aside, checks that the other group members are all right, hears Ali's side, and asks, "What will you do to make this right?" Ali rejoins the group and contributes. Allow 20 minutes. Then present your evaluation and identify one moment where the two responses diverge, and explain what message each sends to the class.

State the difference between responsible action and personal accountability, and give one example of each. (Remember) A teacher sends a disruptive pupil out of the room and the lesson continues. Using this topic's account, explain what that response costs in relational terms. (Analyze) Name the six steps of a caring, accountable response to a behaviour breakdown, in order. (Remember) A pupil becomes ill during a lesson. Using the decision aid, propose the teacher's first three moves. (Apply) Evaluate the claim that "a caring response to disruption is a weak response." Use the six-step model in your answer. (Evaluate)

A caring classroom builds personal accountability through routines that make expectations clear, consequences that are restorative, and reflection that connects action to impact. When behaviour breaks down, a caring, accountable response follows six steps: stop calmly, check for harm, hear both sides, agree a repair, follow up, and restore the relationship. When the unexpected happens, the priority is safety, then learning, then relationship.

I can distinguish responsible action from personal accountability. I can describe the six steps of a caring, accountable response. I can explain why a restorative consequence is different from a punitive one. I can apply the unexpected-event decision aid to a described incident. I can evaluate a described response to a behaviour breakdown.

Over one week, note one behaviour incident and trace how the teacher responded. Using the six-step model, write half a page on which steps were present and which were missing, and what the cost was for the classroom's culture. Do not name the school or the teacher in your write-up.

Community is not a single thing but a set of circles around a classroom, each with a different relationship to the school. Participation is being present; involvement is having a voice. An ethic of care is built from attentiveness, responsiveness, competence and mutual respect, and it is not the same as being permissive: a caring classroom has consequences, but they are restorative rather than punitive. When behaviour breaks down, a caring, accountable response follows six steps and rebuilds the relationship rather than damaging it.

You are placed in a government primary school. A teacher manages mainly through rules and exclusion: pupils who misbehave are sent out, and the community is asked for money but never invited in. c - the classroom itself is the innermost circle. b - attending a meeting is participation; helping to decide what happens there is involvement. b - Marzano et al. found that involvement matters more than participation for the quality of community relationships. b - the four components are attentiveness, responsiveness, competence and mutual respect. b - responsiveness is acting on what you notice; noticing without acting is attentiveness. c - sending a pupil out is a punitive consequence. b - the first step is to stop the behaviour calmly. c - owning the action and committing to repair is personal accountability. a - the priority order is safety, learning, relationship. c - Henley frames mutual respect as the foundation of a proactive classroom.

The four topics follow the logic of an expanding circle. Topic 4.1 asks what community means; Topic 4.2 asks how to bring it into the classroom; Topic 4.3 asks what kind of relationships a caring classroom is built on; Topic 4.4 asks what happens when those relationships are tested. A useful session order is to teach the topics in numerical order across the four weeks the guide allows (Weeks 12 to 15), using the first session of the unit to map the community circles around the trainees' own practicum schools and the last to rehearse the integrative assessment. The unit is designed so that a tutor who needs to compress it can merge the activity time of Topics 4.1 and 4.2 into a single community-mapping workshop without losing the conceptual spine.

These are the misconceptions the unit names explicitly. Surface them early and return to them; trainees often assent to the correct version in a discussion and then revert when they plan. "Community involvement means asking parents for money." This is the most persistent one. Probe it by asking: "If a parent gives money but never visits the school, is that involvement?" Trainees who equate community support with financial contribution will find the distinction counter-intuitive. The figure in Topic 4.1 (participation vs involvement) is designed to make the distinction visible; use it as a poster or handout. "An ethic of care means never correcting a child." Probe it by asking: "If a pupil is about to make a dangerous mistake, does care mean letting them?" The answer is no, and the six-step model in Topic 4.4 is designed to show how correction and care coexist. "A caring classroom has no consequences." Probe it by asking: "If a pupil hurts a classmate and nothing happens, is that caring - for whom?" The answer is that the hurt classmate deserves a response, and the six-step model shows what a caring consequence looks like.

Topic 4.1 - Participation or involvement? (15 minutes). This is a quick classification task. The key teaching move is the debrief: ask trainees to identify the scenario where the boundary is unclear, and use it to make the point that the boundary is a matter of voice, not presence. Topic 4.2 - Plan a community visit (25 minutes). The trap is that trainees produce a vague invitation rather than a six-phase plan. The difference: a vague invitation says "come and talk"; a six-phase plan says what the need is, who the person is, what the first contact says, what the visit looks like, how it is hosted, and what the follow-up is. The debrief question - "identify one moment where the visit could become a performance" - is designed to catch this. Topic 4.3 - Trace one incident twice (20 minutes). This is the most emotionally demanding activity. The key teaching move is to make the comparison explicit: write the two traces side by side and ask, "What is the message to the class in each?" The divergence is usually at step 2: the punitive trace skips "check for harm" and goes straight to blame. Topic 4.4 - Evaluate a response (20 minutes). The trap is that trainees evaluate the outcome (quiet class) rather than the process (relationship rebuilt). Push them back: "The class is quiet in both responses. What is different?" The answer is the relationship, and the six-step model is the tool for making it visible.

Each topic carries a "Try this at your practicum school" task. The unit works best when the tutor sets these up explicitly before trainees leave for practicum and debriefs them when trainees return. Topic 4.1 practicum task (classify school-community interactions) produces a tally. Use it to open Topic 4.2: ask trainees which interactions are participation-only, and use their examples to motivate the six-phase model. Topic 4.2 practicum task (plan a community visit) produces a plan. Use it to make the point that community involvement is a routine, not a one-off event. Topic 4.3 practicum task (note caring teacher moves) produces a list. Use it to make the point that care is a set of practised routines, not a personality trait. Topic 4.4 practicum task (trace a behaviour incident) produces a six-step analysis. Use it to make the point that the unexpected is the moment when the classroom's culture is most visible.

The unit carries eight figures: two concept-map figures that make a relational structure visible (fig-U4-1, fig-U4-3), two flowchart figures that sequence a process (fig-U4-2, fig-U4-4), and four tables that compare options against a criterion (fig-U4-5, fig-U4-6, fig-U4-7, fig-U4-8). The tables are the ones trainees most often try to read as prose. Before you project any of them, ask trainees to read the column headers first and say what the table is comparing.

The 10/10/5 bank is designed to be used in two passes: the MCQs and RRQs as formative checks at the end of Topics 4.2 and 4.4, and the ERQs as a summative task at the end of the unit. ERQ 5 (the integrative item) is the one that most reliably separates trainees who have understood the unit from those who have memorised its definitions. If you use only one ERQ, use that one.

Units 1 to 4 gave you the pieces: a definition of classroom management centred on learning, the theories that explain how learning happens, the curriculum and routines that carry a plan through a day, and the relationships that make a classroom worth learning in. This unit asks you to pull those pieces into one usable philosophy, to test it against the work of your peers, and to close the course with a plan you can use in your own classroom.

By the end of this unit you should be able to: Synthesise the content of Units 1 to 4 into a single, coherent classroom management philosophy. Apply a structured peer-critique protocol to a described classroom management plan. Evaluate a described plan against the principles of the course. Revise a plan in light of structured feedback.

The full content of Units 1, 2, 3 and 4. This unit assumes you have worked through the theories, the curriculum and differentiation, the routines, and the community and care units, and applies that material to a single culminating artefact.

Topic 5.1 - One philosophy from four units - pulling the four preceding units into one classroom-management philosophy. Topic 5.2 - Peer critique of final projects - the peer-critique protocol and how to use it. Topic 5.3 - Presenting and improving the plan - presenting the plan, giving and receiving structured feedback, and revising in light of critique. Topic 5.4 - Summary and close - the course's closing synthesis and the beliefs the course asks you to leave behind.

This is the lightest unit in the course by design. The work here is synthesis and application of material already covered, not new content. The question bank at the end of the unit is shorter than the others and focuses on integration. The summative task is the classroom management plan itself, the course's culminating artefact.

textbook.com.pk At the start of this course, you wrote a personal philosophy of teaching. Now, at the end, you have more to say. You know that management is centred on learning, that three theories explain how learning happens, that curriculum decisions are management acts, that routines buy time, and that care and accountability build the relationships a classroom runs on. This topic is about pulling those pieces into one philosophy you can use.

The guide treats a philosophy not as a statement you write once but as a synthesis you build from the material of the course. The figure above maps the synthesis: each unit contributes a layer, and the layers connect. textbook.com.pk

Unit 1 gave you the foundation. Management is the proactive work of creating and maintaining the conditions in which student learning happens. Three theories explain how learning happens, and a fluent teacher moves between them as the learning target demands. Unit 2 gave you the plan. Curriculum decisions are management acts: what to teach, in what order, at what pace, for whom. Differentiation adjusts the route without lowering the target. Unit 3 gave you the machinery. Routines buy instructional time. The anchor routine, the independent-work routine, and subject-specific routines carry a plan through a day. Unit 4 gave you the relationships. Community, care and accountability build the culture a classroom runs on. A caring classroom has consequences, but they are restorative. The figure above shows how these layers connect. The centre is your philosophy: what you believe learning is, and what that belief implies you should do first, second, third in a classroom. The four layers are the evidence for that philosophy, drawn from the course.

The guide's worked example asks you to build the synthesis in three moves: State your belief. What do you believe learning is? Unit 1's three theories are your options; you do not have to choose one, but you have to say which you draw on most and why. State the implication. What does that belief imply you should do in a classroom? Unit 2's curriculum decisions, Unit 3's routines and Unit 4's relationships are your evidence. State the test. How would you know your philosophy is working? The observable features of a well-managed classroom (Unit 1) are your answer: practised routines, high intellectual demand, teacher withitness, an environment that supports learning.

textbook.com.pk In the guide's worked example, each student teacher presents the classroom management plan they have built across Units 1 to 4. Peers use a structured protocol to critique it: they check the plan for clarity, consistency and coverage, and the author revises in light of the feedback. This topic is about that protocol and about why structured critique produces better plans than unstructured opinion.

The guide treats peer critique not as a conversation but as a protocol, because unstructured feedback produces vague praise or vague criticism, and neither helps the author improve. The protocol is the tool that makes feedback specific, evidence-based and actionable. textbook.com.pk

The figure above maps the protocol. The guide's protocol has three criteria, each with two guiding questions: Clarity. Can I state the author's philosophy in one sentence? Can I identify the theory it draws on? A plan that cannot be summarised is a plan that has not yet been thought through. Consistency. Does the curriculum decision match the philosophy? Does the routine set match the constraint the plan names? A plan that holds a constructivist philosophy but describes a transmission-plan is inconsistent, and the inconsistency is the most useful feedback a reviewer can give. Coverage. Does the plan address all four layers (theory, curriculum, routines, care)? Does it name the constraint it is designed for? A plan that covers three layers and omits the fourth is a plan with a gap, and naming the gap is the reviewer's job.

The figure above maps the criteria. The guide treats the four units as the standard against which a plan is read, not as a checklist to be ticked but as a set of principles to be applied. A plan that names a philosophy but does not connect it to a theory is drawing on Unit 1 incompletely. A plan that describes routines but does not name the constraint they are designed for is drawing on Unit 3 incompletely. A plan that describes care but does not describe consequences is drawing on Unit 4 incompletely. The reviewer's job is to name the gap, not to fill it. The author decides how to revise; the author decides how to revise; the reviewer makes the gap visible.

textbook.com.pk The guide's worked example asks each student teacher to present the classroom management plan they have built across Units 1 to 4. Peers give structured feedback using the protocol from Topic 5.2. The author identifies the most useful feedback, revises the plan, and presents the revision. This topic is about that cycle and about why the revision step is the point.

The guide treats presenting and improving as a cycle, not a one-off event. The figure above maps the cycle: present, receive feedback, identify the most useful feedback, revise, present the revision. The management question is: how do you give feedback that the author can actually use, and how do you receive feedback without defending or dismissing it? textbook.com.pk

The figure above maps the cycle. The guide treats the presentation as a structured event, not a reading-aloud. A strong presentation does three things: States the philosophy in one sentence. The audience needs to know what you believe before they can evaluate what you have planned. Names the constraint the plan is designed for. A plan for a class of twenty is not the same as a plan for a class of sixty; the constraint is part of the plan. Walks through the four layers. Theory, curriculum, routines, care - each gets a moment, and the audience uses the protocol to evaluate each.

The figure above maps the cycle. The guide treats feedback as a skill, not an opinion. Strong feedback follows the protocol: it names a specific criterion (clarity, consistency or coverage), cites a specific passage from the plan, and suggests a specific revision. Weak feedback is vague ("I liked it") or prescriptive ("You should do it my way"). The guide treats receiving feedback as a skill too. The author's job is to listen, to ask clarifying questions, and to decide which feedback to act on. The author does not defend the plan and does not accept every suggestion; the author decides.

The figure above maps the cycle. The guide treats revision as the point of the exercise, because a plan that is presented but not revised is a plan that has not been tested. A strong revision does three things: Names the feedback it is responding to. "My reviewer noted that my philosophy and my curriculum decision were inconsistent. I have revised the curriculum decision to match the philosophy." Shows the change. The revision is visible: the before and after are both present. Explains the reasoning. The author explains why the revision strengthens the plan.

Work in groups of three. Each person presents their plan (5 minutes). Peers give structured feedback using the protocol (5 minutes). The author identifies the most useful feedback and revises one section of the plan (10 minutes). Then the author presents the revision (5 minutes). Allow 30 minutes total.

textbook.com.pk You have worked through four units. You began with a definition of classroom management and a personal philosophy. You end with a plan, a set of routines, and a network of relationships. This topic is about what you leave behind: the beliefs the course asks you to correct, and the evidence you can cite for the beliefs you now hold.

The guide treats the close of the course as a moment of examination, not just celebration. The figure above maps the seven closing misconceptions the guide names, and the evidence against each drawn from the four units. The management question is: what did you believe at the start, and what do you believe now? textbook.com.pk

The figure above maps them. The guide lists them because the review unit is where a teacher examines and corrects the beliefs they held at the start of the course. "The best-managed classroom is one where the teacher, not the student, is in control of learning." The evidence against: a well-managed classroom is defined by the quality of pupil engagement, not by the level of teacher control (Unit 1). "The quietest classrooms are the best managed." The evidence against: silence is a behavioural state, not a learning state; a well-managed classroom is marked by intellectual demand, not by the absence of noise (Unit 1). "The goal of classroom management is peace and discipline." The evidence against: the goal is learning; discipline is reactive, management is proactive (Unit 1). "Classroom management relies on threats and punishment." The evidence against: consequences in a caring classroom are restorative, not punitive (Unit 4). "Classrooms are homogeneous." The evidence against: every classroom is diverse, and differentiation adjusts the route without lowering the target (Unit 2). "Each class has fixed content that must be taught." The evidence against: curriculum decisions are management acts, and a teacher who tries to cover everything sets the class up for rushed explanations and confusion (Unit 2). "The same content must be taught to every student in one class." The evidence against: differentiation by need, interest and level means adjusting the support, the context, or the complexity so that every pupil reaches the same target (Unit 2).

The figure above maps the misconceptions. The guide treats the closing synthesis as a whole-group event: each trainee states one belief they held at the start of the course and one belief they hold now, and the group cites the evidence for the change. The management point is that the course has not given you a set of tips; it has given you a way of thinking about classrooms that you can defend with evidence.

Unit 5 is the lightest unit in the course by design. The work here is synthesis and application of material already covered in Units 1 to 4, not new content. A useful session order is to teach the topics in numerical order across the single week the guide allows (Week 16), using the first session for the synthesis (Topic 5.1), the second for the peer-critique protocol (Topics 5.2 and 5.3), and the third for the closing synthesis (Topic 5.4) and the presentation of revised plans.

Topic 5.1 - Build your philosophy (15 minutes, individual). This is a quiet, individual activity. The key teaching move is the pair share: ask trainees to identify one place where their philosophy draws on a specific idea from one of the four units. If trainees cannot name the connection, their philosophy is still at the level of opinion; push them to cite the evidence. Topic 5.2 - Peer critique in pairs (20 minutes). The trap is that trainees give vague praise or vague criticism. The protocol is the tool that prevents this: remind trainees to name a specific criterion, cite a specific passage, and suggest a specific revision. Circulate and listen for feedback that is specific; if you hear "I like it," ask, "Which criterion does that refer to?" Topic 5.3 - Present and revise (30 minutes, groups of three). This is the most important activity in the unit. The key teaching move is the revision step: ask trainees to name the feedback they are responding to, show the change, and explain the reasoning. If trainees revise without naming the feedback, they are editing, not responding to critique. Topic 5.4 - Examine your beliefs (10 minutes, individual). This is a closing reflection. The key teaching move is the pair share: ask trainees to identify one belief that changed for both of them. The common changes are usually about the management/discipline distinction, the purpose of routines, and the meaning of care.

The summative task for Unit 5 is the classroom management plan, the course's culminating artefact. The guide's sample assignment asks for a plan that covers all four layers: philosophy and theory, curriculum decisions, routines, and care and accountability. What to look for in a strong plan: The philosophy is stated in one sentence and connected to at least two of the three theories. The curriculum decision is explained as a management act, not just a content choice. The routine set is designed for a named constraint, not generically. The care section describes consequences that are restorative, not punitive. Every choice is justified by reference to the described pupils or setting. What to look for in a weak plan: The philosophy is stated but not connected to a theory. The four layers are listed but not integrated. The routine set is generic ("I will use routines to manage the classroom"). The care section describes punishment without naming it as such. The justifications are generic ("this is good practice").

The unit carries four figures: one concept-map figure (fig-U5-1), one flowchart figure (fig-U5-3), and two tables (fig-U5-2, fig-U5-4). The tables are the ones trainees most often try to read as prose. Before you project any of them, ask trainees to read the column headers first and say what the table is comparing.

This course equips student teachers with essential English language skills for effective communication in diverse real-world scenarios. It focuses on developing proficiency in English language usage: word choices, grammar and sentence structure, comprehension and analytical skills, professional writing, public speaking, and intercultural communication.
Assessment follows the GECE default: 60% summative / 40% formative (Constitution Art. III.7).
Recommended sources from the course guide are listed for scope and further reading only; they are never reproduced as content.

This unit builds the foundation on which the rest of the course rests. Before you can communicate effectively, read with understanding, or write with clarity, you need command of the building blocks: words, the rules that govern them, the structures that hold them together, and the sounds that carry them. This unit gives you that foundation.

By the end of this unit you should be able to: Explain how vocabulary functions in context, including register, collocation, and connotation. Identify and correct common grammatical errors in written and spoken English. Describe the main word-formation processes (affixation, compounding, clipping, back formation) and apply them to unfamiliar words. Distinguish the four main sentence structures (simple, compound, complex, compound-complex) and explain how structure affects meaning. Identify the key features of the English sound system that differ from Urdu and apply strategies to improve pronunciation.
No prior course is assumed. The unit starts from the level of a student who has completed intermediate education in Pakistan and uses English as a second or additional language.

Topic 1.1 - Words in context: vocabulary and grammar - vocabulary in context, communicative grammar, and common errors. Topic 1.2 - Building words and sentences - word-formation processes and sentence structures. Topic 1.3 - Sounds of English - the English sound system and pronunciation challenges for Urdu speakers.

The three topics build on each other. Topic 1.1 gives you the vocabulary and grammar you need to understand the examples in Topics 1.2 and 1.3. Work through them in order, and use the glossary terms (marked with underlining) as your reference points throughout the course.

textbook.com.pk Miss Ayesha teaches Class 9 English in a government school in Karachi. She asks her pupils to write a letter to the headteacher requesting a library card. One pupil writes: "I am needing the card for reading books." The grammar is understandable but not natural. Another writes: "Kindly issue me the card at your earliest convenience." The grammar is correct but the tone is too formal for a pupil. This topic is about the choices that make English natural, correct, and appropriate to the situation.

Effective English is not just about knowing words and rules. It is about choosing the right word for the right context and applying grammar so that meaning is clear. This topic covers the two foundations: vocabulary in context and communicative grammar.

A word means different things in different contexts. The word "run", for example, has over forty meanings in English. In a classroom, "run an activity" is different from "run for election" or "a run in your stocking". Understanding vocabulary means understanding these distinctions. Register is the level of formality a situation demands. A conversation with a friend uses an informal register; a letter to a headteacher uses a formal register. Pakistani English often mixes registers in ways that sound unnatural to a fluent speaker. The figure above maps the components of vocabulary knowledge. Collocation is the tendency of certain words to appear together. In English, we make a decision (not do a decision), we take a photo (not make a photo), and we commit a mistake (not make a mistake, though this is common in Pakistani English). Learning collocations is more useful than learning individual words. Connotation is the feeling or association a word carries beyond its literal meaning. "Thin" and "slim" both describe a person of low weight, but "slim" has a positive connotation and "thin" can be negative. Choosing words with the right connotation is part of choosing words with the right register. Synonyms, antonyms and idiomatic expressions. Synonyms are words with similar meanings (big, large, enormous), but they are rarely interchangeable. Antonyms are words with opposite meanings (hot/cold, fast/slow). Idiomatic expressions are phrases whose meaning cannot be guessed from the individual words ("kick the bucket" means to die, not to kick a bucket). Urdu has its own rich set of idioms, and direct translation often produces confusion.

Communicative grammar is the study of how grammar creates meaning in real communication, not as a set of abstract rules. The guide lists several areas where Pakistani learners commonly make errors. Subject-verb agreement. The verb must agree with the subject in number. "The pupils reads" is incorrect because "pupils" is plural. Common difficulties include collective nouns (the team is/ are), indefinite pronouns (everyone is/are), and sentences where the subject and verb are separated by a long phrase. Verb tenses. English has twelve verb tenses, but the most common sources of error are the present perfect ("I have done" vs. "I did"), the past continuous ("I was doing"), and the conditionals ("If I were you, I would..."). Urdu has a different tense system, so direct transfer produces errors. Fragments and run-ons. A fragment is an incomplete sentence that lacks a subject or a verb ("Because I was tired"). A run-on is two complete sentences joined without proper punctuation ("I was tired I went to bed"). Both are common in Pakistani student writing. Modifiers. A modifier describes another word. A misplaced modifier creates confusion ("Running quickly, the finish line appeared" suggests the finish line was running). Dangling modifiers have no clear word to modify. Articles. "A", "an" and "the" are among the hardest parts of English grammar for Urdu speakers because Urdu has no direct equivalent. The rules are complex, but the most common errors are omitting "the" when it is needed (I went to school vs. I went to the school) and using "the" when it is not needed. Word classes. The eight word classes (noun, pronoun, verb, adverb, adjective, preposition, conjunction, interjection) are the building blocks of sentences. Being able to identify them helps you understand why a sentence works or does not. textbook.com.pk The figure above maps the most common grammatical errors, their corrections, and the principle behind each correction. Use it as a reference when you write. Common misconception. "Grammar rules are fixed and universal." They are not. English grammar describes how fluent speakers actually use the language, and usage varies by region, register and context. The goal is not perfection but clarity and appropriateness.

Work in pairs. Take a short text (a newspaper editorial, a textbook paragraph, or a pupil's essay). First, identify five words whose meaning depends on context and explain what they mean in this context. Second, identify three grammatical structures (tenses, articles, subject-verb agreement) and explain why they are used. Allow 25 minutes. Then present your findings to another pair and discuss any disagreements.

(Remember) Identify the article error in this sentence and explain the principle: "She is doctor at the Civil Hospital." (Apply) Rewrite this sentence so the modifier is not dangling: "Walking to school, the rain started suddenly." (Apply)

Vocabulary in context means understanding register, collocation, connotation and denotation, not just memorising word lists. Communicative grammar means understanding how grammar creates meaning in real communication, not just memorising rules. The most common grammatical errors made by Pakistani learners involve subject-verb agreement, verb tenses, fragments, run-ons, modifiers and articles.

textbook.com.pk Mr Tariq teaches Class 7 English in a government school in Multan. He writes "unhappiness" on the board and asks his pupils what it means. One pupil says it means "not happy". Mr Tariq asks how they knew. The pupil says "un means not, and ness makes it a noun". This topic is about the processes that build words and the structures that build sentences.

English has over a million words, but most of them are built from a much smaller set of parts. Understanding how words are formed helps you decode unfamiliar vocabulary. Understanding how sentences are built helps you write with clarity and variety.

textbook.com.pk The figure above maps the four main processes this topic describes. Affixation is the addition of a prefix (at the beginning) or a suffix (at the end) of a word. "Un-happiness" adds the prefix "un-" and the suffix "-ness" to the root "happy". English has over a hundred common prefixes and suffixes. Learning the most common ones (un-, re-, pre-, dis-, -ment, -tion, -ly, -ful, -less) gives you access to thousands of words. Compounding is joining two or more words to create a new one. "Blackboard", "textbook", "notebook" and "keyboard" are all compounds. Some compounds are written as one word, some as two, and some with a hyphen. The meaning of a compound is usually (but not always) related to the meanings of its parts. Clipping is the shortening of a word. "Exam" (examination), "lab" (laboratory), "phone" (telephone) and "maths" (mathematics) are all clippings. They are common in informal English and are often the form that Pakistani learners encounter first. Back formation is the creation of a new word by removing what looks like an affix but is not. "Edit" was formed from "editor" (not the other way around), and "televise" from "television". Back formations are a sign of a living language that is still changing.

A sentence is a group of words that expresses a complete thought. English has four main sentence structures, and the figure above maps them with examples. A simple sentence has one independent clause: a subject and a verb that express a complete thought. "The pupils read their books." A simple sentence can be long ("The pupils in Class 7 read their English books quietly during the free period") but it still has only one clause. A compound sentence has two or more independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction (and, but, or, so, yet, for, nor). "The pupils read their books and the teacher wrote on the board." Each clause could stand alone as a sentence. A complex sentence has one independent clause and one or more dependent clauses (clauses that cannot stand alone). "When the bell rang, the pupils packed their bags." "When the bell rang" is a dependent clause; it needs the independent clause to complete its meaning. A compound-complex sentence has at least two independent clauses and at least one dependent clause. "When the bell rang, the pupils packed their bags and the teacher left the room." This is the most common structure in academic writing. Common misconception. "Longer sentences are better sentences." They are not. The best sentence is the one that communicates the clearest meaning. A mix of simple, compound and complex sentences produces the most readable writing.

Work in groups of three. Take a short English newspaper article (or a textbook paragraph). First, identify five words formed by affixation, compounding, clipping or back formation, and explain the process. Second, identify five sentences and classify each as simple, compound, complex or compound-complex. Allow 25 minutes. Then present and compare with another group.
documents.s: Activity: Analyse word formation and sentence structure

documents.t: Name the four word-formation processes and give one example of each. (Remember) A pupil writes, "The teacher gave us a homework about the exam." Identify the clipping in this sentence and explain its full form. (Understand) Classify the following sentence as simple, compound, complex or compound-complex: "After the rain stopped, the children went outside and played in the mud." (Apply) A friend says, "If I would have known, I would have come earlier." Identify the error in the conditional structure and explain the rule. (Analyze) Explain why "edit" is an example of back formation, not affixation. (Understand)

Word-formation processes (affixation, compounding, clipping, back formation) explain how English builds new words from existing parts. Sentence structures (simple, compound, complex, compound- complex) explain how clauses combine to create meaning. Understanding both helps you decode unfamiliar vocabulary and write with clarity and variety.

I can identify the four word-formation processes and give an example of each. I can distinguish simple, compound, complex and compound-complex sentences. I can explain how affixation and compounding create new words. I can classify sentences by their structure. I can identify back formations and explain why they are not affixation.

textbook.com.pk Miss Hina teaches Class 6 English in a government school in Islamabad. She asks her pupils to pronounce "think". Several pupils say "tink". She asks them to pronounce "this". Several say "dis". She asks them to pronounce "vet". Several say "wet". This topic is about why these errors happen and what to do about them.

English has approximately 44 sounds (phonemes) but only 26 letters. This means that the relationship between spelling and sound is not one-to-one. For Urdu speakers, the challenge is greater because English has sounds that do not exist in Urdu, and Urdu has sounds that do not exist in English.

textbook.com.pk The figure above maps the main categories of English sounds and the challenges they pose for Urdu speakers. Vowels. English has twelve vowel sounds (monophthongs) and eight diphthongs (two vowel sounds blended together in one syllable). Urdu has far fewer vowel sounds, which is why distinctions like "ship/sheep", "full/fool" and "cat/cut" are difficult. The figure above maps the most problematic distinctions. Consonants. English has 24 consonant sounds. Several do not exist in Urdu: the "th" sounds in "think" and "this", the "v" sound in "vet", the "w" sound in "wet", and the "zh" sound in "measure". Urdu speakers often substitute the closest Urdu sound: "t" for "th", "f" for "v", "w" for "v" (sometimes in the wrong direction). Stress. In English, every word of more than one syllable has one syllable that is stressed (louder, longer, higher in pitch). "REcord" (noun) and "reCORD" (verb) are distinguished only by stress. Urdu stress patterns are different, which can make Pakistani English sound flat to a native speaker. Intonation is the rise and fall of the voice across a phrase or sentence. English uses intonation to distinguish statements from questions, to show emphasis, and to signal attitude. Urdu intonation patterns are different, and direct transfer can produce speech that sounds uninterested or rude when no rudeness is intended.

The figure above maps the most common pronunciation challenges. The most frequent are: "th" sounds (think, this, bath, bathe): Urdu has no equivalent; speakers substitute "t/d" or "s/z". "v" and "w" distinction (vet/wet, very/well): Urdu has a sound between the two; speakers confuse them. "p" and "f" distinction (pin/fin, pat/fat): Some Urdu dialects merge these sounds. Final consonant clusters (desks, texts, films): Urdu does not allow clusters at the end of syllables; speakers insert vowels ("deskes"). Vowel length (ship/sheep, full/fool): Urdu does not distinguish these pairs. Common misconception. "Pronunciation does not matter as long as people understand you." It does matter. Poor pronunciation can cause misunderstanding, and in professional contexts it can affect how competent you sound. The goal is not a British or American accent but clarity.

Work in pairs. Take the following minimal pairs (pairs of words that differ by one sound). One partner says one word from a pair; the other identifies which word was said. Then switch. Pair 1 Pair 2 Pair 3 Pair 4 Pair 5 ship / sheep vet / wet think / sink full / fool pin / fin bat / bet this / dis bad / bed cat / cut fan / van Allow 15 minutes. Then discuss: which pairs were hardest to distinguish? What strategy helped?

Explain why English has more sounds than letters, and give one example. (Understand) A pupil says "tink" for "think". Identify the sound that is causing the difficulty and explain why it is difficult for Urdu speakers. (Analyze) Explain the difference between stress and intonation, and give one example of each. (Remember) Write three minimal pairs that would help a Urdu speaker practise the "v/w" distinction. (Apply) A friend says, "I just speak loudly and they will understand." Using this topic's account, explain why volume is not the same as clarity. (Evaluate)

English has approximately 44 phonemes, several of which do not exist in Urdu. The most common challenges for Urdu speakers are the "th" sounds, the "v/w" distinction, final consonant clusters and vowel length. Stress and intonation are as important as individual sounds. The goal is clarity, not a native-speaker accent.
