textbook.com.pk Mr Omar teaches in a government school in Lahore. A visiting teacher from rural Sindh, Miss Zahra, joins the staff. In a staff meeting, the headteacher asks Miss Zahra to share her teaching experience. She speaks softly, begins with a long account of her village and her training, and never directly states her main point. Some colleagues look impatient. Later, Mr Omar asks a British-trained volunteer teacher the same question. The volunteer answers in two sentences: "I focus on group work. My pupils' test scores rose last term." Same question, two very different answers. This topic explains why.

Intercultural communication is the study of how people from different cultural backgrounds communicate with one another, and how cultural assumptions shape the way messages are sent, received and interpreted. English is a global language: the English spoken in Karachi, in London, in Lahore and in New York is not used in exactly the same way. Learning to communicate across these differences is a core skill for a teacher, who works with pupils, parents and colleagues from many backgrounds.

The most influential account of cultural difference in communication comes from Hall (1976), who distinguished high-context and low-context communication. In a high-context culture, much of the meaning is carried by the context: the relationship between the speakers, the shared history, the setting, what is left unsaid. The words themselves may be indirect and understated. The listener is expected to "read between the lines". Many South Asian, East Asian and Middle Eastern communication styles are relatively high-context. Miss Zahra's long, story-like answer in the staff meeting is a high-context style: the meaning is embedded in the account, and a listener who knows the style will hear humility, respect for the group and a gradual build to the point. In a low-context culture, meaning is carried mainly by the words themselves. The speaker is expected to be explicit, direct and efficient, and the listener should not have to guess. Many Northern European, North Australian and North American communication styles are relatively low-context. The volunteer's two-sentence answer is a low-context style: the meaning is in the words, and nothing is left to inference. textbook.com.pk Neither style is better. Hall (1976) is clear that the distinction is a tendency, not a rule: every person and every conversation falls somewhere on the spectrum between the two extremes. A Pakistani doctor explaining a diagnosis to an elderly patient may use a high-context style (gentle, indirect, relationship-focused), while the same doctor writing a referral letter to a specialist uses a low-context style (precise, technical, direct). Why this matters for you. Pakistani classrooms are often high-context environments, but the English textbooks, exams and official documents pupils encounter are written in a relatively low-context style. A teacher who understands both can help pupils navigate between them.

A second dimension of intercultural variation is directness. In some cultures, saying "no" directly is honest and efficient. In other cultures, a direct "no" threatens the relationship and is avoided. Brown and Levinson (1987) describe face as the public self-image every person wants to maintain, and they distinguish two kinds: Positive face: the want to be liked, appreciated and approved of. Negative face: the want to be unimpeded, to have freedom of action without pressure. A face-saving strategy is a way of speaking that protects either your own face or the other person's face. Common face-saving strategies in English include: Hedging: softening a statement. "I wonder if you might…", "Perhaps we could…", "It might be a good idea to…". Giving reasons before a refusal: "I would love to help, but I have a prior commitment" instead of "No, I cannot". Using questions instead of commands: "Could you share the notes?" instead of "Give me the notes". Apologising: "I'm sorry, but I won't be able to attend" signals respect for the other person's invitation. These strategies are not weakness. Brown and Levinson (1987) argue that politeness is a fundamental part of human language, and every culture has its own system of it. The difference is in which face is prioritised and which strategies are considered polite. In many Pakistani settings, protecting the other person's positive face (showing warmth, respect, hospitality) is central. In some low-context Western settings, respecting negative face (not imposing) is more central. Worked example before you analyse one. Consider a parent who arrives late to a meeting with a teacher. A relatively direct (low-context) response: "You are fifteen minutes late. We started without you." A face-saving (higher-context) response: "Thank you for coming. We have just started; please join us." Both communicate the same fact (the meeting has started), but the second protects the parent's positive face and preserves the relationship. A skilled teacher chooses the response the situation and the relationship call for. Common misconception. "Cultural awareness is about memorising facts about other cultures." It is not. Facts are a starting point, but cultural awareness is the habit of noticing that your own way of communicating is not the only way, and of adjusting your style when the situation demands it. Hall (1976) warns against turning cultural tendencies into stereotypes: not every Pakistani is high-context, and not every British person is low-context. The value of the framework is that it gives you a way to notice and interpret differences, not a set of labels to apply to people.

Work in groups of three. Read the following scenario and answer the questions below. Allow 25 minutes. Then present your analysis to another group. A Pakistani teacher on an exchange programme in England emails her mentor: "I was wondering if it might be possible for you to observe my lesson next week, if it is not too much trouble. I completely understand if you are too busy. Perhaps another time would be better." The mentor reads the email as lacking confidence and assumes the teacher does not really want the observation. Using Hall's high-context / low-context framework, explain what is happening. Using Brown and Levinson's face framework, identify the face-saving strategies the teacher uses and how the mentor might interpret them. Rewrite the email so it is clearer for a low-context reader while still sounding polite.

Explain the difference between high-context and low-context communication in your own words, and give one example of each. (Remember) A colleague says, "Low-context communication is just rude." Using Hall (1976), explain what is wrong with that claim. (Understand) A pupil writes in an essay, "Tell me the answer." Rewrite the sentence using two different face-saving strategies from this topic and explain which face each one protects. (Apply) Analyse the staff-meeting scenario at the start of this topic. Identify one high-context feature of Miss Zahra's answer and one low-context feature of the volunteer's answer, and explain how each fits their likely cultural framing. (Analyze)

Intercultural communication is shaped by at least two major dimensions. Hall's (1976) high-context / low-context spectrum describes where meaning lives: in the shared context or in the words themselves. Brown and Levinson's (1987) face framework describes how politeness works: speakers use strategies to protect their own and others' positive and negative face. Neither framework ranks one style above the other; both give you tools to notice, interpret and adapt to the communication patterns you meet as a teacher.

I can explain high-context and low-context communication and recognise each in a described example. I can identify at least three face-saving strategies in a piece of spoken or written English. I can analyse a described cross-cultural communication breakdown using Hall's and Brown and Levinson's frameworks. I can rewrite a direct message in a more face-saving way without losing its meaning. I can reject the claim that one communication style is simply better than another.

Over one week, collect three examples of communication between the school and parents or the community (a letter home, a verbal request, a notice at the gate). For each, note whether the style is closer to high-context or low-context, and identify any face-saving strategies used. Write half a page on what you notice and whether the style fits the audience. Do not name the school, the staff or the families in your write-up.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: Write 400 to 450 words on the following. A teacher in a government school in Punjab sends the following message to a non-governmental organisation (NGO) that works in a low-context, direct communication style: "We are very grateful for your continued support. If it is not too much trouble, and only if it suits your schedule, we were hoping you might consider visiting our school one day. We would not want to impose on your valuable time." The NGO replies that they are unsure whether the school actually wants the visit. Analyse the breakdown using this topic's two frameworks (Hall and Brown and Levinson), and rewrite the message so the request is clear and polite for a low-context reader. Mini-rubric Criterion What a strong response does Use of Hall's framework (Understand) Correctly identifies the high-context features of the original message and explains how a low-context reader misreads them Use of Brown and Levinson's framework (Apply) Identifies the face-saving strategies used and explains the face threat the NGO perceived Rewritten message (Analyze) Produces a message that is direct enough for a low-context reader while remaining genuinely polite, and explains the changes Register and clarity Writes for a colleague, defines any technical term used, stays within the word count

Hall, E. T. (1976). Beyond Culture. Anchor Press. Chapters 6 and 7 set out the high-context / low-context distinction this topic draws on. Brown, P., & Levinson, S. C. (1987). Politeness: Some Universals in Language Usage. Cambridge University Press. Chapter 1 introduces the face framework and the politeness strategies this topic describes.

textbook.com.pk Miss Laila teaches Class 8 in a government school in Jacobabad. She writes a note to parents about an upcoming exam. Her first version reads: "Examinations shall commence on 10 October. Pupils are expected to be seated by 8.30 a.m. Non-compliance will result in denial of entry." The parents, many of whom have limited formal schooling, do not respond. Her mentor suggests rewriting it in plainer, warmer language. This topic is about that rewriting: how to take a message and reshape it for a different reader without losing its meaning.

Topics 4.1 and 4.2 gave you two sets of tools: the professional writing formats, and the cultural knowledge to understand how communication varies across contexts. This topic puts them together. Adapting communication is the skill of taking a message and reshaping its register, tone and content so it works for a new audience or a new purpose. Register is the level of formality a situation demands. Tone is the writer's attitude toward the subject and the audience. A single fact ("The exam is on 10 October") can be expressed in many registers and tones, and the choice depends entirely on who will read it and what relationship the writer wants with them.

The figure above maps the adaptation process. The first step is always to analyse the two situations: Original audience and purpose: Who was this written for, and what should they think, feel or do after reading it? New audience and purpose: Who will read it now, and what do they need? For each audience, ask four questions: What do they already know? (A district education officer knows what an exam timetable is; a parent with limited schooling may not.) What is their relationship to the writer? (Familiar or formal? Equal or hierarchical?) What is their likely communication style? (Higher-context or lower-context? More direct or more face-saving?) What do they need from this message? (The facts only, or also reassurance, motivation or an explanation of why it matters?) Miss Laila's first version assumed a formal, low-context reader who would respond to authority ("shall", "non-compliance", "denial of entry"). Her actual audience was parents who needed a clear, warm, practical message. The mismatch is a register and tone problem, not a grammar problem.

textbook.com.pk The figure above compares three common register and tone combinations you will move between as a teacher. The same core message changes shape in each: Formal-official (to a district officer): "I am writing to inform you that the Class 8 examinations will commence on 10 October. Pupils are required to be seated by 8.30 a.m." Formal-professional (to a colleague): "Just to let you know, the Class 8 exams start on 10 October. Pupils need to be seated by 8.30." Informal-warm (to parents with limited schooling): "Dear parents, please note that the Class 8 exam will begin on 10 October. Kindly make sure your child reaches school by 8.30 a.m. so they can sit the exam on time. Thank you for your support." Notice what changes and what stays the same. The facts (the date, the time) stay the same in all three. What changes is the level of formality (shall/kindly/please), the distance between writer and reader (I am writing to inform you / just to let you know / dear parents), and the attitude (neutral-authoritative / collegial / warm-inviting). Worked example before you adapt one. Miss Laila's first parent note ("Examinations shall commence… Non-compliance will result in denial of entry") is rewritten for her actual audience as: "Dear parents, the Class 8 exam will begin on 10 October. Please send your child to school by 8.30 a.m. on that day. If a child arrives late, they may not be allowed to sit the exam. Your support helps your child do their best. Thank you." The facts are identical. The register is plainer, the tone is warmer, and the reason (your child's success) is made explicit for an audience that needs it.

Adapting communication is sometimes more than swapping formal words for plain ones. It can also mean adding, removing or reordering information: Add what the new reader needs: a reason, a definition, a reassurance. Remove what the new reader does not need: jargon, official phrasing, assumptions. Reorder so the most important information comes first. A busy parent needs the date and time before the background. Hall (1976) and Brown and Levinson (1987) both remind us that what counts as "enough" information varies by context. A low-context reader wants the point first and the reason after. A higher-context reader may expect the relationship and context to be established before the point. Adapting a message means judging which pattern your new reader expects. Common misconception. "One communication style works everywhere." It does not. A message that sounds respectful and professional to a district officer can sound cold and distant to a parent, and a message that sounds warm and plain to a parent can sound unprofessional to a supervisor. The skill is not to pick one "correct" style and use it always; the skill is to read the situation and adapt.

Work in pairs. Take the following message, written by a headteacher to a colleague, and rewrite it for the two other audiences described. For each rewrite, explain in two or three sentences what you changed and why. Allow 25 minutes. Then compare your rewrites with another pair. Original (to a colleague): "The mid-term exam schedule has been moved forward by two days because of the sudden holiday. Papers need to be ready by Friday. Can you handle the Class 7 English paper?" Audiences to adapt for: A formal letter to the district education officer explaining the change. A note to parents informing them of the new exam dates.
documents.s: Activity: Adapt a message for three audiences

documents.t: Explain the difference between register and tone, and give one example of each. (Remember) A teacher writes to a parent: "Your child's academic performance is unsatisfactory and requires immediate remedial intervention." Rewrite this sentence for a parent with limited schooling and explain the changes you made. (Apply) A colleague says, "You should always write professionally, no matter who the reader is." Using this topic's account, explain what that advice overlooks. (Understand) Analyse the two versions of Miss Laila's parent note (the original and the rewrite in the worked example). Identify two specific changes and explain how each one serves the new audience. (Analyze)

Adapting communication means analysing the audience and purpose, then reshaping the register, tone and content of a message so it works for a new reader. The facts usually stay the same; what changes is the level of formality, the distance between writer and reader, the attitude, and sometimes the amount and order of information. The frameworks from Topic 4.2 (Hall's high-/low-context spectrum and Brown and Levinson's face framework) help you judge what a given audience expects and needs. One style does not work everywhere; the skill is to read the situation and adapt.

I can analyse a described audience using the four questions this topic sets out. I can rewrite a message for a different register and tone without changing its facts. I can explain why a given message does or does not fit its intended reader. I can add, remove and reorder information to suit a new audience. I can reject the claim that one communication style is right for every situation.

Find one written communication the school sends to parents or the community (a notice, a letter or a message). Analyse it using this topic's four audience questions. Then rewrite it for a specific parent audience you know (for example, parents with limited formal schooling, or parents who work long hours and read messages quickly). Write half a page on what you changed and why. Do not name the school, the staff or the families in your write-up.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: Write 400 to 450 words on the following. A teacher writes the following message to a group of parents, many of whom are not comfortable reading English: "Guardians are hereby notified that the annual parent-teacher meeting is scheduled for 5 November at 10:00 hours. Attendance is compulsory. Those failing to attend will be sent a show-cause notice." Analyse why this message may fail for the intended audience, rewrite it for that audience, and explain how your rewrite applies at least two principles from this topic. Mini-rubric Criterion What a strong response does Analysis of the original message (Understand) Identifies specific register, tone and content problems for the described audience Quality of the rewrite (Apply) Produces a message that is clear, warm and practical for the described parents Justification by topic principles (Evaluate) Names and applies at least two specific principles (audience analysis, register/tone shift, add/remove/reorder, face-saving) and shows how each shaped the rewrite Register and clarity Writes for a colleague, defines any technical term used, stays within the word count

Hall, E. T. (1976). Beyond Culture. Anchor Press. Chapter 7 discusses how the same message is read differently in high- and low-context settings. Brown, P., & Levinson, S. C. (1987). Politeness: Some Universals in Language Usage. Cambridge University Press. The discussion of positive and negative face (Chapter 1) is the basis for choosing face-saving strategies for a given reader.

Professional writing is the skill of choosing the right format (email, memo, report, formal letter) for the right purpose and audience, and following the conventions each format expects. Every professional document moves through the same writing process: plan, draft, revise, edit, final version. Intercultural communication is shaped by Hall's (1976) high-context / low-context spectrum (where meaning lives) and by Brown and Levinson's (1987) face framework (how politeness works). Adapting communication means analysing a new audience and purpose, then reshaping the register, tone and content of a message so it works for that reader. One style does not work everywhere; the skill is to read the situation and adapt.

In this unit's account, a business email's subject line should be: (Remember) a) left blank so the reader opens the email to find out what it is about b) short and specific, telling the reader what the email concerns c) a full sentence that explains the whole request d) the word "Urgent" followed by as many exclamation marks as possible Which writing format is most appropriate for informing all staff about a changed timetable? (Understand) a) A formal letter b) A short report c) A memo d) A job application letter In Hall's (1976) account, a high-context communication style carries most of its meaning in: (Remember) a) the exact words the speaker uses b) the grammatical structures of the sentences c) the shared context, relationship and what is left unsaid d) the written record of the conversation A teacher writes, "Perhaps we could consider revising the homework policy, if that is all right with everyone." This is an example of: (Apply) a) a face-saving hedge b) a low-context demand c) a formal letter closing d) a report recommendation In the writing process this unit describes, which stage comes immediately after drafting? (Remember) a) Final version b) Editing c) Revising d) Planning Brown and Levinson (1987) describe "negative face" as the want to: (Understand) a) be liked and appreciated b) have freedom of action without pressure c) avoid all forms of politeness d) communicate only in writing Which of the following is a feature of a formal letter but NOT of a business email? (Understand) a) A subject line b) The sender's address and the date at the top c) A polite closing d) A clear opening sentence A teacher adapts a formal-official message for a parent audience by changing "Guardians are hereby notified" to "Dear parents, please note". This is primarily a shift of: (Apply) a) format b) grammar rules c) register and tone d) the writing process A face-saving strategy that gives a reason before refusing is used to protect the listener's: (Apply) a) physical safety b) positive or negative face c) knowledge of grammar d) understanding of register A short report differs from a memo primarily because it: (Remember) a) is always handwritten b) presents findings with an introduction, findings and conclusion c) has no heading d) is sent to people outside the organisation

Explain the difference between a memo and a short report, and give one situation where you would choose each. (Remember) A colleague writes a business email that begins with three paragraphs of background before stating the purpose. Using this unit's account of professional email structure, explain what is wrong and how to fix it. (Analyze) Explain the difference between high-context and low-context communication, and give one example of each. (Remember) Identify two face-saving strategies in the following sentence and explain which face each one protects: "I'm really sorry to bother you, but I was wondering if you might possibly be able to share your notes, if it's not too much trouble." (Analyze) A teacher writes the same message about a school event to a district officer and to a group of parents with limited schooling. Explain two specific changes the teacher should make for the parent audience and why. (Apply) Explain the difference between register and tone, and give one example of each. (Remember) A pupil says, "Face-saving strategies are just dishonest ways of avoiding the truth." Using Brown and Levinson (1987), explain what that claim overlooks. (Evaluate) Arrange the five stages of the writing process in order and explain what happens at each stage. (Understand) A message written in a high-context style is read by a low-context reader. Explain one specific misunderstanding that is likely to happen and why, using Hall (1976). (Apply) Explain why "one communication style works everywhere" is a misconception, and give one example of a situation where adapting your style matters. (Understand)

A teacher needs to write three documents in one week: a request to the headteacher for classroom supplies, an announcement to staff about a changed exam date, and a letter to the district education officer reporting on a school event. For each document, choose the most appropriate professional writing format, explain your choice, and outline the structure and tone you would use. (Analyze) A Pakistani teacher in a multicultural school writes the following to a low-context British colleague: "If it is not too much trouble, and only if you are free, I was hoping you might not mind observing my lesson sometime, but please don't feel you have to." The colleague later says they did not realise the teacher actually wanted the observation. Analyse the breakdown using Hall's and Brown and Levinson's frameworks, and rewrite the request so the meaning is clear and the politeness is preserved. (Analyze) Take a formal notice from a school or office (for example, a fee notice, a holiday announcement or a meeting invitation). Analyse it for register, tone and likely audience. Then rewrite it for a different audience (for example, parents with limited formal schooling, or a group of colleagues). Explain every change you make. Write 400 to 450 words. (Evaluate) Evaluate the claim that "professional writing means using complex vocabulary and long sentences." Use this unit's account of professional writing, register and tone to argue for or against the claim. (Evaluate) Integrative. You are the headteacher of a government school in Sindh. You need to communicate a sudden school closure (due to flooding) to two audiences: (a) the district education officer and (b) the parents of your pupils, many of whom have limited formal schooling. Plan both messages, choose the right format and register for each audience, and justify your choices using this unit's account of professional writing, intercultural communication and audience adaptation. (Create)

b - a subject line should be short and specific, telling the reader what the email is about. c - a memo is the format for informing people within the same organisation about a change. c - high-context communication carries meaning in the shared context, relationship and what is unsaid. a - "Perhaps we could consider" is a hedge that softens the suggestion and protects face. c - the order is plan, draft, revise, edit, final version; revising follows drafting. b - negative face is the want to be unimpeded, to have freedom of action without pressure. b - the sender's address and date at the top are features of a formal letter, not of a business email. c - changing formal-official phrasing to plain, warm phrasing is a register and tone shift. b - giving a reason before refusing is a face-saving strategy that protects the listener's positive or negative face. b - a short report presents findings with an introduction, findings and conclusion/recommendation.

1. (4 marks) A memo informs or instructs people within the same organisation (1); a short report presents findings, often to a supervisor, with an introduction, findings and conclusion (1); the memo situation is genuinely internal (1); the report situation genuinely presents findings or recommendations (1). 2. (5 marks) Identifies the problem: the purpose comes too late (1); explains the principle: a business email states its purpose in the opening sentence so the reader knows immediately why they are reading (1); advises moving the purpose to the first sentence and keeping background brief (1); the reasoning draws on Topic 4.1 (1); the reasoning is coherent (1). 3. (4 marks) High-context communication carries meaning in the shared context, relationship and what is left unsaid (1); low-context communication carries meaning mainly in the words themselves (1); the high-context example is genuinely indirect or context-dependent (1); the low-context example is genuinely explicit (1). 4. (5 marks) Identifies at least two strategies from: apologising ("I'm really sorry to bother you"), hedging ("I was wondering if", "might possibly"), and the conditional softening ("if it's not too much trouble") (2 for two correct); explains that these protect the listener's negative face (freedom from imposition) (2); the reasoning is coherent (1). 5. (5 marks) Names two specific changes (e.g. plainer language, warmer tone, shorter sentences, adding a reason the parents should care) (1 each, up to 2); explains why each change serves the parent audience (e.g. limited schooling, high-context expectations) (1 each, up to 2); the reasoning is coherent (1). 6. (4 marks) Register is the level of formality a situation demands (1); tone is the writer's attitude toward the subject and the audience (1); the register example is genuinely about formality level (1); the tone example is genuinely about attitude (1). 7. (5 marks) Takes the claim at its strongest (1); explains that Brown and Levinson treat politeness as a fundamental, universal part of language, not as dishonesty (1); notes that face-saving strategies protect relationships and reduce threat, which honest directness can damage (1); argues a verdict with reasons (1); the reasoning is coherent (1). 8. (5 marks) Correct order: plan, draft, revise, edit, final version (1); explains planning (purpose, audience) and drafting (first version) (1); explains revising (rethinking structure and content) and editing (fixing grammar, punctuation, tone) (1); explains final version (the polished document) (1); the reasoning is coherent (1). 9. (5 marks) Identifies a likely misunderstanding (e.g. the low-context reader takes indirect phrasing literally and misses the point, or interprets excessive politeness as lack of interest) (1); explains it using Hall's framework (the reader expects meaning in the words, but the message embeds it in context) (2); the reasoning draws on Topic 4.2 (1); the reasoning is coherent (1). 10. (4 marks) Explains that different audiences and purposes demand different register, tone and content (1); explains that a style that works for one reader can confuse or offend another (1); gives a genuine example (e.g. formal-official language for parents, or indirect language for a low-context reader) (1); the reasoning is coherent (1).

These notes are for the instructor. They set out teaching strategies, sequencing, the misconceptions this unit is likely to meet, and the practical work that gives trainees something to do rather than only something to read. This unit carries no assessment items of its own; the question bank lives in unit-assessment.mdx.

The guide lists four teaching strategies for this course: lecture, discussion, question-answer and brain storming. This unit uses all four, but leans heavily on discussion and brain storming because the content (register, tone, cultural awareness) is best learned by comparing examples and arguing about choices, not by memorising rules. Lecture works best for the structural knowledge in Topic 4.1: the parts of a business email, a memo, a short report and a formal letter. A short lecture that names and shows the structure of each format, followed by a worked example, gives trainees the scaffold they need before they write. Discussion works best for Topics 4.2 and 4.3, where there is rarely one right answer. Trainees learn more from arguing about whether a message is "too direct" or "too vague" and why, than from being told the answer. Question-answer is useful for checking understanding of key terms (high-context vs low-context, positive vs negative face, register vs tone). Use it after a reading or an activity, not as the main event. Brain storming is useful at the start of an adaptation task: before trainees rewrite a message, have the whole group list everything they know about the new audience. This makes the audience analysis visible and shared. The guide also lists group work, group assignments, individual assignment and presentations as practical work. This unit's activities are designed for pairs and small groups, with one individual transfer task ("Try this at your practicum school") per topic.

The three topics are designed to be taught in order across Weeks 13 to 16 (derived): Week 13 to 14 (Topic 4.1): professional writing formats and the writing process. Start with the formats trainees are most likely to use (business email, formal letter) before the less common ones (memo, short report). Build in at least one writing task where trainees draft, revise and edit a real document. Week 15 (Topic 4.2): intercultural communication. This is the most abstract topic. Ground it in concrete examples from the trainees' own experience (staff meetings, parent interactions, differences between schools they have worked in). The frameworks (Hall, Brown and Levinson) are tools for interpreting experience, not facts to be memorised in isolation. Week 16 (Topic 4.3): adapting communication. This topic depends on both previous topics, so it should come last. The summative task here is the unit's most integrative piece of writing: trainees analyse an audience, choose a register and tone, and rewrite a message. If time is short, Topic 4.3 can be combined with the revision of Topic 4.2, but do not teach 4.3 before 4.2: the adaptation tasks assume trainees already understand high-/low-context communication and face-saving strategies.

The content-spec names three misconceptions for this unit. All three are durable and worth addressing directly. "Professional writing means using complex vocabulary." Trainees often believe that formal = impressive = long words. Handle it by showing two versions of the same message, one over-formal and one plain, and asking trainees which a real reader would prefer. The note to parents in Topic 4.3 is a good example: the over-formal version is grammatically correct but fails with its audience. "One communication style works everywhere." Trainees may default to the formal-official style they associate with school. Handle it by giving them the same message to rewrite for three audiences and having them compare the results. The Activity in Topic 4.3 is designed for exactly this. "Cultural awareness is about memorising facts about other cultures." Trainees may try to learn a list of "Pakistani traits" or "British traits". Handle it by stressing, as Hall (1976) does, that these are tendencies on a spectrum, not fixed labels, and that the value of the framework is to notice and interpret differences, not to stereotype people.
documents.s: Common misconceptions and how to handle them

documents.t: The unit's practical work is built into each topic's Activity and Summative task. For a cohesive four-week block, consider the following sequence of assessed tasks: Week 13: trainees draft a business email and a formal letter on a given scenario; peer review using a simple checklist (structure, tone, clarity). Week 14: trainees write a short report on a described school activity; revise it after feedback. Week 15: in small groups, trainees analyse a cross-cultural communication breakdown (the Activity in Topic 4.2) and present their analysis to another group. Week 16: the Summative task from Topic 4.3 (analyse and rewrite a message for a new audience) serves as the unit's integrative practical assessment. Across all four weeks, encourage trainees to collect real examples of professional writing and real cross-cultural interactions from their practicum schools. These real examples are the best material for discussion, and they make the frameworks concrete.
This course introduces prospective B.Ed teachers to how learners develop, think, and learn, and to the psychological principles that inform effective teaching in Pakistani classrooms.
Teaching follows the course guide: interactive lectures grounded in local classroom examples, small-group discussion, and case analysis.
Assessment for the affiliated colleges (GECEs) is weighted 60% summative / 40% formative, per the course guide and Constitution III.7.
Recommended books from the course guide are listed for scope and further reading only; they are never reproduced as content.

Every teacher already has a theory of how pupils learn. It may never have been written down, and it may be wrong, but it is there, and it decides what you do when a class goes quiet or a bright pupil stops trying. Educational psychology is the effort to test those theories instead of trusting them. This unit works through what the subject is, where it came from, and what it actually gives you on a Monday morning, in four short topics. Each topic is a complete learning cycle: it opens with a real classroom situation, explains the ideas, gives you an activity, checks your understanding, and ends with something to try on your practicum.

By the end of this unit you should be able to: Define educational psychology and explain what makes it a distinct field rather than psychology in general or teaching experience written down. Describe its scope - the learner, the learning process and the learning situation - and place a given classroom question inside one of the three. Explain why it is called a scientific study, and name the main ways it gathers evidence. Explain the two-way relationship between psychology and education, including what school classrooms give back to psychology. Describe the main ways learners in one class differ, and explain what each difference does and does not tell you about a pupil. Explain how psychological ideas shape planning, classroom management, assessment and a teacher's own reflection, and use them to analyse a described classroom episode.

None beyond HSC-level general study skills. This is the opening unit of the course; no psychology is assumed. What you do bring is years as a school pupil yourself, and several topics start from that.
Topic 1.1 - What educational psychology is Topic 1.2 - How psychology and education meet Topic 1.3 - The learners in front of you Topic 1.4 - Shaping teaching, assessment and reflection

Work through the topics in order. Topic 1.3 uses the scope idea from 1.1, and Topic 1.4 assumes you have met learner differences in 1.3. Do the activity and the "Check your understanding" questions before moving on. They are not graded; they show you which ideas are still shaky while it is cheap to fix that. Keep your Topic 1.4 reflection note. Later units on development, learning theories and motivation each send you back to it. After the four topics, the unit assessment page carries a full question bank with answers and marking guidance, so you can test yourself before a class test.

Miss Shazia teaches Class 6 in a government girls' school in Hyderabad. Two pupils sit at the same desk. Both are taught the same lesson on fractions, by the same teacher, on the same morning. Rukhsana follows it easily. Ayesha copies every step correctly into her notebook and still cannot do a single sum on her own that evening. Staff-room explanations come quickly. "Ayesha is weak." "Ayesha is lazy." "Some girls just cannot do maths." Each of these is a theory about why learning failed, and each one leads somewhere different: a weak pupil gets easier work, a lazy pupil gets a scolding, and a pupil who "cannot do maths" gets quietly given up on. Miss Shazia notices something the explanations miss. Ayesha can halve a roti at home without hesitation. She can split a plate of food between three sisters and argue about fairness. What she cannot do is connect any of that to the symbols on the blackboard. That observation is worth more than all three staff-room theories, because it can be checked. textbook.com.pk

Psychology is the study of mind and behaviour: why people do what they do, and what is going on inside them while they do it. It is a wide field. A psychologist may study memory, fear, friendship, language, or how an infant learns to walk. Educational Psychology is the part of that field that studies mind and behaviour in educational settings. Its question is narrower and more practical: how do people learn, what helps and hinders that learning, and what follows for the person trying to teach them? Two boundaries matter, and new students blur both. It is not simply psychology applied to schools. A general psychologist studying memory wants to know how memory works. An educational psychologist wants to know what a teacher should do differently on Tuesday because of it. The question is asked from inside the classroom. It is not teaching experience written down. Experience is where the questions come from, and an experienced teacher's hunches are usually worth taking seriously. But "in my thirty years I have found" is not evidence that the thing works, or that it works for pupils unlike the ones that teacher taught. Educational psychology is the discipline that tests the hunches. The misconception to clear now. Many trainees arrive believing educational psychology is "common sense with difficult words attached" - that a sensible person could reach the same conclusions without studying it. The trouble is that common sense supplies too many answers, and they contradict each other. "Birds of a feather flock together" and "opposites attract" are both common sense. "Practice makes perfect" and "you either have a gift for it or you do not" are both common sense. Common sense cannot tell you which is true for Ayesha, because whichever way the evidence falls, some proverb will have predicted it. The value of the discipline is not that its answers are surprising. It is that they can be wrong, and so can be checked.
documents.s: What psychology studies, and what makes educational psychology a distinct field

documents.t: The field is usually described as covering three things at once, and almost every question a teacher asks sits in one of them (Seifert & Sutton, 2009). The learner. Who is this pupil? What do they already know, what are they ready for, what moves them, what do they bring from home? Ayesha's fraction sense at the dinner table belongs here. The learning process. What actually happens when someone comes to understand something? How does attention work, how is something held in memory, why does knowledge learnt in one place so often fail to appear in another? Ayesha's inability to carry her roti-halving to the blackboard belongs here, and it has a name: the problem of transfer. The learning situation. What surrounds the learning? The way the lesson is sequenced, the size and noise of the room, whether it is safe to be wrong out loud, what the test rewards. Sixty girls in a hot room with one blackboard is not a neutral background; it is part of the explanation. The three are not separate compartments, and nothing is gained by arguing about which box a question goes in. The reason to hold all three is that teachers reach for one and forget the other two. "Ayesha is weak" is a learner-only explanation. It may be wrong simply because the answer lay in the process, or in the room. textbook.com.pk
documents.s: The scope: the learner, the learning process, and the learning situation

documents.t: The course guide calls educational psychology "the scientific study of human learning, development, and behavior in educational settings". The word doing the work in that sentence is scientific, and it does not mean laboratory coats. It means claims are stated so that evidence could count against them, and then evidence is gathered on purpose rather than remembered selectively. Three ways of gathering it come up constantly in this course. Observation. Watching what actually happens, systematically, rather than what you assume happens. Counting how many pupils Miss Shazia calls on, and who they are, will surprise most teachers who try it. Experiment. Changing one thing on purpose and comparing. Teach the same content to two similar sections, one with worked examples first and one without, and see which does better on the same test a week later. Case study. Following one learner or one class closely and in depth. This will not tell you what is true of all pupils, but it can show you a possibility nobody had considered - which is often where the good questions come from. None of the three is trustworthy alone. An observation may be of an unusual day. An experiment in one school may not hold in another. A case study is a single case. What makes the field scientific is not any one method but the habit of asking how would I know if I were wrong? Notice what this gives Miss Shazia that the staff room did not. "Ayesha is weak" cannot be wrong; it explains any result. "Ayesha has the underlying idea but has not connected it to the symbols" can be wrong, and it tells her exactly what to try next: start from the roti, and build the notation onto it. textbook.com.pk
documents.s: Educational psychology as a scientific study

documents.t: In pairs, about 20 minutes. Below are eight questions a teacher might genuinely ask. Decide for each whether it is mainly about the learner, the learning process, or the learning situation. Expect to disagree; the argument is the point. Why does this class go silent whenever I ask a question? Why can Ayesha halve a roti but not a fraction? Why do my pupils remember the poem but not the grammar rule? Why does Rukhsana finish early and then disturb others? Why did the whole section do worse after we moved to the room by the road? Why do they answer well in Sindhi and badly in English? Why does nobody ask me to repeat anything, even when they have not understood? Why do they do better on the test than on the homework? Then pick the one you would most want a real answer to, and write a single sentence saying what you would observe, count or try in order to get one.

In your own words, define educational psychology without using the words "study" or "learning". (Understand) Give one question a general psychologist might ask about memory, and one question an educational psychologist would ask about the same topic. (Understand) Classify each of these as learner, process or situation, and say why: a pupil who has not eaten breakfast; a lesson that introduces four new terms in five minutes; a pupil who is fluent in Sindhi and hesitant in Urdu. (Apply) A colleague says "I do not need theory, I have taught for twenty years." Give the strongest fair reply you can, in two sentences. (Apply) Miss Shazia wants to know whether starting from everyday examples helps her class with fractions. Describe how she could find out using one of observation, experiment or case study, and name one limit of the method you chose. (Apply)

Educational psychology studies mind and behaviour in educational settings, asking its questions from the teacher's side of the desk. Its scope covers the learner, the learning process and the learning situation, and a teacher who reaches for only one of the three will misread most classrooms. It is called a scientific study because its claims are stated so that evidence could count against them, and gathered through observation, experiment and case study rather than recalled selectively. Its value is not that it replaces a teacher's judgement, but that it gives that judgement something to check itself against.

I can define educational psychology and say what makes it different from psychology in general. I can name the three parts of its scope and give a classroom example of each. I can explain why "it is just common sense" is a weak objection to the field. I can name three ways evidence is gathered and state one limit of each.

Sit at the back of one lesson with a blank page. Do not judge the teaching. Just count one thing: how many pupils are asked a question by name, and where in the room they sit. Mark the seating plan. Afterwards, ask yourself which part of the scope your count belongs to, and what a second lesson's count would need to look like before you would trust the pattern.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: Write 250-300 words on the Ayesha case at the top of this topic. Take the three staff-room explanations ("weak", "lazy", "cannot do maths") and the explanation Miss Shazia reached, and compare them. Your answer must say, for each, what evidence would count against it, and must conclude with which explanation you would act on first and why. Mini-rubric Criterion What a strong answer shows Grasp of the field Uses the scope correctly; does not treat every explanation as a learner explanation. Analysis of the explanations Separates the explanations by what evidence could disconfirm each, not by which sounds kindest. (Analyze) Classroom judgement The chosen next step follows from the analysis and could actually be done by one teacher with sixty pupils. Plain, accurate writing Terms used correctly; no padding; within the word count.

How children learn. Educational Practices Series No. 7. International Academy of Education / UNESCO IBE. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED455955

At an in-service session in Sukkur, a trainer tells forty teachers about a well-known finding: pupils remember more when they are tested on material than when they re-read it. Testing is not just measurement, she says. Testing is itself a way of learning. Three teachers leave and do three different things. Mr Iqbal ignores it. His pupils are already tested constantly and are frightened of it; another test is the last thing his class needs. Mrs Naz adopts it wholesale and starts every lesson with a graded quiz. Within a month the weakest pupils have stopped attempting the quizzes at all, and she concludes the finding was nonsense. Mr Junaid changes one thing. At the end of each lesson he asks three questions, ungraded, with no names recorded, and pupils answer in their notebooks. After a fortnight he checks whether the class does better on the fortnightly test than the previous fortnight's class did. All three heard the same true finding. Only one of them is doing educational psychology. textbook.com.pk

A teacher makes hundreds of decisions a day and has time to think about almost none of them. Do I explain that again or move on? Do I call on the girl at the back who never volunteers? Is this class quiet because they understand or because they have given up? Every one of those is answered by some theory of how learning works. The only question is whether the theory was chosen or inherited. This is the honest case for the subject, and it is worth stating plainly because the dishonest case is so common. Educational psychology will not give you a rule that decides those questions for you. What it gives you is, first, a set of ideas that have survived testing, so your default guesses are better than chance; second, a vocabulary precise enough to describe what you are seeing, so you can discuss it with a colleague and be talking about the same thing; and third, the habit of asking what would tell you that you were wrong. Pakistan's National Professional Standards for Teachers make this explicit rather than optional: one of the ten standards is Human Growth and Development, which requires a teacher to understand how learners develop and to use that understanding in practice (Khizar et al., 2019). The knowledge is part of the job description, not an academic extra.
documents.s: Why a teacher needs educational psychology

documents.t: Psychology brings three things across the border into education. Theories that have been tested. How attention is limited, how something moves into long-term memory, how motivation shifts when a task is graded, how children's thinking changes with age. These are not certainties, but they are far better than staff-room proverbs, and they have been checked against evidence rather than recalled from experience (Seifert & Sutton, 2009). Methods for finding things out. The observation, experiment and case study from Topic 1.1. These transfer directly: Mr Junaid is running a small experiment, whether or not he would call it that. A language for describing learners. "Weak" is not a description; it is a verdict. Working memory, prior knowledge, transfer, motivation, readiness - these let two teachers point at the same thing. Precision here is not decoration. Mrs Naz's failure was that "testing helps memory" and "graded tests help frightened pupils' memory" sounded like the same claim to her.

The traffic runs both ways, and courses often forget to say so. Classrooms give psychology conditions no laboratory can produce: thirty or sixty learners at once, over months, with real consequences attached. A finding that holds for twenty volunteers recalling word lists for an hour may simply not survive a Class 6 room in July, and the only way to discover that is to go there. Classrooms also pose problems psychology would not have thought to ask. Why does knowledge learnt for a test vanish by the next term? Why do some pupils work hard for one teacher and not another? These questions came from teachers, not from laboratories. And classrooms are where theories go to be corrected. Mrs Naz's month is data. It does not show the finding was nonsense; it shows the finding has a condition attached that the trainer did not state, and that condition matters enormously for frightened pupils.
documents.s: What education contributes back to psychology

documents.t: Some sciences aim only to understand. Educational psychology aims to understand in order to improve something, and that changes how it works. It is judged partly by usefulness. A true finding that no teacher could act on is of limited interest to this field, however interesting it is to psychology. It cannot ignore context. Whether a finding holds in a Sindh government school with sixty pupils and no electricity is not a footnote; it is the question. And it carries an ethical weight that pure research does not. You are experimenting on other people's children, in the time they have, and they cannot opt out. This is exactly why Mr Junaid's version is better practice than Mrs Naz's: ungraded and unnamed, his change could not harm a pupil's record while he found out whether it worked. The misconception to clear now. Trainees often assume the flow is one-way - that researchers discover and teachers apply, and a good teacher is one who implements faithfully. Mrs Naz implemented faithfully. The relationship is a loop: a finding arrives, a teacher tries it under their own conditions, and what happens feeds back. A teacher who never asks whether the finding held in their own room is not being scientific, only obedient. textbook.com.pk
documents.s: Applied, not pure: how educational psychology differs from general psychology

documents.t: In groups of three, about 25 minutes. Take one teacher each - Mr Iqbal, Mrs Naz, Mr Junaid - and argue their case as sympathetically as you can. Each of you has two minutes. Then, as a group, agree on answers to these: What exactly did the trainer's finding claim, and what did it leave unstated? Mr Iqbal did nothing. Name the circumstances in which that is the right professional decision, and the circumstances in which it is just avoidance. Mrs Naz concluded the finding was nonsense. What would she have had to change about her month for that conclusion to be fair? Write your group's answer to question 2 in one sentence. Be ready to defend it.

Name the three things psychology contributes to education, and give a one-line example of each. (Remember) Explain, in two sentences, what a classroom can give psychology that a laboratory cannot. (Understand) "Educational psychology is an applied field." Explain what follows from that for how its findings should be judged. (Understand) Mrs Naz's quizzes were graded and named. Using the loop in this topic, explain what went wrong and what one change would have most improved her attempt. (Apply) A trainer tells you that pupils learn better in groups. Write the two questions you would ask before changing anything about your own teaching. (Apply)

A teacher needs educational psychology because teaching is decision-making under time pressure, and every decision rests on some theory of learning - chosen or inherited. Psychology contributes tested theories, methods for finding things out, and a precise language for describing learners. Education contributes back the conditions, the problems and the corrections that laboratories cannot supply. Because the field is applied, its findings are judged by usefulness and by whether they survive real conditions, and acting on them carries an ethical weight: the pupils cannot opt out. The relationship is a loop, not a delivery.

I can state the honest case for why a teacher needs this subject, without overclaiming. I can name what psychology gives education and what education gives back. I can explain what "applied" changes about how a finding should be judged. I can take a research claim and say what I would check before acting on it.

Ask your co-operating teacher this question: "Is there something you were told in training that did not work with your pupils?" Listen for what they changed and what they abandoned. Then ask yourself whether they had any way of telling the difference between a finding that was wrong and a finding whose conditions did not hold in their room. Write down what you would have suggested they check.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: Write 300-350 words taking one claim you have heard about teaching - from a trainer, a relative, a teacher, or a social-media video. State the claim precisely, including the conditions it needs in order to be true. Then say how you would find out whether it holds for one class you have actually seen, and what result would make you abandon it. End by saying which of the three Sukkur teachers your approach resembles, and why that is the right choice for this particular claim. Mini-rubric Criterion What a strong answer shows Precision of the claim The claim is restated with its unstated conditions made explicit, not repeated as a slogan. Analysis of the loop Distinguishes "the claim is false" from "the conditions do not hold here", and shows what evidence would separate them. (Analyze) Ethical judgement The proposed trial could not damage a pupil's record or standing while it ran. Plain, accurate writing Terms used correctly; the argument is followable; within the word count.

N., & Malik, M. A. (2019). Role of National Education Policy-2009 and National Professional Standards for Teachers in developing teachers' professionalism. Bulletin of Education and Research, 41(3), 101-118. https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/EJ1244705.pdf

Mr Bilal has taught the same Class 7 science lesson for six years. This year, three pupils sit out the whole period. Sana copies from the board and answers nothing. Asked directly, she says "I did not understand the last chapter either." Kiran answers everything correctly and then spends the rest of the lesson drawing. Asked why, she shrugs. Hina listens hard, follows every diagram, and freezes whenever she has to say anything aloud. Her written work is among the best in the class. In the staff room all three appear on the same list, under the same heading: not participating. That single heading is the problem. Three pupils have stopped taking part for three unrelated reasons, and the remedy for any one of them would do nothing for the other two. textbook.com.pk

The single best predictor of whether a pupil learns today's lesson is what they already knew when they walked in (Seifert & Sutton, 2009). New understanding attaches to old understanding. Where there is nothing to attach to, the lesson slides off. This is Sana. She is not slow. She is missing the chapter this one is built on, and no amount of attention to today's lesson will supply it. Every week that passes makes the gap wider, because each new lesson assumes the one she did not get. Readiness is the closely related idea: a pupil can be ready for the next step and not for the one after it. Push too far ahead and the work is meaningless; stay too far back and it is boring. Kiran and Sana are in the same room, at opposite ends of that problem. The practical move is unglamorous and it is most of the job: find out what they already know before you teach, not after. Two minutes of questions at the start of a lesson tells you more than a whole test at the end, because at the start you can still act on it.
documents.s: Differences in readiness and prior knowledge

documents.t: Motivation is not a fixed quantity a pupil has more or less of. It shifts with the task, the subject, the teacher and, above all, with whether the pupil expects effort to pay off. That last point is the one teachers most often miss. A pupil who has failed at something repeatedly makes an entirely rational decision to stop trying, because trying and failing in public is worse than not trying. What looks like laziness is often self-protection. Sana's silence is not indifference; it is the cheapest way to avoid being seen not to know. Kiran is the opposite case and gets far less sympathy. She is not under-motivated in general - she draws with great concentration. She is under-motivated by this task, which she finished in four minutes and which asks nothing more of her. Boredom and failure look identical from the front of the room and require opposite responses. Interest matters too, and it is more tractable than teachers assume. A task connected to something a pupil already cares about gets attention that the same task in the abstract does not. This is not entertainment; it is the difference between a fraction on a blackboard and a plate of food divided between three sisters.

In much of Sindh a pupil may speak Sindhi at home, meet Urdu in the corridor, and be taught, examined and judged partly in English. A pupil can understand an idea perfectly and be unable to show it in the language of the test. This is Hina. Her written work is strong because writing gives her time. Speaking in front of sixty classmates in a language she is still building does not. Her silence is a language cost, not a comprehension failure, and treating it as shyness or as weakness both miss it. Home background reaches into the classroom in plainer ways as well: whether there is light and quiet to work in, whether anyone at home can explain a missed chapter, whether a pupil is needed for work or for younger siblings. A teacher cannot change most of this. But a teacher who does not know it will misread the homework that never arrives. The misconception to clear now. Every difference in this topic gets collapsed into a single word: ability. Sana is "weak", Kiran is "careless", Hina is "shy". The word feels descriptive and is in fact a prediction - and a self-fulfilling one, because a pupil labelled weak is given easier work, which guarantees they stay behind. None of the three differences above is a statement about how much a pupil can ultimately learn. Each is a statement about where they are standing right now, and each points to a different next step. textbook.com.pk
documents.s: Differences in language, home background and support

documents.t: In groups of three or four, about 25 minutes. Take Sana, Kiran and Hina. For each one: Name which difference best explains what Mr Bilal is seeing, and say what makes you prefer it to the other two. Write one thing Mr Bilal could do next lesson. It must be something a single teacher with a full class could actually do, not "give her individual attention". Say how he would know within two weeks whether it had helped. Then answer this as a group: all three pupils appeared on the same staff-room list. What is the cost, to a pupil, of being on a list that does not distinguish between them?
documents.s: Activity: Three pupils, three next steps

documents.t: Name the three dimensions of difference in this topic. (Remember) Explain why a pupil who has failed repeatedly may stop trying, and why that is not the same as not caring. (Understand) Why does the text say "boredom and failure look identical from the front of the room"? What follows for a teacher? (Understand) A pupil answers confidently in Sindhi and poorly on the English written test. Give two different explanations, and say what you would do to tell them apart. (Apply) Classify each and justify: a pupil who cannot start the exercise but copies the example perfectly; a pupil who stops writing whenever work is graded; a pupil whose homework arrives only on days the electricity held. (Apply)

Learners in one room differ in ways that a single word like "weak" hides. Readiness and prior knowledge decide whether today's lesson has anything to attach to. Motivation shifts with the task and with whether a pupil expects effort to pay off, so both the failing pupil and the unchallenged one may stop taking part. Language and home background can separate what a pupil understands from what they can show. Each difference looks similar from the front of the class and calls for a different response, which is why reading them apart is a teaching skill rather than a courtesy.

I can name three dimensions along which learners in one class differ. I can explain why what looks like laziness is often self-protection. I can explain why a strong written performance and a silent pupil are not a contradiction. I can take a described pupil and give a defensible first step, not a label.

Before a lesson you are going to observe, ask the teacher to name two pupils who "do not participate". Watch only those two for the whole period. Note what each actually does - not whether they speak, but when they look up, when they write, when they stop. Afterwards, decide which difference in this topic best fits each pupil, and what you would want to find out next to check yourself.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: Write 300-350 words on one pupil you have actually seen in a classroom, taught by you or by someone else. Change the name. Describe what the pupil did, as neutrally as you can. Then give two competing explanations drawn from this topic, and weigh them: what speaks for each, what speaks against, and what evidence would settle it. End with the first thing you would try, and what would tell you within a fortnight that you had chosen wrongly. Mini-rubric Criterion What a strong answer shows Observation before judgement The description reports behaviour rather than assigning a label. Competing explanations weighed Two explanations are genuinely tested against the evidence and against each other, not listed. (Analyze) Practicality The proposed step is workable for one teacher with a full class. Plain, accurate writing Terms used correctly; the pupil is described with respect; within the word count.

Vosniadou, S. (2001). How children learn. Educational Practices Series No. 7. International Academy of Education / UNESCO IBE. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED455955 Seifert, K., & Sutton, R. (2009). Educational Psychology (2nd ed.), Chapters 2 and 6. University of Manitoba. CC BY. https://open.umn.edu/opentextbooks/textbooks/educational-psychology

Miss Farah plans a Class 8 lesson on the water cycle. She has forty minutes and fifty-two pupils. Her first plan is the one she was taught: define evaporation, condensation, precipitation and collection; draw the diagram on the board; pupils copy it; set the textbook questions for homework. She teaches it. The copying is immaculate. The homework, next morning, is not: a third of the class have reproduced the diagram and answered nothing, and several have labelled the arrows in the wrong direction while copying them correctly from their own notebooks. Nobody misbehaved. Nobody was absent. By every visible measure the lesson went well, and almost nothing was learnt. The question this topic asks is what Miss Farah should change - and how she could know whether the change worked. textbook.com.pk

Planning is where most psychological ideas do their quiet work, and where Miss Farah's lesson went wrong before she opened her mouth. Start from what they know. The water cycle is not new to pupils who have watched a puddle dry and rain fall. A plan that begins with four definitions throws away everything they could have attached the lesson to. Respect the limits of attention. Four new terms in the first five minutes is more than working memory will hold while also copying a diagram. Copying and understanding compete for the same limited capacity, which is why the notebooks can be perfect and the understanding absent (Seifert & Sutton, 2009). Show the move before you ask for it. A worked example, done aloud with the reasoning visible, costs five minutes and saves the exercise. Miss Farah asked pupils to explain the cycle without ever modelling an explanation. Decide the one thing. With forty minutes and fifty-two pupils, a plan that tries to cover everything covers nothing. What must they be able to do by the bell that they could not do at the start?
documents.s: Planning: choosing method, sequence and pace

documents.t: Management is usually taught as a set of rules and consequences. That is half of it, and the less useful half. Most of what looks like misbehaviour is a pupil doing something rational given how the lesson feels from their seat. A pupil who cannot start the work and does not want that noticed will find something else to do. A pupil who finished six minutes ago will too. In Topic 1.3 these were Sana and Kiran; from the front they look like the same discipline problem and they are not. So the first management question is not "what is the consequence?" but "what is this behaviour getting them, and what would make it unnecessary?" A task pitched where pupils can start it removes more disruption than any rule. The second is that a classroom is a psychological environment. Whether it is safe to be wrong out loud decides whether anyone will answer a question honestly. A teacher who greets a wrong answer with visible impatience will, within a fortnight, have a class that only volunteers when certain - and will have lost the main instrument for finding out what they know.
documents.s: Classroom management as a psychological task, not only a disciplinary one

documents.t: Assessment in most classrooms means marking, and marking means a number at the end. Psychology suggests two corrections. Assessment is for finding out, and it is most useful while you can still act on it. A test at the end of the chapter tells you what to write in the register. Three questions in the middle of the lesson tell you whether to carry on. Miss Farah discovered the failure the next morning, which was one day too late and fifty-two pupils too wide. Feedback works when it tells the pupil what to do next. A mark tells a pupil where they stand and nothing else; worse, once a mark is attached, most pupils stop reading anything else on the page. Feedback that says which step went wrong, and what to try, is the part that changes performance (Vosniadou, 2001). There is also the matter of what assessment teaches pupils to value. If the test rewards reproducing a diagram, pupils will become excellent at reproducing diagrams. Miss Farah's class did exactly what her assessment asked of them.
documents.s: Assessment and feedback informed by psychology

documents.t: The four steps in the figure above are a cycle, and the fourth is the one that gets skipped. Reflection here does not mean feeling bad about a lesson. It means treating your own classroom as the place where claims get tested - the loop from Topic 1.2, run on yourself. What did I expect? What happened? Which explanation fits, and what would separate it from the rival explanation? Miss Farah's second attempt is a small piece of research. She starts from a puddle in the school yard, models one explanation aloud, cuts the four terms to two, and asks three ungraded questions with ten minutes left. If more pupils can explain the cycle in their own words than last time, she has learnt something about her own teaching. If not, she has learnt something too. This is also a professional obligation rather than a personal virtue: Continuous Professional Development is one of Pakistan's National Professional Standards for Teachers, and it asks for exactly this habit of examining and improving one's own practice (Khizar et al., 2019). The misconception to clear now. Reflection is widely taken to mean writing a diary entry after a difficult lesson - a mood, recorded. On that reading it is honest but useless, because nothing about it could come out unexpectedly. Useful reflection has a prediction in it. "I think they copied without understanding because the terms came before the example" can be wrong, and checking it is what makes the next lesson better. textbook.com.pk
documents.s: The reflective teacher: using evidence to improve one's own practice

documents.t: In groups of four, about 30 minutes. You have forty minutes, fifty-two pupils, a blackboard, and no projector. Decide the one thing pupils must be able to do by the bell. Write it as something they do, not something they know. Sketch the lesson in four moves, and mark where the worked example goes and why it goes there. Write the three questions you would ask with ten minutes left, and say what answer would tell you to slow down. Name one thing you have deliberately left out, and defend leaving it out. Swap plans with another group. Their job is to find the place where a pupil like Sana, from Topic 1.3, would fall out of your lesson.

Name the four steps of the plan-teach-assess-reflect cycle. (Remember) Explain why a class can produce perfect notebooks and still not understand the lesson. (Understand) Why does the text say a mark can get in the way of feedback? (Understand) A teacher says "my class is badly behaved in the last ten minutes." Give two explanations drawn from this topic and say what you would observe to choose between them. (Apply) Rewrite this reflection so that it could turn out to be wrong: "The lesson did not go well. The pupils were not interested. I will try to make it more interesting next time." (Apply)

Psychological ideas shape a teacher's work long before any pupil misbehaves. Planning decides whether a lesson has anything to attach to, whether it exceeds the limits of attention, and whether the move is modelled before it is demanded. Management is better read as a question about what a behaviour is getting a pupil than as a question about consequences, and the emotional climate of a room decides whether a teacher can find out what pupils know. Assessment is most useful while there is still time to act on it, and feedback works when it names the next step rather than the position. Reflection completes the cycle, and it is only useful when it contains something that could be shown to be wrong.

I can name the four steps of the cycle and say which is most often skipped. I can explain why copying and understanding compete, in terms of attention. I can explain the difference between a mark and feedback that changes performance. I can turn a vague reflection into one that makes a checkable prediction.

Ask to see a lesson plan, then watch that lesson. Afterwards, write down the one thing the teacher wanted pupils to be able to do, and how they found out whether it had happened. If they found out after the lesson rather than during it, work out where in the forty minutes a three-question check could have gone, and what it would have cost them.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: Write 350-400 words analysing the Miss Farah episode at the top of this topic. Your answer must do three things. First, explain what went wrong using at least two ideas from this unit, drawn from more than one topic. Second, weigh the ideas against each other - which best explains the wrong-direction arrows in particular, and what makes you prefer it? Third, set out her second attempt, including the evidence she would gather and the result that would tell her she was still wrong. Mini-rubric Criterion What a strong answer shows Range across the unit Draws on ideas from at least two topics and connects them rather than listing them. Analysis of competing causes Explains the specific evidence - the reversed arrows - and argues why one cause fits it better than another. (Analyze) Evaluation of the redesign The second attempt is judged by what it would reveal, including what would count as failure. (Evaluate) Practicality and plain writing Workable with fifty-two pupils and no equipment; terms used correctly; within the word count.

Educational Psychology (2nd ed.), Chapters 8 and 11. University of Manitoba. CC BY. https://open.umn.edu/opentextbooks/textbooks/educational-psychology Khizar, A., Anwar, M. N., & Malik, M. A.
