Bulletin of Education and Research, 41(3), 101-118. https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/EJ1244705.pdf

Educational psychology studies mind and behaviour in educational settings, asking its questions from the teacher's side of the desk. Its scope is the learner, the learning process and the learning situation; a teacher who reaches for only one of the three will misread most classrooms. It is a scientific study because its claims are framed so evidence could count against them, and gathered through observation, experiment and case study. Psychology and education feed each other. Psychology supplies tested theories, methods and a precise language for describing learners. Classrooms supply the conditions, the problems and the corrections that laboratories cannot. Because the field is applied, a finding is judged by whether it survives real conditions, and acting on one carries an ethical weight, since pupils cannot opt out. Learners in a single room differ in readiness and prior knowledge, in motivation and interest, and in language and home support. Each difference looks similar from the front of the class, each is routinely collapsed into the word "ability", and each calls for a different response. Those ideas reach a teacher's work through planning, management, assessment and reflection. Planning decides whether a lesson has anything to attach to and whether it exceeds attention. Management is better read as a question about what a behaviour gets a pupil. Assessment is most useful while there is still time to act on it, and feedback works when it names the next step. Reflection closes the cycle, and earns its place only when it makes a prediction that could turn out to be wrong.

Educational psychology is best described as the study of: (Remember) a) mental illness in school-age children b) mind and behaviour in educational settings c) the history of school systems d) methods of school administration Which of these is not one of the three parts of the scope of educational psychology? (Remember) a) the learner b) the learning process c) the learning situation d) the examination board "Educational psychology is just common sense." The strongest objection to this claim is that: (Understand) a) common sense is usually wrong b) common sense offers contradictory answers and cannot be checked c) psychology uses technical terms d) teachers have no time for common sense A teacher teaches the same topic to two similar sections, changing only the order of the examples, and compares the test results. This is closest to: (Remember) a) a case study b) an experiment c) systematic observation d) a survey The main thing a classroom gives psychology that a laboratory cannot is: (Understand) a) more participants b) faster results c) real conditions in which a finding may fail d) better equipment Calling educational psychology an applied field means chiefly that: (Understand) a) it is easier than pure psychology b) it is judged partly by whether its findings can be acted on c) it does not use experiments d) it applies only to primary schools A pupil copies the board perfectly and cannot do the exercise alone. The most likely explanation offered in this unit is: (Apply) a) the pupil is lazy b) the pupil lacks the prior knowledge the lesson assumes c) the pupil dislikes the teacher d) the pupil has poor handwriting A pupil who finishes early and then disturbs others is best understood as: (Apply) a) badly behaved b) under-motivated by that particular task c) unable to learn d) in need of a stricter rule According to this unit, feedback changes performance mainly when it: (Understand) a) is given as a mark out of ten b) is given in front of the class c) tells the pupil what to do next d) is written in red Which reflection is most useful by this unit's standard? (Apply) a) "The lesson went badly and I felt discouraged." b) "The pupils were not interested today." c) "They copied without understanding, I think because the terms came before the example." d) "I will try harder to make the next lesson interesting."

Answer each in two to four sentences. Define educational psychology and name the three parts of its scope. (Remember) Give one question a general psychologist and one question an educational psychologist might each ask about memory. (Understand) Name the three ways of gathering evidence described in Topic 1.1 and state one limit of each. (Understand) Explain what psychology contributes to education, under three headings. (Understand) Explain what education contributes back to psychology, with one example. (Understand) A trainer reports that testing helps pupils remember. Write the two questions you would ask before changing your own teaching. (Apply) Explain why a pupil who has failed repeatedly may stop trying, and why "lazy" is a poor description of this. (Understand) A pupil speaks confidently in Sindhi and answers poorly on an English written test. Give two explanations and say what would tell them apart. (Apply) Explain why copying a diagram and understanding it can compete with each other. (Understand) Rewrite this so it could be shown to be wrong: "My class is weak in mathematics." (Apply)

Answer each in 300-400 words. "Educational psychology is common sense dressed up in technical language." Set out the strongest case for this claim, then answer it, using the idea of scientific study from Topic 1.1. (Analyze) Three teachers hear the same research finding. One ignores it, one adopts it wholesale, and one changes a single thing and checks. Analyse what each has understood and misunderstood about the relationship between psychology and education. (Analyze) Three pupils in one class have all stopped participating, for three different reasons. Explain how a teacher could tell the reasons apart, and why acting on the wrong one may make matters worse. (Analyze) A lesson produces immaculate notebooks and almost no understanding. Analyse what went wrong using ideas from at least two topics of this unit, and set out a redesigned lesson together with the evidence you would gather to judge it. (Evaluate) "A teacher's own classroom is the place where claims about learning get tested." Evaluate this statement. Consider what a single teacher can and cannot establish, and what would make their evidence worth more than an anecdote. (Evaluate)

b - the definition used throughout the unit; the field is defined by its setting and its question, not by clinical work. d - the examination board belongs to the system around a school, not to the three-part scope. b - the objection is not that common sense is wrong but that it is unfalsifiable, since some proverb predicts every outcome. b - one variable changed on purpose, with a comparison; that is an experiment however small. c - laboratories can supply participants and equipment; only real classrooms supply the conditions under which a finding may fail. b - applied means aimed at improving something, so usefulness is part of how it is judged. b - copying is possible without the prior knowledge the lesson assumes; a and c are verdicts rather than explanations. b - motivation is task-specific; the same behaviour from a failing pupil would have the opposite cause. c - a mark reports position; feedback that names the next step is what alters performance. c - it contains a prediction that could turn out to be wrong; the others record a mood or an intention.

Award marks for the substance below, not for matching wording. The study of mind and behaviour in educational settings (1), plus the learner, the learning process and the learning situation (1 for all three). One question about how memory works in general (1); one asked from the teacher's side, about what to do differently as a result (1). Observation, experiment, case study (1). One fair limit each, for example an unusual day, a result that may not hold elsewhere, a single case (1). Tested theories; methods for finding things out; a precise language for describing learners (2, one mark for two headings, two for all three with examples). Real conditions, problems laboratories do not pose, and corrections when findings fail (1), with a concrete example (1). Any two of: what exactly does the claim state, under what conditions, do those conditions hold in my class, what would count as it failing (1 each). Repeated failure makes trying costly, because failing visibly is worse than not trying (1); "lazy" describes the behaviour as a trait rather than as a response to a situation (1). Two plausible explanations, for example a language cost versus an understanding gap (1); a way to separate them, such as allowing the answer in another form or language (1). Both draw on the same limited attention, so effort spent reproducing the diagram is not available for making sense of it (2). Any rewriting that names a specific, checkable claim, for example "most of my class cannot convert an improper fraction, which I will check with five items on Monday" (2).

For the teacher educator. The course guide allots Weeks 1 and 2 to this chapter, with the second week ending in discussion and a short assessment.
documents.s: Introduction to Educational Psychology - teacher notes

documents.t: The course guide specifies interactive lecture with Pakistani classroom examples, and small-group discussion and case analysis. Both suit this unit, but the order matters. Lead with the case, not the definition. Every topic opens with a classroom situation for a reason. Trainees who meet "educational psychology is the scientific study of..." first will memorise it and learn nothing. Trainees who have spent four minutes arguing about why Ayesha can halve a roti but not a fraction will absorb the definition as an answer to a question they now have. Use their own schooling as data. This is the one topic in the programme where every trainee has twelve years of first-hand evidence. Ask what their own teachers assumed about how learning works, and what those assumptions cost them. It is usually a livelier discussion than the reading. Protect the disagreements. The Topic 1.1 sorting activity is designed to produce arguments about which part of the scope a question belongs to. Do not resolve them. The point is that the three overlap and that a teacher must hold all three; a tidy set of correct assignments would destroy the lesson.

Session Focus Leave time for Week 1, first session Topic 1.1 - what the field is, its scope, its methods the sorting activity in full; it anchors the rest Week 1, second session Topic 1.2 - the two-way relationship, applied character the three-teachers role play Week 2, first session Topic 1.3 - learner differences the three-pupils activity; expect this to overrun Week 2, second session Topic 1.4 - planning, management, assessment, reflection rebuilding Miss Farah's lesson, then the short assessment If a session is lost, compress Topic 1.2's role play rather than Topic 1.3's activity. Trainees can recover the two-way relationship from reading; they rarely recover the distinction between Sana, Kiran and Hina without arguing it through aloud.

"This is just common sense." Do not argue it down. Write two contradictory proverbs on the board - "practice makes perfect" and "you either have a gift for it or you do not" - and ask which one common sense endorses. The point lands better than any defence of the discipline. "Researchers discover, teachers apply." This survives most of the reading. It is best broken by Mrs Naz in Topic 1.2: she implemented faithfully and it failed. Ask what she should have done instead, and trainees will invent the feedback loop themselves. "Ability explains it." The most stubborn one, because it is how most trainees were described at school. Expect resistance when you suggest that "weak" is a prediction rather than a description. The three-pupils activity is the lever: once a group has proposed three different next steps for three pupils on the same staff-room list, the single label is visibly useless. "Reflection means writing how the lesson felt." Address this directly in Topic 1.4 by asking the class to make one of their own reflections falsifiable. Most first attempts still contain no prediction; the second attempt usually does.
documents.s: Misconceptions to expect, and how to handle them

documents.t: Several trainees will be more fluent in Sindhi than in English, which makes Topic 1.3 unusually delicate: you are teaching about language cost to a group experiencing it. Let the discussion work in whichever language carries the argument, and ask for the written summative in the language of assessment. Naming this openly, once, tends to improve participation for the rest of the unit.

The course guide's practical component for this chapter is a discussion task. The version used here: each trainee brings one remembered lesson - their own, from school - in which they genuinely learnt something, and one in which they did not. In pairs, they work out what differed. Collect the factors on the board and sort them into the three parts of the scope from Topic 1.1. Two things reliably emerge: the list is dominated by the learning situation rather than by the learner, and almost nobody names ability. That is the unit's argument, produced by the class rather than asserted by you. Allow twenty-five minutes. It works best at the end of Week 1, after Topic 1.1 and before Topic 1.3.

The unit's formative work sits in each topic's Check your understanding block; across the four topics that is twenty items, comfortably above the five-to-eight floor the pipeline expects for a unit. The unit-assessment page carries the graded bank, with worked responses and rubrics in its final bounded section. The guide's "short assessment" at the end of Week 2 is best served by the Topic 1.4 summative task, which requires trainees to draw on at least two topics and so functions as a unit-level check rather than a topic-level one.

This course equips prospective teachers with a grounded understanding of the teaching profession as a dynamic, ethical, and evolving field of practice - professional ethics and codes of conduct, national and global professional standards, effective and reflective practice, and continuous professional development.

Assessment follows the GECE default: 60% summative / 40% formative (Constitution Art. III.7). This course's guide does not specify a course-wide breakdown of teaching strategies or practical work beyond what each unit's own topics cover - see each unit's Teacher Notes for the strategies used to teach it.
Recommended sources from the course guide are listed for scope and further reading only; they are never reproduced as content.

Before you can grow as a teacher, it helps to be clear about what teaching actually asks of you. This unit works through that question in four short topics. Each topic is a complete learning cycle: it opens with a real classroom situation, explains the ideas, gives you an activity, checks your understanding, and ends with a task you can try on your practicum.

By the end of this unit you should be able to: Define a profession and name the four features that separate it from an ordinary occupation, and use them to judge whether a described job is a profession. Explain the difference between professionalism in teaching and professionalisation of teaching, and place teaching in a comparative view alongside other professions. Describe the shift from an industrial model of teaching to inquiry-based professionalism, and apply that lens to a described lesson. Explain the four dimensions of teacher professionalism and use them to analyse a described teacher's practice. Describe how teacher identity develops through reflection and is shaped by personal beliefs and by the social and policy context, and begin reflecting on your own.

None beyond HSC-level general study skills. This is the opening unit of the course and of the semester; you are not assumed to know any education theory. You are assumed to have been a school student yourself - that experience is a starting point for several of the topics.

Topic 1.1 - What makes teaching a profession Topic 1.2 - From an industrial model to inquiry-based teaching Topic 1.3 - The four dimensions of teacher professionalism Topic 1.4 - Becoming a teacher: developing your identity

Work through the topics in order. Topic 1.3 uses the ideas from 1.1, and Topic 1.4 assumes you have met the four dimensions. Do the activity and the "Check your understanding" questions before you move on. They are not graded; they show you which ideas are still shaky. Keep your Topic 1.4 reflection. You will add to it through the course and return to it in Unit 6 when you build a professional development plan. After the four topics, the unit assessment page has a full question bank with answers and marking guidance so you can test yourself.

textbook.com.pk A parent in a village in interior Sindh comes to the government primary school to enrol a child. She asks the new teacher a fair question: "You studied for two years to do this. The shopkeeper next door started selling on the day he opened. Why does teaching need all that training?" It is a good question, and the honest answer is not "because the rules say so". The answer is that teaching is a profession, and a profession is a particular kind of work with particular demands. This topic sets out what that word means and why it applies to teaching.

Not every job is a profession. In everyday speech people sometimes call any respectable, salaried job "a profession", but the word has a narrower meaning. A profession is an occupation built on a body of specialised knowledge, entered only after an extended period of training, governed by a shared code of conduct, and held accountable to a wider community of practitioners - not only to an employer. A professional is a member of such an occupation who is expected to use judgement, keep learning, and act in the interest of the people they serve even when no one is watching. Carr (2000) argues that this last part - acting for the good of others as a matter of principle, not just following instructions - is central to what "professional" means in teaching. Common misconception - "a profession just means a respectable, well-paid job." Pay and status are not the test. Some well-paid jobs are not professions, and some modestly paid ones are. The test is the four features below.

Four features are usually used to tell a profession apart from an ordinary occupation: Specialised knowledge - a body of knowledge specific to the work that outsiders do not have. Extended training and a qualification - you cannot enter simply by being hired; you must complete a recognised course of study and be certified. A code of conduct - shared standards of ethical behaviour that members agree to follow. Accountability to a professional community - a body of peers, an association, or a regulator that can judge your practice, not only your employer. Worked example. Take the parent's three jobs and check each against the four features. The shopkeeper needs no qualification to start, follows no shared written code, and answers only to the owner - no feature is clearly met, so this is an occupation. The doctor studied for years, belongs to a council that can suspend a licence, follows a medical code of ethics, and uses trained judgement about each patient - all four features are met. The teacher is in the same position as the doctor: subject and pedagogical study, a certified B.Ed route, codes of ethical conduct, and answerability to professional standards bodies as well as to a head teacher. Teaching meets all four features. Some jobs sit in between and are worth arguing about - a pharmacist's assistant, a paramedic, a draughtsman. When you are unsure, name the feature that is only partly met; that is usually where the disagreement is.
documents.s: Features that distinguish a profession from an occupation

documents.t: Two similar-sounding ideas are easy to confuse. Professionalism in teaching is about how one teacher conducts themselves day to day - their skill, their ethics, their judgement, their willingness to keep improving. Professionalisation of teaching is a slower, collective process: the way teaching as a field has built its own training routes, licensing, standards, and associations, in the way that medicine and law did earlier. The two are linked but separate. A teacher can show strong personal professionalism even in a system where professionalisation is still developing. Demirkasımoğlu (2010), reviewing how different writers define teacher professionalism, notes that some accounts stress the individual teacher's expertise and autonomy while others stress the collective structures - standards, bodies, accountability. Both senses are in normal use; keep them apart when you write and talk about the profession. Pakistan's move toward the National Professional Standards for Teachers (Unit 4) is part of the professionalisation process.
documents.s: Professionalism in teaching versus professionalisation of teaching

documents.t: Set against medicine, law, or engineering, teaching is sometimes called a "semi-profession": its training route was historically shorter, its practitioners have had less collective control over entry to the field, and much of the work is done in public institutions under close administrative supervision. Demirkasımoğlu (2010) shows there is no single agreed definition of teacher professionalism - some writers emphasise autonomy and expertise, others accountability and service. The comparison is not a ranking. It is useful because it points to the parts of professional status that teaching is still building: a longer and more rigorous training route, stronger professional bodies, and more room for teachers to exercise informed judgement. Treat "semi-profession" as a description of work in progress, not an insult. textbook.com.pk
documents.s: Comparative perspective: teaching and other professions

documents.t: Work in pairs. About 20 minutes. Pick three jobs you know well - for example a government-school teacher, a shopkeeper, and a doctor at a Rural Health Centre. Draw a table with the three jobs as columns and the four features of a profession as rows. In each cell write yes, no, or partly, with one reason. Decide: which job is clearly a profession? Which is clearly not? Which one do you and your partner disagree about - and what evidence would settle it? Join another pair, compare tables, and agree on one job that is genuinely hard to classify and the feature that makes it hard. Bring that to the whole class.

Define a profession in one sentence, and name its four distinguishing features. (Remember) Give one example of a well-paid job that is not a profession, and one modestly paid job that is. Explain each choice using the four features. (Understand) A colleague says, "Teaching became a profession the day the government issued standards for it." Use the distinction between professionalism and professionalisation to explain what is right and what is wrong in that statement. (Apply) Teaching is sometimes called a "semi-profession". Name two things teaching is still building toward fuller professional status, and say why each one matters. (Apply)

A profession is defined by specialised knowledge, extended training and certification, a shared code of conduct, and accountability to a professional community - not by pay or prestige. Teaching meets all four features. Professionalism is how an individual teacher acts; professionalisation is how the field organises itself; the two develop at different speeds. Compared with older professions, teaching is still strengthening its training route, its professional bodies, and the room it gives teachers to use judgement.

I can define a profession and name its four distinguishing features. I can use the four features to judge whether a described job is a profession, an occupation, or a hard-to-classify case. I can explain the difference between professionalism in teaching and professionalisation of teaching, with an example of each. I can explain why teaching is sometimes called a "semi-profession" without treating that as an insult.

Ask your cooperating teacher which of the four features of a profession they feel most strongly in their daily work, and which they feel least. Note their answer with one concrete example they give, and bring it to the next session.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: Choose any job that is not teaching and that you know well. In about 250–300 words, judge it against the four features of a profession. For each feature say whether the job shows it clearly, partly, or not at all, and give a specific reason. End with a one-sentence verdict: profession, occupation, or borderline - and why. Mini-rubric (10 marks) Criterion Strong Adequate Weak All four features applied to the chosen job (4) Each feature judged with a specific, job-based reason Most features judged; some reasons vague Features defined but not applied Verdict justified (4) Verdict follows clearly from the four judgements; borderline cases named as such (Analyze) Verdict stated with partial support Verdict asserted with no link to the analysis Plain, accurate use of terms (2) Terms used correctly and consistently Minor slips Key terms confused

Carr, D. (2000). Professionalism and ethics in teaching. Routledge. Demirkasımoğlu, N. (2010). Defining "teacher professionalism" from different perspectives. Procedia - Social and Behavioral Sciences, 9, 2047–2051. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sbspro.2010.12.444

textbook.com.pk Two teachers in the same school both teach fractions to Class 5 on the same day. The first follows the textbook exactly, in order, at the planned pace. The class is quiet, the board is neat, and the period ends on time. The second starts the same way, but partway through notices that most of the class is adding the denominators. She stops, puts three wrong answers on the board without names, and asks the class what rule would produce each one. The lesson runs five minutes over. Both lessons are "covered". Only one of them responded to what the pupils were actually thinking. This topic is about the difference between those two pictures of teaching.

Early twentieth-century thinking about schooling borrowed heavily from factory management. On this industrial view, a school is like a plant: pupils are raw material, the curriculum is a fixed production line, and the teacher's job is to deliver it efficiently, keep the class under control, and comply with set procedures. Success is measured by covering the syllabus on time. The industrial model is not simply "bad teaching". It brought real gains - mass schooling, predictable coverage, clear routines - and parts of it are still useful. A teacher who wastes no time and keeps an orderly room is doing something the industrial model valued. The problem is what it leaves out: it treats every class as interchangeable and gives the teacher little reason to ask why a particular group of pupils is or is not learning. Worked example. A teacher marks the same end-of-unit test with the same key every year, in the same order, and never asks why particular questions are missed. The work is orderly and efficient. But nothing in the routine turns the pattern of wrong answers into a change in teaching. That is the industrial model doing exactly what it was designed to do.

Over recent decades the field has moved toward a different picture, often called inquiry-based professionalism: teaching as a practice in which the teacher studies their own classroom, reflects on what worked and why, and adjusts based on evidence rather than habit alone. The learner, not the syllabus, is at the centre. Hargreaves (2000) describes teacher professionalism as passing through four "ages": a pre-professional age in which teaching was seen as simple work learned by watching; an age of the autonomous professional in which teachers won the right to make their own classroom decisions but often worked alone; an age of the collegial professional in which teachers plan, observe, and solve problems together; and a fourth, post-professional or postmodern age in which teachers face competing pressures - greater public accountability, faster change, more stakeholders - and need inquiry and collaboration to cope. The point is not that the industrial model has vanished. It is that professional expectations now include noticing, reflecting, and adjusting. Common misconception - "inquiry-based teaching just means group work and less structure." It is not about a seating plan or about relaxing rules. A tightly run, teacher-led lesson can be fully inquiry-based if the teacher is watching how pupils think and changing the next step in response. The defining move is noticing and adjusting on evidence, not the furniture. textbook.com.pk

Work individually, then discuss. About 25 minutes. Think of one lesson you have seen taught, or plan one on a topic you know well. Describe it as an industrial lesson: fixed procedure, cover the point on time, keep the class quiet, mark against a fixed key. Describe the same lesson as an inquiry-based lesson: the teacher watches how pupils are thinking, notices a common mistake, and changes the next step in response. Name one concrete change that would move the industrial version toward the inquiry-based one. It must be something a teacher could actually do next week - not "care more". In groups of four, read out your one change. Pick the change that would make the biggest difference for the least effort, and be ready to say why.
documents.s: Activity: The same lesson, two ways

documents.t: Name two things the industrial model of teaching values, and one important thing it leaves out. (Remember / Understand) In two or three sentences, explain what "inquiry-based professionalism" means, using the phrase noticing and adjusting. (Understand) A teacher runs a strict, silent, teacher-led classroom. A visitor says this cannot be inquiry-based teaching. Explain why the visitor might be wrong. (Apply) Give one concrete, do-able change that would move a described lesson toward inquiry-based professionalism, and explain why it would help. (Apply)

Ideas about teaching have shifted from an industrial model - efficiency, control, compliance, covering the syllabus - toward inquiry-based professionalism, in which the teacher notices how pupils are thinking and adjusts on evidence. Hargreaves' "four ages" show this as a long change from working alone toward working collegially and inquiringly, not a simple before-and-after. Both models still appear in real schools; the inquiry stance is a habit of noticing and adjusting, not a particular seating arrangement.

I can describe the industrial model of teaching and name what it values and what it leaves out. I can explain inquiry-based professionalism as noticing and adjusting on evidence. I can tell the difference between "inquiry-based" and "unstructured", and explain why a strict classroom can still be inquiry-based. I can take a described lesson and name one realistic change that makes it more inquiry-based.

Watch any ten minutes of a lesson. Note one moment that looked "industrial" (a fixed routine carried out regardless of pupil response) and one moment that looked "inquiry-based" (the teacher changed something because of what a pupil said or did). Do not judge the teacher - you are practising the lens, not rating a person. Bring both notes.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: Take a lesson you know and write two short descriptions of it, about 150 words each: one industrial, one inquiry-based. Then, in a final paragraph, name one realistic change that moves the industrial version toward the inquiry-based one and explain, using the idea of noticing and adjusting, why it would help learning. Mini-rubric (10 marks) Criterion Strong Adequate Weak Two contrasting descriptions of the same lesson (4) Both clearly recognisable; the difference is noticing and adjusting, not just tone Descriptions differ but the key contrast is blurred One description only, or the two are near-identical The proposed change (4) Specific, do-able next week, and its effect on learning is explained (Analyze) Named but generic ("be more flexible") Missing or unrelated to the descriptions Plain, accurate use of terms (2) "Industrial" and "inquiry-based" used correctly Minor slips Terms confused
Hargreaves, A. (2000). Four ages of professionalism and professional learning. Teachers and Teaching, 6(2), 151–182. https://doi.org/10.1080/713698714

textbook.com.pk A secondary-school science teacher in Hyderabad joins a national science-teachers' association. Through it she gets a termly journal, an annual conference, and a short written code the association asks members to follow - be fair in assessment, keep learning, do not misrepresent results. Her head teacher did not require any of this. She did it because it is part of what she thinks being a professional teacher means. Her choice touches all four dimensions of teacher professionalism. This topic sets out those four and how they fit together.

The first dimension is a distinct knowledge base: knowledge of the subject, knowledge of how learners of a given age develop, and pedagogical content knowledge - knowing the best ways to represent a particular topic so that particular learners understand it. Hurst and Reding (2009) describe this knowledge as something built through a recognised programme of study and continued reading, not picked up casually on the job. Worked example. Knowing Urdu grammar is subject knowledge. Knowing that Class 3 pupils in a multi-grade room grasp tenses faster through short spoken drills than through written rules is pedagogical content knowledge - and building that kind of knowledge is a main purpose of a B.Ed programme.

The second dimension is a shared code of conduct: agreed standards for how a teacher behaves toward pupils, colleagues, parents, and the wider community - fairness in assessment, honesty, protecting pupils from harm, respecting confidentiality. Carr (2000) argues that teaching is a fundamentally ethical practice, because almost every classroom decision affects the interests and development of children. A teacher does not follow the code because they are watched; they follow it because the work is ethical by nature. Unit 2 examines these codes and ethical frameworks in detail.
documents.s: A professional code of conduct and ethical behaviour

documents.t: The third dimension has three parts that must be held in balance: Accountability - answering for the quality of your work to pupils, parents, employers, and standards bodies. Autonomy - the room to use professional judgement about how to teach a class, rather than following a rigid script. Collegiality - working with, learning from, and being answerable to fellow teachers. Hargreaves (2000) shows how the weight given to these three has shifted across the "ages" of professionalism - from strong autonomy but little collegiality, toward more collaboration and, lately, much stronger external accountability. The practical point for you is the balance. Too much accountability with no autonomy pushes teaching back toward the industrial model. Too much autonomy with no collegiality leaves each teacher isolated and unchecked. Professional practice needs all three at once. Common misconception - "professionalism is mainly dress, punctuality, and discipline." Those matter, and a professional keeps them, but they are not the centre. The centre is knowledge, ethical judgement, the accountability–autonomy–collegiality balance, and continuing to learn.

The fourth dimension is organised structure. Associations represent members and often maintain a code; accreditation bodies judge whether a training programme or institution meets agreed standards. Demirkasımoğlu (2010) treats the presence of such bodies as one of the markers writers use when they call an occupation a profession. In Pakistan, teacher-education programmes are accredited against national criteria, and bodies such as the National Accreditation Council for Teacher Education set expectations for how teachers are prepared. Belonging to these structures is part of what makes teaching a profession rather than a private arrangement between a worker and an employer. textbook.com.pk
documents.s: The role of professional associations and accreditation bodies

documents.t: Work in groups of three or four. About 15 minutes. Professional practice needs accountability, autonomy, and collegiality together. For each situation below, decide which of the three is missing, and say one thing a school could do about it. A teacher is told exactly what to say in every lesson and is checked daily against the script. A teacher plans alone, never sees another teacher teach, and never has their marking looked at by anyone. A teacher is free to teach however they like, and no one ever asks what their pupils have learned. Then write one more situation of your own in which two of the three are missing, and swap it with another group to solve.

Name the four dimensions of teacher professionalism. (Remember) Give one example of pedagogical content knowledge that is not just subject knowledge, set in a Pakistani classroom. (Apply) Explain, with a short example, why accountability, autonomy, and collegiality have to be held in balance rather than maximised one at a time. (Understand / Apply) A teacher keeps perfect attendance, dresses smartly, and maintains strict discipline, but marks unfairly and never updates her methods. Which dimensions is she meeting, and which is she failing? (Apply)

Teacher professionalism has four dimensions: a specialised knowledge base built through training; a shared ethical code of conduct; the balance of accountability, autonomy, and collegiality; and organised professional bodies - associations and accreditation. The dimensions work together: strong subject knowledge does not make up for unfair assessment, and autonomy without collegiality leaves a teacher isolated. Judging a teacher's practice means looking across all four, not picking the one that is easiest to see.

I can name and briefly explain the four dimensions of teacher professionalism. I can give an example of pedagogical content knowledge from a real classroom. I can explain why accountability, autonomy, and collegiality must be balanced, using an example of what goes wrong when one is missing. I can look at a described teacher's practice and say which dimensions are strong and which are weak, pointing to specific details.

Ask to see any written code of conduct, professional-standards document, or association membership your cooperating teacher works under. Note one expectation it sets that goes beyond what an employer would demand, and bring it to the next session.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: Your teacher will give you a one-page description of a teacher's classroom practice (real or realistic - for example, a teacher in a Sindh government school). Read it carefully, then write a structured analysis of about 500–700 words that does all three of the following. Dimensions present. Judge the described practice against the four dimensions (specialised knowledge; an ethical code of conduct; the accountability–autonomy–collegiality balance; organised professional bodies). For each dimension say whether the description shows it clearly, partly, or not at all, and point to the specific detail that tells you. One strong, one weak. Identify one dimension that is strong and one that is weak or missing, and justify both with evidence from the text. Industrial or inquiry-based? Using Topic 1.2, decide whether the practice sits closer to the industrial model or to inquiry-based professionalism, supported by at least two specific details. Then propose one realistic change that would strengthen the weak dimension you named, and explain why it would help. Rubric (20 marks) Criterion Excellent (full marks) Adequate (about half) Weak (low marks) Analysis against the four dimensions (6) All four judged; each judgement tied to a specific detail from the description Most dimensions judged; some judgements not evidenced Dimensions listed or defined but not applied One strong, one weak - justified (5) Both clearly identified and justified with evidence (Analyze) Identified but justification thin or one-sided Named without linking to the case Industrial vs inquiry-based judgement (5) Clear position supported by two or more specific details; nuance where the case is mixed Position with one detail, or details vague Assertion with no evidence from the text Proposed change (2) Realistic, specific, tied to the weak dimension Named but generic ("care more") Missing or unrelated Structure and plain, accurate language (2) Organised, clear, terms used correctly Understandable but loosely organised Hard to follow; key terms misused

Hurst, B., & Reding, G. (2009). Professionalism in teaching. Pearson Education. Carr, D. (2000). Professionalism and ethics in teaching. Routledge. Hargreaves, A. (2000). Four ages of professionalism and professional learning. Teachers and Teaching, 6(2), 151–182. https://doi.org/10.1080/713698714 Demirkasımoğlu, N. (2010). Defining "teacher professionalism" from different perspectives. Procedia - Social and Behavioral Sciences, 9, 2047–2051. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sbspro.2010.12.444

textbook.com.pk A trainee grew up in a village in interior Sindh, in a multi-grade primary school with one teacher and few books. He is now on practicum in a well-resourced city school. He notices he keeps expecting pupils to sit silently and copy, the way he was taught - and that this is not what his cooperating teacher does, or what his B.Ed course recommends. That gap between how he was taught and how he now wants to teach is where teacher identity is formed. This topic is about how that identity develops and how to work on it deliberately from the start.

Your teacher identity is your evolving sense of who you are as a teacher - your purposes, your values, and the relationships you want with pupils. Beijaard, Meijer, and Verloop (2004), reviewing research on teacher identity, stress that it is formed in relation to context, not in isolation: the status teachers hold in a society, how they are paid and trusted, the language and cultural background of their pupils, and the national policies and standards they work under all shape what "being a professional teacher" feels like. Worked example. A teacher in an under-resourced rural school in Sindh, working across three grades in one room, is forming a professional identity under very different pressures from a teacher in a well-equipped city school - even though both follow the same national standards. The rural teacher's identity may come to centre on resourcefulness and multi-grade management; the city teacher's on subject depth. Neither is more "professional"; the context has pulled their identities in different directions.
documents.s: The influence of sociocultural and policy context

documents.t: Identity is also shaped from the inside. It is strongly influenced by your own experience as a pupil: the teachers you admired or feared, what you came to believe about how learning happens, and why you chose teaching. Beijaard and colleagues (2004) note that teachers' prior beliefs act as a filter through which new ideas from training are accepted, adapted, or quietly resisted. Two trainees can complete the same course and still teach differently, because they bring different beliefs about what matters.
documents.s: How personal beliefs and values shape teacher identity

documents.t: Identity does not settle once and stay fixed. It keeps developing through reflection - deliberately looking back at your teaching, noticing the gap between what you intended and what happened, and asking what that says about your assumptions. Brookfield (2017) describes the critically reflective teacher as one who examines their practice from several viewpoints - their pupils', their colleagues', the research literature, and their own past - rather than trusting first impressions. Suarez and McGrath (2022), writing for the OECD, similarly treat teacher identity as something that must be actively developed and supported, especially during periods of change, rather than left to form on its own. Common misconception - "reflective practice just means keeping a diary." A diary is a record. Reflection is using that record to find and question an assumption, and to change what you do next. Six dated notes that each name one belief a lesson challenged are reflection; six pages of "today we did fractions, it was fine" are not.
documents.s: Reflection and self-awareness in teacher-identity formation

documents.t: A useful habit from the very start of training is to ask, and keep returning to, one question: who am I becoming as a teacher? Answering it honestly - in a journal, in conversation with a mentor, after a difficult lesson - turns experience into learning instead of letting it pass by. It is itself a professional practice, and it connects directly to the reflective tools you will meet again in Unit 6. textbook.com.pk
documents.s: "Who am I becoming as a teacher?"

documents.t: Individual writing. About 15 minutes. Keep this; you will add to it through the course. Write half a page answering these prompts honestly. It is not marked for "correct" answers. Name one teacher from your own schooling who influenced how you think a class should be run. What did they do? Complete the sentence: "I believe pupils learn best when…" - then give one reason you believe it. Why did you choose teaching? Name one thing about teaching you are not yet sure you can do well. Date the page. You will look back at it in Unit 6 when you build your professional development plan.
documents.s: Activity: First reflection - who am I becoming as a teacher?

documents.t: Define teacher identity in one sentence. (Remember) Give two ways the social or policy context a teacher works in can shape their professional identity, with an example of each. (Understand) Explain, in two or three sentences, why keeping a teaching diary is not the same as reflective practice. (Understand) "Two trainees can finish the same B.Ed course and still teach differently because…" - complete this and link your answer to the idea of prior beliefs acting as a filter. (Apply)

Teacher identity is your developing sense of who you are as a teacher. It is shaped from the outside by sociocultural and policy context - status, trust, pupils' backgrounds, national standards - and from the inside by your own beliefs and values, which filter what you take from training. Identity keeps changing through reflection: examining your practice from several viewpoints and questioning your assumptions, not just recording events. Returning regularly to "who am I becoming as a teacher?" is a professional habit that turns experience into learning.

I can define teacher identity and explain that it develops rather than being fixed. I can give examples of how context and personal beliefs each shape a teacher's identity. I can explain the difference between recording events and reflecting on them. I have written and dated a first reflection on who I am becoming as a teacher.

Ask your cooperating teacher one question: "What is one way you teach now that is different from how you were taught, and what changed your mind?" Write down their answer and one thing it makes you think about your own beliefs.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: In about 300–400 words, analyse one influence on your own developing teacher identity - for example your own schooling, your family's view of teaching, the community you will teach in, or a national policy you have met in this course. Your analysis must: name the influence and describe it concretely; explain how it is shaping the kind of teacher you are becoming - your purposes, values, or the relationships you want with pupils; name one belief it has given you that you want to keep, and one you want to question, and say why. Mini-rubric (10 marks) Criterion Strong Adequate Weak The influence described concretely (3) Specific, real, and clearly relevant to identity Named but thin or generic Vague or not really an identity influence How it shapes the teacher you are becoming (4) Traces a clear line from the influence to purposes/values/relationships (Analyze) Some connection made but under-explained Asserts influence with no reasoning One belief to keep, one to question (3) Both named with honest reasons Both named, reasons thin One or both missing

Beijaard, D., Meijer, P. C., & Verloop, N. (2004). Reconsidering research on teachers' professional identity. Teaching and Teacher Education, 20(2), 107–128. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tate.2003.07.001 Brookfield, S. D. (2017). Becoming a critically reflective teacher (2nd ed.). Jossey-Bass. Suarez, V., & McGrath, J. (2022). Teacher professional identity: How to develop and support it in times of change (OECD Education Working Paper No. 267). OECD Publishing. https://doi.org/10.1787/b19f5af7-en

A profession is defined by specialised knowledge, extended training and certification, a shared code of conduct, and accountability to a professional community - not by pay or prestige. Teaching meets all four features (Topic 1.1). Professionalism (how one teacher acts) and professionalisation (how the field organises itself) are related but different, and develop at different speeds. Against older professions, teaching is still building a longer training route, stronger bodies, and more room for judgement (Topic 1.1). Ideas about teaching have shifted from an industrial model - efficiency, control, compliance, covering the syllabus - toward inquiry-based professionalism, the habit of noticing how pupils think and adjusting on evidence. Hargreaves' "four ages" describe this as a long change, not a simple before-and-after; both models still appear in real schools (Topic 1.2). Teacher professionalism has four dimensions: a specialised knowledge base; a shared ethical code of conduct; the balance of accountability, autonomy, and collegiality; and organised professional bodies. Judging practice means looking across all four (Topic 1.3). Teacher identity is a developing sense of who you are as a teacher. It is shaped by sociocultural and policy context and by personal beliefs that filter what you take from training, and it keeps changing through reflection - examining practice from several viewpoints and questioning assumptions (Topic 1.4).
Every item is tagged with its Bloom level. Work through a section, then check yourself against ## Answers and marking guidance at the end of this page.

Which of these is the best test of whether a job is a profession? (Remember) A) It is respectable and reasonably well paid. B) It rests on specialised knowledge, extended training, a code of conduct, and accountability to a professional community. C) It is done mostly in an office or an institution. D) It requires a uniform and fixed working hours. A shopkeeper trains no one, follows no shared written code, and answers only to the owner. Against the four features of a profession, the shopkeeper's work is best described as: (Understand) A) a profession, because it needs skill. B) a semi-profession. C) an occupation. D) impossible to classify. "Two years of B.Ed study builds knowledge of how particular learners understand particular topics." This is closest to which feature or dimension? (Understand) A) A code of conduct. B) Accountability to a professional community. C) Pedagogical content knowledge within the specialised knowledge base. D) Membership of a professional association. A teacher shows strong personal skill, ethics, and judgement, but works in a system with weak licensing and few professional bodies. This situation best illustrates: (Apply) A) high professionalism with still-developing professionalisation. B) high professionalisation with low professionalism. C) neither professionalism nor professionalisation. D) that the teacher is not really a professional. On the industrial model of teaching, success is measured mainly by: (Remember) A) how well the teacher adjusts to evidence about learning. B) covering the set syllabus on time and keeping order. C) how much pupils collaborate. D) the teacher's membership of an association. A teacher runs a strict, quiet, teacher-led room but stops mid-lesson to address a mistake she notices most pupils making, changing her next step. Her teaching is best described as: (Apply) A) purely industrial, because the room is strict. B) inquiry-based, because she is noticing and adjusting on evidence. C) neither, because inquiry-based teaching needs group work. D) unprofessional, because she departed from her plan. Which set names the three parts of the third dimension of teacher professionalism that must be held in balance? (Remember) A) Efficiency, control, compliance. B) Accountability, autonomy, collegiality. C) Knowledge, ethics, associations. D) Planning, teaching, assessing. A teacher plans alone, is never observed, and never has her marking checked, though she is asked about pupil results. Which part of the third dimension is most clearly missing? (Apply) A) Accountability. B) Autonomy. C) Collegiality. D) Specialised knowledge. Teacher identity, according to the unit, is best described as: (Understand) A) a fixed set of personality traits a teacher is born with. B) a developing sense of who one is as a teacher, shaped by context and beliefs. C) the same thing as a teaching licence. D) decided entirely by national policy. A trainee keeps a page each week that names one belief a lesson challenged and what she will try differently. This practice is best described as: (Apply) A) a diary, which is the same as reflective practice. B) reflective practice, because the record is used to question an assumption and change what comes next. C) not reflection, because it is written down. D) reflection only if a mentor reads it.

In one or two sentences, define a profession and name its four distinguishing features. (Understand) Give one example of a well-paid job that is not a profession and one modestly paid job that is, and justify each using the four features. (Analyze) Explain the difference between professionalism in teaching and professionalisation of teaching, with one example of each. (Understand) Name two things the industrial model of teaching values and one important thing it leaves out. (Understand) A visitor says a strict, silent classroom cannot be inquiry-based. In two or three sentences, explain why the visitor may be wrong. (Analyze) Name the four dimensions of teacher professionalism, and give one classroom example of pedagogical content knowledge that is not merely subject knowledge. (Understand) Explain, with a short example, why accountability, autonomy, and collegiality must be held in balance rather than maximised one at a time. (Analyze) Give two ways the sociocultural or policy context a teacher works in can shape their professional identity. (Understand) Explain in two or three sentences why keeping a teaching diary is not, by itself, reflective practice. (Understand) A teacher keeps perfect attendance, dresses smartly, and maintains strict discipline, but marks unfairly and never updates her methods. Analyse which dimensions of professionalism she is meeting and which she is failing. (Analyze)

Choose any job that is not teaching and that you know well. Evaluate it against the four features of a profession - feature by feature, with specific reasons - and reach a justified verdict of profession, occupation, or borderline. (Evaluate) Using a lesson you know, write a short account of it as an industrial lesson and as an inquiry-based lesson, then argue for one realistic change that would move the first toward the second, explaining its likely effect on learning. (Analyze / Create) You are given a one-page description of a teacher's practice. Analyse it against the four dimensions of teacher professionalism, identify one strong and one weak dimension with evidence, and recommend one change to strengthen the weak one. (Analyze) Analyse one influence on your own developing teacher identity: describe it, explain how it is shaping your purposes and values, and name one belief from it you want to keep and one you want to question. (Analyze) Integrative. You are given a description of a teacher in a Sindh government school. Classify the practice against all four dimensions of professionalism and the industrial-versus-inquiry frame, judge whether this is a "professional" practice overall, and justify your judgement using at least four specific details from the description. (Evaluate)
Use this section to check your own work after you have attempted the questions.

B - the four features are the test; A describes status, C and D describe surface conditions. C - none of the four features is clearly met, so it is an occupation, not a semi-profession. C - knowing how particular learners understand particular topics is pedagogical content knowledge. A - strong individual practice (professionalism) in a system whose collective structures (professionalisation) are still developing. B - the industrial model measures success by timely coverage and order. B - the defining move of inquiry-based teaching is noticing and adjusting on evidence, regardless of how strict the room is. B - accountability, autonomy, and collegiality are the three to balance. C - she is answerable for results (accountability) and plans her own lessons (autonomy), but works with no colleague input, so collegiality is missing. B - identity is developing and shaped by context and beliefs, not fixed or policy-decided. B - using the record to question an assumption and change practice is what makes it reflection rather than a diary.

Model: a profession is an occupation built on specialised knowledge, extended training and certification, a shared code of conduct, and accountability to a professional community. Marks (3): 1 - usable definition; 2 - all four features named. Model: names one well-paid non-profession (e.g. a property dealer - no required qualification, no shared code, no professional body) and one modestly paid profession (e.g. a government primary teacher - trained, certified, code-bound, standards-accountable), with feature-based reasons for each. Marks (4): 1 per example named; 1 per example justified against at least two features. Model: professionalism = how an individual teacher acts (skill, ethics, judgement, learning); professionalisation = how the field builds training routes, licensing, standards, bodies; one example of each. Marks (3): 1 - distinction clear; 1 per apt example. Model: values efficiency/timely coverage and order/control; leaves out responsiveness to how particular pupils are actually learning. Marks (3): 1 per value named; 1 for the omission. Model: inquiry-based teaching is defined by noticing how pupils think and adjusting on evidence, not by seating or noise level; a strict teacher-led lesson can do exactly that. Marks (3): 1 - names the defining move; 2 - applies it to the strict-classroom case. Model: specialised knowledge; ethical code of conduct; accountability–autonomy–collegiality balance; organised professional bodies. PCK example, e.g. teaching tenses to a multi-grade Class 3 through short spoken drills rather than written rules. Marks (4): 2 - all four dimensions; 2 - a genuine PCK example (not just subject knowledge). Model: maximising accountability alone crushes autonomy and returns teaching to the industrial model; maximising autonomy alone with no collegiality leaves a teacher isolated and unchecked; balance keeps judgement and answerability together. Marks (3): 1 - states the balance principle; 2 - an example of what goes wrong when one is over-weighted. Model: any two of - teacher status/trust in society; pay and conditions; pupils' language and cultural background; national policies and standards - each with a brief example. Marks (2): 1 per way with an example. Model: a diary records events; reflection uses the record to surface and question an assumption and to change the next action. Marks (3): 1 - record vs use; 2 - the questioning-an-assumption step. Model: she meets the surface expectations often mistaken for professionalism (punctuality, dress, discipline) but fails the ethical code of conduct (unfair marking) and the specialised-knowledge dimension's expectation of continued learning (never updates methods). Marks (4): 2 - dimensions met, with reasons; 2 - dimensions failed, with reasons.
