documents.t: Analytic rubric (12). Feature-by-feature evaluation (0–4: each of the four features judged with a job-specific reason) · Verdict justified (0–4, Evaluate: verdict follows from the four judgements; borderline named where features are partly met) · Use of terms (0–2) · Structure and clarity (0–2). Analytic rubric (12). Two contrasting accounts of one lesson (0–3: the contrast is noticing-and-adjusting, not tone) · Proposed change (0–5, Analyze/Create: specific, do-able, with a reasoned effect on learning) · Use of the industrial/inquiry terms (0–2) · Clarity (0–2). Analytic rubric (15). Analysis against all four dimensions (0–6: each judged against a specific detail) · One strong, one weak, justified (0–5, Analyze: evidence from the text for both) · Recommended change (0–2: tied to the weak dimension) · Structure and accurate terms (0–2). Analytic rubric (10). Influence described concretely (0–3) · How it shapes purposes and values (0–4, Analyze: a clear line from influence to the teacher being formed) · One belief to keep, one to question, with reasons (0–3). Analytic rubric (20). Classification against all four dimensions (0–6) · Industrial vs inquiry judgement with evidence (0–4) · Overall judgement of "professional" practice (0–6, Evaluate: weighs strengths and weaknesses across the frameworks rather than listing them) · At least four specific details used (0–2) · Structure and clarity (0–2).

This is the opening unit of EFMP-302 and, for most students, the opening unit of the B.Ed. It covers Weeks 1–3. Students arrive with strong everyday opinions about teaching and almost no technical vocabulary for it. The unit's job is to give them that vocabulary - profession, professionalism, professionalisation, the four dimensions, teacher identity - and the habit of examining a case rather than reacting to it. Units 2–4 build directly on the "dimensions" and "identity" material. The unit is built as four topic cycles plus a unit-assessment page: Topic Focus Sub-topics 1.1 What makes teaching a profession U1-01…U1-04 1.2 Industrial model → inquiry-based teaching U1-05, U1-06 1.3 The four dimensions of teacher professionalism U1-07…U1-10 1.4 Becoming a teacher: developing your identity U1-11…U1-14 Each topic is a complete lesson: a real classroom situation, an explanation, an activity, a formative check, a summary, a self-assessment checklist, a practicum transfer task, a summative task, and further reading. Teach them in order - 1.3 relies on 1.1, and 1.4 assumes the four dimensions.

The course description names interactive lecture with local examples, case analysis, reflective practice, and collaborative inquiry. Use all four: Open each topic with its "real classroom situation", not a definition. For Topic 1.1, ask students to name one job they would call a "true profession" and one they would not, and why, before you give the four features. This surfaces the "well-paid job" misconception straight away. Teach the industrial → inquiry shift (Topic 1.2) as a contrast, not a history lecture. Describe one lesson two ways in two minutes of talk (scripted/procedural, then reflective/adjusting). Students grasp the distinction far faster from a concrete contrast. Hargreaves' "four ages" can be mentioned for students who want the fuller picture - do not make it the centre. Use think–pair–share for the Topic 1.1 and 1.3 activities so every student commits to a judgement before the whole-class comparison. Protect time for the Topic 1.4 "First reflection" activity. It is short but important - the first entry in a habit the course returns to in Unit 6. Do not let it be squeezed out. The Topic 1.3 summative task needs a case. Give students the one-page description of a teacher's practice at least a few days early; the same case type reappears in the unit-assessment ERQs.

Misconception What to do "A profession = a respectable, well-paid job." Push for the four features; ask for a well-paid job that is not a profession and a modestly paid one that is. "Teaching is a profession only because the state says so." Separate recognition from basis: the knowledge base and ethical code exist whether or not policy names them. "Inquiry-based teaching = group work / less structure." Show a strict, teacher-led lesson that is still inquiry-based because the teacher notices and adjusts. The defining move is evidence-based adjustment, not the furniture. "Reflection = keeping a diary." Contrast a record with using the record to question an assumption and change the next action (Topic 1.4 activity). "Professionalism is dress and discipline." Acknowledge these matter, then weight the discussion toward knowledge, ethics, the accountability–autonomy–collegiality balance, and continued learning. Treating "semi-profession" as an insult. Frame it as a description of what teaching is still building (longer training, stronger bodies, more judgement), not a ranking.
documents.s: Likely misconceptions and how to handle them

documents.t: The Topic 1.2 summative doubles as practical work. Each student describes one real or imagined lesson two ways - industrial framing, then inquiry-based framing - and names one concrete, do-able change between them. Collect a sample aloud so the class hears that "inquiry-based" is a habit of noticing and adjusting, not an abstract label. Mini-observation (optional, if a practicum school is available). Ask students to watch ten minutes of any lesson and note one moment that looked "industrial" and one that looked "inquiry-based", with no judgement of the teacher. Discuss patterns, not individuals. This is the Topic 1.2 "Try this at your practicum school" task. The per-topic practicum tasks are cumulative. By the end of the unit each student should have four short practicum notes and one dated identity reflection. Ask to see them before the unit-assessment.

The per-topic "Check your understanding" items are diagnostic - mark lightly, look for which key ideas are shaky, and reteach before the topic's summative task. The per-topic summative tasks reach Apply/Analyze. The Topic 1.3 task reaches Analyze in full - breaking a real case into parts and relating it to the four dimensions. The most common shortfall is asserting an industrial/inquiry judgement without quoting specific details; flag that explicitly when you set the task. The unit-assessment page carries the full 10 MCQ / 10 RRQ / 5 ERQ bank with answers and marking guidance. Students can self-check; you may also use selected RRQs/ERQs as a graded end-of-unit test. Weighting follows the course default: 60% summative / 40% formative.

Unit 1 listed a code of conduct as one of the four marks of a profession. This unit opens that mark up. It asks what professional ethics actually are, who a teacher owes them to, and what you do on the morning when two things you owe pull in opposite directions. That last question is the real work. Most ethical difficulty in a classroom is not a choice between doing right and doing wrong, which is usually obvious. It is a choice between two things that are both right, where honouring one costs you the other. This unit gives you two models for working through exactly that.
documents.s: Models and Frameworks of Professional Ethics and Behaviors

documents.t: By the end of this unit you should be able to: Define professional ethics and distinguish them from personal morality and from the law, and explain why the teacher-pupil relationship needs a shared ethic of its own. Describe what a code of ethical conduct requires of a teacher toward students, toward their own practice and performance, toward parents and the community, and toward colleagues, and say what a written code can and cannot settle. Explain Rest's four-component model of moral behaviour and name where a well-meaning teacher most often fails in it. Apply the four-step Empathy, Context, Reflect, Action framework to a classroom ethical dilemma and justify the course of action you reach. Analyse a dilemma involving grading, confidentiality, social media or equity in which two duties genuinely conflict, and defend a decision rather than merely describe the difficulty.

Unit 1, in particular the code-of-conduct dimension of professionalism and the accountability, autonomy and collegiality triad. This unit assumes you have met those ideas and opens up the first of them; it does not re-teach Unit 1. No prior study of philosophy or ethics is assumed. Where a technical term is needed it is defined where it first appears.

Topic 2.1 - What professional ethics are, and why teaching needs them - what the phrase means, how it differs from personal morality and from law, and why the imbalance of power between a teacher and a pupil is what makes a shared ethic necessary. Topic 2.2 - Codes of conduct, and the four people a teacher owes them to - what is owed to students, to your own practice, to parents and community, and to colleagues, and how the local and international codes fit together. Topic 2.3 - Models for deciding: Rest, and the four-step framework - two models of how an ethical decision is actually made, and the four distinct ways it can fail. Topic 2.4 - Dilemmas in your own classroom - grading fairness, confidentiality, social media and equity, worked through with the models from Topic 2.3.

Your course guide sets out this unit in three sections, 2.1 to 2.3. This book teaches it in four, because the guide's section 2.3 covers both the decision models and their application to classroom dilemmas, and those are enough work to warrant separate sittings. Topic 2.4 is not a fourth guide section; it is the second half of guide section 2.3. Nothing in the guide has been added or left out.
documents.s: A note on how this unit is divided

documents.t: Each topic is a complete learning cycle and takes roughly one sitting. Work through them in order, because Topic 2.4 applies the models built in Topic 2.3, which in turn assume the codes described in Topic 2.2. Do the activity in each topic with at least one other person if you can. Ethical reasoning improves by being challenged, and a dilemma you have only thought about privately tends to feel more obvious than it is. The question bank at the end of the unit covers all four topics together. Its answers and mark schemes are in a clearly marked section at the foot of that page; try each item before you read them.

textbook.com.pk Miss Rabia teaches Class 8 mathematics in a government girls' school in Karachi. On the day she returns the monthly test, she reads the marks aloud, starting with the highest and working down, so that the class can hear where everyone stands. She has done this for years. She believes it motivates the girls at the bottom to work harder. Nothing Miss Rabia has done is against any rule. No law has been broken. No line in any service regulation forbids reading marks aloud. Ask her about her own character and you would find a conscientious person who arrives early, prepares her lessons and has never taken a rupee she was not owed. And yet something has gone wrong. Sana, who scored 11 out of 40, has heard her failure announced to thirty classmates. She will carry that into every future maths lesson. Whatever Miss Rabia intended, what she actually did was use a pupil's weakness as a public instrument. This topic is about the space that situation occupies: the space where you break no rule and are not a bad person, and still act wrongly as a teacher.

Professional ethics are the standards of conduct that belong to a particular occupation, owed by the people who practise it because of the position that practice puts them in. They are not a private matter and not an optional extra. They come with the job. Three things are easy to confuse, and the difference between them is the whole of this topic. Personal morality is what you believe is right, formed by your family, your faith, your conscience and your experience. It is yours. It varies legitimately between people, and a teacher's own morality is not what a pupil signed up for. The law is what the state requires and will punish you for breaching. It is the same for everyone and it is enforceable, but it is also a floor rather than a standard. The law sets out what is intolerable, not what is good. Professional ethics sit in between and cover what neither reaches. They are shared rather than private, so unlike personal morality they can be stated, taught and argued about. They are aspirational rather than minimal, so unlike the law they describe good practice rather than the edge of the punishable. Miss Rabia's case sits exactly in that gap. The law is silent. Her personal morality is untroubled, because she meant well. Only professional ethics has anything to say, and what it says is that a teacher does not trade a child's dignity for a motivational effect. This is also the answer to a common objection, which is worth naming because you will hear it: ethics is just being a good person, so it cannot really be taught. If professional ethics were personal morality, that would be true. But being a decent person did not tell Miss Rabia what was wrong with reading marks aloud, and no amount of additional decency would have. What tells her is a professional understanding of what her position does to an ordinary act. That can be taught, which is why this unit exists. A second objection is the mirror image: if it is not in the code, it is allowed. Miss Rabia breached no written rule. A code is a summary of settled judgement, not an exhaustive list of forbidden acts, and it is always shorter than the situations a teacher meets. Topic 2.2 returns to what a code can and cannot settle.
documents.s: What "professional ethics" means, and how it differs from personal morality and from law

documents.t: Every profession with an ethic has one feature in common: the practitioner holds something the client cannot hold for themselves, and the client cannot easily tell whether it is being held well. A patient cannot assess a diagnosis. A litigant cannot audit their own lawyer. The imbalance is the reason the ethic exists. Teaching has this imbalance in an unusually strong form, for three reasons. The gap is large and permanent. A pupil is a child and the teacher is an adult. Where a patient may be the doctor's equal in every respect except medical knowledge, a Class 8 pupil is the teacher's junior in knowledge, age, status and institutional power simultaneously. The pupil cannot leave. A dissatisfied client changes accountants. A pupil in a government school in a village with one school cannot change teachers, cannot appeal, and in practice cannot even complain without cost. Consent, which does a lot of ethical work in other professions, is largely unavailable here. The effects are formative and invisible for years. A pupil who concludes at thirteen that they are "bad at maths" may not discover the cost of that belief until they are excluded from a course at twenty. Neither Miss Rabia nor Sana will connect the two events. Carr (2000) makes this the ground of teaching's ethical claim: the work is not the delivery of a service to a customer but the formation of a person who cannot yet judge what is being done to them. That is why a teacher's ethics cannot be left to individual conscience. The person most affected is least able to hold you to account. Carr's book is print-only and could not be obtained while this unit was written, so treat that attribution as uncorroborated: the argument is reported here, not read from the text. The point itself rests on the reasoning above, which you can check against your own schooling.
documents.s: Why teaching needs a shared ethic: the power asymmetry between teacher and pupil

documents.t: textbook.com.pk Authority in a classroom looks like it comes from position. It does not, or not for long. A teacher who is not trusted can compel silence but cannot produce learning, because learning requires a pupil to risk being wrong in front of someone. Think of trust as working capital. It is accumulated slowly through ordinary reliable acts: marking returned when promised, a question answered rather than deflected, a confidence kept. It is spent invisibly. And it can be destroyed in a single act far faster than it was built, because the pupil's inference from one betrayal is not "that was unlike her" but "I was wrong about what she is." Four parties extend this trust, and the figure above maps them. Pupils entrust their learning and their safety. Parents entrust their children, often the only asset they have. The state entrusts its curriculum and its certification, since a mark you award is a public claim. Colleagues entrust the standing of the profession itself, which is why one teacher's misconduct damages every teacher in the district. Icka and Kochoska (2024) put the point about pupils sharply: a teacher functions as an ethical model whether or not they intend to, because pupils learn conduct by watching an adult who holds authority. A teacher who announces they value fairness and then grades a relative's child gently has taught something about fairness. It is simply not the lesson they announced. That article could not be retrieved while this unit was written either, so its attribution is likewise uncorroborated. The claim is one you can test directly: think of a teacher whose stated values and observed conduct differed, and ask which of the two you actually learned from.
documents.s: Trust as the working capital of a teacher's authority

documents.t: The word "ethics" suggests rare, dramatic dilemmas. In teaching, the opposite is true. The ethical weight of the work sits in decisions so routine that they are not experienced as decisions at all: Which pupil you call on when several hands are up, and which you stop calling on. Whether you mark the last ten scripts as carefully as the first ten. What you say about a pupil in the staff room. Whether you prepare a lesson properly for a class you find tiring. Whether a parent's gift changes anything about how you treat their child. None of these will ever reach a disciplinary hearing. All of them are decisions about what a pupil is owed, and all of them are noticed. A class knows, with considerable accuracy, which pupils their teacher has given up on. Recognising these as ethical decisions is the practical payoff of this topic. You cannot reason carefully about a choice you have not noticed making, which is exactly where the model in Topic 2.3 begins.
documents.s: Significance in practice: the everyday decisions that are ethical decisions

documents.t: Work in groups of three. Below are eight short descriptions of a teacher's action. For each one, decide together whether it is primarily a matter of law, of personal morality, or of professional ethics, and be ready to defend the placement. Some belong in more than one column, which is the interesting part. A teacher strikes a pupil. A teacher reads the class's marks aloud in rank order. A teacher does not pray. A teacher tells a colleague, in the staff room, which pupils in the class are "hopeless". A teacher accepts a large gift from a parent before the examinations. A teacher arrives ten minutes late to every lesson. A teacher posts a photograph of their class on a public social media account. A teacher lends money to a struggling student's family. Allow 20 minutes. Then compare with another group and find one placement you disagree on. Spend your last five minutes on that disagreement rather than on the seven you agreed about.

In your own words, state the difference between the law and professional ethics, and give one teaching example that the law does not reach. (Understand) Miss Rabia broke no rule and meant well. Explain why her action is still a professional failure. (Apply) Name the three features that make the teacher-pupil power imbalance stronger than the imbalance in most other professions. (Remember) A teacher says: "My private life is my own business, so my personal morality has nothing to do with my professional ethics." Identify what is right and what is wrong in that claim. (Analyze) Give two examples from your own schooling of routine decisions by a teacher that you now recognise as ethical decisions. (Apply)

Professional ethics are the shared standards of conduct that come with a professional position. They are not personal morality, which is private and varies; they are not the law, which is a floor rather than a standard. They occupy the large space between the two, and most of a teacher's ethical life happens there. Teaching needs such an ethic because of the size and permanence of the gap between teacher and pupil, the pupil's inability to leave, and the delayed invisibility of the harm. Trust is the working capital that makes teaching possible, and it is extended by pupils, parents, the state and colleagues at once. The ethical weight of teaching sits mostly in decisions too routine to feel like decisions.

I can define professional ethics and distinguish them from personal morality and from law. I can explain why the teacher-pupil relationship needs a shared ethic rather than leaving conduct to individual conscience. I can explain what trust does in a classroom and name the four parties who extend it. I can identify ethical decisions inside routine teaching acts that do not look like decisions. I can answer the objection that ethics is just being a good person and therefore cannot be taught.

Over one full teaching day, keep a private tally of a single decision: which pupils the teacher calls on. Record the name or seat position each time a pupil is invited to answer. At the end of the day, look at the distribution. Who was never called on? Was the pattern visible to the teacher? Write half a page on whether the pattern you found was an ethical decision, and note whether anyone in the room, including you, would have described it as one at the time. Do not show the tally to the teacher or discuss individual pupils by name.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: Write 350 to 400 words on the following. A teacher in your practicum school says: "I follow the rules and I have a clear conscience. What more can anyone ask of me?" Write a reply that takes the claim seriously rather than dismissing it, explains what it leaves out, and uses one concrete classroom example of your own to show the gap between following the rules and acting professionally. Mini-rubric Criterion What a strong response does Grasp of the distinction (Understand) States accurately what the law covers, what personal morality covers, and what neither reaches Use of example (Apply) The example is concrete, classroom-based, and genuinely occupies the gap rather than being a plain rule-breach Analysis of the claim (Analyze) Identifies what is legitimate in the teacher's position, not only what is wrong with it, and shows why a clear conscience is insufficient evidence of good practice Register and clarity Writes for a colleague, defines any technical term used, stays within the word count

Carr, D. (2000). Professionalism and ethics in teaching. Routledge. Chapters 1 and 2 set out why teaching's ethical claims rest on the nature of the teacher-pupil relationship. Could not be retrieved while this unit was written; see this course's source register. Icka, E., & Kochoska, J. (2024). The influence of teachers as an ethical model on students' development. International Journal of Education Teacher, 27, 99-107. Could not be retrieved while this unit was written; see this course's source register.

textbook.com.pk Mr Aslam teaches Class 9 biology. A pupil, Bilal, fails the term examination badly. Four things happen in the following week. Bilal asks Mr Aslam privately whether he is simply not capable of biology. Mr Aslam, tired, says he should "think about a different subject". Bilal's mother arrives and asks what happened; Mr Aslam tells her Bilal does not work, which is not quite true. The head of department asks for the mark sheet; Mr Aslam has not finished marking and copies forward last term's marks for the six scripts he has not reached. In the staff room, he mentions to a colleague that Bilal's family "are not educated people". Four separate failures, to four different parties, arising from one bad week. No single one of them would be described as a scandal. Together they are a fair picture of what it looks like when a teacher's obligations quietly stop being met.

A code of ethical conduct is a written statement of what a profession's members owe and to whom. Codes differ in wording, but almost all of them organise the obligation by the party it is owed to. That organisation is the useful part, because it lets you check your practice against four questions rather than one vague one.

The first and heaviest domain. At minimum a code requires that a teacher protects pupils from harm, including harm the teacher causes; treats them without discrimination on grounds of sex, ethnicity, religion, disability or family background; respects their dignity in public and in private; and does not exploit the relationship for personal advantage, financial or otherwise. Mr Aslam's answer to Bilal breaches this domain. A pupil asked a question about his own capacity at a moment of maximum vulnerability, and received a verdict. The verdict may even have been accurate about the examination. It was not a defensible thing to hand a fifteen-year-old as a settled fact about himself. Note what makes this hard to see: nothing was done to Bilal. A sentence was said. Breaches in this domain are usually made of ordinary speech.

The second domain is about competence rather than kindness, and it is the one trainee teachers most often leave out of their picture of ethics. It requires that you are prepared, that you teach the curriculum you are employed to teach, that you keep your subject knowledge current, and that your assessment is honest. Assessment honesty matters more than it looks. A mark is a public claim about a pupil that others will rely on. Mr Aslam copying forward last term's marks is the clearest breach in the vignette, and the one most likely to be defended as a small administrative shortcut. It is not. Six pupils now carry a mark that describes work nobody read. If one of them is placed in a lower set on that basis, the harm is real and untraceable. Being under-prepared is the same category of failure, more slowly. A teacher who has not prepared is charging a class the cost of their own time.
documents.s: Ethical conduct in practice and performance

documents.t: The third domain covers honesty with parents, respect for the family's circumstances, and the teacher's standing in the community they serve. It requires accurate reporting about a child, not a comfortable version or a punitive one. It requires that difficult information is delivered in a way a parent can act on. And it requires that a family's poverty, language, caste or lack of schooling never becomes a reason to treat the child as less entitled to your effort. Mr Aslam told Bilal's mother that Bilal does not work. It was near enough to true to feel honest and far enough from true to be useless: it gave her nothing to act on and told her that the problem was her son's character. A parent who cannot read the textbook can still change what happens at home, if you tell her something specific.
documents.s: Ethical conduct toward parents and the community

documents.t: The fourth domain is the one most easily dismissed as workplace politeness. It is not. It covers fair dealing with colleagues, not undermining them in front of pupils, contributing to shared work rather than free-riding on it, and declining to damage the profession's standing. Mr Aslam's staff-room remark about Bilal's family belongs here and in the first domain at once. A remark like that circulates. Within a term, several teachers hold a view of Bilal formed from a sentence nobody examined, and the pupil is taught by all of them. The professional standing point is the part trainees underestimate. Teaching's claim to be treated as a profession rests on public confidence, and that confidence is collective. One teacher who sells examination papers lowers the standing of every teacher in the province.
documents.s: Ethical conduct toward colleagues and the profession

documents.t: textbook.com.pk Codes exist at several levels, and they are not rivals. At the international level, UNESCO and the International Task Force on Teachers set out a global framework of professional teaching standards, which gives a reference point independent of any one employer. At the national level in Pakistan, the National Professional Standards for Teachers (2009) state what a teacher is expected to know, value and be able to do, and Standard 9 carries the code-of-conduct element directly. Below both, individual schools and systems hold their own service rules. Neither of those two documents could be opened from where this unit was written: the UNESCO framework and the National Professional Standards for Teachers both refused every route tried. The levels described above follow the course guide and secondary accounts of them, and the attribution of the code-of-conduct element to Standard 9 in particular is uncorroborated. Read the standards themselves before you cite a numbered standard in an assignment. Your course guide also names "NACTE guidelines" at this point. The National Accreditation Council for Teacher Education is Pakistan's accreditation body for teacher education programmes. This unit does not tell you what those guidelines say, because the reference could not be verified against a primary document while the unit was written. Ask your tutor which NACTE document is meant, and read it; the gap is recorded in this course's source register rather than filled with a guess. Reading them together is the skill. An international framework says what the profession everywhere aspires to. A national document says what this country has committed to and can hold you to. A school's rules say what happens on Monday. When they conflict, the conflict itself is information: it usually marks a place where local practice has drifted from what the profession claims. Now the limitation, which matters as much as the content. A code cannot settle every case, and it is not trying to. Three reasons: Codes are general and situations are particular. "Respect pupil dignity" does not tell you whether to correct a pupil's error in front of the class. Codes conflict with themselves. Honesty toward a parent and protection of a pupil's confidence can point in opposite directions, as Topic 2.4 shows in detail. Codes are silent on almost everything. Miss Rabia in Topic 2.1 breached no code. This is why the rest of the unit is about models for deciding rather than more rules to follow. A code tells you what is settled. Judgement is what the profession asks of you everywhere else, and the nested circles in the figure above are drawn with gaps for exactly that reason.
documents.s: Local and international codes, and what a written code cannot settle

documents.t: Work in groups of four. Take the Mr Aslam vignette at the top of this topic. Assign one domain to each group member: students; practice and performance; parents and community; colleagues. Each person writes, alone and in five minutes, what their domain required Mr Aslam to do differently in that week. Then read them aloud in turn. Two questions for the group afterwards. First: did any two of your prescriptions conflict? Second: which domain would have been noticed if Mr Aslam had breached it alone? Spend ten minutes on the second question, because the answer explains why the quietest failures persist. Allow 25 minutes in total.

Name the four domains a code of ethical conduct typically organises obligations by. (Remember) Explain why copying forward unmarked scripts is an ethical failure and not merely an administrative one. (Understand) A teacher says a code of conduct is pointless because "it cannot cover every situation". Explain what is right in that observation and why the conclusion does not follow. (Analyze) Classify each of Mr Aslam's four failures by domain, and say for each who would notice first. (Apply) Give one example of information about a pupil that is accurate but useless to a parent, and rewrite it so the parent can act on it. (Apply)

A code of ethical conduct states what a teacher owes and to whom, and it organises that obligation by party: students, one's own practice and performance, parents and the community, and colleagues and the profession. Breaches in the first domain are usually made of ordinary speech; breaches in the second are usually defended as shortcuts; breaches in the third often take the form of accurate but unusable information; breaches in the fourth spread. Codes exist at international, national and school level, and reading them together is a professional skill. But a code is a summary of settled judgement, not a decision procedure. It is general where situations are particular, it conflicts with itself, and it is silent on most of what a teacher actually does.

I can name the four domains of conduct a code addresses and give an example breach in each. I can explain why assessment honesty is an ethical obligation and not an administrative one. I can describe how the international framework, the national standards and a school's own rules relate to one another. I can state three reasons a written code cannot settle every case. I can rewrite unusable feedback to a parent into something the parent can act on.

Ask to see whatever written code, service rules or staff handbook your practicum school operates under. Many schools have something, even if it is only a page. Read it with the four domains in front of you. Which domains does it cover in detail? Which does it barely mention? Write half a page on what the document's emphasis tells you about what the school has had trouble with in the past, and note one situation you have witnessed on placement that the document does not reach. If the school has no written code at all, that is itself the finding. Write about what fills the gap instead.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: Write 400 to 450 words. Using the Mr Aslam vignette, take the two failures you judge most serious and the one you judge least serious. Justify the ranking. Your answer must name the domain each failure belongs to, explain the harm in each case including who bears it and when, and defend your judgement about the least serious one against the strongest objection you can construct. Mini-rubric Criterion What a strong response does Domain identification (Understand) Correctly assigns each chosen failure to its domain and shows why it belongs there Account of harm (Apply) Names who is harmed, how, and over what time scale, rather than asserting seriousness Justified ranking (Evaluate) Defends the ranking with a stated criterion of seriousness, and answers the strongest objection to the least-serious judgement rather than a weak one Use of sources Refers accurately to at least one code or standard rather than to ethics in general

textbook.com.pk Two teachers watch the same thing happen. In the corridor between periods, a group of Class 7 boys surround a smaller boy, Imran, and push his books out of his hands. It takes about four seconds. Then everyone moves on. Mr Khalid, walking behind, does not register it as anything. Boys jostle; books get dropped. He is thinking about his next lesson. Miss Nadia sees it and knows exactly what it is, because it is the third time this month with the same boy. She also knows that raising it means a conversation with the head, who dislikes complaints, and that the ringleader's father is a member of the school management committee. She decides to keep an eye on it. Neither teacher acts. But they failed in completely different places, and a model that cannot tell those two failures apart is useless for improving either one.

James Rest's model, set out by Bebeau, Rest and Narvaez (1999), makes one central claim: acting well is not a single act but four distinct things that must all succeed. Fail any one and no ethical action occurs, no matter how well the other three worked. Moral sensitivity is noticing that a situation has an ethical dimension at all, and recognising who is affected and how. This is perception, not reasoning. Mr Khalid failed here. No amount of ethical knowledge would have helped him, because he never saw a situation to apply it to. Moral judgement is working out which course of action is right. This is the part that looks like ethics, and it is the part most teaching about ethics concentrates on. It draws on principles, codes and reasoning about consequences. Moral motivation is choosing to prioritise the ethical course over competing values. The competing values are rarely wicked ones. They are usually ordinary: a quiet life, a manageable workload, a good relationship with the head, the wish not to make trouble for a colleague. Miss Nadia failed here. She noticed correctly and judged correctly, and then the cost outweighed the judgement. Moral character is following through: persistence, and enough courage to carry out the action once distraction, fatigue or resistance appears. A teacher who reports the incident, is told to drop it, and drops it has failed at this fourth stage rather than the third. The practical value is diagnostic. When you find yourself or a colleague not acting well, the useful question is not "why was that wrong?" but which of the four failed? The remedy differs completely at each stage. The table below is this unit's diagnostic gloss, not a direct quotation from Rest or from Bebeau, Rest and Narvaez (1999): Component The failure What actually helps Sensitivity Did not notice Practice in reading situations; hearing colleagues describe what they saw Judgement Noticed, reasoned poorly Codes, principles, worked cases, discussion Motivation Judged well, chose otherwise Honest reckoning with what competes; institutional support Character Intended well, did not follow through Rehearsal, allies, small commitments made in advance Notice that the most common remedy offered to teachers, which is more instruction in what is right, only addresses the second. Rest's point is that a great deal of unethical behaviour comes from people who know perfectly well what is right. This also dismantles a misconception worth naming: if a teacher knows the right thing, they will do it. Rest's model exists precisely because that is false, and the two teachers in the vignette show the two most common ways it fails.
documents.s: Rest's four-component model of moral behaviour

documents.t: textbook.com.pk Rest's model describes how ethical action happens or fails. It does not tell you what to do on Tuesday. The four-step framework is the working procedure, and it maps onto Rest: the first two steps build sensitivity, the third does judgement, the fourth demands motivation and character. This framework is named in your course guide. No published source verifying it was found while the unit was written, so it is taught here as a guide-given procedure; the gap is recorded in this course's source register. Empathy. Ask who is affected and what this looks like from where they stand. Not "what would I feel", but what they feel given what they know and what they can do about it. For Imran, the four seconds in the corridor are not four seconds; they are a standing condition of his school day. Context. Establish the facts and the constraints before deciding. What actually happened, how often, what has been tried, what the school's rules require, what you are permitted and obliged to do, who else knows. Miss Nadia had unusually good context, which is what made her inaction a motivation failure rather than an ignorance one. Reflect. Weigh the options against your obligations, not against your comfort. Name the competing goods honestly. Ask the test question: if the reasoning behind this decision were published, would it stand? Ehrich and colleagues (2011) argue, in a conceptual model illustrated by constructed scenarios rather than by survey data, that the first move in a dilemma is recognising it as one and naming the multiple forces at play in it. Action. Decide, do it, and then close the loop. The return arrow in the figure is the part most often dropped. What happened? Was the pupil better off? What would you do differently? The framework is drawn as a loop rather than a line for a reason. A decision that is never reviewed cannot teach you anything, and most ethical skill in teaching is accumulated from cases you handled imperfectly and thought about afterwards.
documents.s: The four-step ethical decision-making framework: Empathy, Context, Reflect, Action

documents.t: Reflective decision making is the habit of treating your own decisions as things to be examined rather than defended. It is what makes the loop above work, and it is a professional disposition rather than a procedure. Three things distinguish it from simply thinking about your day. It is structured. "I felt bad about that lesson" is not reflection. "I did not call on any girl in the back three rows, and I think it was because they answer slowly and I was behind" is. It seeks disconfirmation. A reflective teacher goes looking for the evidence that their decision was wrong. This is uncomfortable and it is the whole value. It is habitual, not exceptional. A teacher who reflects only after something goes badly will only ever examine dramatic cases, which are rare and unrepresentative. Most of what needs examining is routine, as Topic 2.1 argued. A practical form: at the end of each teaching week, write three sentences on one decision you made about a pupil and are not certain was right. Three sentences, once a week, sustained for a term, will teach you more about your own practice than a course will.
documents.s: Reflective decision making as a standing habit

documents.t: Work in pairs. Below are four short accounts of a teacher who did not act well. For each, identify which of Rest's four components failed, and state what would actually have helped that teacher, using the remedy column in the table above. A teacher marks a colleague's relative generously without ever consciously deciding to. A teacher knows a pupil is being bullied, plans to raise it at the staff meeting, and does not because the meeting runs late and the moment passes. A teacher believes that publicly comparing pupils' marks is an effective motivator and continues to do it. A teacher realises mid-year that a pupil cannot see the board, and says nothing because the parents cannot afford spectacles and raising it would embarrass them. Then swap with another pair. Where you disagree about which component failed, argue it out: the disagreements are usually about whether the teacher genuinely did not notice, or noticed and looked away, and that distinction is the hardest and most useful one in the model. Allow 25 minutes.

Name Rest's four components in order and state what each one does. (Remember) Explain why a teacher who knows exactly what is right may still fail to act, using two different components to give two different explanations. (Understand) Apply the four-step framework to Miss Nadia's situation. What does each step require of her? (Apply) Distinguish a failure of moral sensitivity from a failure of moral motivation, and say what evidence would let you tell them apart from outside. (Analyze) Why is the four-step framework drawn as a loop rather than a line? (Understand)

Rest's four-component model holds that ethical action requires four separate things to succeed: noticing the ethical dimension (sensitivity), working out what is right (judgement), prioritising it over what competes (motivation), and carrying it through (character). Failure at any one produces the same visible result, which is why diagnosis matters: the remedy differs at every stage, and only judgement is addressed by being told more rules. The four-step framework, Empathy, Context, Reflect and Action, is the working procedure that maps onto those components. Drawn as a loop, it makes reviewing the decision part of the decision. Reflective decision making is the standing habit that keeps the loop turning: structured, seeking disconfirmation, and applied to routine cases rather than only dramatic ones.

I can name Rest's four components and explain what failing at each one looks like in a classroom. I can diagnose which component failed in a described case rather than simply judging the teacher. I can work a situation through Empathy, Context, Reflect and Action and say what each step requires. I can explain why more instruction in what is right fixes only one of the four components. I can describe what distinguishes structured reflection from simply thinking about my day.

For one week, keep a decision log. At the end of each teaching day, write three sentences about one decision you made involving a pupil that you are not certain was right. At the end of the week, read the five entries together and ask Rest's diagnostic question of each: had you not acted well, which component would have been the one to fail? Most people find the same component recurring. That recurrence is the single most useful thing this unit can tell you about yourself. Keep the log private and do not name pupils.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: Write 400 to 450 words. Take Miss Nadia's situation from the top of this topic. Work it fully through the four-step framework and reach a decision. Your answer must complete all four steps, state a specific decision rather than a sentiment, and identify honestly what competes with the ethical course in her case. Finish by saying which of Rest's components your proposed course of action most depends on, and why that makes it fragile. Mini-rubric Criterion What a strong response does Completeness (Apply) Works all four steps, with Context establishing facts rather than restating the problem Specificity of decision (Apply) Reaches a concrete, actionable decision that another teacher could carry out Analysis of what competes (Analyze) Names the competing goods honestly, including the teacher's legitimate self-interest, rather than treating the obstacle as simple cowardice Self-critique Identifies which component the plan depends on and why that is its weak point

C., Kimber, M., Millwater, J., & Cranston, N. (2011). Ethical dilemmas: A model to understand teacher practice. Teachers and Teaching: Theory and Practice, 17(2), 173-185. Ehrich et al. 2011

textbook.com.pk Miss Farah teaches Class 10 English in a small private school in Hyderabad. Three weeks before the board examination, a pupil named Ayesha submits an essay that is plainly not her own work. It is fluent in a way Ayesha has never been, and two sentences appear verbatim in a guide book sold outside the school gate. Miss Farah knows several other things. Ayesha's father died in January. Her results have collapsed since. The school's rule on plagiarism is a zero mark and a report to the head, and the head has told staff that the school's board results this year are "a matter of survival". Ayesha has never done anything like this before. Every option Miss Farah has costs her something she is obliged to protect. That is what makes this a dilemma rather than a hard decision.

An ethical dilemma is not a choice between right and wrong. That is a temptation, and while it can be difficult to resist it is not difficult to analyse. A dilemma is a situation in which two or more things you are genuinely obliged to do cannot both be done. Whatever you choose, you fail an obligation. Ehrich and colleagues (2011) built their model of teacher practice around exactly this kind of conflict between competing forces. This unit sorts those competing claims into four that teachers in Pakistan can recognise quickly: the individual pupil's interest, the other pupils' interest, the institution's interest and the wider public interest. This matters practically. If you approach a dilemma expecting to find the option with no cost, you will search for it, fail to find it, and then either freeze or pick the option that is cheapest for you and call it the right one. Accepting at the outset that something will be lost is what makes a reasoned choice possible. In Miss Farah's case the competing goods are clear once named: honesty in assessment, which she owes every other pupil and the board; and a duty of care to a grieving child who may be in more trouble than the essay suggests. Both are real. Neither cancels the other.
documents.s: What makes a dilemma a dilemma

documents.t: Grading dilemmas are the most common kind a teacher meets, because a mark is simultaneously a piece of feedback to one pupil and a public claim relied on by others. The recurring pressures are worth naming in advance, because they arrive with a plausible justification attached: Sympathy. A pupil whose circumstances are genuinely terrible submits weak work. Pressure from above. A school needs results; a head asks for marks to be "looked at again". Relationship. The pupil is a colleague's child, or a relative, or simply one you like. Consistency drift. The last ten scripts are marked more harshly, or more kindly, than the first ten, because you are tired. The principle that resolves most of these is a distinction between the mark and the response. The mark is a claim about the work. It is not a reward, not a message of sympathy, and not yours to trade. What you do besides the mark is where a teacher's care operates, and it is almost unlimited: time, a second chance where the rules allow one, a conversation with the family, a referral. Applied to Miss Farah: the essay cannot receive a mark it did not earn, because that mark would be a false claim and other pupils would carry its cost. But "zero and report" is not the whole of what she owes Ayesha either. textbook.com.pk The figure above works the case through. Empathy: from Ayesha's side, three weeks before the board, a father dead in January, and a guide book on sale at the gate. Context: first offence, rule is zero and report, head under results pressure, and a fact Miss Farah does not yet have, which is what else has changed at home. Reflect: honesty in assessment against duty of care, with the school's interest in results as a third pressure that is not one of her obligations and must be named as such so it can be set aside. Action: the mark stands at zero because the work is not Ayesha's; the report is made because the rule is not Miss Farah's to waive privately; and she asks for the pastoral consequence to be handled separately, having first spoken to Ayesha so the girl is not ambushed. That decision costs something. It is defensible because the cost is borne where it belongs.

Confidentiality. A pupil tells you something in confidence. The obligation to keep it is real, and it is not absolute. A common and damaging misconception is that confidentiality means never telling anyone anything. In practice a teacher holds information in trust with a known limit: where a pupil is at risk of harm, the obligation to protect overrides the obligation to keep the confidence. The professional skill is to make the limit known in advance rather than discovering it in the moment. "I will keep what you tell me private unless you are in danger, and if that happens I will tell you before I tell anyone else" is a promise that can be kept. "You can tell me anything" is not. Social media. Two distinct issues get confused here. The first is your conduct toward pupils in online spaces: private messaging, adding pupils as contacts, photographs. The default is the same as it would be offline, and the reason is the power imbalance from Topic 2.1, which does not weaken because the medium changed. The second is your own personal account. Trainees often say that what they post privately is nobody's business. As a claim about privacy that is reasonable; as a claim about professional consequence it is simply false. A teacher is an ethical model to pupils who can see them, and the standing of the profession is collective. Posting a photograph of a class, or a complaint about a named pupil, or material that would make a parent doubt your fairness, has professional consequences whoever owns the account. Equity. The hardest of the four, because equity dilemmas rarely announce themselves. Treating pupils identically is easy to defend and often produces unequal outcomes: the same homework expectation lands differently on a girl who does housework until nine and a boy with a desk and a lamp. Treating them differently to reach a fairer outcome is right in principle and opens two risks at once, that you patronise a pupil by lowering what you expect of them, and that other pupils see favouritism. There is no formula. The workable test is whether you could state your reason to the whole class and to the affected pupil's parents without embarrassment. Adjusting the conditions for success usually survives that test. Adjusting the standard usually does not.

Work in groups of three. Each person writes, privately and in five minutes, a short account of a real dilemma they have witnessed or heard about in a school, with names removed. It must be a genuine dilemma: two obligations that cannot both be met. Pass each account to the person on your left. They work it through the four steps in writing, ending with a specific decision. Pass again. The third person's job is different: they must construct the strongest possible objection to the decision reached. Return all three to the original writer and discuss. Allow 30 minutes. If someone's account turns out not to be a dilemma, because one option is simply wrong, that is a useful finding and worth naming as a group.

State the difference between an ethical dilemma and a temptation, and explain why the distinction changes how you should approach it. (Understand) Explain the distinction between the mark and the response, and apply it to a pupil whose work is weak because of genuine hardship. (Apply) Why is "you can tell me anything" a promise a teacher should not make? Rewrite it as one that can be kept. (Apply) A trainee says their personal social media account is private and therefore professionally irrelevant. Identify what is correct in that claim and where it fails. (Analyze) Give one example of adjusting the conditions for success and one of adjusting the standard, and explain why the first usually survives the public-reason test and the second does not. (Analyze)

A genuine dilemma is a conflict between obligations you actually hold, not between right and wrong. Accepting that something will be lost is what makes reasoned choice possible; searching for the costless option produces paralysis or self-serving rationalisation. Grading dilemmas turn on separating the mark, which is a claim about the work and cannot be traded, from the response, which is where a teacher's care operates and is nearly unlimited. Confidentiality is real but bounded, and the bound should be stated in advance. Social media carries the classroom's power imbalance into a new medium and does not dissolve it at the boundary of a personal account. Equity dilemmas are hardest because identical treatment is easy to defend and frequently unfair; the working test is whether your reason could be stated openly to the class and to the parents.

I can distinguish a genuine dilemma from a simple right-and-wrong choice and explain why it matters. I can name the competing goods in a described case rather than asserting one is obvious. I can apply the mark-and-response distinction to a grading pressure. I can state the limit of confidentiality in a way I could say to a pupil in advance. I can use the public-reason test to judge an equity decision.

Ask your mentor teacher this question: "What is a decision you have had to make here where whatever you chose, something was lost?" Listen without proposing a solution. Afterwards write half a page identifying the two obligations that conflicted, which one your mentor prioritised, and what they did to limit the cost of the one they could not honour. That last part is where experienced teachers differ most from trainees, who tend to think the decision ends when the choice is made. Do not record identifying details of any pupil.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: Write 450 to 500 words on Miss Farah's case, from the top of this topic. Reach a decision, defend it, and then argue against yourself. Your answer must name both competing obligations explicitly, identify which pressure on Miss Farah is not one of her obligations and explain why it must be set aside, state a specific course of action, and then set out the strongest case that your decision is wrong before explaining why you still hold it. Mini-rubric Criterion What a strong response does Naming the conflict (Understand) States both obligations accurately and shows why neither cancels the other Separating pressure from obligation (Apply) Identifies the school's results pressure as a pressure rather than a duty, and says why that distinction matters Self-objection (Evaluate) Constructs the strongest counter-argument rather than a weak one, and answers it without retreating to "it depends" Specificity The proposed action is concrete enough that another teacher could carry it out on Monday

Ehrich, L. C., Kimber, M., Millwater, J., & Cranston, N. (2011). Ethical dilemmas: A model to understand teacher practice. Teachers and Teaching: Theory and Practice, 17(2), 173-185. Ehrich et al. 2011 UNESCO / International Task Force on Teachers (2019). Global framework of professional teaching standards. UNESCO teacher standards Could not be retrieved while this unit was written; see this course's source register.

Professional ethics are the shared standards of conduct that come with a professional position. They are neither personal morality, which is private and varies legitimately, nor the law, which sets a floor rather than a standard. Teaching needs such an ethic because the gap between teacher and pupil is large, permanent and impossible for the pupil to escape, and because the harm of a bad decision often becomes visible only years later. Trust is the working capital that makes teaching possible, and it is extended at once by pupils, parents, the state and colleagues. A code of ethical conduct states what is owed and to whom, organised by party: students; one's own practice and performance; parents and the community; colleagues and the profession. Codes exist at international, national and school level and are read together. But a code is a summary of settled judgement rather than a decision procedure, and it is silent on most of what a teacher does. Where the code runs out, two models take over. Rest's four-component model holds that ethical action requires sensitivity, judgement, motivation and character, and that failure at any one produces the same visible result by a different route, requiring a different remedy. The four-step framework, Empathy, Context, Reflect and Action, is the working procedure, drawn as a loop so that reviewing the decision is part of making it. A genuine dilemma is a conflict between obligations you actually hold. Grading dilemmas turn on separating the mark, which is a claim about the work, from the response, which is where care operates. Confidentiality is real and bounded, and the bound is stated in advance. Social media carries the classroom's power imbalance into a new medium. Equity dilemmas are hardest, and the working test is whether your reason could be stated openly to the class and to the parents.

Professional ethics differ from the law chiefly because the law: (Understand) a) applies only to employees of the state b) sets out what is intolerable rather than what is good c) is written down whereas ethics are not d) changes more often than professional standards A teacher reads pupils' marks aloud in rank order. No rule forbids it. This is best described as: (Apply) a) a legal breach b) a failure of personal morality only c) a professional-ethics failure that no written rule reaches d) acceptable, since no rule was broken Which feature of the teacher-pupil relationship most distinguishes it from a doctor-patient relationship? (Understand) a) The teacher is paid by the state b) The pupil cannot leave and cannot meaningfully consent c) The teacher has more subject knowledge d) The relationship lasts a fixed term Copying forward unmarked scripts from last term belongs to which domain of a code of conduct? (Understand) a) Conduct toward students b) Conduct in practice and performance c) Conduct toward parents and community d) Conduct toward colleagues Telling a parent only that "your son does not work" fails chiefly because the statement is: (Understand) a) untrue in every respect b) a breach of confidentiality c) accurate enough to feel honest but useless to act on d) too technical for a parent to follow Which element of Pakistan's National Professional Standards for Teachers carries the code-of-conduct requirement? (Remember) a) Standard 1, subject matter knowledge b) Standard 5, assessment c) Standard 9, continuous professional development and code of conduct d) Standard 10, teaching of English as a second or foreign language A teacher notices nothing wrong when a pupil is repeatedly excluded from group work. In Rest's model this is a failure of: (Understand) a) moral sensitivity b) moral judgement c) moral motivation d) moral character A teacher knows what is right, intends to act, and lets the moment pass at a staff meeting. This is a failure of: (Apply) a) moral sensitivity b) moral judgement c) moral character d) moral motivation A teacher must choose between reporting a grieving pupil's plagiarism and protecting her at a fragile moment. Both obligations are real. This is best described as: (Understand) a) a temptation b) a genuine ethical dilemma c) a breach of the code of conduct d) a failure of moral sensitivity A pupil who does housework until nine every evening submits the same work as a pupil with a desk and a lamp. Treating them identically is easy to defend and produces an unfair outcome. This is best described as: (Understand) a) a grading dilemma b) an equity dilemma c) a failure of moral character d) a confidentiality dilemma

In no more than 80 words, distinguish professional ethics from personal morality, and give one teaching example that belongs to the first and not the second. (Understand) Explain why the delayed and invisible nature of harm in teaching strengthens the case for a shared professional ethic rather than individual conscience. (Analyze) Explain what is meant by describing trust as the "working capital" of a teacher's authority, and name two of the four parties who extend it. (Understand) Name the four domains a code of ethical conduct organises obligations by, and give one example breach in each. (Understand) Explain why assessment honesty is an ethical obligation rather than an administrative one. Refer to who bears the cost of a false mark. (Understand) A colleague argues that a written code is pointless because it cannot cover every situation. Set out what is correct in the observation and explain why the conclusion does not follow. (Analyze) State Rest's four components in order and give, for each, the one remedy most likely to help a teacher who fails there. (Understand) Distinguish a failure of moral sensitivity from a failure of moral motivation, and state what evidence would allow an observer to tell them apart. (Analyze) Explain the distinction between the mark and the response, and apply it to a pupil whose work is weak because of severe family hardship. (Apply) Rewrite the promise "you can tell me anything" into a statement about confidentiality that a teacher can actually keep, and explain in one sentence why the original cannot be kept. (Apply)

"Following the rules and keeping a clear conscience is all anyone can ask of a teacher." Evaluate this claim, using the distinction between law, personal morality and professional ethics, and at least one worked classroom example of your own. (Evaluate) Analyse the Mr Aslam vignette from Topic 2.2 across all four domains of a code of conduct. For each failure, identify the domain, the person harmed, and the time scale over which the harm becomes visible. Conclude by arguing which failure a school is least likely to detect, and why. (Analyze) Using Rest's four-component model, explain why increasing teachers' knowledge of what is right is an incomplete strategy for improving ethical conduct in a school. Propose one practical measure for each of the three components that instruction does not address. (Create) Take a classroom dilemma involving equity, in which treating pupils identically would produce an unfair outcome. Work it through the four-step framework, reach a decision, and defend it against the objection that you have shown favouritism. (Evaluate) Integrative. A teacher discovers that a colleague has been inflating the marks of pupils whose families pay for private tuition with that colleague. The teacher has strong but circumstantial evidence, no formal authority, and a good working relationship with the colleague. Work this situation through both Rest's four-component model and the four-step framework. Then argue which of the two produced the more useful guidance in this particular case, and explain what that tells you about what each model is for. (Evaluate)

b - the law marks the boundary of the punishable; ethics describes good practice above it. c - no rule is breached and the teacher means well, which is precisely the gap professional ethics occupies. b - the pupil's inability to exit or consent is the structural difference; subject knowledge (c) is common to both. b - it is a failure of competent, honest practice, not of kindness toward the pupil. c - the statement's uselessness, not its falsity, is the failure; it gives the parent nothing to act on. c - Standard 9 pairs continuing professional development with the code of conduct, which is why Unit 2's obligations and Unit 6's development sit under one standard. a - the teacher never perceived an ethical situation, so judgement was never engaged. c - the teacher intended to act, so motivation was present; what failed was follow-through, which is character. A motivation failure (d) would have been choosing not to act at all. b - two genuine obligations are set against each other, so neither choice is costless; a temptation has an obvious right answer. b - identical treatment producing an unfair outcome is the definition of an equity dilemma, which Topic 2.4 identifies as the hardest kind because it rarely announces itself.

1. (4 marks) Professional ethics are shared, statable standards attaching to a professional role (1); personal morality is private, self-formed and legitimately variable (1); the example belongs to the role rather than the person (1); the example is a genuine gap case rather than a rule breach (1). 2. (4 marks) Names the delay between act and visible harm (1); explains that the pupil cannot connect the two events and so cannot hold the teacher to account (1); concludes that accountability cannot rest on the affected party (1); links this to why a shared, external standard is required (1). 3. (4 marks) Trust is accumulated slowly through ordinary reliable acts (1); it is spent invisibly and destroyed fast (1); without it a teacher can compel behaviour but not produce learning, because learning requires risking being wrong (1); names two of pupils, parents, state, colleagues (1). 4. (8 marks) One mark per domain correctly named (4); one mark per apt example breach (4). Examples must sit in the domain claimed. 5. (4 marks) States that a mark is a public claim relied on by others (1); names who bears the cost, including other pupils and any body acting on the mark (1); distinguishes this from a private matter between teacher and pupil (1); identifies the shortcut justification and rejects it (1). 6. (5 marks) Concedes accurately that codes are general, self-conflicting and silent on most situations (2); explains that a code is a summary of settled judgement, not an exhaustive prohibition list (1); argues that incompleteness is an argument for judgement alongside a code, not against having one (2). 7. (8 marks) Sensitivity, judgement, motivation, character, in order (4). Remedies: practice in reading situations; codes, principles and worked cases; honest reckoning with competing values and institutional support; rehearsal, allies and advance commitment (4). 8. (5 marks) Sensitivity failure means the ethical dimension was never perceived (1); motivation failure means it was perceived and judged but outweighed (1); evidence distinguishing them includes whether the teacher can describe the situation accurately afterwards (1), whether they show discomfort at the time (1), and whether they have acted on similar cases before (1). 9. (5 marks) The mark is a claim about the work and is not the teacher's to trade (2); the response is everything else the teacher does and is where care operates (2); applies both to the hardship case without collapsing one into the other (1). 10. (3 marks) Rewrite states a limit tied to risk of harm (1); promises to tell the pupil first (1); explains that an unlimited promise must be broken in precisely the cases that matter most (1).
