This unit references Pakistan's National Professional Standards for Teachers (2009) throughout and does not reproduce it, following the course's citation policy. Obtain a copy before Week 9. Topic 4.2's practicum task and the indicator-writing activity both assume trainees can read at least one standard in full. If you cannot supply copies, the unit still teaches the architecture, but the activities become hypothetical and lose most of their value. The unit's own source record notes a verification limitation worth passing on: the document was not retrievable from the authoring environment, and the names of the ten standards used in Topic 4.2 were corroborated from secondary sources rather than read from the primary text. Check them against your copy. If any differ, that is a correction to make in the unit, not an error to teach around.
documents.s: Before you teach: obtain the primary document

documents.t: Four topics over three weeks: 4.1 in Week 9, 4.2 in Week 10, and 4.3 with 4.4 in Week 11. Give 4.1 a full week even though it is conceptually the lightest. The four uses of a standard are the analytical tool the rest of the unit runs on, and a cohort that has not internalised them reads 4.4 as an opinion about bureaucracy rather than as a design argument. Topics 4.3 and 4.4 belong together in the same week. Read separately, 4.3 sounds like an exhortation to be honest and 4.4 like a complaint about administration. Read together, they are one argument: honest self-evaluation is professionally valuable, and it only survives if the system is built so that honesty is not punished.

"Standards and a code of conduct are the same thing." Near-universal, because both are official documents about teachers. The Topic 4.1 comparison table exists for this. Press on the question each answers rather than on what each contains, since the contents do overlap. "A standard tells you how to teach." Correct this early or trainees will read the NPST as a prescribed method and resent it. The space a standard deliberately leaves is where Unit 3's professional judgement operates. "Meeting the indicators is the goal." The most consequential of the four, because acting on it produces exactly the behaviour the framework was built to prevent. The indicator-gaming activity in Topic 4.2 is the intervention; do not shorten it. "Appraisal and professional development are the same process." Trainees have usually only met systems where they are combined. Ask how many have ever told an appraiser something they were bad at. The answer in the room makes the argument better than the text does.

The Topic 4.2 indicator-writing activity depends on pairs genuinely trying to defeat each other's indicators. Groups that are polite to one another produce indicators nobody attacked, and the lesson does not land. Set it up as adversarial and explicitly reward the pair that finds the cleverest way to satisfy an indicator without the competence. Trainees are often reluctant, because it feels like teaching dishonesty. Name that objection directly: you are teaching them to anticipate how a measure will be gamed, which is exactly what whoever designs their appraisal should have done and frequently has not.
documents.s: The activity that most often goes wrong

documents.t: Read one standard in full (Week 10). The Topic 4.2 practicum task. The reliable finding is that the dispositions part is nearly impossible to evidence by observation, which sets up Topic 4.3's material on evidence types. Collect a show of hands on that question rather than the written work; it is faster and the pattern is what matters. One full self-evaluation cycle (Week 11). The Topic 4.3 task. Three lessons will usually be too few for the re-collection stage to show change, and trainees should report that as a finding rather than manufacture a result. Say so in advance, or you will receive five reports of successful improvement in a fortnight. Ask one question in the debrief and give it time: were you tempted to improve the record rather than the practice? An honest cohort will say yes. That admission is the unit's most important learning moment and does not survive being rushed. Appraisal enquiry (Week 11). The Topic 4.4 task asks what really happens in the school's appraisal. Prepare for the common finding of a process that is formally summative and decides nothing. The unit does not cover that case, and it is worth ten minutes of discussion: an appraisal with no consequence is not neutral, because it teaches that the standards are decoration.

The bank is on the unit assessment page with model answers and analytic rubrics. ERQ 2 is the integrative item and the best single indicator of whether the unit landed, because it requires the three-part internal division to be applied to specific described behaviours rather than recited. The rubrics cap a response that does not reach "Adequate" on the analysis, evaluation or creation criterion at 10 out of 20. In this unit the characteristic strong-looking weak answer is a fluent summary of what standards are for that never applies them to anything.

The four units before this one described teaching as it should be: a profession with an ethic, identifiable components of effectiveness, and written standards. This unit describes the conditions under which you will actually try to do all of that. That is not a change of subject. A trainee who leaves a course knowing what good teaching looks like and nothing about why it is hard to sustain will meet the gap in their first term and conclude that either the course was naive or they are failing. Usually neither is true. The work is genuinely difficult under the conditions most Pakistani teachers meet, and knowing the shape of that difficulty in advance is what lets you plan for it instead of being surprised by it. The unit ends where it should: on what is actually within your control.
documents.s: Issues and Challenges in the Teaching Profession

documents.t: Much of the research on teacher stress, burnout and workload was done in places that look nothing like a government school in Sindh. Where this unit cites a study it tells you where the study was done and with whom, because a finding from 262 Norwegian teachers may or may not travel. Where no research supports a claim about Pakistani conditions, the unit says that too, and describes the condition from the course guide and from ordinary observation instead of borrowing authority it does not have.
documents.s: A note on the evidence in this unit

documents.t: By the end of this unit you should be able to: Describe what actually consumes a teacher's working week, and distinguish stress from burnout in terms of what each is and what each requires. Explain the specific demands of multilingual and multi-grade classrooms, and why neither is solved by working harder. Analyse the competing expectations placed on a teacher by pupils, parents, heads, districts and the public, and explain how an increased focus on accountability changes what teachers do. Explain the relationship between a profession's socio-economic status and its public recognition, and what parts of it a teacher can and cannot affect. Evaluate a proposed use of classroom technology against what it adds, what it costs and what it replaces, and describe responsible conduct on digital platforms. Separate what is within your control from what is not, and design one response to a named challenge that is actually within reach.
Units 1 to 4. Topic 5.2 assumes Unit 4's account of accountability and appraisal; Topic 5.3 assumes Unit 2's obligations, which do not change because the medium did.

Topic 5.1 - The conditions you will actually teach in - workload, stress and burnout, resources, and the multilingual and multi-grade classroom. Topic 5.2 - What is asked of you, and by whom - accountability, competing stakeholder expectations, and the status of the profession. Topic 5.3 - Professionalism in the digital age - the pressure to integrate technology, and responsible use of digital platforms. Topic 5.4 - Responding: growth rather than endurance - separating what you control from what you do not, and acting on the first.

Your course guide sets out this unit in three sections, 5.1 to 5.3. This book teaches it in four. The guide's section 5.1 carries six separate bullets, more than any other section in the course, and they divide naturally into the conditions you work in and the demands placed on you from outside. Topics 5.1 and 5.2 are both guide section 5.1; topics 5.3 and 5.4 are guide sections 5.2 and 5.3. Nothing has been added or left out.
documents.s: A note on how this unit is divided

documents.t: Read Topic 5.4 last and do not skip it. The first three topics describe difficulty, and a unit that stopped there would be demoralising and useless. The point of describing the conditions accurately is to make the final topic possible: you cannot act on what you have not named. If you are already teaching, the transfer tasks in Topics 5.1 and 5.4 are the two worth doing properly.

textbook.com.pk Miss Shahnaz teaches Class 4 in a government primary school outside Nawabshah. Her timetable says she teaches six periods a day. Last Tuesday she taught eight, because a colleague was absent and there is no cover arrangement. She marked forty-three notebooks. She completed a district enrolment return that took ninety minutes because the format changed this year. She spoke to two parents at the gate about a child who has stopped attending. She prepared nothing, because there was no time left, and taught Wednesday's lesson from memory. None of this is unusual, and none of it appears in any account of what she does. Ask a member of the public what a primary teacher's job is and you will be told: six periods a day, and long holidays.

The figure above itemises the week. The pattern it shows matters more than the individual rows: the parts of the job that are invisible from outside are the parts that expand. Timetabled teaching is fixed and visible. Everything else, the marking, the returns, the cover, the parent contact, the duties assigned at short notice, is elastic, invisible, and lands on whoever will absorb it. A conscientious teacher absorbs more of it than a disengaged one, which produces the first hard fact of this unit: under these conditions the workload falls hardest on the teachers who care most. Three consequences follow. Preparation is the first casualty. It is the only substantial part of the job with no external deadline. Nobody notices on Tuesday that Wednesday's lesson was not prepared, and by the time anyone notices the pattern it has become normal. The official workload and the actual workload diverge, and only the official one is used in planning, staffing and public discussion. Arguments about teacher workload frequently fail because the two sides are counting different things. The elasticity is invisible until it fails. A school running on teachers absorbing extra duties looks fine right up until the moment a teacher stops absorbing them.
documents.s: Workload, and what actually consumes a teacher's week

documents.t: Burnout is not a strong word for stress, and treating the two as the same thing is the most consequential misconception in this topic. Stress is the response to demands that exceed resources in the moment. It is normal, it is episodic, and it resolves when the demand passes or the resources arrive. The week before examinations is stressful, and the week after is not. Burnout is what chronic, unresolved demand produces over time. Maslach and Leiter (2016) describe it as having three dimensions: exhaustion, the depletion of energy; cynicism or depersonalisation, a growing distance from the work and from the people in it; and a reduced sense of personal accomplishment or efficacy, the feeling that nothing you do makes a difference. Note the scope of that source honestly: Maslach and Leiter review burnout across human-service occupations, health care in particular, and their paper is not about teachers. The construct is theirs; the application to a classroom is an extension. For teachers specifically, Skaalvik and Skaalvik (2020) followed 262 Norwegian high-school teachers across a school year, measuring job demands and job resources at one point and burnout, job satisfaction and intention to leave teaching later. The demands they measured were time pressure, low student motivation and a dissonant value context, meaning a workplace whose values conflict with the teacher's own. The resources were autonomy and supervisory support. That study was done in Norway, in high schools, with teachers whose conditions differ from Miss Shahnaz's in almost every material respect. What travels is not the numbers but the shape of the model: burnout is produced by the relationship between demands and resources, not by demands alone. This matters practically, because it means there are two levers, and the second one is usually the neglected one. The dimensions also explain something trainees find puzzling. A burnt-out teacher is often not the one who looks overwhelmed. Exhaustion is visible; cynicism looks like competence, because the teacher has stopped investing and therefore stopped being visibly distressed. The colleague who says "do not waste your time on that class, they will not pass anyway" is not giving you practical advice. They are describing the second dimension. textbook.com.pk The figure above adds the practical part. Because burnout comes from the balance, it can be interrupted by removing a demand or by adding a resource, and the second is often available when the first is not. Miss Shahnaz cannot stop the enrolment return. She might be able to secure a cover arrangement, or an hour of protected preparation time, or a colleague who takes half the marking in exchange for half of hers.
documents.s: Stress and burnout, and how the two differ

documents.t: The resource side of that balance is where Pakistani conditions bite hardest, and it is worth being concrete rather than general. Missing resources in a typical government school include: Physical: textbooks arriving late or not at all, no blackboard space, no electricity in summer, a room built for thirty holding sixty. Human: no teaching assistant, no subject specialist to ask, no cover when a colleague is absent. Instructional: no library, no manipulatives, one copy of the teacher's guide for the school. Structural: no protected preparation time, no functioning referral route for a struggling pupil. The last two categories are the ones trainees underestimate. A missing blackboard is obvious and gets discussed. The absence of anyone to ask about a pupil who cannot decode at Class 4 is not discussed, and it is the more damaging gap, because it converts a solvable problem into a permanent one. A note on what this unit will not do. It will not tell you that a resourceful teacher can substitute for these things. Some can be worked around, and Topic 5.4 deals with that honestly. Others cannot, and pretending otherwise puts the responsibility for a system's failure onto the individual standing in front of the class.

Many Pakistani classrooms contain pupils whose home language is not the language of instruction, and often several home languages at once: Sindhi, Siraiki, Balochi, Pashto, Urdu, and English arriving as a third or fourth. The instructional difficulty is real. A pupil processing a lesson in their second or third language carries a cognitive load their classmates do not, and that load shows up as slowness or inattention that is easily misread as low ability. Unit 3's warning about mistaking a condition for a trait applies directly. The misconception to defeat here is that the home language is the problem and should be excluded. Treating a child's home language as an obstacle teaches them that part of who they are does not belong at school, and it removes the one resource they have for understanding a difficult idea. The workable practices are the opposite: let pupils discuss a concept in the language they think in before they write it in the language of instruction; take an answer in whatever language it arrives in when the thinking behind it is sound, then supply the words for it in the language of instruction; pair pupils who share a home language deliberately. This unit cites no research for those practices, because none was verified while it was written. They are offered as reasoned practice consistent with the general point about cognitive load, not as findings. Treat them as worth trying and worth evaluating with the Topic 3.5 researcher method.

A multi-grade classroom is one in which a single teacher is responsible for pupils of two or more grade levels at the same time, in the same room. It arises wherever enrolment is too small or teachers too few for one class per grade, which in Pakistan means a large share of rural primary schools. Little (2001) argued that multigrade teaching deserved an international research and policy agenda of its own, which tells you something about its status: it is extremely common and has been treated as an aberration rather than as a normal condition requiring its own preparation. The difficulties are specific and do not reduce to "more work": Two or more curricula must be planned for the same period. Direct instruction can only be given to one group at a time, so the others must be doing something worthwhile unsupervised. Assessment multiplies, and so does record-keeping. Most teacher preparation, including most of this course, implicitly assumes one grade. Naparan and Alinsug (2021) interviewed ten multigrade teachers in Zamboanga del Sur in the Philippines about what they actually do, and found strategies clustering around classroom management, collaborative learning, differentiated instruction, connecting teaching to real-life situations, and integrating technology. That is ten teachers in one district of one country, so treat it as an existence proof rather than a prescription: these are things multigrade teachers find workable, not a validated method. The honest summary is that multi-grade teaching is a distinct skill, it is widely required, and it is barely taught. If you are posted to such a school, you will be learning it on the job, and knowing that in advance is itself useful.

Work in groups of three or four. Between you, reconstruct one week of a government primary teacher in as much detail as you can: every activity, a rough time for each, and two marks against it - is it visible to someone outside the school, and is it counted in the official workload? Then answer two questions as a group. First, which activities would a teacher drop first under pressure, and what is the consequence? Second, which single added resource would relieve the most pressure, and is it one a school could actually supply? Allow 30 minutes. If anyone in the group has taught, build the week from their experience rather than from imagination.

Distinguish stress from burnout, and name the three dimensions of burnout. (Understand) Explain why, under the conditions described, workload falls hardest on the most conscientious teachers. (Understand) Explain why preparation is the first thing to be dropped, and what makes that hard to notice. (Apply) A colleague advises you not to waste effort on a weak class. Identify what this most likely indicates, using the burnout dimensions. (Apply) Explain why excluding a pupil's home language is both a pedagogical and an ethical mistake. (Analyze) Name three specific difficulties of multi-grade teaching that do not reduce to "more work". (Remember)

A teacher's week is dominated by parts of the job that are invisible from outside and therefore elastic: marking, returns, cover, parent contact, assigned duties. The elastic parts land on whoever absorbs them, so workload falls hardest on the most conscientious, preparation is dropped first because it alone has no external deadline, and official workload diverges from actual workload in a way that defeats most arguments about it. Stress is episodic and resolves; burnout is what chronic unresolved demand produces, and it has three dimensions: exhaustion, cynicism or distancing, and a reduced sense of accomplishment. It comes from the relationship between demands and resources, which means adding a resource is a lever when removing a demand is not. Cynicism is the dimension that looks like competence. Missing resources in Pakistani government schools are physical, human, instructional and structural, and the last two are the most underestimated. Multilingual classrooms impose a real cognitive load that is easily misread as low ability, and excluding the home language removes the pupil's best resource. Multi-grade teaching is a distinct, widely required and barely taught skill.

I can distinguish stress from burnout and name burnout's three dimensions. I can explain the demands-and-resources relationship and identify both levers. I can recognise cynicism as a burnout dimension rather than as realism. I can name the four categories of missing resource and say which are underestimated. I can describe the specific demands of multilingual and multi-grade classrooms without reducing either to "more work". I can state where this topic's claims come from, and which have no research behind them.

For one full day, shadow a teacher and record every activity with a time, including the short ones: signing a register, answering a parent at the gate, covering five minutes of another class. Total the time that appears on the timetable and the time that does not. Write half a page on the ratio you found and on which of the uncounted activities would be the first to be dropped. Show the teacher your total if they want to see it; most are surprised by it, because the uncounted work is invisible to the person doing it as well.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: Write 450 to 500 words. Miss Shahnaz's Tuesday is described at the top of this topic. Analyse it using the demands-and-resources idea, and propose the two interventions you judge most likely to help. Your answer must distinguish demands from resources, identify which of her demands could realistically be removed and which could not, and defend your two interventions against the objection that they require someone else to act. Say explicitly which parts of your analysis rest on research and which are reasoned from the conditions described. Mini-rubric Criterion What a strong response does Use of the model (Apply) Separates demands from resources accurately and applies both to the specific Tuesday described Realism about constraints Distinguishes what a teacher, a head, and a district can each change Defence of the interventions (Analyze) Engages with the objection that the proposals depend on others, and says what remains possible if nobody else acts Evidence honesty States which claims rest on the cited studies and which are reasoned, including the studies' scope

textbook.com.pk In one week, Mr Rafiq is told four things. His head tells him the school's Class 10 results must improve. A parent tells him her son is being pushed too hard and is not sleeping. The district office sends a circular requiring a new monthly assessment return. A newspaper column, which several colleagues have read, says that government teachers are paid to do nothing. Every one of these is a legitimate voice with a real interest in his work. No two of them are asking for the same thing, and one of them is asking for something incompatible with another. He has one week and one Class 10.

Accountability in teaching has grown steadily over the last three decades, in Pakistan and almost everywhere else. Unit 4 gave the mechanisms: standards, appraisal, licensing, inspection. This topic asks what their accumulation does to the person being held accountable. The case for accountability is strong and this unit does not dispute it. A profession that cannot be held to account has no claim on public trust, as Unit 1 argued, and in a system where teacher absence and unprepared teaching are real problems, the demand for accountability is not an insult. What is worth understanding is what accountability does when it arrives without the other half of the bargain. Isoré (2009), reviewing teacher evaluation across OECD countries, found the tension between accountability and development to be the central design problem of evaluation systems. Accountability mechanisms measure, compare and impose consequences. They do not, by themselves, supply anything that makes the measured work easier to do. So a predictable pattern follows, and you should expect to see it: What is measured becomes what is done. If results are measured and understanding is not, teaching narrows toward results. Unit 3 made this point about effectiveness; it is the same mechanism. Effort moves from the work to the record of the work. The monthly return in Mr Rafiq's week is real work that produces no learning. Accountability without autonomy produces compliance rather than improvement. A teacher held responsible for an outcome they are given no power to affect will manage their exposure, which is rational. Hargreaves (2000), tracing the historical phases of teacher professionalism, situates this: the demand for accountability is part of a long movement in how societies relate to teaching, not a recent invention or a local grievance. The practical conclusion for a trainee is narrow and useful. When you meet an accountability demand, ask what it measures and what it supplies. If it measures and supplies nothing, it will change your behaviour without improving your teaching, and knowing that lets you protect the teaching.
documents.s: The increased focus on teacher accountability

documents.t: The figure above maps the parties and, crucially, distinguishes what each wants from what each measures. Those two are different for almost every party, and the gap is where most of a teacher's difficulty lives. Pupils want to be treated fairly and to understand. What they can judge is mostly fairness and clarity, not whether the curriculum was covered. Parents want their child to succeed and be safe. Many measure by marks, because marks are the only signal the system gives them. The head wants a school that runs and results that hold up. Measures attendance, compliance, and examination outcomes. The district wants returns filed and standards met. Measures paperwork, because paperwork is what travels up a system. The examination system wants coverage of the syllabus. Measures one paper. The public wants a profession worth funding. Measures by anecdote and by newspaper column. Three things follow. The demands genuinely conflict: the parent asking Mr Rafiq to ease off and the head asking for better results cannot both be satisfied by the same action. No party sees the whole job, so each judges from a partial view that feels complete from where they stand. And the teacher is the only person positioned to see all of it, which is a responsibility and also the reason the work feels isolating. What a professional does with this is not satisfy everyone, which is impossible, but decide explicitly whose claim takes priority when they conflict, and be able to say why. Unit 2's dilemma material is the tool: name the competing goods, accept that something will be lost, and choose where the loss falls. In Mr Rafiq's case the pupil's welfare and the pupil's results are both his to weigh, and the newspaper column is not a claim on him at all.
documents.s: High expectations from many stakeholders at once

documents.t: Demirkasimoglu (2010), reviewing how teacher professionalism has been defined, opens from the long argument over whether teaching is a profession or a semi-profession, given the limits placed on teacher autonomy and decision-making. That argument is the background to everything in this section: the markers below are the ones that argument is conducted in. textbook.com.pk Occupational status is the standing a society accords a line of work: what it pays, who it attracts, how it is spoken about, and how much independence its members are granted. Teaching's status is uneven rather than simply low, and the figure above is built to show that. Against medicine or law, teaching in Pakistan typically has lower pay, a less selective entry route and less day-to-day autonomy. Against many other occupations it has greater security, substantial social respect in some communities, and a moral standing that survives even hostile newspaper columns. This unit cites no research for that comparison, because none was verified while it was written. The pattern is offered as reasoned description consistent with the definitional debate Demirkasimoglu reviews, not as measured national figures, and the figure above carries the same caveat on its face. Treat it as a claim to check against your own system, and note that the markers move independently: an occupation can score well on recognition and badly on autonomy. The relationship between status and recognition runs in both directions, and this is the part worth thinking about carefully. Status shapes who enters. Where teaching is a fallback rather than a first choice, the profession recruits accordingly, and Unit 3's discussion of attitude toward the profession becomes a live problem rather than an abstraction. Practice shapes recognition. A public forms its view of teachers from the teachers it meets: its own, its children's, the one at the gate who did or did not have time to talk. The newspaper column that angered Mr Rafiq's colleagues was written by someone with their own school memories. And recognition is not the same as status. A teacher can be genuinely respected in their community while the occupation remains poorly paid and weakly trusted nationally. Conflating the two produces the misconception this section exists to correct: a teacher's status is fixed by society and nothing a teacher does affects it. The occupation's structural position is not something one teacher can shift. The recognition extended to teachers in one community, by the people who deal with them, is affected by what those teachers do every day, and Unit 2's account of the profession's collective standing is the same argument. That is not a call to be satisfied with poor pay and to seek respect instead. Structural conditions require structural remedies, and Topic 5.4 is explicit that some things are not within a teacher's control. It is a statement about which part of the problem is in your hands.

Work in groups of four. Take Mr Rafiq's week from the top of this topic and assign one demand to each member: the head's, the parent's, the district's, the newspaper's. Argue your assigned party's case as strongly as you can, in turn, including what that party would say about the others' demands. Then decide as a group: which demands are genuine claims on Mr Rafiq, which are not claims on him at all, and in what order should the genuine ones be honoured? You must reach a ranking and be able to state the criterion you used. Allow 30 minutes. The most useful disagreement is usually about the newspaper column.

Explain what accountability mechanisms measure and what they do not supply. (Understand) Give two predictable effects of accountability arriving without autonomy. (Remember) For any three stakeholders, state what that party wants and what it actually measures. (Apply) Explain why no single party is in a position to judge a teacher's whole job, and what follows from that. (Analyze) Distinguish occupational status from public recognition, and explain why conflating them leads teachers to conclude that nothing they do matters. (Analyze)

Accountability in teaching has grown steadily and the case for it is sound. What it does not do by itself is supply anything that makes the measured work easier. Where it arrives without autonomy or resources, three things follow predictably: what is measured becomes what is done, effort shifts from the work to the record of the work, and teachers manage their exposure rather than improving their practice. Many parties make demands on a teacher, and for almost all of them what they want and what they measure are different things. The demands genuinely conflict, no party sees the whole job, and the teacher is the only person who does. The professional response is not to satisfy everyone but to decide whose claim takes priority and be able to justify it. Teaching's status is uneven rather than simply low. Status shapes who enters the profession; practice shapes the recognition a community extends to it. The two are not the same, and conflating them produces the belief that nothing a teacher does affects how teaching is regarded, which is false of recognition even where it is true of structural status.

I can state the case for accountability and what it fails to supply. I can predict what accountability without autonomy does to behaviour. I can distinguish what each stakeholder wants from what each measures. I can rank conflicting demands and state the criterion I used. I can distinguish status from recognition and say which part is affected by my own practice.

Ask three people connected to your practicum school what they think makes a good teacher: a pupil, a parent if you can, and a teacher or the head. Write half a page comparing the three answers against what each of them is actually in a position to observe. The usual finding is that each answer is accurate about the part they see and incomplete about the rest, which is the topic's central point arriving as evidence rather than assertion.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: Write 450 to 500 words. Mr Rafiq has four demands and one week. Decide what he should do, and justify the order. Name each demand, say what the party wants and what it measures, identify which are genuine claims on him and which are not, and give a ranking with the criterion it rests on. Then address the objection that ignoring the head's demand is not realistic for someone whose confirmation and transfer depend on that head's report. textbook.com.pk A donor gives Ms Sundas's school forty tablets. There is no budget for electricity beyond the existing supply, which fails most afternoons in summer. No one has been trained. The tablets carry a drill application in English, which is the third language of most of her Class 5. The district office has asked for photographs of the tablets in use for a report. Ms Sundas has thirty minutes a day in which the tablets might realistically be used, and a class that cannot yet read fluently in any language. What should she do?

The pressure is real and it comes from several directions at once: donors with equipment, district offices with targets, private schools advertising their facilities, and a general public belief that technology and modernity are the same thing. Very little of that pressure originates in a question about learning. This is the first thing to notice, and it is not cynicism: a donor measuring tablets delivered, an officer measuring photographs filed, and a parent comparing schools are all doing something reasonable from where they stand. None of them is measuring whether a child reads better. Hennessy and colleagues (2022) reviewed the use of technology for teacher professional development in low- and middle-income countries. Note that scope carefully: their subject is technology for developing teachers, not technology in the hands of pupils, so their review cannot settle Ms Sundas's tablet question. What it does establish is that teacher development opportunities in such countries are limited and often not informed by research evidence, that technology offers real potential to extend both formal programmes and informal peer learning, and that outcomes so far are mixed. Mixed is the operative word, and it is the honest summary for educational technology generally: it does some things well, many things poorly, and nothing automatically. So the professional skill is not enthusiasm and not refusal. It is judgement about particular uses, and the figure above gives the three questions worth asking of any of them. What does it add that was not possible before? A projector that shows a diagram too complex to draw by hand adds something. A tablet drilling multiplication that a worksheet drills equally well adds convenience at best. What does it cost? Not only money. Time to set up, time lost when it fails, training you do not have, and attention spent on the device rather than the content. What does it replace that was already working? This is the question nobody asks and it is the most important. A video lesson replacing a teacher's own explanation removes the one thing a video cannot do, which is notice that a particular pupil has not understood and stop. Applied to Ms Sundas: the tablets add English drill to a class that cannot decode, cost her the only thirty minutes she has, depend on electricity that fails, and would replace reading practice that is the actual bottleneck. The defensible answer is that she uses them minimally, if at all, for their stated purpose, and says so plainly when asked. That is a harder answer to give than to write, which is why this is a professionalism topic and not a technology topic. The misconception to name: integrating technology means using it in every lesson. It does not. Integrating technology means deciding where it earns its place, which sometimes means almost nowhere, and being able to justify that decision in the same terms you would justify any other instructional choice.

textbook.com.pk Unit 2 established a teacher's obligations toward pupils, parents, colleagues and the profession. None of them changes because the medium changed. The power imbalance that makes a private conversation with a pupil a matter of care does not weaken because the conversation is on a phone. Four situations account for most of the difficulty, and the figure above places them. Private messaging with pupils. The default is not to. Where contact is necessary, use a group rather than a private thread, or a channel a parent or colleague can see. This protects the pupil and it protects you, and the second reason is not the important one. Class groups on messaging platforms. Useful, and they carry three quiet problems: pupils without a phone are excluded from whatever is announced there; the group runs at all hours, so the expectation of a teacher's availability expands without anyone deciding it should; and a message sent in haste is permanent and forwardable. Agree the hours and the purpose when the group is created, and put anything that matters through the school's official route as well. Your personal accounts. Discussed in Unit 2 and worth repeating because trainees resist it: the claim that a personal account is private is reasonable about privacy and false about professional consequence. A photograph of a class, a complaint about a named pupil, or material a parent would read as evidence of unfairness has professional consequences whoever owns the account. Pupil data and images. Marks, assessment records, medical or family information, and photographs of children are not yours to circulate. A photograph of a class posted to demonstrate that tablets were used, as the district asked of Ms Sundas, involves children who did not consent and cannot refuse. Digital resources. Two obligations. Check what you take: a worksheet found online may be wrong, may be pitched for a different curriculum, and frequently is not aligned to anything your pupils are being examined on. And credit what you use, because the citation discipline Unit 4 expects of your own evidence applies to your teaching materials too.
documents.s: Responsible use of digital platforms and resources

documents.t: Work in pairs. Below are four proposed classroom uses of technology. Take each through the three questions - what does it add, what does it cost, what does it replace that was working - and reach a verdict. A projector used to display the same notes the teacher would otherwise write on the board. A WhatsApp group for a Class 9 to receive homework reminders. Forty tablets running an English drill application in a class that cannot decode fluently. A short video of a science experiment the school has no equipment to perform. Then swap verdicts with another pair and challenge one of theirs. Allow 25 minutes. Note which of the four divides the room. In most cohorts it is the second, because the costs are social rather than technical and therefore easy to miss.

Name three sources of pressure to integrate technology, and state what each actually measures. (Understand) State the three questions to ask of any proposed classroom use of technology. (Remember) Apply the three questions to the tablets in Ms Sundas's school and reach a verdict. (Apply) Explain why "what does it replace that was already working" is the question most often missed. (Analyze) Give two quiet problems with a class messaging group that are not about the technology itself. (Understand) Explain why a teacher's obligations do not weaken when a conversation moves to a phone. (Understand)

Pressure to integrate technology comes from donors, districts, competing schools and public belief, and almost none of it originates in a question about learning. Research on technology for teacher development in low- and middle-income countries reports mixed outcomes, and mixed is the honest summary for educational technology generally: it does some things well, many poorly, and nothing automatically. The professional skill is judgement about particular uses, tested by three questions: what does it add that was not possible before, what does it cost in money, time, training and reliability, and what does it replace that was already working. The third is the one most often missed. Integrating technology means deciding where it earns its place, not using it everywhere. Obligations do not change with the medium. Private messaging with pupils has a default of no; class groups exclude pupils without phones, expand availability by default and are permanent; personal accounts carry professional consequence whatever their privacy settings; and pupil data and images are not a teacher's to circulate. Digital resources must be checked for accuracy and alignment, and credited.

I can name where the pressure to use technology comes from and what each source measures. I can apply the three questions to a proposed use and reach a defensible verdict. I can explain why replacing something that was working is a real cost. I can state the default for private contact with pupils and why it exists. I can identify what pupil information and images I may not circulate.

Find one use of technology in your practicum school, however small: a projector, a phone used for a register, a class group, a photocopied resource taken from the internet. Take it through the three questions and write half a page. Pay particular attention to the third question, and ask the teacher directly what the technology replaced. The common finding is either that it replaced nothing, which is fine, or that it replaced something the teacher misses, which is the interesting case.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: Write 400 to 450 words. Ms Sundas has forty tablets, unreliable electricity, an untrained staff, a drill application in a third language, a class that cannot decode, and a district asking for photographs. Decide what she should do and defend it. Work at least two of the proposed uses through the three questions, state what you would tell the district office and in what terms, and address the objection that refusing to use a donated resource is ungrateful and will harm the school's standing with donors. Mini-rubric Criterion What a strong response does Use of the three questions (Apply) Applies all three to specific uses, including what is replaced Handling the photograph request Recognises the pupil-image issue rather than treating the request as merely administrative Answering the objection (Evaluate) Takes the donor-relations cost seriously and proposes something defensible that does not require pretending the tablets are working Realism The recommendation is something a teacher in her position could actually carry out

Hennessy, S., D'Angelo, S., McIntyre, N., Koomar, S., Kreimeia, A., Cao, L., Brugha, M., & Zubairi, A. (2022). Technology use for teacher professional development in low- and middle-income countries: A systematic review. Computers and Education Open, 3, 100080. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeo.2022.100080 The subject is teacher development, not pupils' classroom use.

textbook.com.pk Two teachers leave the same staff meeting, at which the head has announced that nothing can be done about class sizes this year. Mr Bilal goes back to a Class 6 of sixty-two and continues exactly as before, more tired each term. When a trainee asks him about group work he says there is no point with these numbers. He is not wrong about the numbers. Miss Ayesha goes back to a Class 6 of sixty-two and changes one thing: she stops trying to mark every exercise in every notebook and instead marks one question thoroughly for every pupil, in rotation, and uses the time saved to prepare the first ten minutes of each lesson properly. Her class is still sixty-two. Her Tuesdays are different. Neither of them changed the class size. Only one of them changed anything.

The figure above divides a teacher's situation into three regions, and the division is the whole content of this topic. What you control. Your preparation, your first ten minutes, how you speak to a pupil who is wrong, what you read, whose advice you seek, how you mark, what you do with the time you have. This region is smaller than a trainee hopes and much larger than a demoralised teacher believes. What you can influence. A colleague's practice, a departmental habit, a head's decision, the way a routine works in your part of the school. You do not command these, and you are not powerless over them either. Unit 3's change-agent role operates here, and so does its warning that influence requires standing earned by doing the ordinary work well. What you do not control. Pay scales, class size, the examination system, the electricity supply, the district's paperwork, the newspaper column. These are real, they are the source of most of the difficulty in this unit, and no amount of individual effort moves them. The practical claim is simple and uncomfortable: most professional frustration comes from spending effort in the third region. Mr Bilal's conclusion about class size is accurate, and it is being used to justify inaction in the first region, where he does have room. That substitution is so common it is worth naming as the characteristic failure of an experienced teacher in a hard system. A caution, so this is not misread. Naming the third region as outside your control is not the same as saying it is acceptable, and this topic is not an argument that teachers should quietly absorb whatever conditions they are given. Class sizes of sixty-two are an institutional failure. Teachers collectively, through associations and professional bodies as Unit 1 described, are exactly who should be pressing on that. What the distinction says is narrower: while it is unresolved, you still have Tuesday, and what you do with Tuesday is yours. This is where the misconception about resilience belongs. The answer to difficult conditions is resilience. Resilience is a real quality, named in Unit 3 among the seven, and offered as the whole answer it becomes a way of relocating a system's failure into an individual's character. A teacher who burns out under sixty-two pupils and no support has not failed at resilience. The useful question is not how much you can endure but what, within the first two regions, would actually reduce the load.
documents.s: Separating what is within a teacher's control from what is not

documents.t: Endurance and growth look similar from outside for about a year, and then they diverge sharply. Skaalvik and Skaalvik's (2020) study of 262 Norwegian high-school teachers is useful here for its structure rather than its numbers. They measured demands against resources, and the resources were autonomy and supervisory support. What that framing supplies is the practical point of this whole unit: when you cannot reduce a demand, the other lever is a resource. Growth is what deliberately adding resources looks like over a career. The resources actually available to a teacher in a Pakistani government school are smaller than the ones in that study and are not nothing: A colleague who will talk honestly about teaching. The single most valuable and most neglected resource in any school. It costs nothing and requires only that you ask. A method that reduces work. Miss Ayesha's rotation is one. Marking less thoroughly but more usefully is not a compromise; it is often better assessment, as Unit 4's material on evidence argued. Knowing something well. The preparation burden falls sharply once you genuinely understand the content, which is why subject study is a workload intervention and not only a quality one. A small, real improvement that worked. Unit 3's researcher role produces these, and their second value is psychological: a teacher who has changed one thing and seen it work holds a different belief about the next thing. textbook.com.pk The figure above is the method, and three stations deserve emphasis. Name the challenge precisely. "My class is impossible" cannot be acted on. "Eleven of my sixty-two cannot read the textbook" can. Place it honestly. Most challenges have a part in each region. Class size is outside; what happens in the first ten minutes with a class that size is inside. Decide in advance what would show it worked. Unit 3's researcher discipline, and the station most often skipped. Without it you will conclude whatever you hoped. The unit ends here deliberately. Four topics have described conditions that are genuinely hard and, in several respects, not your fault. That description is only worth having if it ends in something you can do on Monday, and the honest list of what you can do is short, real, and enough to build a career on.
documents.s: Growth and development as a response rather than endurance

documents.t: Work individually for ten minutes, then in pairs. Write down three challenges you expect to face, or already face, in a Pakistani classroom. Be specific: not "lack of resources" but the particular thing that is missing and what it stops you doing. For each, place it in the three regions and mark which parts fall where. Then choose the one with the largest share inside your control and take it through the flowchart to a single change and a piece of evidence you would collect. In pairs, attack each other's plans on one question: could you actually do this next week without anyone's permission? If not, the change is too large; make it smaller. Allow 30 minutes.
documents.s: Activity: Place it, then change it

documents.t: Name the three regions and give two examples of a teacher's situation in each. (Remember) Explain why most professional frustration comes from effort spent in the third region. (Understand) Mr Bilal is right about class size. Explain precisely where his reasoning fails. (Apply) Explain why offering resilience as the answer to structural conditions relocates a system's failure onto an individual. (Analyze) Give three resources available to a teacher in a poorly resourced school, and say what each one reduces. (Apply) Why is deciding the evidence in advance the station most often skipped, and what goes wrong when it is? (Analyze)

A teacher's situation divides into what they control, what they can influence, and what they do not control. The first is smaller than a trainee hopes and larger than a demoralised teacher believes; the second is where the change-agent role operates and requires standing; the third contains most of the conditions described in this unit. Most professional frustration comes from effort spent in the third region, and the characteristic failure of an experienced teacher in a hard system is to use an accurate judgement about the third region to justify inaction in the first. Naming something as outside your control is not saying it is acceptable. Structural conditions require structural remedies and collective action; the distinction is about what remains available while they are unresolved. Because burnout comes from the balance of demands and resources, adding a resource is a lever when removing a demand is not. The resources genuinely available include an honest colleague, a method that reduces work, knowing the content well, and one small improvement that demonstrably worked. The method is to name the challenge precisely, place it honestly, choose the smallest change that touches it, decide the evidence in advance, act, and check.

I can place a challenge accurately in the three regions. I can explain why an accurate complaint about conditions can still be an excuse. I can answer the claim that resilience is the response to structural difficulty. I can name resources available to me that cost nothing. I can turn a named challenge into one change small enough to make without permission.

Do the method once, in full, on something real. Name a challenge you have actually met on placement. Place it. Choose the smallest change inside your control. Decide in advance what evidence would show whether it worked. Make the change for one week. Check. Write half a page, and include the honest answer to one question: was the change too small to matter, or did it matter more than you expected? Both answers are useful findings. Trainees consistently underestimate how much a change in the first ten minutes of a lesson can alter the rest of it.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: Write 450 to 500 words. Mr Bilal and Miss Ayesha left the same meeting with the same class size. Analyse the difference between their responses, then take one challenge from Topic 5.1, place it in the three regions, and design a response. Your answer must state what you are not claiming to fix, defend your change against the charge that it is too small to matter, and address the objection that asking teachers to adapt to bad conditions lets the system off the hook. Mini-rubric Criterion What a strong response does Use of the regions (Apply) Places a real challenge accurately, including the parts that fall outside control Honesty about limits States plainly what the proposed change does not fix Defence of a small change (Evaluate) Argues why a small change within reach beats a large one that requires permission, without pretending it solves the structural problem Answering the systemic objection (Analyze) Engages seriously with the charge that individual adaptation excuses institutional failure, rather than dismissing it

Skaalvik, E. M., & Skaalvik, S. (2020). Teacher burnout: Relations between dimensions of burnout, perceived school context, job satisfaction and motivation for teaching. A longitudinal study. Teachers and Teaching, 26(7-8), 602-616. https://doi.org/10.1080/13540602.2021.1913404 Cited here for its demands-and-resources structure; the study is of 262 Norwegian high-school teachers. Hargreaves, A. (2000). Four ages of professionalism and professional learning. Teachers and Teaching, 6(2), 151-182. https://doi.org/10.1080/713698714

A teacher's week is dominated by work that is invisible from outside and therefore elastic: marking, returns, cover, parent contact, assigned duties. It lands on whoever absorbs it, so workload falls hardest on the most conscientious, and preparation is dropped first because it alone has no external deadline. Stress is episodic and resolves. Burnout is what chronic unresolved demand produces, and it has three dimensions: exhaustion, cynicism or distancing, and a reduced sense of accomplishment. It comes from the relationship between demands and resources, so adding a resource is a lever when removing a demand is not. Cynicism is the dimension that looks like realism. Missing resources are physical, human, instructional and structural, and the last two are the most underestimated. Multilingual classrooms impose a cognitive load easily misread as low ability, and excluding the home language removes the pupil's best resource. Multi-grade teaching is a distinct, widely required and barely taught skill. Accountability has grown and the case for it is sound; what it does not supply is anything that makes the measured work easier. Without autonomy it produces narrowing, effort shifted to the record of the work, and managed exposure. Many parties make demands, and for nearly all of them what they want and what they measure differ. The demands conflict, no party sees the whole job, and the teacher is the only one who does. Teaching's status is uneven rather than low; status shapes who enters, practice shapes the recognition a community extends. Pressure to use technology rarely originates in a question about learning. Judge a use by what it adds, what it costs, and what it replaces that was working. Obligations do not weaken because the medium changed. A teacher's situation divides into what they control, what they can influence, and what they do not. Most frustration comes from effort spent in the third region, and the characteristic failure is using an accurate judgement about conditions to justify inaction where there is room. Resilience offered as the whole answer relocates a system's failure into a person's character.

The part of a teacher's workload that expands under pressure is characteristically: (Understand) a) timetabled teaching b) work specified in the service rules c) examination duties d) the work that is invisible from outside the school The dimension of burnout that most often looks like competence to a colleague is: (Understand) a) reduced sense of accomplishment b) exhaustion c) cynicism or distancing d) time pressure A pupil sends a teacher a private message on a messaging app. The professional default is to: (Apply) a) reply on a channel a parent or colleague can see, rather than privately b) reply privately but keep the exchange brief c) not reply at all, in any form d) reply privately and delete the thread afterwards Excluding a pupil's home language from the classroom is a mistake mainly because it: (Apply) a) breaks a school rule b) removes the pupil's best resource for understanding a difficult idea c) slows the syllabus d) is unpopular with parents An accountability mechanism that measures but supplies nothing will typically: (Understand) a) reduce workload b) improve teaching directly c) be ignored entirely d) change behaviour without improving teaching For most parties making demands on a teacher, what they want and what they measure: (Remember) a) are the same thing b) differ, and the gap is where much of the difficulty lives c) are both set by the district d) are both invisible to the teacher Teaching's occupational status is best described as: (Understand) a) uneven across markers, so that pay, autonomy and recognition do not move together b) determined entirely by pay c) equal to medicine and law d) uniformly low across every marker The question most often missed when judging a classroom use of technology is: (Apply) a) what does it cost in money b) what does it add c) what does it replace that was already working d) who supplied it A teacher who is accurate that class size cannot be changed, and uses that to justify changing nothing at all, has: (Apply) a) acted as a change agent b) correctly identified what is outside their control c) failed at resilience d) used a true judgement about one region to excuse inaction in another Offering resilience as the whole answer to structural conditions chiefly: (Understand) a) relocates a system's failure into an individual's character b) applies only to multi-grade classrooms c) contradicts the evidence on burnout dimensions d) is good advice for new teachers

Explain why workload falls hardest on the most conscientious teachers under the conditions described. (Understand) Distinguish stress from burnout, name burnout's three dimensions, and state where each of this unit's two burnout sources was conducted. (Understand) Name the four categories of missing resource and explain why the instructional and structural ones are the most underestimated. (Analyze) Give two predictable effects of accountability arriving without autonomy or resources. (Understand) For any three stakeholders, state what that party wants and what that party actually measures. (Apply) Distinguish occupational status from public recognition, and explain what follows for a teacher who believes nothing they do affects how teaching is regarded. (Analyze) State the three questions to ask of any proposed classroom use of technology, and explain why the third is the hardest to answer honestly. (Understand) Give two problems with a class messaging group that are social rather than technical. (Understand) Name the three regions into which a teacher's situation divides, with two examples in each, and explain why most challenges cannot be placed wholly in one region. (Understand) Explain why "decide in advance what would show it worked" is the station most often skipped, and what goes wrong when it is. (Analyze)

Analyse Miss Shahnaz's Tuesday using the demands-and-resources idea. Identify which demands could realistically be removed and which could not, propose the two interventions most likely to help, and state which parts of your analysis rest on the cited research and which are reasoned from the described conditions. (Analyze) Mr Rafiq receives four demands in one week from his head, a parent, the district and a newspaper. Rank them, state the criterion your ranking rests on, and address the objection that deprioritising the head is unrealistic for someone whose confirmation depends on that head's report. (Evaluate) Ms Sundas is given forty tablets she cannot usefully deploy and a request for photographs of them in use. Decide what she should do, work at least two uses through the three questions, and address the objection that refusing a donated resource is ungrateful. (Evaluate) Take one challenge described in this unit, place it in the three regions, and design a response that is within a teacher's control. State what your change does not fix, and answer the charge that individual adaptation lets the system off the hook. (Create) Integrative. A teacher in a rural government school has a multi-grade Class 4 and 5 of fifty-one pupils across three home languages, no cover arrangement, a district requiring monthly returns, and a head asking for better results. She has begun telling trainees not to bother with group work. Analyse her situation across conditions, demands and response: identify what is happening to her, distinguish the structural from the personal, and say what could realistically change and who would have to act. (Evaluate)

d - the invisible work is elastic, so it absorbs pressure; the timetable does not move. c - a teacher who has stopped investing is no longer visibly distressed, which reads as competence or realism. a - the obligations from Unit 2 do not change because the medium changed, and the power imbalance that makes a private conversation a matter of care does not weaken on a phone. A visible channel protects the pupil first and the teacher second. Refusing to reply at all abandons a pupil who may need the contact; deleting the thread destroys the record that protects both parties. b - the home language is the pupil's working resource for a difficult idea, not an obstacle. d - measurement changes behaviour; without supplied resources the behaviour change is not an improvement in teaching. b - the want-measure gap is the topic's central analytical point. a - uneven; teaching scores differently on pay, entry selectivity, autonomy and recognition. c - the replacement question is the one nobody asks, and the one that catches a video replacing a teacher who can notice confusion. d - the judgement about class size is correct and is doing work it cannot do. a - it converts an institutional failure into a personal deficiency.

1. (4 marks) The elastic work is invisible and unallocated (1); it lands on whoever absorbs it (1); conscientious teachers absorb more (1); so the burden correlates with commitment rather than with formal duty (1). 2. (6 marks) Stress is episodic and resolves (1); burnout follows chronic unresolved demand (1); exhaustion, cynicism or distancing, reduced accomplishment (3); names Maslach and Leiter as human-service occupations generally and Skaalvik and Skaalvik as 262 Norwegian high-school teachers (1). 3. (5 marks) Physical, human, instructional, structural (2); instructional and structural absences are invisible and undiscussed (1); they convert solvable problems into permanent ones (1); an example such as having nobody to ask about a pupil who cannot decode (1). 4. (4 marks) Two of: what is measured becomes what is done; effort moves from the work to the record of the work; teachers manage exposure rather than improving practice. Two marks per effect, one for naming and one for the mechanism. 5. (6 marks) Two marks per stakeholder: what they want and what they measure, correctly distinguished. 6. (5 marks) Status is the occupation's structural standing, recognition is what a community extends (2); structural status is not shiftable by one teacher (1); recognition is affected by the teachers people actually meet (1); so the belief is false of recognition even where true of status (1). 7. (5 marks) What does it add, what does it cost, what does it replace that was working (3); the third is hardest because it requires admitting that the existing practice had value (1); and because nobody proposing the technology is asking it (1). 8. (4 marks) Two of: pupils without a phone are excluded from what is announced; availability expectations expand without decision; messages are permanent and forwardable. Two marks each. 9. (7 marks) Names the three regions (3, one mark each); two apt examples in each (2); explains that most challenges divide across the regions rather than sitting wholly in one, with an illustration - the number of pupils in a class is outside a teacher's control while the response to it is inside (2). 10. (4 marks) It is skipped because it is not required to act (1); and because deciding afterwards is easier (1); what goes wrong is that a measure chosen after the fact confirms whatever was hoped (1); so the result cannot surprise you and no learning occurs (1).
