One intervention, three stages Criterion Limited (1-2) Adequate (3) Strong (4-5) Use of the stages One or two stages All three with their needs Needs stated specifically rather than as "more support" Recognition of constraint Proposes three interventions Accepts one Explains what makes the choice genuinely exclusive Defended choice (Evaluate) Preference stated Choice with reasons States the criterion and answers the group not served Realism Not deliverable Deliverable Deliverable once a year on a district budget ERQ 3 - The head's twelve teachers Criterion Limited (1-2) Adequate (3) Strong (4-5) Comparison One route Three routes on some criteria Three or more on cost, reach and principles What is given up Not stated Stated Stated precisely, including who loses Protection (Create) None General intent Concrete defences against the three named failure modes Constraint (Evaluate) Assumes protected time Notes the difficulty Argues whether a head in an understaffed school can actually defend it ERQ 4 - Miss Hina's six goals, critiqued and rewritten Criterion Limited (1-2) Adequate (3) Strong (4-5) Diagnosis Says six is too many Names the one-goal rule Explains why six goals defeat a plan before March, not merely that they do Against the six blocks Names one or two missing blocks Names the missing blocks Identifies that the gap and its evidence were never stated, so nothing could be reviewed Critique against the principles (Analyze) Asserts the plan is weak Applies the principles of Topic 6.1 Shows which principles the plan could not have satisfied, and why that follows from its structure The rewrite One goal, no evidence One goal with evidence named Evidence chosen in September that could be compared in March, with the choice of goal justified ERQ 5 - Your own plan, defended (integrative) Criterion Limited (1-2) Adequate (3) Strong (4-5) The plan itself Blocks missing All six present The gap is stated so an observer could confirm or disconfirm it Fit of the activity Chosen by preference Justified Justified against what that route can actually deliver Evidence design (Create) Vague or retrospective Decided in advance Capable of showing the goal was not met, and the candidate says so Use of the course and self-diagnosis (Evaluate) No earlier units used Draws on three units Uses them substantively and names the plan's own weakest point honestly

This is the last unit of the course and the one that determines whether the previous five leave anything behind. Every earlier unit ends in a promise that only continuing development keeps: a profession rests on developing knowledge, competence is an ethical obligation, effectiveness components are not fixed, standards are for self-evaluation, and conditions are hard so what is within your control matters. The deliverable is Topic 6.4's one-page plan. If the block runs short, protect that session above everything else, including the assessment. A cohort that leaves with a real plan has got more from this course than one that leaves with a good examination mark and no page.

Four topics over three weeks: 6.1 in Week 14, 6.2 and the first half of 6.3 in Week 15, the rest of 6.3 and 6.4 in Week 16. Topic 6.3 is the longest in the unit and 6.4 must not be squeezed by it. If you are behind, cut the conference and online-platform sections of 6.3 to a brief treatment, and keep professional learning communities and lesson study, which are the two routes trainees can actually use. Teach 6.1 before anything else and teach the six principles properly. Every later topic is scored against them, and a cohort that has not internalised them will read 6.3 as a list of options rather than as a comparison.

"Professional development means attending a workshop." The commonest belief in the field and the one the whole unit argues against. Mr Naeem's folder is the intervention; let the class reach the diagnosis rather than stating it. "Development is what a system provides, so if none is provided none happens." Common and understandable in cohorts who have seen poor provision. The response is Topic 6.3's professional learning communities and reflective tools, which cost almost nothing, and Unit 5's control distinction. "Experienced teachers have finished developing." Trainees hold this and so, quietly, do many serving teachers. The inverse arrangement of capacity and pressure in Topic 6.2 is the repair. "A development plan is a document you write for an appraiser." If this survives, Topic 6.4 produces a page written to look good and the unit fails. Address it directly, and connect it to Unit 4's argument about mixing development with judgement, which the cohort has already accepted in another context. "Reflective practice means keeping a diary." Correct with the three-sentence structure from Unit 3 rather than by argument: show them what a reflective entry looks like beside a diary entry.

Topic 6.4's activity is the most important thirty-five minutes in the unit, and it fails in three predictable ways. Trainees write six goals. They will, despite the one-goal rule, because narrowing feels like admitting defeat. Enforce it during the session rather than in marking. Ask each person to read their goal aloud; a six-goal plan cannot be read aloud as one sentence and the exercise exposes itself. Gaps are stated as virtues. "I want to be more patient" is not a gap. Require that every gap names something an observer could see, and be prepared to send several people back to this block. The time question is skipped. "Where does the hour come from" is the block trainees leave blank and the one that decides whether anything happens. Do not accept a plan without it. Have trainees keep the page. Ask them to photograph it. A plan collected by you and filed becomes exactly the appraiser's document the topic warns against.

Development audit (Week 14). The Topic 6.1 task asks three teachers what development they have attended and what they do differently. Brief the framing carefully: this is not an audit of whether those teachers are good, and if it is heard that way the answers will be defensive and useless. Stage interviews (Week 15). The Topic 6.2 task asks a new and an experienced teacher what would actually help them. The answers are usually more modest and more specific than the topic predicts, and where they differ from the text, say plainly in the debrief that the teachers are the better evidence. Observation question (Week 16). The Topic 6.3 task asks whether teachers in the school ever watch each other teach, and why not. The third reason, about how an observation would be received, is the one worth drawing out. The plan (Week 16). Topic 6.4, described above.

ERQ 5 is the integrative item and the closing task of the whole course. It requires a real plan, a defence of each block, substantive use of at least three earlier units, and an honest naming of the plan's own weakest point. It is the best single indicator of whether the course was understood, because it cannot be answered from Unit 6 alone. Two marking notes. The rubric rewards a candidate who names their plan's vulnerability; a plan presented as having no weak point should not reach the top band, because the self-diagnosis is the skill being assessed. And a gap that an observer could not confirm or disconfirm caps the first criterion however well the rest is written. If you have time in the final session, do one thing: ask how many trainees expect to reopen their page in March. Take the honest count rather than the polite one, and say plainly that the count is what the course was for.
documents.s: Marking the unit assessment, and closing the course

documents.t: GNAS-301 Environmental Science is a 3 (2-1) credit General Education course in Semester 1 of the B.Ed (4-Year) programme. It builds a comprehensive understanding of the interactions between humans and their environment, from ecosystems and natural resources through pollution, waste and occupational safety to toxicology, environmental law and climate change, with Pakistan's own environment as the running case.

By the end of this course, students will be able to: Explain fundamental concepts of environmental science, including ecosystems, natural resources, and human-environment interactions. Analyze major environmental issues such as pollution, climate change, and resource depletion at local and global levels. Evaluate environmental health risks and the effects of physical, chemical, and biological hazards on human health. Apply environmental management tools and techniques for pollution control, waste management, and risk assessment. Develop sustainable solutions and demonstrate responsible environmental behavior in personal and professional contexts.

Environmental Science and Ecosystems - what environmental science studies, the four spheres of planet Earth, the human-activity nexus, ecosystems and natural resources, and the individual's part. Water and Waste Management - global and Pakistani water resources, water pollution and effluent treatment, the waste hierarchy, and hazardous hospital and industrial waste. Air, Noise and Environmental Hazards - air and noise pollution, the five hazard classes, and the risk assessment and management cycle. Occupational Safety and Health - sector hazards, OSH management systems and the PDCA cycle, regulation and internal control, duties and rights, HSE principles, statutes, plans and tools. Toxicology Essentials and Environmental Governance - atmospheric agents, the fate of toxins, natural detoxification, risk management, multilateral environmental agreements, the SDGs and Pakistan's environmental law. Toxic Substances, Climate Change and Smog - toxicology proper, effect classes, bioaccumulation, the greenhouse effect, smog, and climate change mitigation and adaptation.

From the course guide: interactive lectures, seminars, group work, case studies, presentations, guided reading, home study and individual tutorials. Students are encouraged to read widely and keep abreast of current trends and issues; discussions and presentations develop course themes and the sharing of ideas and knowledge.
Component Marks Mid-term 30 Final term 50 Assignment / presentation 10 Attendance 10 Total 100

Cited by reference only, never reproduced. The guide's list carries two verified works, Planetary Health (Haines & Frumkin, Island Press) and Occupational Health (Harrington & Gill, Blackwell), and five further titles that do not resolve as printed; all are flagged per the owner's ruling on unretrievable sources, and the course's in-prose citations rest on verified open-access sources instead. Haines, A., & Frumkin, H. (Eds.). Planetary Health. Island Press. Harrington, J. M., & Gill, F. S. (Eds.). Occupational Health. Blackwell. Holland, W. W. (Ed.). Oxford Textbook of Public Health. (Guide's closest real work.) Park, J. E., & Park, K. Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine. (Guide's closest real work.) Shilling, R. S. F. Occupational Health Practice. (Guide's closest real work.)

Before you can manage pollution, waste or climate change, you need a map of what you are managing. This unit draws that map. It begins with what environmental science is and how planet Earth is structured, then follows the thread that runs through the whole course: human activities and the environment shape each other. It closes with the two living foundations, ecosystems and natural resources, and with the part an individual, including a teacher, can play.

By the end of this unit you should be able to: Define environmental science, state its scope, and explain why it matters for Pakistan. Describe the natural environment using the four-sphere picture of planet Earth. Explain the nexus between environmental problems and human activities, with examples. Classify environmental issues as global, regional or local, and give a current example of each. Explain what an ecosystem is, why ecosystems matter, what threatens them, and how they are conserved. Distinguish renewable from non-renewable natural resources and describe how each is managed. List concrete individual responsibilities for protecting the natural environment.
None beyond HSC-level general study skills. This is the opening unit of the course. No prior biology or geography beyond HSC is assumed, and none may be assumed.
What environmental science studies, and the planet it studies People, activities and environmental problems Ecosystems and natural resources Protecting the environment: the individual's part

Each topic is one complete learning cycle: a real classroom situation, an explanation, an activity, a check on your understanding, a summary, a self-assessment, a practicum task, a summative task and further reading. Work the topics in order, because each builds on the one before it. Keep a notebook for the activities: several of them ask you to collect real observations from your own surroundings, and those notes become the raw material for this unit's summative tasks and for later units on pollution and waste.

Miss Farzana teaches Class 8 in a government girls' school in Karachi. It is November, and the city's air has turned grey. Before the annual sports day, she checks the air quality index, or AQI, on her phone the way other teachers check the weather. The reading is "unhealthy". She moves the races to the morning, shortens them, and tells the girls with asthma to sit out the long-distance events. A colleague asks her, half joking, "Since when are you a scientist?" Miss Farzana answers, "Since the air started deciding whether my pupils can run." Her decision used a measurement, a standard, a health effect, and a judgement. That is environmental science in one classroom moment. This topic defines the field, maps its scope, and describes the planet it studies.

Environmental science is the study of the natural environment and the way people interact with it. It asks three linked questions: what is in our surroundings, how do human activities change those surroundings, and how do the changes come back to affect people? It is not one discipline but a meeting point of several: chemistry for pollutants, biology for living things, physics for energy and climate, geography for where things happen, and the social sciences for why people act as they do. The scope of the subject is easiest to see as five areas of questioning. The table below shows each area with one question a teacher in Sindh might actually ask. textbook.com.pk The importance of the subject is practical. Pakistan faces real environmental pressures: city air that repeatedly crosses unhealthy levels, a river system under strain, and a climate that is warming. A teacher who understands the subject can read an AQI number, explain why a canal smells, and answer pupils' questions with evidence instead of guesses. The World Health Organization reports that almost the whole world's population, 99 per cent, breathes air that exceeds its guideline levels (WHO, 2024). That single fact explains why this course exists. A note on the word itself: the natural environment means everything around us that is not made by people: air, water, soil, rocks, plants, animals and the climate, together with the processes that link them. A classroom is not part of the natural environment, but the air its windows open onto is.
documents.s: What environmental science is, and why it matters

documents.t: Scientists describe the natural environment as four great spheres that meet and overlap. The atmosphere is the envelope of gases around the Earth. Its lowest layer, where weather happens, holds the air we breathe and the pollutants we add to it. The monsoon winds that water Sindh's crops are atmosphere at work. The hydrosphere is all the water: oceans, rivers, lakes, groundwater, glaciers and ice. The Indus river system, the Arabian Sea and the water under the Thar desert are all hydrosphere. The lithosphere is the solid outer part of the Earth: rocks, soil and the landforms they make. The soil that grows Sindh's wheat and the coal seams beneath Thar sit in the lithosphere. The biosphere is the thin zone where life exists, where the other three spheres meet: the mangrove forests of the Indus Delta, the fish in Keenjhar Lake, the crops in the fields, and the people in the cities. Beneath the biosphere, the Earth itself is layered: a thin crust, a thick mantle, and a core of iron. The crust matters most for this course, because that is where soil forms, water is stored, minerals sit and everything we build stands. When we speak of "using natural resources", we almost always mean taking something from the crust, the hydrosphere or the biosphere faster than it can be replaced. textbook.com.pk The figure above gathers the four spheres around one Earth, with a school building standing in the biosphere. A worked example. Place a cup of tea on the desk. The water came from the hydrosphere, boiled by gas from the lithosphere. The tea leaf grew in the biosphere, in soil weathered from the lithosphere, watered by the hydrosphere, under the atmosphere's rain. The cup, the gas stove and the price of the tea belong to human systems, which environmental science also studies, because people are part of the environment, not visitors to it. One object, four spheres, one human system. That is the analytical habit this topic wants you to build. Common misconception. Many people think "the environment" means nature far away from people: mountains, forests, wild animals. The four-sphere picture corrects this. People live inside the biosphere, drink the hydrosphere, farm the lithosphere and breathe the atmosphere. There is no "away". A city street is as much an environment as a mangrove creek, and the subjects of this course, from air quality to waste, are mostly about the environments people live in every day.
documents.s: The natural environment and the structure of planet Earth

documents.t: Work in pairs. Your teacher will give you eight short newspaper headlines from a Pakistani paper, for example "Smog closes Lahore schools", "Indus flows low at Kotri", "New coal plant approved", "Fish deaths reported at Keenjhar". For each headline, decide two things: which scope area it belongs to (air, water, land, living things, human systems), and which spheres are involved. Be ready to defend one answer that surprised you. Allow 20 minutes.

Define environmental science in one sentence, in your own words. (Remember) Name the four spheres and give one example of each from your own district. (Understand) A pupil says, "Environmental science is just about pollution." Give two reasons why this is too narrow. (Understand) Place these three things in their sphere: the Indus river, Thar coal, the Indus Delta mangroves. Then explain why the mangroves belong to more than one sphere. (Apply)

Environmental science studies the natural environment and the human-environment interaction across five scope areas: air, water, land, living things and human systems. The natural environment is organised into four overlapping spheres: atmosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere and biosphere, with people living inside the biosphere. The Earth beneath is layered into crust, mantle and core, and the crust is where most resources sit. The subject matters in Pakistan because its pressures, unhealthy city air, a strained river system and a warming climate, are already inside every classroom.

I can define environmental science and name its five scope areas. I can name the four spheres and give a Pakistani example of each. I can explain why people are part of the biosphere, not separate from it. I can take one everyday object and trace it through the four spheres.

Walk once around the school building with a notebook. Find one example of each sphere inside or beside the school grounds: the air over the courtyard, the water source or water tank, the soil in the garden or the dust on the windowsill, and any living thing from a tree to a sparrow. Write four sentences, one per sphere, naming what you found and one human activity that affects it. Do not name the school or any pupil.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: Write 150 to 200 words on the following. A colleague tells you, "The environment is not our department. We teach, nature looks after itself." Using this topic's account of environmental science, the four spheres and the scope table, explain what the colleague is missing. Support your explanation with at least two examples from Pakistan. In a boys' high school in lower Sindh, the science teacher takes his Class 9 pupils to the edge of a field near the school. The crop stands in patches: some plants green, some yellow and dying. An old farmer tells them, "Our fathers grew good wheat here. Now the water stands too long in some parts and the soil has turned white in others." Back in the classroom, the teacher writes two words on the board: waterlogging and salinity. "This field," he says, "is not just a farming problem. It is a story about us." The field is a story about people changing their environment, and the environment answering back. This topic is about that two-way relationship, which the course guide calls the nexus between environmental problems and anthropogenic activities, and about how such problems appear at three scales: global, regional and local.

Anthropogenic means caused by people. An anthropogenic environmental problem is one that either did not exist before human activity created it, or existed only mildly and was made worse by it. The nexus is the two-way link: activities change the environment, and the changed environment returns the harm to people, sometimes to the same people, often to different and poorer people, and sometimes years later. The chain usually runs in four steps. An activity, such as farming, industry, transport, energy use or waste disposal, takes something from the environment or puts something into it. The environment responds: water tables rise, air goes grey, forests thin. The response crosses back into human life: crops fail, illness rises, floods damage homes. And the human response to that harm often starts the chain again, as when a failing crop pushes farmers to clear more land. textbook.com.pk A worked example, fully traced. Take the yellow field near the Sindh school. Step one, the activity: farmers in the last century expanded canal irrigation across lower Sindh to grow more food. Step two, the environmental response: canals seeped, fields were watered more than the soil could drain, the water table rose, and the salts naturally present in the soil were drawn up and left on the surface as the water evaporated. Step three, the harm returned: waterlogged and salt-affected soil yields less, and the white crust you can see is the evidence. Step four, the response: some farmers abandon the land or dig tube wells, which can draw up even saltier water. One chain, four steps, every link human and environmental at once. The same four-step structure fits the other big activities. Industry and transport burn fuel and load the air with pollutants. Energy choices, from coal to firewood, drive both local smoke and global greenhouse gases. Waste disposal, when it means open dumping or burning, moves the problem from the bin to the air, the soil and the water. The United Nations Decade on Ecosystem Restoration describes the present situation plainly: there has never been a more urgent need to revive damaged ecosystems (UN, 2021).
documents.s: The nexus between environmental problems and human activities

documents.t: Environmental problems are usually sorted by how far their causes and effects reach. Global issues affect the whole planet, whatever their source. Climate change is the clearest case: greenhouse gases mix through one shared atmosphere, and the World Health Organization reports that about 3.6 billion people already live in places highly susceptible to its effects (WHO, 2023). The loss of biodiversity is the second: the WHO also reports that around one million species face extinction risk (WHO, 2025). Ozone depletion, now slowly recovering thanks to a global agreement, is the third. Regional issues cross borders or cover a region. South Asia shares the smog that builds each winter, the waters of the Indus and its tributaries, and the Himalayan glaciers whose melt feeds the rivers. The Indus system's stress is a regional issue: what happens upstream in one country changes the flow downstream in another. Local issues are tied to a place, though they repeat everywhere. A neighbourhood's burning garbage heap, a village's contaminated hand pump, a school's dusty courtyard, one city's traffic noise. textbook.com.pk The scales are connected, which is the point of showing them together. A local burning heap adds carbon to the global atmosphere. A global rise in temperature shows up locally as heatwaves in Karachi. When you analyse an issue, name its scale, but also ask how it crosses to the others. Common misconception. Many people think global problems are the "real" environmental problems and local ones are too small to count. The reverse error also appears: that only local problems matter because they are the ones we can see. Both are wrong. Global problems are built from millions of local activities, and local people suffer global problems first and worst. The scales are one system, not a competition.
documents.s: Global, regional and local issues and their current status

documents.t: Work in groups of three. Your teacher will give you one week of environmental headlines from a Pakistani newspaper. Sort each headline into global, regional or local. For two headlines, one that surprised your group and one you argued about, write one sentence naming the human activity behind the problem and one sentence naming a connection to a different scale. Allow 25 minutes, then each group presents its two headlines.

Define "anthropogenic" in one sentence and give one anthropogenic problem from your own district. (Remember) Trace the four steps of the nexus for one activity other than irrigation, such as transport or waste burning. (Apply) A classmate says, "Smog in Lahore is a local issue." Give two reasons why the regional and global scales are also involved. (Analyze) Name one current global environmental issue and state one figure from this topic that describes its status. (Remember)

Environmental problems and human activities are linked in a two-way nexus: activities change the environment, and the changed environment returns harm to people. The chain runs activity, environmental response, harm returning, human response. Irrigation-induced waterlogging and salinity in lower Sindh is one complete worked chain. Issues appear at three scales, global such as climate change and biodiversity loss, regional such as the Indus system and winter smog, and local such as a burning waste heap, and the scales connect in both directions.

I can define anthropogenic and use it correctly in a sentence. I can trace a human activity through the four nexus steps to its returning harm. I can classify an environmental issue as global, regional or local with a reason. I can explain how one local issue connects to a global one, with an example.

Find the nearest environmental problem to the school gate, a drain, a heap, a dusty road, a smoky stove. In half a page, name the scale you would call it, the human activity that drives it, and one way it connects to a bigger scale. Ask one person who lives nearby how long it has been there. Do not name the school or the person.

Trace it through the four nexus steps, then explain one connection it has to a regional or global issue. Finish with one sentence naming who bears most of its harm. Every year, teachers from Hyderabad take their pupils on a trip to Keenjhar Lake, the large freshwater lake about two hours away. The pupils see fishermen casting nets, birds wading in the shallows, and thick green plants at the edge. One pupil asks, "If the fishers catch fish every day, why are there still fish?" The teacher turns the question back to the class: "What do the fish need to keep being fish?" By the end of the discussion the pupils have listed food, clean water, shelter and young, and one of them says, "So the lake has to stay a lake." That is an ecosystem: a living community together with its non-living surroundings, functioning as one system. This topic explains ecosystems, why they matter, what threatens them and how they are conserved, and then turns to the natural resources people take from them.

An ecosystem has two kinds of parts. The living parts, plants, animals, fungi and micro-organisms, are its biotic community; the non-living parts, water, soil, air, sunlight and temperature, are its abiotic surroundings. Energy from sunlight enters through plants, which make their own food; animals eat plants or each other; decomposers return the remains to the soil. This one-way flow of energy and the cycling of materials are what make an ecosystem a system rather than a list of species. Ecosystems come in broad types. Forests, grasslands, deserts, freshwater lakes and rivers, coastal waters and wetlands each carry a characteristic community. Pakistan holds examples of nearly all of them: the conifer forests of the north, the thorn forests of the Indus plains, the Thar desert, the rivers and lakes of Sindh, and the mangrove creeks of the Indus Delta. A national assessment using satellite imagery ranks the Indus Delta as the world's fifth-largest mangrove forest and has mapped how Pakistan's cover changed over time (Abbas et al., 2012), which is itself an example of environmental science at work. Why ecosystems matter has a name: ecosystem services, the benefits people receive from functioning ecosystems. The mangroves are a full worked example. Their roots hold the delta soil against the sea and soften storm waves, which protects coastal villages. Their fallen leaves feed the creek food web that supports fish and shrimp catches. Their trees shelter young fish and birds. And they store carbon. The World Health Organization lists clean air, fresh water, food security, medicines and disease and climate regulation among the services biodiversity underpins, and reports that about one million species now face extinction risk (WHO, 2025). textbook.com.pk The threats are the human activities from Topic 1.2, arriving at once. Habitat loss, when a wetland is drained or a forest cleared; overuse, when fish, reeds or timber are taken faster than they renew; pollution, when waste enters the water or air; invasive species, when a foreign plant or animal displaces native ones; and climate change, which shifts temperature and rainfall faster than communities can move. The WHO reports that 35 per cent of the world's wetlands were lost between 1970 and the present (WHO, 2025), a warning directly relevant to Sindh's lakes. Conservation answers each threat with a matching tool. Protected areas, such as national parks and wildlife sanctuaries, hold habitat. Sustainable use rules, such as fishing seasons and mesh-size limits, slow overuse. Pollution control, the subject of later units, removes the stress. Restoration rebuilds what was lost, which is the explicit aim of the United Nations Decade on Ecosystem Restoration, 2021 to 2030 (UN, 2021). Conservation is not the protection of nature from people; it is the management of the relationship between them.
documents.s: Ecosystems: types, importance, threats and conservation

documents.t: A natural resource is anything from the environment that people use to meet their needs. The basic sorting is by renewal. Renewable resources renew themselves on a human timescale if not overused: water in the Indus system, sunlight falling on Thar, wind, the fish in the lakes, the soil itself, and the forests and reeds that regrow. Non-renewable resources exist as fixed stocks that renewal cannot rebuild on any human timescale: Thar's coal, Sindh's natural gas, rock salt from the Salt Range, and groundwater in deep aquifers laid down over thousands of years. The sorting matters because it sets the management question. For a renewable resource, the question is the rate of use: stay below the rate of renewal and the resource lasts; exceed it and it behaves like a non-renewable one on its way out. For a non-renewable resource, the question is the order and speed of use, and what replaces it when the stock ends. The Indus system is the national example: researchers writing in an open-access hydrology journal analyse its water management as a sustainability problem under changing climate and socio-economic conditions (Archer et al., 2010), which is exactly the rate question at basin scale. textbook.com.pk A worked example. Groundwater in lower Sindh. Rainfall is thin, so the water under the fields is old water, recharged slowly. Where tube wells pump faster than recharge, the water table falls and wells go dry or salty. The resource is renewable in name and non-renewable in practice, because of the rate. Management, metering, drip irrigation, recharge ponds, crop choice, is exactly the discipline of keeping use below renewal. Common misconception. "Resources are infinite because nature renews them." Nature renews some things, at set rates, and renews others not at all. The WHO's figure of over 2 billion people living in water-stressed countries (WHO, 2023) describes what happens when use runs ahead of renewal on the most renewable resource of all. Renewability is a rate, not a permission.
documents.s: Natural resources: types, services, issues and management

documents.t: Work in two groups. One group represents a fishing community on Keenjhar Lake; the other represents a factory that wants the lake's water for cooling. Each group lists what it needs, at what rate, and what happens to the other side if it takes that rate. Then find one rule both groups could accept, such as a catch limit, a season, or a closed zone. Allow 25 minutes, then each side presents the rule it accepted and why.

Define an ecosystem and name its two kinds of parts. (Remember) List three ecosystem services of the Indus Delta mangroves and explain how each protects or feeds people. (Understand) Why is groundwater in Sindh behaving like a non-renewable resource? Name the rate that decides the answer. (Analyze) Classify these as renewable or non-renewable: Indus water, Thar coal, lake fish, natural gas. Give one management rule for the renewable ones. (Apply)

An ecosystem is a living community plus its non-living surroundings, joined by a one-way flow of energy and the cycling of materials. People receive ecosystem services from functioning ecosystems: protection, food, water, climate regulation. The threats are habitat loss, overuse, pollution, invasive species and climate change, and conservation answers each with protected areas, sustainable use rules, pollution control and restoration. Natural resources sort into renewable and non-renewable, and the management question differs: rate of use for renewables, order and replacement for non-renewables. Groundwater shows how a renewable resource turns non-renewable when use exceeds renewal.

I can define an ecosystem and name its biotic and abiotic parts. I can give three ecosystem services with a Pakistani example of each. I can name the five main threats to ecosystems and match a conservation tool to each. I can classify a resource as renewable or non-renewable and state the management question that follows.

Make a one-page resource map of the school and its street. Mark one renewable resource the school uses (water, sunlight, a tree's shade) and one non-renewable one (gas, grid electricity from fossil plants, a concrete source). Under each, write the rate question: how much, how fast, from where. Show the map to the school's clerk or caretaker and note one thing they monitor that you had not thought of.

Identify the ecosystem your school belongs to, name two services it provides, and analyse one resource the school uses: is it renewable, at what rate is it used, and what would a sustainable rule for it look like? After the Keenjhar trip, a Class 8 pupil tells Miss Farzana, "Everything we learned is about the government and the factories. What can I do? I am one person in Karachi." Miss Farzana does not answer with a speech. She asks the class to write down everything they threw away yesterday, from the wrapper of a biscuit to the plastic bag that carried it. The lists are long. Then she asks, "Multiply your list by every pupil in this school, by every school in this city." The class goes quiet. One pupil says, "So the heap outside the gate is partly mine." That quiet moment is the beginning of individual responsibility. This topic is about what one person, and one teacher, can actually do, and why it counts.

Individual responsibility begins with a fact from Topic 1.2: environmental problems are built from millions of individual actions, so they can be unbuilt the same way, partly and beginning now. Sustainability is the working test: can this action continue, as it is, at this scale, without exhausting what it depends on? Applied to a person's own habits, the test turns "what can I do" from a helpless question into a checkable one. The practical path has five steps, and each step is a real responsibility, not a slogan. textbook.com.pk Notice. Keep the one-week log: what you use, what you throw away, what runs while unneeded. You cannot manage what you have never counted. Learn. Follow one item from your list: where does the water come from, where does the bag go after the heap. Topics 2 and 3 of this unit gave you the tools: the nexus and the rate question. Reduce. The strongest step, because waste never made is never managed: a cloth bag instead of a plastic one, a filled bottle instead of bought water in single-use plastic, a tap closed while brushing, lights and fans off in an empty room. Reuse and recycle. Give things a second life, and separate what your collector actually takes, which in most Pakistani neighbourhoods means keeping paper, cardboard, metal and some plastics apart from food waste, because the recovery chain buys clean material. Influence others. A teacher's step is the widest of all: a class that runs a waste audit, a school that keeps one clean-water rule, habits that travel home through forty pupils at a time. textbook.com.pk A worked example. Take the biscuit wrapper from Miss Farzana's class. Notice: it is on the list, and so are eleven others. Learn: it is single-layer plastic, the kind most collectors in Karachi do not buy, so it ends at the heap and often in a drain. Reduce: buy one large tin instead of twelve packets, or refuse the bag for one item. Reuse: the tin becomes a pencil box. Influence: the class agrees on a "no wrapper pile" corner for one week and counts the difference. Nothing here needs permission from anyone. All of it needs the five steps. Common misconception. "Conservation is the government's job, not an individual's." Both halves are half true, which is why the idea survives. Governments set rules and run systems, and those matter more than any one person's habits. But rules are made and enforced by people, systems are fed by households, and the culture that tolerates a heap or refuses it is made of individuals. The honest statement is: individual action is not a substitute for policy, and it is not worthless; it is the part that is in your hands today, and the part a teacher multiplies by a classroom.
documents.s: Individual responsibilities to protect the natural environment

documents.t: Work in pairs. For one week, each of you keeps a daily two-line log: one line for what you threw away, one for what you used without needing to. In the second week, agree on one reduce action each, keep the log again, and compare the two weeks. Present the pair's before-and-after counts and name the action that made the biggest difference. Allow 15 minutes to set up, then two weeks of logging at home.

Name the five steps of the individual action path in order. (Remember) Explain, using the nexus from Topic 1.2, why reducing waste is stronger than recycling it. (Understand) Your log shows you buy four single-use plastic bottles on a school day. Design a reduce action and predict what it changes, using the rate idea from Topic 1.3. (Apply) A colleague says individual action is pointless next to factory pollution. Give the honest answer this topic gives, with both halves. (Analyze)

Individual responsibility is the five-step path: notice, learn, reduce, reuse and recycle, influence others. The strongest step is reducing, because waste never made never needs managing. A teacher's influence multiplies a habit through a whole class. Individual action is not a substitute for policy, and it is not worthless; it is the part in your hands, and sustainability is the test you apply to it: can this continue?

I can name the five steps of the action path and give an example of each. I can explain why reduce comes before reuse and recycle. I can run a one-week use-and-waste log on my own habits. I can give the honest answer to "individual action is pointless".

Start one small system, not one small act: with your cooperating teacher's agreement, set up a two-bin separation for one classroom, paper and cardboard in one, food waste in the other, for two weeks. Count the bags each week. Report back the two counts and one thing that surprised you about what a class throws away.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

Run it through the five steps of the action path, and finish by naming the one change you will actually keep, and what would make it fail. Environmental science studies the natural environment and the human-environment interaction across five scope areas: air, water, land, living things and human systems. The natural environment is organised into four overlapping spheres, atmosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere and biosphere, and people live inside the biosphere, not beside it. Environmental problems are anthropogenic: human activities change the environment through the four-step nexus of activity, environmental response, harm returning and human response, as Sindh's waterlogging and salinity shows. Issues appear at global, regional and local scales, and the scales connect in both directions. Ecosystems provide services people depend on, face five main threats, and are conserved by protected areas, sustainable use, pollution control and restoration. Natural resources sort into renewable and non-renewable, and the management question is rate for the first and replacement for the second. Individual responsibility is the five-step path: notice, learn, reduce, reuse and recycle, influence others.

(Create) Take one local environmental issue, such as a burning waste heap or a drying lake, and analyse its connections to the regional and global scales. Conclude by proposing who should act at each scale, and what one individual teacher can actually do. (Evaluate)

b - environmental science studies the environment and the human interaction with it; the other options each describe only one small part. c - natural gas is extracted from rock layers, which is the lithosphere. a - anthropogenic means caused by people, from the Greek for human. d - canal seepage and over-watering raised the water table and drew salts to the surface; that is the worked example in Topic 1.2. c - smog shared across several countries at once is regional; its sources and effects cross borders. b - the living (biotic) and non-living (abiotic) parts; producers and consumers are only two roles within the living part. b - the mangroves' roots soften storm waves and hold the delta soil, protecting coastal villages. d - when use exceeds recharge, a renewable resource behaves as non-renewable; the rate of pumping decides. a - reduce; waste never made needs no collection, separation or processing. a - reduce; the tin replaces many wrappers, so the waste is never created.

Model: A street is part of the biosphere people live in; its air, dust, drainage and shade are the surroundings that affect living things, so it is an environment. Marks (2): 1 for placing people inside the biosphere; 1 for naming a street-level environmental element (air, dust, drainage). Model: hydrosphere, the boiled water; lithosphere, the gas that burned; biosphere, the tea leaf that grew; atmosphere, the steam and the rain that watered the leaf. Marks (4): 1 per correct sphere with its item. Model: activity, environmental response, harm returning, human response; the salt crust is the environmental response (or the returning harm if framed as lost yield; accept either with a reason). Marks (3): 1 for the four steps in order; 1 for placing the crust; 1 for the one-sentence reason. Model: first, the sources are shared, vehicle and industrial emissions and crop burning occur across the region; second, the air itself crosses borders, so one city's emissions add to another's. Marks (2): 1 per reason. Model: global greenhouse gases raise temperatures everywhere; locally this appears as heatwaves, such as Karachi's, or changed rainfall. Marks (2): 1 for the mechanism; 1 for a specific Pakistani example. Model: renewable resources renew on a human timescale if not overused, such as Indus water or lake fish; non-renewable resources are fixed stocks, such as Thar coal or natural gas. Marks (2): 1 for the distinction; 1 for both examples. Model: recharge is slow because rainfall is thin, and pumping exceeds it, so the water table falls; the rate of pumping versus the rate of recharge decides. Marks (2): 1 for the pumping-versus-recharge explanation; 1 for naming the deciding rate. Model: habitat loss to protected areas; overuse to sustainable use rules such as catch limits; pollution to pollution control. Justification example: a catch limit slows overuse because it caps the take below renewal. Marks (3): 1 per correct match; the justification must link tool to threat. Model: reduce prevents the waste from existing, while reuse and recycle only manage waste that has already been made; preventing beats managing. Marks (2): 1 for the prevention-versus-management contrast; 1 for clarity. Model: part one, individual action is not a substitute for policy, and factories and systems matter more than habits; part two, individual action is not worthless, because systems are fed by households and a teacher multiplies habits through a class. Marks (2): 1 per half, both needed.

The four topics form one arc. Topic 1.1 gives the map (the field, the spheres). Topic 1.2 gives the engine (the nexus and the scales). Topic 1.3 applies both to living systems and resources. Topic 1.4 hands the whole thing to the learner. Teach them in order across the two weeks the guide allows, and keep the worked examples alive across topics: the Karachi air from 1.1 returns as a scale example in 1.2, and the Keenjhar Lake from 1.3 returns as the resource-rate debate and the ecosystem map.

The guide names interactive lectures, seminars, group work, case studies, presentations, guided reading, home study and individual tutorials. This unit leans on three of them: interactive lecture for the four spheres and the nexus (pause every few minutes and ask for a local example), group work for the headline sort and the resource debate, and case study for the waterlogging chain and the mangrove services. The home-study element is the one-week log in Topic 1.4, which needs to be set up in week one, not discovered in week two.

"The environment means nature far away." Probe with the school itself: ask what the air over the courtyard, the water tank and the soil in the garden have in common with a forest. The answer you want is that both are surroundings affecting living things, which is the definition. "Global problems are the real ones; local ones are too small." Probe with the multiplication question from Topic 1.4: one wrapper times one class times one city. The scales are one system. "Resources are infinite because nature renews them." Probe with the tube-well example: if renewal is a rate, what happens when pumping is a faster rate? The word to land on is "rate", not "shortage". "Conservation is the government's job." Do not dismiss this; half of it is true. The honest answer, which the unit teaches, is that policy matters more and individual action still counts, especially a teacher's.

Topic 1.1, Sort the questions (20 minutes, pairs). The trap is sorting by topic word ("smog" to air) without asking which spheres are involved. Push for the second question. Keep eight headlines ready on cards; Dawn and The News environment pages give a week's worth. Topic 1.2, Headline scale sort (25 minutes, groups of three). Arguments are the point. The judgement call between regional and global (Indus water stress, for example) is where the learning happens. Ask the arguing group to state the rule they used, not just the answer. Topic 1.3, Resource rate debate (25 minutes, two groups). Assign roles firmly; pupils argue better as fishers or managers than as themselves. The debrief question is the one to protect time for: what rule could both sides accept, and why? Topic 1.4, The one-week audit (set up in 15 minutes, two weeks at home). The setup session must produce a real, shared log format, two lines a day. Pairs compare weeks in the follow-up session; the before-and-after counts are the presentation.

Each topic carries a practicum task, and Topic 1.4's two-bin classroom trial is the unit's main practical: it needs the cooperating teacher's agreement, two weeks, and nothing else. The guide allocates a practical hour each week under the (2-1) credit split; the audit and the trial are its natural carriers in this unit. Debrief all four tasks in the last session of the unit, because Unit 2 (water and waste) picks up exactly where the log and the trial leave off.

Unit 1 ended with a rate: use below renewal. This unit follows the two things a city moves most, water and waste, and shows what happens when that rate is exceeded on both sides: too little clean water in, too much polluted water and solid waste out. It runs from the global water balance to a hospital's sharps bin, and every scale in between.

By the end of this unit you should be able to: Describe the distribution of water on Earth, and explain why a flooded district can still be water-scarce. Describe Pakistan's water resources and the challenges to its water security. Explain the sources, types, impacts and remedies of water pollution. Explain how industrial effluents are treated and recycled. Apply the principles of municipal solid waste management, including the waste hierarchy. Distinguish hazardous hospital and industrial waste from ordinary waste, and describe how each is managed.
Unit 1 (natural resources, the human-activity nexus, the rate question). You should be able to name a renewable resource and explain what exceeding its renewal rate does.
Water on Earth, and in Pakistan Water pollution and industrial effluents Solid and hazardous waste

Work the topics in order: the first sets the supply, the second the pollution, the third the waste stream, and each builds on the one before. Keep your Unit 1 waste log running: Topic 2.3 asks you to re-read it as a waste stream rather than a personal habit. The activities need a water bill, a map of your neighbourhood and your school's bins, all ordinary things.

After the 2022 floods, a teacher in a village near Khairpur gives her class a puzzle. "Three months ago," she says, "this district was under water. Sindh had a third of the country drowned. And this week, the tanker driver says the neighbourhood tank is running low and the price has gone up." A pupil asks the question the whole class is thinking: "How can we have too much water and too little water at the same time?" That question is this topic. The answer has two halves: most of Earth's water is not usable where and when people need it, and water security is not about how much water a country receives, but about how much clean water reaches people reliably.

Start with the global picture, drawn as 100 droplets. The United States Geological Survey puts the oceans at about 96.5 per cent of all Earth's water, so call it 97 droplets of salt (USGS, 2019). Of the roughly 3 that are fresh, more than two-thirds is locked in ice caps and glaciers, and most of the rest sits underground. The share in rivers and lakes, the water people can see, pump and treat cheaply, is a small fraction of one droplet. There is a great deal of water on Earth; there is very little of it in the form, the place and the season that a household, a field or a city needs. textbook.com.pk That is why the Khairpur puzzle has an answer. The flood delivered a huge volume of the wrong water, salty in places, contaminated everywhere, arriving in weeks and leaving destruction, while the tanks and wells that supply daily drinking water depend on a steady, clean supply the flood did not provide. Scarcity is a match between need and usable supply, not a count of litres that fell. Pakistan's water resources are dominated by one system. The Indus and its tributaries, fed by snowmelt and glacial melt and monsoon rain, carry most of the country's surface water; the Indus basin irrigation system is among the largest in the world. Beneath it lie aquifers, recharged slowly, and along the coast the Arabian Sea. Rainfall is uneven: high in the north, thin in Sindh and Balochistan. Researchers analysing the basin describe Pakistan's water resources as already highly stressed, by the ratio of withdrawals to runoff and by per-capita availability, and increasingly so with population growth (Archer et al., 2010). textbook.com.pk Water scarcity is usually measured per person. As Pakistan's population has grown, the same river system now serves far more people than it served a generation ago, and researchers describe its resources as already highly stressed by per-capita water availability (Archer et al., 2010). The World Health Organization reports that over 2 billion people worldwide already live in water-stressed countries (WHO, 2023). Quality is the second half of security. A well can be abundant and still unsafe. In Taluka Chachro, in the Thar desert, researchers tested thirty-two groundwater samples and found the physicochemical parameters, including total dissolved solids, exceeded WHO drinking-water guideline levels (Samtio et al., 2022). Water security, in the definition this course uses, is reliable access to water of acceptable quality and quantity for health and livelihoods. Quantity and quality fail separately, and a country must manage both. A worked example. Read a household water bill or a neighbourhood tanker price in Hyderabad, and answer three questions. Where does the water come from (river, canal, groundwater, tanker)? What does the price per litre imply about scarcity? And what happens to it after use, which is Topic 2.2's question. One bill, the whole system. Common misconception. "Floods mean there is no water scarcity." A flood is a timing and quality failure, not a supply success. The opposite error is also common: "nothing can be done, it is all climate." Both halves are wrong: storage, metering, pricing, treatment and leak repair are all management levers that work whatever the sky does.
documents.s: Global water distribution, Pakistan's water resources, and water security

documents.t: Work in groups of four. Your teacher gives each group 100 small counters (beans, pebbles or bottle caps). Sort them into salt water, ice, groundwater and surface water to match the figure. Then, on paper, split your group's "usable" share among four uses a household makes in a day: drinking and cooking, washing, latrine flushing, and the garden or animals. Argue for your split and defend it to another group. Allow 25 minutes.

Of every 100 units of Earth's water, roughly how many are salt water, and where is most of the fresh water held? (Remember) Explain, in two sentences, how a flooded district can still face drinking-water scarcity. (Understand) A colleague says Pakistan's water problem is only about rainfall. Use two other parts of the system to show what the statement misses. (Analyze) What did the Chachro study find about Thar's groundwater, and which half of water security does it fail, quantity or quality? (Apply)

About 97 per cent of Earth's water is salt; most fresh water is ice and groundwater, and the visible rivers and lakes are a fraction of one per cent. Water security is reliable access to acceptable quality and quantity, so floods and scarcity coexist. Pakistan's resources centre on the Indus system, already highly stressed and increasingly so, plus slowly recharged groundwater that can be abundant yet unsafe, as Thar's Chachro samples showed. Quantity and quality fail separately, and both are managed, not endured.

I can draw the 100-droplet picture from memory and label its parts. I can define water security and explain why it has a quality half and a quantity half. I can name Pakistan's four main water resources and one challenge to each. I can explain the flooded-but-scarce puzzle to a pupil in plain words.

Find out where the school's water comes from: the tap, the tank, the tanker or the hand pump. Ask the clerk or caretaker what it costs per month and whether the supply was cut in the last year. Write half a page naming the source, one quantity fact and one quality fact (colour, smell, taste, or a test the school has done). Do not name the school.

In a settlement on the edge of Hyderabad, a hand pump stands twenty paces from an open drain. The drain carries grey water from houses and, twice a week, a dark discharge from a small textile unit upstream. A grandmother tells the health visitor, "The pump water looks clear, but three of my grandchildren have had loose motions this month." The visitor takes a sample bottle from her bag. Clear, she says, is not the same as clean. That drain and that pump are the whole of this topic in one picture: a source, a pathway, a receptor, and a health effect waiting to be measured.

Water pollution is the addition of substances or heat to water at a level that harms its use by people or by living things. Its logic is always the same chain: a source releases a pollutant, a pathway carries it, water in a river, canal, drain or aquifer, and a receptor receives it: a drinking well, a fish, a swimmer, a crop. Every remedy in this topic is a cut made at one link of that chain. textbook.com.pk The main pollutant types, with their usual sources: Pathogens, disease-causing organisms from human and animal waste. The world's heaviest water burden: the WHO estimates about 505,000 diarrhoeal deaths each year from microbiologically contaminated drinking water (WHO, 2023). Organic matter, food, slaughterhouse and dairy waste, that decays in water and uses up its oxygen, suffocating fish. Nutrients, nitrogen and phosphorus from fertiliser run-off and detergent, which over-fertilise water. The algal bloom that follows, and the oxygen collapse when it dies, is eutrophication. Heavy metals, chromium, lead, arsenic, from industry and old geology; they persist and accumulate. Heat and suspended solids, less discussed but real: hot discharge and silt both change what a water body can support. textbook.com.pk Remedies sit at the three links. At the source: latrines and sewerage, phasing phosphorus detergents, keeping waste out of the drain. At the pathway: treatment (chemical dosing, filtration), protecting wellheads, and sanitation figures show what source control is worth: the WHO attributes 1.4 million deaths a year to inadequate water, sanitation and hygiene (WHO, 2024). At the receptor: boiling or chlorinating drinking water, and closed wells with proper sealing.
documents.s: Water pollution: sources, types, impacts and remedies

documents.t: An effluent is the liquid waste a facility discharges. Textile dyeing, tanning, sugar, paper and steel each produce a characteristic one: tanneries carry chromium, dye houses carry colour and salts, sugar mills carry a heavy organic load. Untreated, the effects arrive down the chain: a drain that kills fish, land that burns crops irrigated with it, and groundwater that carries the metals for decades. Treatment runs in stages, each removing a different kind of load. Primary treatment screens and settles: grit and a share of solids drop out. It is cheap and removes the visible load. Secondary treatment puts bacteria to work on the dissolved organic matter, in tanks or trickling filters, and settles their remains. This is the step that restores oxygen to the receiving water. Tertiary treatment polishes what is left: filtration, adsorption and special steps for metals, salts or nutrients, so the water can be reused or discharged safely. Recycling closes the loop. A factory that treats its own effluent can return it to washing, cooling or irrigation instead of the river, which cuts both its draw on fresh water and its discharge. Pakistan's National Environmental Quality Standards, the discharge limits the law sets, are the yardstick a treatment plant is built to meet; the standards name the pollutant, the receiving water and the maximum concentration allowed. A worked example. Take the Hyderabad drain. The textile unit is the source; primary treatment would settle its fibre bits, secondary would eat its dye organics, tertiary would treat its salts and colour. The household grey water needs a different, cheaper chain, and the well needs a sealed head and a test. One drain, three links, different remedies at each. Common misconception. "Water that looks clear is safe." The most dangerous pollutants are invisible: pathogens by the million, dissolved metals, nitrate. Clear is a colour, not a test. The only clear water you may trust is water that was treated or boiled after it came from a protected source.
documents.s: Industrial effluents: sources, impacts, treatment and recycling

documents.t: Work in pairs. Your teacher gives each pair a sketch map of a neighbourhood with one canal, six buildings (houses, a workshop, a clinic) and two hand pumps marked. Mark every possible source of water pollution on the map, draw the pathway arrows to the canal and the pumps, and mark who or what receives each. Then choose the single cheapest remedy that would cut the most arrows. Allow 20 minutes, then compare maps with another pair.

Name the three links of the pollution chain and give one example of each from your own surroundings. (Remember) Which pollutant type causes eutrophication, and what happens in the water when it does? (Understand) A tannery discharges chromium. Which treatment stage is built for it, and what remains if that stage is skipped? (Apply) Explain why "the water looks clear" is not evidence that a well is safe. Use two different pollutant types in your answer. (Analyze)

Water pollution runs source, pathway, receptor, effect, and every remedy cuts one of those links. The pollutant types, pathogens, organic matter, nutrients, heavy metals, heat and silt, each pair a usual source with a matching impact and remedy. Industrial effluents carry a concentrated mix and are treated in stages, primary for solids, secondary for organics, tertiary for metals, salts and colour, after which the water can be recycled instead of discharged. Clear water is not tested water: the deadliest pollutants are invisible.

I can name the three links of the pollution chain and a remedy at each link. I can match each of the five pollutant types to its usual source and impact. I can explain the three treatment stages and what each removes. I can explain why water recycling serves both the factory and the river.

Find the school's nearest drain or watercourse. Walk ten minutes along it, note what enters it (pipes, open channels, dumped waste) and where it goes. Draw the chain, source, pathway, receptor, for the two biggest inputs, and name one remedy for each that a neighbourhood committee could actually ask for. Do not name the school or any person.

documents.t: Write 170 to 200 words on the following. Your neighbourhood committee has one budget line for water. Using the pollution chain and the treatment stages, argue for the single best use of that money, and name one thing that should NOT be funded first, with reasons for both. A trainee teacher on practicum in Karachi walks past the school gate at 7 a.m. The sweeper is burning the day's rubbish in a corner of the lane: paper, plastic bags, food scraps and, on top, a cardboard box with a red stripe that has come loose from the clinic next door. The smoke drifts across the assembly line. The trainee has just read about the waste hierarchy, and she now sees three failures in one heap: waste that should have been reduced, waste that should have been separated, and clinical waste that should never have been in the lane at all. This topic gives you the principles that heap breaks: how a city manages its solid waste, and how the hazardous part, hospital and industrial waste above all, is kept apart.

Municipal solid waste is the everyday waste of households, shops, schools and offices: food scraps, paper, plastic, glass, metal, garden waste and dust. Managing it is a system with five stages: generation, storage at source, collection, transport, and disposal or recovery. A city fails at whichever stage it neglects; the burning heap at the school gate is a storage and collection failure before it is anything else. The ordering principle for the whole system is the waste hierarchy, a staircase from best to worst. textbook.com.pk Reduce comes first because waste never made needs no bin, no truck and no landfill. This is Unit 1's strongest step, restated for a city. Reuse gives an object a second life without reprocessing it. Recycle turns material into material, and depends on the recovery chain buying clean, separated stock: paper, cardboard, metal, some plastics. Recover extracts what is left, compost for organic waste, or energy where a proper facility exists. Dispose is the last resort, and even then a lined, managed site, not an open heap. The stakes are real. A study of Pakistan's metropolitan dumpsites estimated decades of methane emissions and leachate from Lahore's disposal systems alone at about 108 million tonnes of carbon-dioxide equivalent, and leachate, the liquid that drains from waste, is a direct threat to groundwater (Ilmas et al., 2026). The WHO reports that 44 per cent of household wastewater worldwide is discharged without safe treatment (WHO, 2024); the solid waste story is the same shape. Segregation at source, keeping the streams apart while they are still clean, is the step that makes every later step possible.
documents.s: The principles of municipal solid waste management

documents.t: Hazardous waste is waste whose properties make it dangerous to people or the environment: infectious, toxic, flammable, corrosive or sharp. The cardinal rule is that it never mixes with the ordinary stream, because a bag of hospital waste in a municipal heap turns the whole heap hazardous. Hospital, or clinical, waste sorts into two streams. The World Health Organization reports that about 85 per cent of health-care waste is general, comparable to household waste, while the remaining 15 per cent is hazardous, infectious, toxic, flammable or corrosive (WHO, 2024). The general stream, offices and kitchens, behaves like municipal waste. The risk stream is what the rules exist for: sharps (needles, blades), infectious waste (dressings, laboratory cultures), pathological waste, pharmaceutical waste and chemical waste. Its handling rules are simple and strict: segregate at the point of generation into colour-coded containers, a sharps container that cannot be reopened, and a covered infectious bin; label and date them; store briefly in a secured area; and hand them to a licensed handler for treatment, autoclaving or incineration, before final disposal. The people most at risk when the rules fail are the sweeper, the waste picker and the nurse, in that order. Industrial hazardous waste, solvent sludges, electroplating liquids, chemical drums, follows the same logic with its own paperwork: characterise the waste, minimise it, store it in contained, labelled space, and transfer it with a manifest so its path can be traced from generator to licensed disposer. textbook.com.pk A worked example. Return to the burning heap. The paper and food scraps belong lower on the hierarchy, separated for the recovery chain and for compost. The plastic bags are a reduce failure from the day they were issued. And the red-striped box is the sharpest lesson: clinical waste in the municipal stream, burning at a school gate, exposing the sweeper, the pupils and the whole lane to smoke from infectious material. Three streams, three rules, one heap that broke all of them. Common misconception. "Waste management means collection." Collection is one stage of five, and it is not the first. The first is what household and shop decide to generate and separate. A city cannot recycle, compost or safely dispose what arrives mixed and dirty; the sorting that happens at the bin decides the fate of everything after it.
documents.s: Hazardous waste management: hospital and industrial waste

documents.t: Work in groups of three. With permission, examine one day of your classroom block's waste (avoid touching anything: use tongs or gloved hands and a spread sheet). Sort it into three streams on the spread sheet: recoverable (clean paper, cardboard, metal), organic (food, garden), and residual (the rest, including anything soiled). Weigh or count each stream, then answer: what share never needed to be generated? Allow 30 minutes, including washing hands afterwards.

Name the five steps of the waste hierarchy in order, from best to worst. (Remember) Why does reduce sit above recycle, and what does recycling depend on that reduce does not? (Understand) A clinic's dressings end up in the municipal bin. Name the rule that was broken and two groups of people put at risk. (Apply) Your city has money for one change: a fleet of trucks, or a segregation campaign with bins. Use the hierarchy and the dumpsite evidence to argue for one. (Analyze)

Municipal solid waste runs through five stages, generation, storage, collection, transport, disposal or recovery, ordered by the waste hierarchy: reduce, reuse, recycle, recover, dispose. Pakistan's open dumpsites show the cost of skipping the hierarchy in methane and leachate. Hazardous waste, hospital risk waste and industrial waste above all, must never enter the municipal stream: segregate at the point of generation, label, store briefly and securely, and transfer to licensed treatment. The people the rules protect first are the workers who handle the waste with their hands.

I can name the five stages of the waste system and the five steps of the hierarchy. I can explain why segregation at source decides everything downstream. I can list the hospital risk-waste categories and the handling rule for each. I can read a waste heap and name the failures it shows, as the worked example did.

With your cooperating teacher's agreement, run the two-bin classroom separation from Unit 1 for one week, then extend it by one stream: a covered bin for anything wet or soiled, kept out of the recoverable bin. Count the three streams at week's end and report the shares. Note one thing the school could change so that the residual stream shrinks.

Write a one-page plan outline, in your own words, for moving the school up the waste hierarchy: name the first change, the second change, who must agree to each, and how you would show the head teacher it is working by the end of the term. About 97 per cent of Earth's water is salt, and most fresh water is ice and groundwater, so water security is a match between need and usable supply, not a count of litres. Pakistan's resources centre on the Indus system, already highly stressed, plus groundwater that can be abundant yet unsafe, as Thar's Chachro samples showed. Water pollution runs source, pathway, receptor, effect, and its types, pathogens, organic matter, nutrients, heavy metals, heat and silt, each match a source, an impact and a remedy at one link. Industrial effluents are treated in stages, primary for solids, secondary for organics, tertiary for metals and colour, and can then be recycled. Municipal solid waste runs through five stages ordered by the hierarchy, reduce, reuse, recycle, recover, dispose, with segregation at source deciding everything downstream. Hazardous hospital and industrial waste never enters the municipal stream: colour-coded segregation at generation, secure storage, licensed treatment.

Of every 100 units of water on Earth, roughly how many are salt water? Model: a flood is the wrong water, contaminated and arriving at once, while drinking water needs a steady, clean, treated supply. Security is a match between need and usable supply, not total volume. Marks (2): 1 for the quality/timing point; 1 for the security definition applied. Model: Indus river system, stressed and seasonal; glaciers and snowmelt, shrinking and shifting; groundwater, slowly recharged and often unsafe; rainfall, uneven and thin in the south. Marks (5): 1 per resource (4); 1 for at least two correct challenges. Model: quality; the samples' physicochemical parameters, including TDS, exceeded WHO drinking guidelines, so the water is unusable even if the aquifer is not empty. Marks (2): 1 for quality; 1 for the finding as evidence. Model: source, remedy: latrines or effluent treatment; pathway, remedy: protect the well head or treat the water; receptor, remedy: boil or chlorinate drinking water. Marks (3): 1 per link with its remedy. Model: primary removes settleable solids; secondary removes dissolved organic matter biologically; tertiary removes metals, salts, nutrients or colour. Marks (3): 1 per stage. Model: pathogens are invisible and cause disease; dissolved heavy metals or nitrate are invisible and toxic or persistent; clarity says nothing about either. Marks (2): 1 per pollutant type used correctly. Model: the factory cuts its fresh-water draw and its discharge volume, and the river receives a smaller, cleaner load, so both the supply side and the pollution side of security improve. Marks (2): 1 for the factory benefit; 1 for the river benefit. Model: waste never made needs no collection, sorting or processing, and recycling depends on clean separated material arriving, which reduce does not. Marks (2): 1 for the no-management-needed point; 1 for the dependency point. Model: sharps, infectious waste, pharmaceutical waste (also pathological or chemical); sharps go in a sealed, puncture-proof container that cannot be reopened, handed to a licensed handler. Marks (3): 1 for three categories; 2 for the full sharps rule. Model: argue for segregation, because the hierarchy's later steps, recycling, composting, safe disposal, all collapse on mixed waste, and trucks alone move the problem to the dumpsite, where the unit's leachate and methane evidence shows it does not disappear. Marks (3): 1 for a clear choice; 1 for hierarchy-based reasoning; 1 for use of the dumpsite evidence.
