The three topics run supply, pollution, waste. Topic 2.1 sets the water frame (the 100-droplet picture and water security); 2.2 follows the water out (pollution and treatment); 2.3 turns to the solid stream. Hold the worked examples together: the Hyderabad drain from 2.2 returns in 2.3's burning heap, and the Unit 1 waste log returns in the bin audit. Teach in order across the two weeks the guide allows.

The guide names interactive lectures, seminars, group work, case studies, presentations, guided reading, home study and individual tutorials. This unit leans on case study (the flooded-but-scarce puzzle, the Chachro study, the burning heap) and guided reading of two figures (the 100-droplet strip and the waste hierarchy staircase). The home-study element is the water bill or tanker-price question in Topic 2.1, which needs one adult conversation at home, not a special trip.

"Floods mean no scarcity." Probe with the 100-droplet picture: which droplet did the flood deliver, and which droplet does a household drink from? The answer separates volume from usable supply. "Clear water is safe water." Probe with two invisible pollutant types, pathogens and dissolved metals. Ask what a sample bottle would need to test that the eye cannot. "Waste management means collection." Probe with the five stages: what happens before the truck, and what happens after it? The heap at the gate is a storage failure, not a truck shortage. "Hospital waste is just like household waste." Do not argue; walk the chain. Who touches the bag between the clinic and the dump? The sweeper and the picker answer the question for you.

Topic 2.1, The 100-droplet class (25 minutes, groups of four). Counters make the abstract share physical. The argument to protect time for is the household split: groups discover that the visible-water droplet cannot serve four uses generously, which is the whole point. Topic 2.2, Trace the drain (20 minutes, pairs). The map is the tool. Watch for pairs that mark receptors (wells, pumps) but forget pathways (seepage into ground). Ask: how does the pollutant travel from that pipe to that pump? Topic 2.3, Bin audit, three streams (30 minutes, groups of three). Safety first: tongs or gloved hands, a spread sheet, no clinical or sharp material, and handwashing after. If the school's waste is not safe to audit, use photographs of a sorted heap instead. The debrief question is: what share never needed to be generated?

Topic 2.3's practicum extends the Unit 1 two-bin trial with a third stream, which is the unit's main practical. The guide's (2-1) practical hour can also carry the water-source walk in Topic 2.1. Debrief both in the unit's last session; the water findings feed Unit 3's hazards work, and the waste findings return in Unit 5's governance discussion of the rules behind the bins.

Unit 2 followed water and waste. This unit turns to what surrounds everyone, all the time: the air and the sound, and then to the field that grew up to manage their dangers: health, safety and environment. It ends with the one tool that organises everything after it, the risk management cycle, which Unit 4 will take into whole workplaces.

By the end of this unit you should be able to: Explain the causes, effects and control strategies of air pollution. Explain the sources, human health impacts and control measures of noise pollution. Describe the HSE field and its idea of a hazard. Classify hazards as physical, mechanical, biological, chemical or psychological. Explain the link between health and environment, and what environmental safety means. Apply the hazard identification and risk management process to a real situation.
Units 1 and 2 (the human-activity nexus; the source-pathway-receptor logic of pollution). The air-pollution chain in Topic 3.1 reuses Unit 2's chain with air in place of water.
Air pollution Noise pollution Hazards in health, safety and environment Risk assessment and management

Work the topics in order: two pollution topics first, then the hazard framework they feed into, then the risk cycle that answers them. The activities use a phone (an air quality app and a sound meter app) and one walk around a building. Keep the notes: Unit 4's workplace audit builds directly on Topic 3.4's risk scoring.

Every winter, schools in Lahore watch the sky turn the colour of dishwater. In November, Miss Farzana's cousin, a headteacher there, checks the air quality index each morning the way coastal people check the tide. On a bad day the AQI passes 300, "hazardous", and the government closes the schools. Her pupils stay home, and the news argues about whose fault the smog is: India's crop burning, the brick kilns, the traffic, the weather. This topic gives you the tools to read that argument properly: what is in the air, where it comes from, what it does to people, and what can actually be done about it.

Air pollution is the presence of substances in the air at levels that harm people, other living things or materials. Its logic is the same chain you met for water in Unit 2, with air as the pathway. textbook.com.pk The pollutants that matter. Particulate matter, PM10 and the finer PM2.5, is soot, dust and droplets small enough to reach deep into the lungs; it is the pollutant most linked to the health burden. Nitrogen dioxide and sulfur dioxide come from burning fuel at high temperature, in engines and furnaces. Carbon monoxide is the silent one: colourless, odourless, and it takes up the seat in blood that oxygen needs. Ground-level ozone is not emitted directly; sunlight cooks it out of other pollutants, which is why it peaks in hot afternoons. Lead, from some fuels and paints, damages the developing brain; there is no safe level. textbook.com.pk How big is the problem? The World Health Organization estimates ambient, outdoor, air pollution caused 4.2 million premature deaths worldwide in 2019, and that 99 per cent of the world's people breathe air exceeding its guideline levels (WHO, 2024). Its 2021 global air quality guidelines set the levels the table's controls are trying to reach (WHO, 2021). The worked case: Lahore's winter smog. A 2026 open-access study combined satellite observations over winter seasons (2019 to 2021) with a survey of the people who work outdoors in smog season, labourers, street vendors and traffic police, and found winter smog critical for both environment and public health in Lahore district (Anwar et al., 2026). A temperature inversion, cold air trapped under warm, holds the city's own emissions over it. The causes are shared: vehicle exhaust, brick kilns, industry, waste burning and crop-residue burning across the region. No single owner, no single fix. Control strategies sit at the three links. At the source: cleaner fuel, upgraded kilns, engine standards, an end to open burning. In the pathway: dispersion helps only a little; the honest answer is that the pathway cannot be cleaned, only shortened by reducing emissions. At the receptor: masks (a good one, worn properly), indoor air filtration, school closures on the worst days, and asthma plans for the vulnerable. A teacher's tools are mostly at the receptor end: the AQI check, the morning timing of sports, the classroom with windows shut on a hazardous day. Common misconception. "Clean air means air you cannot see," and its winter cousin, "smog is a winter problem only, and only in Lahore." Both halves of both claims fail. Lahore's smog is visible, but the most dangerous pollutant there, PM2.5, is invisible particle by particle; a clear sky can still carry an unhealthy index. And the same pollutants burden Karachi's air and the summer afternoons' ozone, so the eye and the calendar are not measuring instruments either. The AQI is.
documents.s: Air pollution: causes, effects and control strategies

For each day, name the band (good, moderate, unhealthy, hazardous), and write one sentence of school advice for that day. Then answer: which day would you cancel the sports day, and which would you move it to the morning? Allow 20 minutes.

Air pollution runs the same source-pathway-receptor chain as water pollution, with six pollutants that matter: particulates, nitrogen dioxide, sulfur dioxide, carbon monoxide, ozone and lead. The WHO estimates 4.2 million premature deaths a year from outdoor air, and nearly everyone breathes air above its guidelines. Lahore's winter smog, trapped by inversions and fed by vehicles, kilns and burning, is the national case. Controls act at the source, weakly in the pathway, and at the receptor, where a teacher's AQI check and timing decisions live.

I can name the six major pollutants and one effect of each. I can read an AQI band and say what a school should do in it. I can explain the inversion that traps Lahore's winter smog. I can name a control at each link of the air chain.

For one week, record the AQI for the school's city every morning at the same time, and one thing the school actually did in response, even if that was nothing. Bring back the seven readings and one sentence on whether the school's response matched the index. Do not name the school.

A school in Karachi sits where two main roads meet. By afternoon, the Class 6 teacher has stopped shouting over the traffic; she uses a hand signal and the pupils copy notes from the board in silence. A visitor asks whether the noise bothers them. "Bother?" says the teacher. "We have stopped noticing it. That is what worries me." She is right to worry. Not noticing is not the same as not being harmed. This topic is about the pollution people cannot see, often stop noticing, and are still injured by.

Sound becomes noise pollution when it is loud enough, or persistent enough, to harm health or wellbeing. Loudness is measured in decibels, dB, on a logarithmic scale: every 10 dB is a tenfold increase in sound energy. A whisper is about 30 dB, normal conversation 60, a busy Karachi road 85 to 95, a pressure horn at the window over 110. Sustained exposure above about 85 dB damages hearing; a single very loud event can do it instantly. textbook.com.pk The sources in Pakistan are the ones you can list from any window: road traffic, pressure horns, construction and generators, loudspeakers, workshops and industry. The health impacts go beyond the ear. Hearing loss is the clearest: it is gradual, painless and permanent. The World Health Organization reports that about 430 million people, including 34 million children, already need rehabilitation for disabling hearing loss, and names loud noise exposure among its causes (WHO, 2026). But sustained noise also raises blood pressure and stress hormones, disturbs sleep, and, in classrooms, measurably slows learning: a teacher shouting over traffic is spending her voice and the pupils' attention at the same time. textbook.com.pk Control measures, once again, sit at the three links. At the source: silencers, horn bans that are actually enforced, quieter machinery, maintenance (a loose part is a loud part). In the pathway: distance, barriers, green belts, and siting, the decision that keeps schools away from main roads, which is the cheapest control of all. At the receptor: ear protection for workers, quiet rooms and, for a school, double glazing and classroom scheduling that keeps the sensitive hours away from peak traffic. A worked example. The school at the crossroads measures its courtyard with a free sound meter app: 72 dB in the morning, 88 dB at the evening rush. The 16 dB difference is not "a bit louder"; it is about forty times the sound energy. The school moves its listening exercises to the morning, plants a hedge along the wall, and writes to the union council about the pressure horns. Three links, three actions, two of them free. Common misconception. "Noise is annoying but not a health hazard." Annoyance is the smallest of its effects. Hearing loss is permanent, cardiovascular effects are documented, and children in noisy schools lose learning time daily. Noise is pollution by the same standard as smoke: a physical agent that harms at a dose.
documents.s: Noise pollution: sources, human health impacts and control measures

documents.t: Work in pairs. Using a free sound meter app on one phone, measure three spots for one minute each: the classroom in silence, the corridor at break, and the nearest road at dismissal time. Record the three numbers, compare them with the ladder figure, and write one sentence per spot naming who is exposed and for how long. Allow 20 minutes, including walking.

What does it mean that decibels are logarithmic? Use a 10 dB example. (Understand) Name four health impacts of noise pollution, only one of which is hearing loss. (Remember) The corridor measures 70 dB and the road 90 dB. Explain why this is not "twice as loud" in energy terms. (Analyze) Your school is beside a main road. Name one control at each of the three links, with the cheapest first. (Apply)

Noise pollution is sound at levels that harm health: hearing loss that is gradual and permanent, plus raised blood pressure, stress, disturbed sleep and lost learning. Decibels are logarithmic, so small number jumps are large energy jumps, and the damage zone begins around 85 dB. Sources are traffic, horns, construction, generators and loudspeakers. Controls act at the source, in the pathway, where distance and siting are cheapest, and at the receptor.

I can explain why 90 dB is far more than "a bit louder" than 70 dB. I can name four health impacts of noise beyond annoyance. I can measure sound with an app and place the reading on the ladder. I can name one noise control at each link of the chain.

With permission, take three one-minute readings at the school: a quiet classroom, the courtyard at break, and the gate at dismissal. Note the time of day for each. Bring back the three numbers and one recommendation you could make at a staff meeting, with the cheapest option first.

After the 2022 floods, a school in Dadu became a relief camp. Within a week, the head teacher had dealt with a scorpion bite, a child's cut from a broken window, a gas cylinder moved next to the cooking fire, and two volunteers who could not sleep. When a health officer visited, she said, "You are running a small HSE operation, you know." The head teacher had never heard the term. "I call it Tuesday," she said. This topic names what she was doing. Health, safety and environment, HSE, is the field that studies hazards to people and the environment together, and it begins with one word used precisely: hazard.

A hazard, in the HSE sense, is anything with the potential to cause harm. The word names the thing or condition, not the event: the wet floor is the hazard; the slip is the incident. Health, safety and environment as a field exists because the three belong together: the same factory smoke is a safety hazard to the worker at the furnace, a health hazard to the neighbourhood, and an environmental hazard to the crops downwind. The World Health Organization describes occupational health as the promotion of the highest degree of physical, mental and social well-being of workers, and lists heat stress, airborne particulates and mental health among its concerns (WHO, n.d.). Hazards sort into five classes, and the sorting matters because each class is controlled differently. textbook.com.pk Physical hazards are energy and conditions: heat, noise, vibration, poor lighting, electricity. A Sindh summer classroom at 45 degrees is a physical hazard, and so is the generator exhaust beside it. Mechanical hazards come from moving things and falls: machinery parts, vehicles, ladders, collapsing structures. The construction site next door is full of them. Biological hazards are living things and their products: bacteria in flood water, mould after damp, insects, hepatitis in clinics. Chemical hazards are substances: cleaning acids, pesticides, fumes, dusts. A farm spraying season is a chemical-hazard season. Psychological hazards are conditions that harm the mind: unmanageable workload, fear, harassment, disaster stress. The two sleepless volunteers in Dadu had a real hazard exposure, by the same standard as the scorpion. textbook.com.pk A Karachi study of a construction site found its most common hazards were excavation work, unsafe working practices and missing or unused protective equipment, alongside faulty, unmaintained machinery (Abbasi et al., 2022). Notice what that list is: one mechanical source, and then human and organisational factors. Real hazard profiles are always mixed.

Health and environment are one subject seen from two ends. The environment is where the exposures come from; health is where they arrive. The same dust that dirties a classroom carries PM2.5 into lungs; the same flood water that ruins a house carries disease into a relief camp. Environmental safety is the management of that connection: keeping the surroundings, the school, the worksite, the water, the air, in a state that does not injure the people inside them. A worked example. Take the Dadu school, one week, all five classes: physical, heat and standing water; mechanical, the broken window and a collapsing wall section; biological, water-borne disease and insects; chemical, the cylinder by the fire and bleach stored with food; psychological, displacement and loss. The head teacher's week, sorted, becomes a hazard register, which is Topic 3.4's tool. Common misconception. "Hazards mean dramatic accidents." Falls and fires are real, but the burden runs through the quiet exposures: heat, dust, noise, stress, contaminated water. The five-class sorting exists precisely so the quiet ones are not missed because the loud ones get the attention.

Work in pairs. With permission, walk one loop of the school building and its yard, inside and out. Find at least one hazard in each of the five classes, write each on a card with its class name, and rank your five cards from most to least likely to injure someone this term. Allow 25 minutes. Handle nothing; observe only.

Define hazard, and distinguish it from an incident, with one example of each. (Understand) Name the five hazard classes and give one example of each from a school. (Remember) Why is "the two volunteers cannot sleep" a hazard finding and not a private matter? (Analyze) The Karachi site study found hazards mostly in practices and missing protection, not machinery alone. What does that suggest about where controls belong? (Analyze)

HSE studies hazards to people and the environment together. A hazard is anything with the potential to cause harm, and hazards sort into five classes, physical, mechanical, biological, chemical and psychological, each controlled differently. Health and environment are one connection seen from two ends, and environmental safety is its management. Real hazard profiles mix all five classes, and the quiet exposures, heat, dust, noise, stress, carry as much burden as the dramatic accidents.

I can define hazard and distinguish it from an incident. I can name the five hazard classes with a school example of each. I can explain why psychological harms belong on a hazard register. I can read a real situation, like the Dadu week, and sort it into the five classes.

Do the hazard-spotting walk with your cooperating teacher's agreement. Bring back your five cards, one per class, and ask the caretaker which one they would fix first. Compare their answer with your ranking and note the difference.

Back from the hazard-spotting walk (Topic 3.3), a pair of trainees argue. One has put "the broken window" at the top of the cards; the other insists on "the uncovered water tank". The first says, "A cut is a certainty; someone will lean on that frame this week." The second answers, "But the tank is a drowning; one child, once, is enough." They have discovered, without being taught it, the two axes of risk: likelihood and severity. This topic gives their argument a name, a grid, and a process.

A hazard is the potential; risk is the chance and the seriousness of the harm actually occurring, in real conditions. The broken window and the open tank are both hazards; their risks differ in both directions. Risk is judged on two axes, how likely, and how severe, and the classic tool is a simple grid. textbook.com.pk Step one: identify. Find the hazards before they find someone. The tools are ordinary: the walk-around inspection, the checklist, the incident register, and the most under-used one, asking the people who work there, who usually know. A Karachi site study found its hazards through exactly such community and site methods (Abbasi et al., 2022). textbook.com.pk Step two: assess. Score each hazard on likelihood and severity, low, medium, high is enough precision for a school. The broken window scores high likelihood, medium severity; the open tank scores lower likelihood, highest severity. Both land in the act-now corner, which is the point of the grid: it ranks, so the loudest hazard is not automatically the first one fixed. Step three: control. Controls have a hierarchy, best to worst: remove the hazard entirely; replace it with something safer; guard or barrier between hazard and person; procedures and training; and last, personal protective equipment. PPE is last because it protects only one person, only while worn, only if correct. The Karachi study's finding, missing and unused protection, is exactly what a reliance on the bottom of the hierarchy looks like in practice. Step four: monitor and review. A control that is not checked quietly stops existing: the guard is removed for convenience, the checklist stops being filled. The cycle repeats, which is why it is drawn as a loop. A worked example, completed. The arguing pair take their two cards to the grid. The window: high likelihood, medium severity, act now; control, board it up (removal, the top of the hierarchy), cost, nothing. The tank: medium likelihood, highest severity, act now; control, a lockable cover (a barrier), cost, one visit to the market. Both done the same afternoon. The rest of their cards, the generator exhaust, the unlit stair, the stress of exam week, are scored, ranked, and two go on the head teacher's desk with dates. Common misconception. "Risk assessment is paperwork done after the danger is controlled." Read backwards, that is exactly wrong: the paperwork is the walk, the grid and the choice of control, done before someone is hurt. A form nobody walked the building for is not a risk assessment; it is a decoration.
documents.s: Hazard identification, risk assessment and the risk management process

documents.t: Work in pairs. Take the five hazard cards from Topic 3.3's walk. Score each on the likelihood-severity grid, agree a control for each using the hierarchy, and prepare to defend one choice to another pair who will argue for a different order of fixing. Allow 25 minutes, then ten minutes of cross-examination.

Define risk, and explain its two axes with the window and tank examples. (Understand) List the five levels of the hierarchy of controls from best to worst. (Remember) Why does personal protective equipment sit at the bottom of the hierarchy? (Analyze) Score these on the grid and justify the order you would fix them: a loose electric wire in a corridor (high likelihood, high severity), a wobbly ladder used once a year (low likelihood, high severity), exam-week stress (high likelihood, low severity). (Apply)

Risk is the chance and seriousness of harm, judged on likelihood and severity, and ranked on a grid so fixing follows evidence rather than noise. The risk management cycle is identify, assess, control, monitor, and it repeats. Controls follow a hierarchy, removal best and personal protection last, and the Karachi site evidence shows what relying on the bottom of it produces. The walk, the grid and the hierarchy are ordinary tools; used before an injury, they are the whole of the method.

I can define risk and distinguish it from hazard. I can score a hazard on the likelihood-severity grid. I can list the hierarchy of controls and say why PPE is last. I can run the four-step cycle on a real building and hand over a ranked list.

Turn your hazard walk into a mini risk assessment: five hazards, each scored on the grid, each with one control named and its level in the hierarchy. Hand the list to your cooperating teacher, and when you visit again, check which controls happened. Record the difference.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: Write 170 to 200 words on the following. Write a one-page risk assessment brief for the school fair: the food stalls, the generator, the bouncy ride and the crowd. Identify at least four hazards across at least three classes, score them on the grid, and name a control for each with its place in the hierarchy. Finish with your monitoring plan for the day. Air pollution runs the source-pathway-receptor chain through the air, carried by six pollutants that matter: particulate matter, nitrogen dioxide, sulfur dioxide, carbon monoxide, ground-level ozone and lead. The WHO estimates 4.2 million premature deaths a year from outdoor air, and nearly the whole world breathes air above its guidelines; Lahore's inversion-trapped winter smog is the national case, and controls act at the source, weakly in the pathway, and at the receptor, where a teacher's AQI decisions live. Noise pollution harms at a dose: hearing loss that is permanent, plus blood pressure, sleep and learning effects, with decibels logarithmic and the damage zone beginning near 85 dB. HSE studies hazards to people and environment together; hazards sort into five classes, physical, mechanical, biological, chemical and psychological, each controlled differently. Risk is likelihood times severity, ranked on a grid, controlled through a hierarchy that puts removal first and personal protection last, in a cycle of identify, assess, control, monitor that repeats.

Which pollutant is a colourless, odourless gas that takes up oxygen's place in blood? (Remember) a) sulfur dioxide b) carbon monoxide c) ground-level ozone d) PM2.5 Ground-level ozone is distinctive because it: (Understand) a) is emitted directly by vehicles b) only exists indoors c) forms when sunlight acts on other pollutants d) disappears in winter In the air pollution chain, "school closures on hazardous days" acts at the: (Apply) a) source b) pathway c) receptor d) cause Every 10 decibels of increase represents: (Remember) a) a tenfold increase in sound energy b) a doubling of sound energy c) ten times the loudness as heard d) no physical change A sound meter reads 70 dB in the corridor and 90 dB at the gate. In energy terms the gate is: (Apply) a) about 20 per cent louder b) about twice as loud c) about a hundred times the energy d) the same, since hearing adjusts Which of these is a psychological hazard by this unit's classification? (Understand) a) a scorpion in the store room b) a broken window frame c) pesticide spray drift d) unmanageable workload during floods The five hazard classes are: (Remember) a) air, water, land, noise, light b) physical, mechanical, biological, chemical, psychological c) source, pathway, receptor, effect, control d) likelihood, severity, control, monitor, review A hazard differs from a risk in that the hazard is: (Understand) a) the potential to cause harm, the risk the chance and seriousness of it occurring b) the chance of harm, the risk the potential c) always physical, while risks are not d) the same thing after an incident In the hierarchy of controls, the best level is: (Remember) a) personal protective equipment b) training and procedures c) removing the hazard entirely d) warning signs The Karachi construction study found its most common hazards were: (Understand) a) machinery failures alone b) weather only c) excavation, unsafe practices and missing protection d) unmeasurable

Explain, in two sentences, why a temperature inversion worsens a city's winter smog. (Understand) Name two reasons why "the wind will clean the air" is a weak control strategy. (Analyze) Name four health impacts of noise pollution, only one of which is hearing loss. (Remember) A school beside a main road asks for the cheapest noise controls. Name one control at each of the three links, source, pathway and receptor, cheapest first. (Apply) Distinguish a hazard from an incident with one example of each from a school. (Understand) Name the five hazard classes and give one flood-camp example of each. (Understand) Why does psychological harm belong on a hazard register, by the same standard as a scorpion? (Analyze) Define risk and name its two axes. (Remember) Why does personal protective equipment sit at the bottom of the hierarchy of controls? (Analyze) A loose wire (high likelihood, high severity) and a yearly-used wobbly ladder (low likelihood, high severity): which do you fix first, and why? (Analyze)

A parents' committee says the smog is another country's fault, so nothing should change. Using the chain and the Lahore case, give an honest answer that names what is shared, what is ours, and what a school can still do. (Analyze) A school beside a main road is told nothing can be done about the noise. Using the three links and the health evidence, write the reply, ending with the two cheapest actions for this term. (Evaluate) Your school becomes a flood relief camp for a month. Write a hazard brief for volunteers: at least four hazards across at least three classes, each with a same-day control. (Analyze) Write a risk assessment brief for the school fair: at least four hazards across three classes, grid-scored, each with a control at a named hierarchy level, plus a monitoring plan. (Evaluate) Integrative: a school downwind of a brick kiln has dusty classrooms, a noisy road in front and an unlit stair inside. Analyse the full situation, air, noise and physical hazards, through the risk cycle, and present one ranked action list with the reasoning shown. (Evaluate)

b - carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin, taking the seat oxygen needs. c - ozone is secondary, cooked by sunlight from other pollutants, peaking in hot afternoons. c - closures protect the receptors, the pupils; they do not touch the source. a - decibels are logarithmic: 10 dB is ten times the energy. c - 20 dB is two tenfold steps, about a hundred times the energy. d - workload and disaster stress are psychological hazards; the scorpion is biological, the window mechanical, the spray chemical. b - physical, mechanical, biological, chemical, psychological. a - the hazard is the potential; the risk is chance and seriousness in real conditions. c - removal eliminates exposure for everyone; PPE protects one person, while worn. c - the study named excavation, working-practice variation and missing or unused PPE, with faulty machinery.

Model: the inversion traps cold air, and the city's emissions, under a warm lid, so pollutants cannot disperse upward and accumulate over the city. Marks (2): 1 for the trapping mechanism; 1 for the accumulation consequence. Model: first, dispersion only moves the problem, it does not remove the pollutant; second, in winter inversions there is little dispersion to help with. Marks (2): 1 per reason. Model: hearing loss plus any three of raised blood pressure, stress hormones, disturbed sleep, slowed learning in noisy classrooms. Marks (4): 1 per impact, max 1 for hearing loss. Model: source, enforced horn bans or smoother traffic flow; pathway, distance, barriers, green belts, or siting the classrooms away from the road (cheapest of all when chosen at planning); receptor, double glazing, quiet rooms, or scheduling listening work away from peak traffic. Marks (3): 1 per link with a correct control; 1 for naming siting or distance as cheapest. Model: hazard, the wet floor or broken frame, the potential; incident, the slip or cut, the event. Marks (2): 1 per definition with example. Model: physical, heat and standing water; mechanical, a collapsing wall; biological, water-borne disease; chemical, cylinder or bleach storage; psychological, displacement stress. Marks (5): 1 per class with an example. Model: the register exists to capture anything with the potential to cause harm; psychological harms meet that standard, are predictable after disasters, and are controllable, like any other class. Marks (2): 1 for the same-standard argument; 1 for predictability or controllability. Model: risk is the chance and seriousness of harm occurring in real conditions; the axes are likelihood and severity. Marks (2): 1 for the definition; 1 for both axes. Model: PPE protects only one person, only while correctly worn, and fails silently when forgotten; higher levels protect everyone by changing the hazard or the path to it. Marks (2): 1 for the one-person/while-worn limits; 1 for the comparison upward. Model: the wire first, high likelihood and high severity is the act-now corner, and the fix is cheap; the ladder is controlled meanwhile by tagging it out of use. Marks (2): 1 for the choice with grid reasoning; 1 for interim handling.

Two pollution topics, then the framework, then the tool. Topics 3.1 and 3.2 deliberately reuse Unit 2's source-pathway-receptor chain so the chain itself becomes the thing students know best; 3.3 reframes the same exposures as hazard classes; 3.4 hands over the risk cycle that Unit 4 will scale up to whole organisations. The hazard walk in 3.3 and the risk brief in 3.4 are one continuous project across two weeks: do not let the pairs change their five cards between them.

The guide names interactive lectures, seminars, group work, case studies, presentations, guided reading, home study and individual tutorials. This unit leans on case study (the Lahore smog episode, the Karachi site study, the Dadu relief camp) and on the two measurement activities, the AQI reading and the sound meter, which convert abstract scales into numbers the trainees produced themselves. Individual tutorials have their natural place after the risk brief: each pair's ranking deserves five minutes of argument.

"Clean air means air you cannot see." Probe with PM2.5: which pollutant carries the heaviest burden, and can you see it? The AQI reading settles the argument. "Noise is annoying but harmless." Probe with the permanent, painless nature of hearing loss and the 430 million WHO figure. Ask: what would we accept if smoke damaged hearing instead of lungs? "Hazards mean dramatic accidents." Probe with the quiet exposures: heat, dust, stress, standing water. The five-class table exists so the quiet ones are not missed. "Risk assessment is paperwork." Probe with the order of events: when was the walk done, when was the form filled? The form nobody walked for is decoration.

Topic 3.1, Read the index (20 minutes, pairs). Have a real week of AQI values ready; Pakistani cities are covered by the usual apps. The judgement to protect is the cancel-or-move decision, which rehearses receptor-end thinking. Topic 3.2, Measure three places (20 minutes, pairs). One phone per pair is enough. The debrief question is the comparison with the ladder figure: where do our numbers sit against the damage zone? Topic 3.3, Hazard-spotting walk (25 minutes, pairs). Safety first: observe only, handle nothing. The ranking argument at the end is the bridge to 3.4; do not skip it. Topic 3.4, Score and defend (25 minutes, pairs, then cross-examination). The cross-examination is the teaching move: another pair argues for a different order, and the grid has to answer, not the loudest voice.

The hazard walk and the risk brief are the unit's main practicals and feed directly into Unit 4's workplace audit. The guide's practical hour can also carry one AQI week (3.1) and one three-spot sound survey (3.2). Debrief all of them together: the same five cards have now been through classification, scoring and control, which is the whole unit in one artefact.

Unit 3 ended with the risk cycle for one building. This unit scales the same thinking up to whole workplaces and the systems that govern them: what goes wrong in factories, on construction sites, in fields and in service workplaces; how management systems are built to prevent it; and what Pakistan's own statutes, duties and professionals contribute.

By the end of this unit you should be able to: Describe the OSH issues of the industry, construction, agriculture and service sectors. Explain accidents, injuries and workplace fatalities, and what a real case shows. Explain an occupational safety and health management system, international and national. Describe safety management, HSE regulation, and internal control. State the duties and rights of employers, workers and government, and the OHS professional's roles. Apply key management and HSE principles, measures and models. Describe HSE statutes and regulations in Pakistan, and how an HSE plan is established. Analyse health challenges within the working environment, the external environment, and the tools and instruments that answer them.
Unit 3 (hazard classes, hierarchy of controls, the risk cycle). This unit assumes you can score a hazard and name a control at each level.

The workplace as an environment OSH management systems Safety management, regulation and internal control Duties, rights and the OHS professional Principles, measures and models of HSE management HSE statutes, regulations and plans Health challenges, the external environment and tools

The topics run from the concrete to the systemic: sectors first, then the systems that manage them, then the law and the profession, and finally the principles, plans and tools. Topic 4.1's sector portraits and 4.2's PDCA cycle are the two things every later topic reuses, so give them the time they need.

In Faisalabad, a trainee teacher's uncle has worked in a spinning mill for nineteen years. He is proud of the job and coughs a little when he says so. "Cotton gets into everyone," he says, waving at the air. "You get used to it." A study of eleven Faisalabad spinning mills found exactly what his wave hides: workers carrying respiratory disease and losing work days to it (Khan et al., 2024). His workplace, like every workplace, is an environment with its own exposures, and this topic begins there.

Every sector has a characteristic hazard portrait, a mix of the five classes from Unit 3. textbook.com.pk Industry (textiles, leather, steel, chemicals): dust and fumes breathed for years, unguarded machines, noise, heat beside furnaces, and chemical handling. In the Pakistani textile industry the prevalence of workplace respiratory illness, including byssinosis, cotton-dust lung disease, is high (Nafees et al., 2019). Construction: falls from height, falling objects, excavation collapse, electrical contact, and the least formal employment of any sector, which is why the Karachi site study found its hazards in excavation, unsafe practices and missing protection (Abbasi et al., 2022). Agriculture: pesticide exposure without protection, machinery injuries, heat, and the same dust burden as industry carried in a more scattered workplace. Services (shops, schools, hospitals, transport): long standing, lifting, stress, violence and harassment, and in health work, infection. The World Health Organization names mental health at work and workplace violence among its occupational concerns (WHO, n.d.). The portrait matters because controls must match it: a dust mask programme answers industry, guardrails answer construction, pesticide training answers agriculture, and staffing and dignity answer services.
documents.s: Workplace environment: OSH issues in industry, construction, agriculture and services

documents.t: An incident is any unplanned event that did or could have caused harm; the injury, the fatality and the near-miss are its grades. The famous case in Pakistan is the garment factory fire in Karachi in September 2012, in which more than 250 workers died, most of them trapped behind locked and barred exits, among the world's worst industrial fires of that decade. Read against this unit's later topics, the case is a checklist of absent elements: no functioning alarm and evacuation, exits locked against theft, stored combustibles, no enforced housekeeping, and no management system that would have made any of these visible. The fire is extreme in its toll but ordinary in its mechanism: several small failures lining up. textbook.com.pk A worked example. Take the uncle's mill and run it through the incident grades. The near-miss he does not report, a cotton bale falling short of a walkway; the injury his colleague carries, a hand caught in an unguarded roller; the fatality the mill has so far avoided; and the chronic illness, his cough, that fatality statistics never count. A workplace's real safety picture includes all four grades, and the quiet ones carry more burden than the loud ones, exactly as Unit 3's hazard teaching predicted. Common misconception. "Accidents happen to careless workers." Carelessness exists, but the record points elsewhere: workers enter unsafe workplaces because they need the wage, not because they misjudge the risk. A locked exit is not a worker's carelessness. The remedies that work change the workplace, not the worker's attitude.

Work in four groups; each takes one sector. In fifteen minutes, list at least five hazards for your sector, classify each into Unit 3's five classes, and name the one control you would demand first if your group were the safety committee. Then each group presents its portrait in ninety seconds. Allow 25 minutes in total.

Name the four sectors this topic covers and one characteristic hazard of each. (Remember) Why does the textile sector's hazard profile centre on dust? Use the Faisalabad and MultiTex findings. (Understand) The 2012 Karachi fire is described as "ordinary in its mechanism". Explain what that means, using the idea of small failures lining up. (Analyze) A farm worker sprays pesticide without protection because the employer provides none. Which control level is missing, and who holds the duty to supply it? (Apply)

Each sector, industry, construction, agriculture and services, carries a characteristic hazard portrait drawn from the five classes, and controls must match the portrait: extraction and masks for industry's dust, guardrails and trench support for construction, training and protection for agriculture's chemicals, staffing and dignity for services. Incidents grade from near-miss to fatality, and chronic illness is the grade statistics under-count. The 2012 Karachi factory fire shows small failures lining up behind a locked door. Workers accept risk for the wage; the remedies that work change the workplace.

I can name the four sectors and a characteristic hazard portrait of each. I can grade an event as near-miss, injury, fatality or chronic illness. I can read a real case, like the mill or the fire, as a checklist of absent controls. I can explain why "careless workers" is the wrong first explanation.

A school is a service workplace. Walk it as one: list five hazards the staff face, from lifting the water drum to exam-week stress, classify them, and name the one control the school's own safety committee, if it had one, should demand first. Do not name the school or any person.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: Write 160 to 200 words on the following. Your cousin is about to join a spinning mill, a construction site or a shop, and asks which is "safest". Using the sector portraits and the incident grades, write an honest answer: what each workplace is likely to expose them to, what question they should ask the employer, and what they should look for on the first walk-through. After the 2012 fire, a factory owner could honestly have said: we had safety measures, we had a fire extinguisher. Such a statement would not be a lie, and that is the point of this topic. An extinguisher on a wall is not a system. A system is what decides, before any fire, who checks the extinguisher, whether the alarm works, whether the doors are unlocked during shifts, and what happens to a manager who lets any of those slide.

An OSH management system is the organised set of elements, policy, organisation, planning, procedures, checking and review, through which a workplace manages its hazards continuously rather than after each disaster. The international reference points are the ILO's Convention No. 155 on occupational safety and health (1981), which obliges member states to build national policy and enforcement, and ISO 45001:2018, the management-system standard workplaces can be certified against. Pakistan's national framework rests on its factory and labour legislation and its provincial enforcement, which national safety reforms have strengthened since the 2012 fire. The engine of any of these systems is the same loop, borrowed from quality management: plan, do, check, act, PDCA. textbook.com.pk Plan: write the policy, identify the hazards (Unit 3's walk and register), list the legal requirements, and set measurable objectives, for example, "all exits unlocked during every shift, checked hourly". Do: put the controls in place with the hierarchy from Unit 3, train the workers, and communicate the rules in a language the floor actually speaks. Check: inspect, measure, audit. Leading indicators, inspections completed, near-misses reported, count what the system is doing; lagging indicators, injuries and fatalities, count what already went wrong. A system steered only by injury counts is steered by its failures. Act: management reviews the results, corrects what the checking found, and raises the bar for the next cycle. textbook.com.pk A worked example. Run PDCA on the burned factory, backwards, to see what was missing. Plan: no policy, no objectives, no legal check, so no unlocked-doors rule. Do: an extinguisher, but no training and no alarm drill. Check: no inspection had walked the escape routes for years. Act: no review had ever asked why previous small fires were extinguished and forgotten. Each element's absence is ordinary; the fire was their sum. Common misconception. "A management system is paperwork for auditors." The paperwork is the residue, not the system. The system is the unlocked door at 3 p.m., the near-miss report that reaches the manager the same day, and the review that changes a rule because the numbers moved. Where those things happen, the paperwork describes them; where they do not, no binder of documents is a system.
documents.s: Occupational safety and health management systems (international and national)

documents.t: Work in pairs. Take one hazard from your Unit 3 school walk, the loose wire or the open tank, and run the full PDCA cycle on it: write the objective, name the control and its hierarchy level, define the check with a leading indicator, and state what the end-of-term review would read. Then swap with another pair and mark one gap in theirs. Allow 20 minutes.

Name the four PDCA stages and one element of each. (Remember) Distinguish leading from lagging indicators, with one example of each. (Understand) Why is a system steered only by injury counts "steered by its failures"? (Analyze) Your school has a fire drill but no alarm test schedule. Which PDCA stage is weakest, and what would you add? (Apply)

An OSH management system manages hazards continuously through the PDCA loop: plan the policy, hazards and objectives; do the controls, training and communication; check with inspection, measurement and audit, preferring leading indicators; act on review and correction. The ILO's Convention 155 and ISO 45001:2018 are the international reference points, with national frameworks resting on factory and labour law. The extinguisher on the wall without the loop around it is what the Karachi fire already taught.

I can name the four PDCA stages and their elements. I can give one leading and one lagging indicator for the same hazard. I can run PDCA on a hazard from my own school walk. I can explain why documents alone are not a system.

Ask whether the school has a fire drill, and then ask the caretaker when the alarm was last tested and by whom. Write three sentences: what exists, what is missing, and which PDCA stage the missing piece belongs to. Do not name the school.

A new safety officer at a Lahore workshop posts the required rules on the wall. Within a month the sheet is yellow and the foreman still has the wire guard off the lathe, because, he says, "it slows the job and the target is the target." The safety officer writes a report; the owner reads it and does nothing. Two months later the guard is still off, and the rules are still on the wall. The sheet was regulation. The foreman's calculation was management philosophy. What stood between them, or failed to, was internal control. This topic is about those three layers.

Safety management is the discipline of running the Unit 4.2 system day to day, and regulation is the state's part in it. The instruments of regulation form a ladder, from the broadest to the most specific: the act (parliament's law, for example factory and labour legislation), the rules and regulations made under it (the enforceable detail), the codes of practice (accepted good methods), and guidance (advisory, not binding). Each instrument answers a different question: acts say what must be achieved, regulations say how, codes say what counts as doing it well, and guidance helps where the situation is unusual. textbook.com.pk Enforcement is the state's half of the bargain: inspections, improvement notices, and penalties when the rules are broken. The Karachi site study's method, community consultation beside site inspection, is a reminder that enforcement works best when the people exposed are part of it (Abbasi et al., 2022).
documents.s: Safety management: regulations of health, safety and environment

documents.t: Internal control is the set of measures an organisation uses to make sure its own rules are actually followed: authorisation, records, supervision, reconciliation, review. In safety terms it is a stack of layers, each catching what the one above misses. textbook.com.pk The top layer is the one everything else inherits: management philosophy, what the organisation's leadership actually rewards. If the foreman's target is output and the owner ignores the report, the guard stays off, whatever the sheet on the wall says. If production stops when a guard is missing, the guards stay on. The philosophy is read off what gets rewarded, not what gets written. A worked example. Return to the workshop and add one layer at a time. A procedure that says "guard off, machine off"; supervision with the authority to stop the line; a near-miss book the owner reads weekly; and a philosophy that counts a stopped line as the system working. With all four, the foreman's calculation changes, because the target now includes the guard. Internal control did not make him careful; it made carelessness expensive for the right person. Common misconception. "Regulation is what makes workplaces safe." Regulation sets the floor and the penalty, but the floor is only as real as the internal control that lives on it. The world's best act does not unbolt a guard; a supervisor with authority and a philosophy that backs him does. Both halves are needed, which is why this topic carries them together.

Work in groups of three. Your teacher gives you four workplace situations, for example "a farm wants to know the legal limit for pesticide re-entry" or "a mill wants to prove its dust controls meet the standard". For each, decide which instrument of the regulatory ladder answers it. Then take one situation and design the internal-control stack for it: philosophy, policy, procedure, supervision, record. Allow 25 minutes.
documents.s: Activity: The ladder and the stack

documents.t: Name the four instruments of regulation from broadest to most specific. (Remember) Why do codes of practice sit between regulations and guidance? (Understand) The foreman keeps the guard off because "the target is the target". Which layer of internal control is failing first, and why? (Analyze) Design the two cheapest internal-control layers a ten-worker workshop could add this month. (Apply)

Safety management runs the system daily, and regulation supplies the ladder of instruments, act, regulations, codes and guidance, each answering a different question, with enforcement as the state's half. Internal control is the organisation's half: philosophy, policy, procedure, supervision and records, stacked so each layer catches what the one above misses. The philosophy layer, what leadership actually rewards, decides whether the others function. Regulation sets the floor; internal control makes it real.

I can name the four regulatory instruments and what each answers. I can list the five layers of internal control in order. I can read a real workshop story and name the failing layer. I can design a cheap internal-control stack for a small workplace.

Find one rule the school has on paper, for example the fire drill. Trace its internal control: who supervises it, what is recorded, who reads the record, and what would happen if the head teacher cancelled it without cause. Write four sentences naming the layers.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

Using the regulatory ladder and the internal-control stack, explain what the law cannot reach and what the workshop must build itself, ending with the one layer that matters most. At the mill gate, the trainee teacher's uncle is asked what he would do if the line were unsafe. He laughs without unkindness. "Do? I would keep working. There are fifty men outside the gate who want my seat." His nephew, who has read this unit, does not argue. He writes down the question the topic exists to answer: what is owed to a worker who cannot afford to refuse?

Occupational safety and health law rests on a triangle of duties: the employer's duty of care, to provide a workplace without avoidable harm, the information, training and equipment that safety needs; the worker's duties, to follow the safe procedures and use the protection provided, and to report what is dangerous; and the government's duty, to set the law, inspect and enforce it. Against the duties stand the rights, strongest for the weakest party: the right to know the hazards, the right to the protection the law requires, the right to refuse work with imminent serious danger, and the right to raise concerns without punishment. textbook.com.pk The strategies that follow are as old as the triangle: give the weakest party the information, the protection and the voice to make the duty enforceable. The goals are measurable versions of the same: every worker informed, every hazard controlled, every refusal investigated, every concern answered. The uncle's answer at the gate is why the rights matter: a worker who can be replaced will not enforce his own safety by bargaining; the system must carry it for him.
documents.s: Duties and rights; strategies and goals

documents.t: The OHS professional is the person the system employs to make its safety work: in Pakistan, factory welfare and safety officers, and the growing corps of HSE officers in industry and construction. The role is a web, not a chair. textbook.com.pk Adviser: brings the hazard knowledge to management's decisions, before the machine is bought, not after the injury. Trainer: turns the rules into a language the floor speaks. Inspector: walks the workplace with the register from Unit 3 and the authority to ask for a stop. Investigator: after an incident, finds the lining-up failures, not the guilty worker. Record keeper: maintains the registers the law and the system both read. Communicator: carries the floor's knowledge upward, which is the direction it travels worst. One boundary defines the profession: the professional advises, checks and records, but the employer holds the legal duty. An officer who is heard is worth ten who are certified; the Karachi fire's factories had paperwork too. A worked example. Give the uncle's mill a real officer, and run the web once. The officer measures the dust, advises extraction, trains the sweepers who clean the byssinosis-causing waste, inspects the guards monthly, investigates the bale near-miss, keeps the register, and tells the owner what the coughs cost in lost days, in the owner's own language, money (Khan et al., 2024). Every spoke is ordinary; together they are the system. Common misconception. "Safety is the safety officer's job." The officer is the system's instrument, not its owner. Where the philosophy layer (Topic 4.3) is sound, the officer's advice is taken and the duty is discharged; where it is not, the officer joins the workers in being exposed, with a clipboard.
documents.s: Roles and responsibilities of occupational health and safety professionals

documents.t: Work in three groups: employer, workers, government. Each group receives the same scenario card, a mill with unguarded rollers and cotton dust, and writes its duties, the rights it must honour, and the one action it would take first. Then the three groups meet and negotiate a single one-page agreement. Allow 25 minutes, then five minutes to read the agreements aloud.

Name the three corners of the duties triangle and one duty of each. (Remember) Why does the right to refuse dangerous work exist, given the uncle's answer at the gate? (Understand) Which of the OHS professional's six roles is weakest in most Pakistani workplaces, and what does its weakness cost? (Analyze) A safety officer's report is ignored by the owner. Which layers from Topic 4.3 have failed, and who still holds the duty? (Apply)

OSH law rests on the triangle of employer, worker and government duties, with rights, know, protect, refuse, raise, designed to make the weakest party's safety enforceable. The strategies give that party information, protection and voice; the goals are measurable versions of the same. The OHS professional works the web, advising, training, inspecting, investigating, recording, communicating, while the employer holds the duty. Where management's philosophy is sound the officer is heard; where it is not, paperwork is the only thing that survives.

I can state the triangle and one duty per corner. I can name the four worker rights and explain why each exists. I can list the OHS professional's six roles with one example each. I can explain who holds the duty when an officer is ignored.

Schools rarely have a safety officer, so someone else carries the role informally. Find out who checks the building, the equipment and the first-aid box, and which two of the six roles that person plays. Write four sentences naming the person's role, not their name.

A student asks the safety officer from topic 4.3's workshop why he keeps the near-miss book at all. "Nothing in it is an accident," she says. He shows her the page: a dropped spanner, a slipped ladder, a smoke smell. "The pyramid says the accidents live under these," he says. "Count the small ones and you have counted the big one's shadow." This topic is the theory behind his notebook: the principles that connect management to safety, the measures that make it visible, and the models that explain why small things are big things in disguise.

Management runs on four functions, plan, organise, lead, control, and HSE borrows them wholesale. Applied to safety: plan the objectives and controls (Topic 4.2's PDCA), organise people, equipment and authority around them, lead by what is rewarded (Topic 4.3's philosophy layer), and control by measuring and correcting. The principles that tie the functions to HSE are old and reliable: safety is a line responsibility, not a staff department; every hazard gets an owner; and what is measured is what gets managed. textbook.com.pk The measures are the indicators of Topic 4.2, led by the leading kind, plus audits and safety-climate surveys that ask the workers what management's philosophy actually is. The models give the measures their meaning. The incident pyramid: for every serious injury, a large number of minor injuries and a very much larger number of near-misses and unsafe acts sit beneath it. The exact ratios are debated; the shape is not. The spanner and the smoke smell are the base of a pyramid whose apex is the fatality. The Swiss cheese model of accident causation: defences are slices of cheese with holes, and harm passes through when the holes line up. The Karachi fire's locked door, missing alarm, stored combustibles and unaudited housekeeping were four holes lining up. Every model of control is an attempt to keep the holes from aligning. Near-miss reporting, formalised, is the cheapest measure in the set: the pyramid's base is where the next apex is visible. textbook.com.pk
documents.s: Key principles of management and HSE; measures and models

documents.t: The organizational environment is the workplace's own climate: how work is actually divided, how pressure is applied, how bad news travels. It is the medium the models live in. A mill where the near-miss book is read has a different organisational environment from one where it is used to blame, and the two will produce different pyramids from identical machinery. The environment is measurable, by the questions workers answer about who gets punished for reporting, and it is manageable, by the same philosophy layer as ever. A worked example. Read the uncle's mill through the models. The near-misses, the dropped bale, the unreported cough, are the pyramid's base. The defences, the guard, the mask rule, the annual medical, are cheese slices with holes (the guard off for convenience, the mask rule unenforced). The near-miss book, if the officer from 4.4 opens one, is the measure that shows both. Nothing new is needed except the reading. Common misconception. "The pyramid's ratios mean small accidents cause big ones." Near-misses do not cause fatalities; they share causes with them. That is the point: the base and the apex grow from the same soil, so gardening the base, fixing the small failures, shrinks the apex you never see coming.

Work in pairs. Your teacher gives you the Karachi fire's four failures as cards: locked exits, no alarm, stored combustibles, no housekeeping audit. Draw four cheese slices, place one hole per slice, and show the arrow of harm passing through. Then add a fifth slice of your own design that would have stopped the arrow, and name which control level it sits at. Allow 20 minutes.

Name the four management functions and match each to one HSE action. (Remember) What does the shape of the incident pyramid tell a safety officer to count, and why? (Understand) The Swiss cheese model calls defences "slices with holes". Explain the Karachi fire in those terms. (Analyze) A near-miss book exists but is empty. Is that good news? Use the pyramid and the organizational environment in your answer. (Analyze)

HSE management borrows management's four functions, plan, organise, lead, control, and binds them to safety by principles: safety is a line responsibility, every hazard has an owner, and what is measured is managed. The measures are led by leading indicators and near-miss reporting; the models, the incident pyramid and the Swiss cheese model, explain why the small and the serious share causes and why defences fail by alignment. The organizational environment, how pressure and bad news actually travel, is the medium that decides whether the models are used or ignored.

I can match the four management functions to HSE actions. I can explain the pyramid's shape and what to count because of it. I can redraw a real case as cheese slices and add a working slice. I can explain why an empty near-miss book is not good news.

Start a one-week near-miss book for the school: any event that could have hurt someone but did not, one line each, no names. At week's end, read the entries aloud without comment and count them. Bring back the count and one sentence on what the pyramid says about it.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

A school fair is planned: food stalls, a generator, a bouncy ride, four hundred visitors. The head teacher asks the trainee teacher, "You did the safety course. Write me the safety plan." The trainee freezes, then remembers Topic 3.4's risk brief, and says, "It is the same walk, on paper, with names and dates." The head teacher says, "One page. Friday." This topic is how that page gets written, and what stands behind it in law.

Pakistan's HSE statute book is built in layers. At the top, the Pakistan Environmental Protection Act 1997 governs discharges and waste, with the National Environmental Quality Standards (NEQS) as its enforceable limits, the same yardstick Unit 2's effluent treatment aimed at. For workplaces, the Factories Act 1934 and the provincial factory legislation built on it carry the classic duties: guarding, ventilation, hours, and the welfare provisions. Labour law, including the Industrial and Commercial Employment (Standing Orders) Ordinance and the provincial labour codes, carries the employment-side duties. After the 18th Constitutional Amendment in 2010, labour and much environmental competence devolved to the provinces, so Sindh, Punjab and the others maintain their own acts and enforcement, for example Sindh's environmental protection legislation. The practical consequence for a workplace is that it must know both its national floor and its provincial detail. textbook.com.pk

An HSE plan is the document that turns the statute book and the PDCA cycle into a named, dated commitment for one workplace. Its steps are few and fixed. textbook.com.pk Scope: one activity, one site, one period. A fair, a mill's dye house, a construction phase. Plans that try to cover everything cover nothing. Hazards: the walk and the register from Unit 3, in this scope only. Objectives: measurable, with dates. "Zero locked exits during operating hours, checked hourly" is an objective; "safety first" is a poster. Controls and resources: each hazard matched to a control at its hierarchy level, with the person and the budget named. Training and communication: who must know what, in which language, before the activity starts. Monitoring and review: who checks what, when; and the date the plan is re-read. A worked example. The fair plan, one page. Scope: the school grounds, 9 a.m. to 2 p.m. Hazards: the generator's exhaust and fuel (chemical, physical), the ride's anchorage (mechanical), the food stalls' gas cylinders (chemical), crowd crush at the gate (physical), lost children (psychological). Objectives: generator sited downwind and fuelled cold; ride inspected before opening; cylinders on firm ground away from flames; one gate open in and one out; a lost-child point staffed all day. Controls and resources: caretaker for the generator, ride operator's certificate, stallholders' briefing, two senior pupils at the gates, one teacher at the lost-child point. Training: a ten-minute all-staff briefing on the morning. Monitoring: the head teacher walks the grounds at 11 and 1; review the Monday after. That is the whole method, and it fits on one page. Common misconception. "A plan is a folder the inspector asks for." The inspector asks for the statutes; the plan is what the workplace writes for itself, because the statutes cannot know where the generator will stand. A folder nobody signed is a wish; a page with names and dates is a plan.

Work in pairs. Using the worked example's six steps, write your own one-page HSE plan for the school fair, but for your own school's layout: name the two gates, the generator corner and the rides' surface. Swap with another pair, who must find one hazard you missed and one name or date you left blank. Allow 25 minutes.

Name the two national instruments this topic places at the top of the statute layers, and one thing each governs. (Remember) Why did the 18th Amendment change a workplace's legal homework? (Understand) Which step of the HSE plan does "safety first" fail to satisfy, and what would satisfy it? (Analyze) Your plan's monitoring line says "the head teacher will check". Improve it in one sentence. (Apply)

Pakistan's HSE statutes layer the Pakistan Environmental Protection Act 1997 with its NEQS, the Factories Act 1934 and provincial factory law, the labour codes, sector rules and the international instruments, with much competence devolved to the provinces since 2010. An HSE plan turns the layers into a one-workplace commitment through six fixed steps: scope, hazards, objectives, controls and resources, training and communication, monitoring and review. The test of a plan is names and dates, not pages.

I can name the statute layers and one thing each governs. I can explain what devolution changed for a workplace's legal duties. I can write the six steps of an HSE plan from memory. I can turn any objective into a measurable one with a date.

Ask for the school's most recent event, a fair, sports day, exam series, and whether any written plan existed. If yes, read it against the six steps and name the missing steps; if no, write the missing one-page plan for the next event, with names and dates.

It is June, and the examination hall has no load-shedding schedule to respect: the fans stop at 11 a.m. By noon, the invigilator has a headache, two pupils have asked for water, and one has put his head on the desk. Outside, the road works add a smell of tar to the still air. Nothing here is an "accident". Everything here is occupational health: the exposures that wear people down without ever making a report. This topic closes the unit with the quiet exposures, the surroundings that feed them, and the toolbox that answers them.

The working environment's health challenges are the chronic exposures, and they map onto Unit 3's classes with a time axis added. Heat: a Sindh summer is a heat exposure for every outdoor and uncooled indoor worker; heat exhaustion has a fatality grade, a truth Karachi's heatwaves have demonstrated at city scale. Dust: the mill lesson of this whole unit, cotton, silica, wood, and its slow diseases, byssinosis among them (Nafees et al., 2019). Noise: Unit 3's ladder, worn for years, becomes the hearing loss the WHO counts in the hundreds of millions (WHO, 2026). Stress and mental health: workload, insecurity and harassment; the WHO estimates 12 billion working days are lost each year to depression and anxiety (WHO, 2026b). Ergonomics: lifting, standing, and the repeating screen, the injuries of posture rather than impact. textbook.com.pk
documents.s: Challenges of health within the working environment

documents.t: The external environment is everything outside the workplace's gate that crosses it: season and heat, air quality, floods, the neighbourhood's traffic and noise, and the supply of water and power. The examination hall's June afternoon is heat outside becoming heat inside; a school beside a main road is the external environment writing its own line in the hazard register. The interaction runs both ways: the workplace also exports its exposures, its noise, its effluent, its commuting traffic, which is Unit 2's chain seen from the employer's side. Safety management that stops at the gate is half a system.

The HSE toolbox is ordinary, and every tool supports one element of the 4.2 system. textbook.com.pk For planning: the hazard register (Unit 3), the legal register (this topic's statutes), the plan template (4.6). For doing: training kits, signs and labels, safe-work checklists, and personal protective equipment, the hierarchy's last resort, used knowingly. For checking: inspection forms, the audit programme, the near-miss book (4.5), and monitoring devices, sound meters, dust samplers, thermometers, which turn exposures into numbers. For acting: the review agenda, incident report forms, and the corrective-action tracker that keeps a fix from being forgotten. A worked example. The examination hall, tooled up. The thermometer (check) reads 38 degrees at noon; the water point (do) is moved inside; the schedule (plan) shifts the hardest paper to the morning; the invigilators' briefing (do) names the heat-exhaustion signs; the caretaker's log (check) records the fans' repair; and the Monday review (act) moves the whole exam series a fortnight earlier next year. Six tools, four elements, one quiet exposure managed. Common misconception. "Health at work means first aid." First aid is the ambulance at the bottom of the cliff. The health challenges of this topic are the exposures that send people there slowly, and the toolbox's real work is measuring them and designing them out, one register line at a time.

Work in pairs. Your teacher calls out eight HSE tools one at a time, for example the near-miss book, the sound meter, the legal register, the training kit. For each, name the management-system element it supports and one workplace situation where it would earn its keep. First pair to agree on all eight reads their answers out. Allow 20 minutes.

Name the five health challenges of the working environment with one workplace example each. (Remember) How does the external environment turn a classroom into a hazard? Give two mechanisms. (Understand) The WHO's 12-billion-working-days figure belongs to which challenge, and what does its size imply for management? (Analyze) Match these tools to their system element: the near-miss book, the legal register, the corrective-action tracker, the training kit. (Apply)

The working environment's health challenges are the chronic exposures: heat, dust, noise, stress and ergonomics, each wearing people down without a single report. The external environment, season, air, water, floods, traffic, crosses the gate in both directions, so safety management that stops at the fence is half a system. The toolbox is ordinary, registers, checklists, training kits, meters, books and trackers, and every tool feeds one element of the PDCA system, which is how quiet exposures get measured and designed out.

I can name the five health challenges and a symptom of each. I can give two ways the external environment crosses into a workplace. I can match any HSE tool to its management-system element. I can tool up a real situation, like the hot exam hall, across all four elements.

Take one school day and log the quiet exposures as they come: the heat of the afternoon rooms, the noise at break, the lifting of the water drum, the stress of the invigilation. Bring back five lines, each with the challenge named and one tool that would measure it.

Each workplace sector, industry, construction, agriculture and services, carries a characteristic hazard portrait, and incidents grade from near-miss through injury and fatality to the under-counted chronic illness; the 2012 Karachi factory fire shows small failures lining up behind a locked door. An OSH management system runs the PDCA loop, plan, do, check, act, with leading indicators preferred over injury counts, under the international reference points of ILO Convention 155 and ISO 45001. Regulation supplies the ladder of act, regulations, codes and guidance; internal control supplies the layers, philosophy, policy, procedure, supervision, records, that make rules real, and the philosophy layer decides the rest. The duties triangle, employer, worker, government, carries the rights, know, protect, refuse, raise, and the OHS professional works the six- role web while the employer holds the duty. The incident pyramid and the Swiss cheese model explain why small failures and serious harm share causes. Pakistan's statutes layer the 1997 Environmental Protection Act with its NEQS, the Factories Act 1934 and provincial law, with much competence devolved since 2010; an HSE plan turns them into one page with names and dates. The quiet exposures, heat, dust, noise, stress, ergonomics, are managed by ordinary tools mapped to the system's elements.

Write the reply using the incident pyramid, the leading-versus-lagging distinction and the organizational environment, ending with two measurements to start this month. (Evaluate) Write the one-page HSE plan outline for your practicum school's sports day: scope, five hazards across three classes, one measurable objective per hazard with its hierarchy level, the training line, and the monitoring line with names and times. (Create) Integrative: the school's June examination series is the workplace. Write the full HSE plan outline for it, covering the quiet health exposures, heat, noise and stress, the external environment that feeds them, and the toolbox, naming actual tools, that makes each measurable, with the monitoring and review lines to close the loop. (Create)

b - the study found respiratory disease and work absence in Faisalabad's spinning mills. b - locked exits, no alarm, stored combustibles and no audit lined up; each alone is ordinary. b - plan, do, check, act, the loop borrowed from quality management. b - regulations say how; codes say what counts as doing it well; guidance advises. b - the duty of care: a workplace without avoidable harm, with information, training and equipment. c - near-misses and unsafe acts are the base; the serious injury is the apex. b - injury counts are lagging; two quiet years may mean no reporting, not no failures. b - devolution moved labour and much environmental competence to the provinces. c - the legal register feeds planning; the near-miss book and meters feed checking; the tracker feeds acting. d - depression and anxiety cost an estimated 12 billion working days a year.

Model: industry, dust and unguarded machines; construction, falls and excavation collapse; agriculture, pesticides and machinery; services, lifting, stress and infection. Marks (4): 1 per sector-hazard pair. Model: fatality and injury statistics count events; chronic illness develops slowly, often after leaving the job, and is attributed to the person rather than the exposure, so it misses the registers, as the uncle's cough shows. Marks (2): 1 for the slow-development point; 1 for the attribution point. Model: injury counts record what already went wrong, so the system reacts after harm; leading indicators, inspections done, near-misses reported, measure what the system is doing before harm. Marks (2): 1 for the reactive point; 1 for naming leading indicators. Model: philosophy, policy, procedure, supervision, records; the others inherit from philosophy, what leadership actually rewards. Marks (3): 2 for all five layers; 1 for naming philosophy as the parent. Model: know, protect, refuse, raise; refusal without the right to know and to raise concerns is blind and punished, so the rights work as a set. Marks (3): 2 for four rights; 1 for the interdependence argument. Model: count the base, near-misses and unsafe acts, because they share causes with the apex, so the base is where the next fatality is visible and cheapest to fix. Marks (2): 1 for what to count; 1 for the shared-causes reason. Model: the locked door, missing alarm, stored combustibles and missing audit were four slices with holes; the harm passed when the holes lined up, and any working slice would have stopped it. Marks (2): 1 for slices and holes; 1 for the alignment. Model: scope, hazards, objectives, controls and resources, training and communication, monitoring and review. Marks (3): all six in order for 3; four or five for 2; two or three for 1. Model: any two of heat crossing into uncooled rooms, road noise and air entering from the street, floods interrupting travel and supply, power cuts stopping fans and pumps. Marks (2): 1 per mechanism. Model: legal register to plan; training kit and checklists to do; inspection forms, near-miss book, sound meter to check; review agenda and corrective-action tracker to act. Marks (4): 1 per correct pairing.
