Seven topics, one arc: the sectors and their failures (4.1), the system that answers (4.2), the layers that make it real (4.3) and the people who carry it (4.4); then the theory (4.5), the law and the plan (4.6), and the quiet exposures with the toolbox (4.7). The mill family from 4.1 returns in every topic, so protect that first lesson; and 4.6's one-page plan is the assessment's ERQ-4 rehearsal, so leave time for the fair-plan activity before the unit test.

The guide names interactive lectures, seminars, group work, case studies, presentations, guided reading, home study and individual tutorials. This unit leans on case study (the mill, the Karachi fire, the ignored safety officer) and on group work for the triangle negotiation in 4.4 and the tool match in 4.7. The home-study element is the near-miss book in 4.5, which runs for one week at the practicum school and is the unit's most transferable artefact.

"Accidents happen to careless workers." Probe with the locked exit and the wage-bound uncle: who chose the lock, and who could afford to refuse? "A management system is paperwork." Probe with the extinguisher-on-the-wall story: which PDCA stage does an extinguisher without a check belong to? "Safety is the safety officer's job." Probe with the ignored report: if the officer is ignored, who still holds the duty? "No accidents means safe." Probe with the empty near-miss book: what does silence measure?

4.1, Portrait of four sectors (25 minutes, four groups). Push groups past the obvious hazard to the quiet one, dust, stress, in each portrait; the ninety-second format keeps the presentations honest. 4.2, PDCA on your school (20 minutes, pairs). The swap-and-mark-one-gap step is the teaching move; gaps found by peers land harder than gaps found by tutors. 4.4, The triangle in practice (25 minutes, three groups). Assign the roles firmly. The negotiation usually stalls on cost, which is the moment to introduce the uncle's question: what is the worker's alternative to accepting? 4.5, Find the holes (20 minutes, pairs). Drawing matters; the fifth slice of their own design is where the hierarchy from Unit 3 gets used without being named. 4.6, The one-page fair plan (25 minutes, pairs). Enforce the one-page limit. The missing-name-and-date hunt in the swap teaches more than the drafting. 4.7, Tool match (20 minutes, pairs). Speed round; keep the tools on cards so the matching is physical.

The near-miss book (4.5) and the one-page plan (4.6) are the unit's practicals, and both run at the practicum school. The guide's practical hour can also carry the sector-portrait research in 4.1, an interview with one working relative. Debrief all three together: the book supplies the hazard list, the plan organises it, and both feed Unit 5's governance discussion of the law behind them.

Unit 4 managed hazards from the outside. This unit follows them inside the body: what a toxic agent does once it is absorbed, how the body defends itself, and how the risk of harm is managed. Then it turns outward again to the frameworks that govern whole countries and the planet: the multilateral environmental agreements, the Sustainable Development Goals, and the environmental laws that carry them.

By the end of this unit you should be able to: Explain the toxic impacts of the major atmospheric agents. Trace the fate of absorbed toxins and xenobiotics, including detoxification and bioactivation. Describe the body's natural detoxification processes. Apply the risk management process to an environmental health risk. Explain what multilateral environmental agreements are and name the major ones. Explain the Sustainable Development Goals and their environment-health targets. Describe environmental laws, policies, guidelines and strategies related to public health.
Units 1-4 (the pollution chain; hazard classes; risk assessment; the PDCA cycle). Topic 5.4's risk management reuses Unit 3's cycle at environmental scale.
Toxic impacts of atmospheric agents Fate of toxins: detoxification and bioactivation Natural detoxification processes Global frameworks: MEAs, SDGs and environmental law

The topics run inward then outward: the agents (5.1), the body's handling of them (5.2, 5.3), the management of the risk (5.4's first half), and the governance frameworks that manage it at scale (5.4's second half, which the topic list folds into one large topic). The CO generator example threads through 5.1 to 5.3; keep it in view.

In a Karachi apartment block, the July load-shedding arrives at midnight and a family starts the generator on the landing, door closed against thieves. By 3 a.m. the grandfather has a headache and nausea; by morning he is in the emergency unit with carbon monoxide poisoning. The doctor's first question is not "what factory is near you?" It is "where was the generator?" The poison came from inside the house. This topic follows that question: how the agents in air, mostly invisible, travel from a source to a target organ and do their harm.

A toxic agent is a substance that harms a living organism when it reaches a sensitive site in enough amount. For atmospheric agents the journey has a fixed shape: emission, inhalation, entry into the blood, and arrival at a target organ, and each agent differs in where it ends up and what it does there. textbook.com.pk Carbon monoxide (CO) is the quiet killer of the worked example: colourless, odourless, and it binds the blood's oxygen seats hundreds of times more tightly than oxygen itself, so the body suffocates with clean-looking lungs. The WHO names it among the pollutants of concern in its global air quality guidelines (WHO, 2021). Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen dioxide dissolve in the airways' lining and inflame them; asthma worsens on high days. Ozone, at ground level, is a lung irritant cooked by sunlight from other pollutants, worst on hot afternoons. Particulate matter (PM2.5) carries the burden the WHO counts: fine particles cause cardiovascular and respiratory disease and cancers, part of the 4.2 million premature deaths a year the WHO attributes to outdoor air pollution (WHO, 2024). Lead attacks the developing brain; no safe level exists. textbook.com.pk Two ideas organise the whole table. Dose matters: the harm depends on how much reaches the target, which depends on concentration and time; the family on the landing had a high concentration for hours. The route matters: the same substance can be a different poison by a different door, and toxic agents are not only atmospheric. Sindh's groundwater carries arsenic, a toxic agent that reaches people by the water route, and a study of twenty-four districts along the Indus found levels demanding health-risk assessment (Alibhatti et al., 2017). Air is this topic's door; Unit 6 opens the others. A worked example, completed. Trace the grandfather's CO. Emission: the generator's incomplete combustion on a closed landing. Inhalation: high concentration, hours of it. Blood: CO takes the oxygen seats. Target: the oxygen-hungry brain. Effect: headache, nausea, collapse. Protection, at the receptor: never indoors; at the source: a vented generator. The chain you learned for pollution in Unit 2 is the same chain, walked inside the body. Common misconception. "If you cannot smell it, it is not poisoning you." CO is the standing refutation, but the rule is general: the sensory system did not evolve to detect industrial chemistry. Detection is an instrument's job, which is why CO alarms exist and noses do not.

Work in pairs. Your teacher assigns each pair one agent from the table. In ten minutes, draw the agent's chain, emission to effect, on one sheet, marking the one link where protection is cheapest. Then each pair presents in sixty seconds and the class votes on which protection saves the most lives per rupee. Allow 25 minutes in total.

Name the six atmospheric agents with one target organ of each. (Remember) Why does carbon monoxide harm without damaging the lungs at all? (Understand) The family ran the generator for hours in a closed room. Explain the dose idea using concentration and time. (Apply) Arsenic reached Sindh's families by a different route than the table's agents. Which idea, dose or route, does its case underline? (Analyze)

Atmospheric agents travel a fixed chain, emission, inhalation, blood, target organ, effect, and differ in their destination and their damage: CO takes the blood's oxygen seats, sulfur and nitrogen dioxide inflame airways, ozone irritates on hot afternoons, PM2.5 causes cardiovascular and respiratory disease and cancers, and lead attacks the developing brain with no safe level. Dose, concentration times time, and the route of entry decide the harm, and toxic agents arrive by water as well as air, as Sindh's arsenic shows. What cannot be smelled can still poison.

I can name the six agents and one effect of each. I can draw the emission-to-effect chain for any agent in the table. I can explain dose as concentration times time with a real example. I can explain why odour is not a poison detector.

Count the combustion sources within one hundred metres of the school gate: generators, kitchens, traffic, burning waste. For each, name the agent it emits most and the protection that applies. Bring back the list and mark the one source the school could actually influence.

A farm worker in lower Sindh sprays cotton without gloves. That evening his hands tingle and his vision blurs at the edges. The health worker who sees him is puzzled by one thing: the pesticide container says the chemical is "weak", yet the man is sicker than the label promised. The puzzle's answer is inside his liver: the body, trying to disarm the chemical, turned it into something more poisonous first. The body has a waste-treatment plant, and it is honest work to learn its plumbing. This topic is that plumbing.

A xenobiotic is any chemical foreign to the body, pesticides, drugs, industrial solvents, pollutants. Once absorbed, every xenobiotic follows the same four-stage journey. textbook.com.pk Absorption: entry by the lung (fastest, Unit 5.1's door), the gut, or the skin, the farm worker's door. Distribution: the blood carries the chemical everywhere, but each has its favourite parking places, the liver, the fat, the bones, the brain. Biotransformation: the liver's chemical workshops, and the body's main defence, rework the chemical to make it easier to export. Usually this works. The reworked product is less harmful and more water-soluble, and the kidneys can send it out: this outcome is detoxification. But the same machinery can also produce, mid-process, a product more poisonous than the original: this outcome is bioactivation, and it is the answer to the health worker's puzzle. Excretion or storage: the finished products leave by kidney, breath or bile; the stubborn ones park in fat and bone, sometimes for years. textbook.com.pk A worked example, two of them. Detoxification: the grandfather's CO from Topic 5.1 does not stay bound forever; the lungs slowly breathe it back out once he is in clean air, and the body's own repair clears the rest. That is detoxification by exit. Bioactivation: some organophosphate pesticides, the cotton-field kind, are weak in the container and are converted by the liver into their active, nerve-attacking form, which is why the sprayer's evening symptoms outran the label. The WHO's chemical-safety work, through its programme on chemical safety, exists precisely because the container's label is not the body's biography (WHO, n.d.). Common misconception. "The liver detoxifies, so a chemical becomes harmless once it is inside." Two errors hide in that sentence. Biotransformation is not always detoxification, as the sprayer learned; and even successful detoxification takes time, during which the dose is doing its work. The liver is a treatment plant with a queue, not a shield.
documents.s: Fate of absorbed toxins and xenobiotics, including detoxification and bioactivation

documents.t: Work in pairs. Your teacher gives each pair one substance card: CO, a pesticide, lead, alcohol. Draw the four-stage journey for your card, naming the entry door, the parking place, the liver's likely outcome, and the exit. Mark the stage where the harm actually happens. Then compare maps with the pair who had the same card. Allow 20 minutes.

Define xenobiotic and name the three doors of absorption. (Remember) What is the difference between detoxification and bioactivation? One sentence each. (Understand) Why did the sprayer get sicker than the label promised? Name the stage responsible. (Analyze) Lead parks in bone for years. Which two stages of the journey does that fact connect? (Apply)

Every absorbed xenobiotic follows the same journey: absorption by lung, gut or skin; distribution by the blood to its parking places; biotransformation in the liver, whose outcome is usually detoxification, a less harmful, exportable product, but sometimes bioactivation, a more poisonous one, as the cotton-sprayer's organophosphate showed; and excretion by kidney, breath or bile, or storage in fat and bone. The liver is a treatment plant with a queue, not a shield, and the label is not the body's biography.

I can define xenobiotic and name the three absorption doors. I can draw the four-stage journey and place any substance on it. I can explain bioactivation with the pesticide example. I can say why "the liver detoxifies" misleads twice.

Ask the school's clerk what chemicals the school stores, cleaners, pesticides, lab reagents, and where. For the two most hazardous, note the door of absorption a spill would use and the first-aid response the school would take. Do not name the school.

After the sprayer's recovery, his neighbour sells him a "liver cleanse" tea, guaranteed to "flush the toxins". The health worker, asked whether to buy it, gives the trainee teacher watching the case a look that means: this one is yours. The trainee has just learned what the liver actually does. She starts there. This topic is the body's own detoxification system, the real one, and the honest answer to the tea.

The body runs a permanent, three-organ waste system, and it needs no help from a box. textbook.com.pk The liver is the hub, working in two phases. Phase 1 chemically reworks the xenobiotic, the biotransformation of Topic 5.2. Phase 2 attaches a handle to the product, a small molecule that makes it water-soluble and ready for export. The phases must stay in balance: a fast phase 1 with a slow phase 2 can raise the bioactivation risk. The kidneys filter the finished water-soluble products into urine, the busiest exit for many chemicals, which is why kidney function matters in every poisoning case. The lungs exhale gases, CO's exit, and volatile solvents. The gut carries out what the liver dumps in bile, and its contents, including its bacteria, can re-release some chemicals, a loop toxicologists account for. What genuinely helps this system is unglamorous: hydration keeps the kidneys' filtration running; nutrition, protein and the vitamins in ordinary food, supplies phase 2's raw materials; avoidance removes the queue's workload, clean air, no smoking, safe water, protective equipment at work; and time, because every exit has a rate. What genuinely hinders it: repeated exposure that keeps the queue full, malnutrition that starves phase 2, and liver disease that slows the whole plant. textbook.com.pk A worked example. The sprayer's recovery, read through the system: away from the cotton field, his exposure stopped (avoidance); the drip rehydrated him (hydration); food restored phase 2's supplies (nutrition); and over days his liver finished the rework and his kidneys exported the products (time). The tea did none of these. Nothing in the system's plumbing is flushed by a drink, and the word "cleanse" describes a marketing hope, not a renal process. Common misconception. "Detoxification means juice cleanses and special diets." The body's detoxification is the organ system above, running since birth. Commercial "detox" products claim to improve it; the honest evidence for those claims is absent, while the evidence for hydration, nutrition and avoidance is the whole of physiology. A teacher's job is not to sell the tea but to name the system it borrows.

Work in groups of three. Your teacher gives each group one "detox" product claim, a tea, a foot pad, a juice week. In fifteen minutes, write the honest label: which organ, if any, the claim touches, what would genuinely help that organ, and what the product's price buys instead. Then present your label in ninety seconds. Allow 25 minutes in total.

Name the liver's two phases and what each does, in one sentence each. (Remember) Which exit does carbon monoxide use, and why not the kidneys? (Understand) Why can a fast phase 1 with a slow phase 2 raise the bioactivation risk? (Analyze) A friend spends a week's wage on a cleanse tea. Using the helps list, write your honest advice in two sentences. (Evaluate)

Natural detoxification is the liver's two-phase rework-and-attach sequence feeding three exits, kidneys, lungs and gut, with a storage branch to fat and bone. What helps is unglamorous: hydration, nutrition, avoidance and time. What hinders is repeated exposure, malnutrition and liver disease. The commercial "detox" borrows the system's name without touching its plumbing, and the honest answer to the tea is the system itself.

I can name the two liver phases and the three exits. I can explain why the phases must stay in balance. I can list the four genuine helps and the three hinders. I can give the honest two-sentence answer to a cleanse claim.

Find out what the staffroom and the first-aid box offer for "heat" and "weakness", the everyday word for feeling unwell. List two items that genuinely help the body's system, water, rest, food, and two claims you would now question. Bring the list.

A trainee teacher reads two news items on the same morning. The first: another round of global climate talks ends with a promise to "pursue efforts" toward limiting warming. The second: a union council in her district cannot say which law, if any, covers the drain behind the school. She asks her tutor the fair question: what do the world's agreements have to do with that drain? This topic is the answer: the same risk management she already knows, run at planetary scale, and the laws that carry it down to the drain.

Risk management at environmental scale is Unit 3's cycle enlarged: identify the hazard (arsenic in a district's wells, PM2.5 in a city's air), assess the risk (who is exposed, at what dose, with what severity), control it (Unit 3's hierarchy still applies: remove the exposure, treat the water, clean the air), and monitor and review (test again, measure again). The management options have names worth learning: avoid the exposure altogether, reduce it by treatment or control, transfer the burden, insurance, compensation, and accept it knowingly when the cost of removing it exceeds the harm. A school near a busy road can avoid (relocate the playing time), reduce (filtration, green belts), transfer (health cover for asthmatic staff), or accept (with the AQI watch running), and the honest choice is usually a mix.

A multilateral environmental agreement, or MEA, is a treaty among many states that commits them to manage a shared environmental problem. States negotiate, sign, ratify, and then report against their commitments, which is what makes an MEA more than a press release. The major ones a teacher should recognise: textbook.com.pk Stockholm 1972, the first world environment conference, where the framework began. Basel 1989, controls the cross-border trade in hazardous waste. Rio 1992, the Earth Summit, produced the climate convention (UNFCCC) and the biodiversity convention. Stockholm POPs 2001, bans or restricts persistent organic pollutants, the long-lived chemicals that build up in bodies; researchers note its monitoring challenge, that POPs harm even at low levels, which is exactly why it exists (Guardans & Castro-Jimenez, 2013). Minamata 2013, controls mercury, named for the Japanese bay whose poisoning taught the world the word. Paris 2015, the climate agreement: hold warming well below 2 degrees and pursue 1.5, through five-yearly national pledges, adopted by 195 parties (UN, n.d.).

The Sustainable Development Goals, adopted by all United Nations member states in 2015, are seventeen goals for 2030, and this course lives inside half of them: SDG 3 (health), 6 (water and sanitation), 7 (clean energy), 11 (sustainable cities), 12 (responsible consumption), 13 (climate action) and 15 (life on land) (UN, 2015). Each goal carries targets and indicators, which is what turns a wish into something a ministry can be asked about. textbook.com.pk

Pakistan's framework carries the same architecture down to the drain. The Pakistan Environmental Protection Act 1997 is the statute, with the National Environmental Quality Standards (NEQS) as its enforceable limits, the yardstick Unit 2's effluent treatment aimed at. Under it sit the provincial environmental protection acts and agencies since the 2010 devolution, and the National Climate Change Policy, which sets the strategies, mitigation and adaptation, that the Paris pledges report against. Policies state goals, laws make them enforceable, guidelines tell how, and strategies sequence the work; the drain behind the school is covered by the NEQS and the provincial agency's complaint desk, which is the practical answer to the trainee's question. A worked example. Run the full stack on arsenic. The hazard is identified (Alibhatti et al., 2017, twenty-four districts); the risk is assessed (who drinks the water); the controls are the hierarchy (safe-source substitution, treatment, testing); and the governance stack above it, SDG 6's water target, Pakistan's drinking-water quality standards, the provincial agency's testing duty, is what makes the control someone's legal job rather than a family's private misfortune. Risk management without law is advice; law without risk management is paper; the course needs both. Common misconception. "International agreements are toothless talk shops." An MEA has no police, which is a real limit; but its reporting cycles, its lists of banned chemicals and its funding mechanisms change what states do, and the POPs banned under Stockholm 2001 are measurably fewer in bodies than they were. The honest statement is slower and stronger than the cynicism: MEAs work at the speed of reporting cycles, not at the speed of headlines.
documents.s: Environmental laws, policies, guidelines and strategies related to public health

documents.t: Work in groups of four. Build the MEA timeline on the classroom wall from six cards your teacher shuffles, each naming an agreement and its year without its subject. Place them, then match each to its subject, then add one card of your own: the next agreement you would want, its year, and the problem it would control. Allow 25 minutes, then a gallery walk.

Name the four steps of the risk management cycle and the four management options. (Remember) What makes an MEA more than a press release? (Understand) Why does the Stockholm POPs convention exist, in terms of what the chemicals do in bodies? (Analyze) The drain behind the school: name the statute, the standard and the office that answer the trainee's question. (Apply)

Risk management at environmental scale is the same cycle, identify, assess, control, monitor, with the options avoid, reduce, transfer, accept. Multilateral environmental agreements commit states to manage shared problems through negotiation, ratification and reporting: Stockholm 1972, Basel 1989, Rio 1992, Stockholm POPs 2001, Minamata 2013 and Paris 2015 are the markers. The SDGs turn the goals into targets and indicators, half of them this course's own ground. Pakistan's stack carries it down: PEPA 1997, the NEQS, the provincial agencies and the climate policy, which is how a global agreement reaches a drain.

I can run the risk cycle at environmental scale with the four options. I can name six MEAs with years and subjects. I can name the seven environment-health SDGs with one target each. I can trace a local problem to its statute, standard and office.

Take the school's nearest environmental complaint, the drain, the dust, the noise. Find out which office owns it, the union council, the provincial EPA, the water board, and which law or standard that office would cite. Write the three-line answer: problem, office, instrument. Do not name the school.

Atmospheric agents travel emission, inhalation, blood, target organ, effect, and differ in destination and damage: CO takes the blood's oxygen seats, sulfur and nitrogen dioxide inflame airways, ozone irritates on hot afternoons, PM2.5 causes cardiovascular and respiratory disease and cancers, lead attacks the developing brain with no safe level. Dose, concentration times time, and the route of entry decide the harm, and toxic agents arrive by water as well as air. Absorbed xenobiotics follow absorption, distribution, biotransformation, whose outcome is usually detoxification but sometimes bioactivation, then excretion or storage. Natural detoxification is the liver's two-phase sequence feeding the kidneys, lungs and gut, helped by hydration, nutrition, avoidance and time, and hindered by repeated exposure, malnutrition and liver disease. Risk management at scale runs the same cycle with the options avoid, reduce, transfer, accept. Multilateral environmental agreements, Stockholm 1972 to Paris 2015, commit states through reporting cycles; the SDGs turn goals into targets; and Pakistan's stack, PEPA 1997, the NEQS and the provincial agencies, carries it down to the drain.

Model: the sensory system did not evolve for industrial chemistry; CO is colourless and odourless yet poisons, so detection is an instrument's job, which is why CO alarms exist. Marks (2): 1 for the CO fact; 1 for the general principle. Model: biotransformation; the liver converted the weak organophosphate into its active, nerve-attacking form, so the harm outran the label. Marks (2): 1 for the stage; 1 for the mechanism. Model: distribution (the blood parks it in bone) and excretion-or-storage (the storage branch, for years). Marks (2): 1 per stage. The unit runs inward then outward: 5.1 the agents, 5.2 the body's handling, 5.3 the honest version of 5.2 that pupils will meet as marketing, and 5.4 the governance that manages it all at scale. The CO generator threads 5.1 to 5.3; the arsenic case threads 5.1 to 5.4. Topic 5.4 is deliberately the largest, folding risk management and the frameworks; give it the guide's full week plus the spill-over from 5.3.

The guide names interactive lectures, seminars, group work, case studies, presentations, guided reading, home study and individual tutorials. This unit leans on case study (the generator, the sprayer, the tea) and on the wall timeline, which is a presentation format every pupil can walk. The home-study element is the staffroom inventory in 5.3, a gentle first audit of health claims.

"If you cannot smell it, it is not poisoning you." Probe with CO and the instrument question: what did the nose evolve to detect? "The liver detoxifies, so chemicals become harmless inside." Probe with the sprayer: what is bioactivation, and what does the queue mean? "Detox means juice cleanses." Probe with the plumbing: which organ does the tea touch? Name the four helps. "MEAs are toothless talk shops." Do not dismiss the frustration; answer it with the POPs evidence and the reporting-cycle mechanism, then let the honest limit stand.

5.1, Chain the agent (25 minutes, pairs). The vote on protection-per-rupee teaches cost-effectiveness without naming it; keep the voting quick and unweighted. 5.2, Journey map (20 minutes, pairs). Comparing maps between pairs with the same card is the point: two correct maps can differ in the harm's stage, and the argument is the learning. 5.3, The honest label (25 minutes, groups of three). Handle the product claims with respect for the buyer; the activity teaches evaluation, not mockery. The ninety-second format keeps it kind. 5.4, The wall timeline (25 minutes, groups of four). The fourth card, the agreement they would want, is the bridge from recall to creation; gallery-walk the results.

The staffroom inventory (5.3) and the three-line answer, problem, office, instrument (5.4), are the unit's practicals, and both run at the practicum school. The guide's practical hour can also carry the chemical-storage walk in 5.2. Debrief together: the governance stack of 5.4 answers who owns the hazards of Units 2 to 4, which is the course's whole argument in one session.

The course closes where it opened, at the human-environment interaction, now seen whole. Unit 5 followed a toxin inside one body; this unit opens the full toxicology toolkit, substances, doses, effects, accumulation, and then turns to the largest interaction of all: a warming climate, the smog it worsens, and the mitigation and adaptation that answer it. The 2022 floods and the Karachi heatwave return as the capstone cases.
documents.s: Toxic Substances, Climate Change and Smog

documents.t: By the end of this unit you should be able to: Define toxicology and its core questions. Classify toxic substances and distinguish anthropogenic from natural poisons. Explain acute, chronic, genotoxic, mutagenic, teratogenic, carcinogenic and sensitizing effects. Explain the biological properties of organic and inorganic pollutants, essentiality and toxicity, routes of absorption, bioaccumulation and bio-magnification. Explain the greenhouse effect, its causes and its enhancement, and global warming. Explain smog, its types, causes, health effects and control measures. Explain climate change, its causes and effects, and evaluate mitigation strategies and adaptation.
Units 1-5 (the whole course). Topic 6.2 builds on Unit 5's xenobiotic journey; 6.4 and 6.5 re-engage Unit 3's air pollution; 6.6 draws on every unit for the capstone.

What toxicology studies: substances and their classes Effects of toxic substances Pollutants in the body: essentiality, absorption, accumulation The greenhouse effect and global warming Smog Climate change: mitigation and adaptation

The topics run from the microscope to the atmosphere: substances and doses (6.1-6.3), then the planetary half (6.4-6.6). The dose-response idea from 6.1 carries through the whole unit, and the climate topics deliberately reuse every earlier unit's tools, the chain, the hierarchy, the governance stack, so the course ends integrated rather than appendicised.

At a village health day near Tharparkar, a trainee teacher holds up two bottles for the Class 8 pupils: one is a pesticide from the cotton fields, the other is the salt from their own kitchen. "Which one is the poison?" she asks. Every hand points at the pesticide. Then she reads the label of a poisoning case the health worker told her about: a child hospitalized after drinking the salty water of a hand pump, and another treated for pesticide rash. "Both bottles hurt someone this month," she says. "The difference is the dose." That is the door into toxicology, and this topic opens it.

Toxicology is the study of the adverse effects of chemicals on living organisms. It asks four questions about any substance: what is it, how does it enter, what does it do, and how much does it take? The last question is the founding one: dose is the amount that reaches a sensitive site, and for most substances the harm depends on it. Water in excess harms; the pesticide diluted a million-fold may not. The classic saying, the dose makes the poison, is the discipline's first law and its first caveat, because some agents, lead and the genotoxic class of Topic 6.2, carry no safe level at all. textbook.com.pk

Toxic substances classify usefully along three axes, by origin, by use, and by the effect they produce, and the third axis belongs to Topic 6.2. By origin: anthropogenic poisons, made or concentrated by people, pesticides, industrial solvents, lead in paint; and natural poisons, made by living things or geology, snake venom, plant alkaloids, arsenic in rock that dissolves into groundwater. By use: pesticides, drugs at the wrong dose, household chemicals, industrial chemicals, and cosmetics. The properties that matter most to behaviour are the ones Unit 5 met: solubility, where it parks, and how long it stays. textbook.com.pk Anthropogenic and natural poisons. The village bottles show the axis. The pesticide is anthropogenic, designed to kill, and the Sindh cotton season exposes the sprayers. Arsenic is natural, dissolved from rock into the Indus basin's groundwater, and the twenty-four-district study of Unit 5 found it in the water families drink (Alibhatti et al., 2017). Snake venom, another natural poison, is the health unit's monsoon visitor. The axis matters because controls differ: an anthropogenic poison can be banned or replaced, a natural one can only be managed, tested, treated, avoided. The WHO's chemical-safety programme spans both, natural and manufactured, for exactly that reason (WHO, n.d.). A worked example. Run the four questions on the kitchen salt. What: sodium chloride, essential to life. Route: by mouth, in food and water. Effect: in excess it raises blood pressure and, in the Thar child's case, the salty well pushed the body's water balance past its limits. Dose: the kitchen pinch is nutrition, the well is a poisoning. Toxicology does not divide the world into safe and dangerous substances; it asks how much, by which door, to whom. Common misconception. "Natural means safe, synthetic means dangerous." Both halves fail. Arsenic and snake venom are natural and lethal; the synthetic class includes life-saving medicines, whose toxicity is a matter of dose and purpose. The honest axis is not origin but information: what the substance is, at what dose, by which route, to whom.
documents.s: Classification and properties of toxic substances

documents.t: Work in pairs. Your teacher gives each pair two substance cards, one natural, one anthropogenic, drawn from the table. For each card, answer the four toxicology questions in one line each, then decide which of the two your pair would rather have spilled in a classroom, and defend the choice with the dose idea. Allow 20 minutes, then three pairs present.

Define toxicology and name its four questions. (Remember) Classify these as anthropogenic or natural: pesticide, arsenic, snake venom, lead paint. (Understand) Why do controls differ for an anthropogenic poison and a natural one? (Analyze) The kitchen salt and the salty well are the same substance. Which question of the four separates nutrition from poisoning? (Apply)

Toxicology studies the adverse effects of chemicals on living organisms through four questions, the agent, the route, the effect and the dose, with dose the founding one and its caveat, the no-safe-level agents. Substances classify by origin, anthropogenic like pesticides and lead paint versus natural like arsenic and snake venom, by use, and by effect. The origin axis decides the control: made poisons can be banned, natural ones only managed. Toxicology divides the world not into safe and dangerous substances but into informed answers.

I can define toxicology and name the four questions. I can classify a substance by origin, use and expected effect. I can explain why natural poisons need managing rather than banning. I can use the dose idea on two exposures to the same substance.

List the six toxic substances closest to the pupils: the cleaner in the toilet block, the chalk dust, the pesticide in the garden, the water source, whatever is really there. For each, note the class, the likely route of exposure for a child, and the one question you would need answered before calling it safe. Do not name the school.

Two patients share a district hospital ward. The first is a farm worker carried in an hour after spraying, sweating, blurred, weak. The second is a woman of fifty from the same village, in for a biopsy, who has drunk the same well water for thirty years. The nurse tells the trainee teacher on placement, "Same village, same chemicals, different clocks." The worker's clock is an hour; the woman's is a lifetime. The two clocks name the two great classes of effect, and behind them wait the special classes this topic adds.

An acute effect appears quickly after a single or short exposure, the sprayer's hour. A chronic effect develops slowly over long, often low-level exposure, the thirty-year well. The distinction organises everything: acute poisoning is an emergency with an antidote clock; chronic disease is a public-health programme with a testing clock. Behind them sit the special classes, named for what they attack: Genotoxic agents damage DNA, the cell's instruction manual; the damage can then be copied forward. Mutagens cause mutations, changes in the DNA sequence; most mutagens are genotoxic, and the effect may wait a lifetime to appear. Teratogens harm the developing unborn child, causing birth defects; the timing of exposure, not only the dose, decides the harm, which is why pregnancy warnings carry their own logic. Carcinogens cause cancer, the uncontrolled growth that begins with one damaged cell; asbestos and tobacco smoke are the classic examples, and the WHO's chemical-safety work lists its major concerns (WHO, n.d.). Sensitizers train the immune system to overreact: the first exposure teaches, the later ones attack, which is why a worker fine with a chemical for years can suddenly develop a rash that never leaves. textbook.com.pk The dose-response relationship ties all the classes to a picture. For most effects, plot dose against harm and the line rises from a threshold, a dose below which the body's repair handles the exposure. For the genotoxic-carcinogenic class the line is drawn without a known safe threshold, which is why regulation treats them with no-level strictness. Note the picture's honest limit: it summarises populations, and the individual, the unborn child, the sensitized worker, can sit far from the average. textbook.com.pk A worked example. Read the ward through the classes. The sprayer's collapse is acute, organophosphate poisoning, Unit 5's bioactivation at speed. The woman's biopsy question is chronic, thirty years of low-dose exposure, and if the well carries a genotoxic carcinogen, arsenic is one, her clock had no threshold to hide behind. The same village, the same chemicals: the classes are the difference between an antidote and a screening programme. Common misconception. "A small dose of anything is harmless." True for the threshold class, false as a general law: the no-threshold agents break it, and the sensitizers break it differently, the first small dose being the lesson the immune system never forgets. The dose idea of Topic 6.1 needs this topic's classes to finish the sentence.
documents.s: Acute and chronic effects; the special classes

documents.t: Work in groups of three. Your teacher gives each group four case cards, real exposure scenarios on one side. For each, name the effect class, the clock it runs on, and the one control that would have prevented it, at the source, the pathway or the receptor. Then each group reads its most instructive card aloud. Allow 25 minutes.

Define acute and chronic effects with one example of each. (Remember) What makes a teratogen's harm depend on timing as well as dose? (Understand) Why are genotoxic carcinogens regulated with no safe level? (Analyze) A worker develops a rash after years of safe use of a solvent. Which class, and what does it mean for her return to that job? (Apply)

Effects divide first by clock, acute after one exposure, chronic over years, then by target: genotoxic agents damage DNA, mutagens change it, teratogens harm the unborn, carcinogens start cancers, sensitizers train the immune system to overreact. The dose-response curve pictures harm rising from a threshold for most effects and from no known safe level for the genotoxic class. The classes decide the response: antidote and emergency for the acute clock, testing and prevention for the chronic one.

I can define acute and chronic effects with real examples. I can name the five special classes and what each attacks. I can read a threshold curve and a no-threshold curve correctly. I can classify a real exposure scenario and name its prevention point.

Ask the school's first-aider about the two most common chemical complaints, a headache from the store room, a rash from the cleaner. Class each one by effect class and clock, and note the one control the school already has in place for it. Do not name the school.

On a school trip to Keenjhar Lake, the guide points to the fishing families and says what the pupils' textbook says not: "The big fish are the worst to eat, if the water is dirty." A pupil asks why. The guide draws in the dust: small plants, small fish, big fish, family. "What the water carries a little of," he says, "the big fish carries a lot of, and the family eats the big fish." He is drawing bio-magnification, and this topic is the explanation behind his dust diagram.

Pollutants behave in the body according to their chemistry. Organic pollutants, built on carbon, pesticides, solvents, dioxins, tend to dissolve in fat, which makes them slow to leave and prone to the accumulation this topic builds to. Inorganic pollutants, the metals and minerals, lead, mercury, arsenic, cadmium, do not break down at all; the body can store them in bone and tissue, and some bind the body's own working parts, which is how they do harm. Essentiality and toxicity sit on one ladder, not two shelves. Essential substances, iron, zinc, copper, even fluoride in small amounts, are required for life; the same substances at higher dose poison, and the ladder's position differs by substance. Iron cures anaemia at one dose and hospitalises a child at another. Arsenic, famously non-essential, is toxic at every rung. The WHO's chemical-safety work treats the essential and the non-essential with the same question, how much reaches whom (WHO, n.d.).
documents.s: Biological properties of organic and inorganic pollutants; essentiality and toxicity

documents.t: Unit 5 named the three doors: the lung (fastest, the air pollutants' door), the gut (food and water, arsenic's door), and the skin (the sprayer's door). The route changes the dose that reaches the blood, and the same substance can be a different exposure by a different door: a farm worker takes in the same pesticide by skin, breath and hand-to-mouth, and the route mix decides how much rides Unit 5's journey. textbook.com.pk

Two words, two scales. Bioaccumulation is within one organism: a substance that enters faster than it leaves builds up over time in the organism's fat or bone. Bio-magnification is up the food chain: each predator eats many prey and inherits what they accumulated, so the concentration rises step by step toward the top, the big fish, the fish-eating bird, the fishing family. textbook.com.pk A worked example. The Keenjhar dust diagram, explained. If the water carries a trace of a fat-loving pollutant, the plankton hold a little; each small fish eats many plankton and holds more; each big fish eats many small fish and holds a lot; the family eats the big fish and receives the whole chain's collections. The guide's warning is the food-chain arithmetic, and it is why the top predators, birds of prey, big fish, and people, are the monitoring stations of environmental poisoning, the story the Minamata bay's mercury taught the world. Common misconception. "If the water is only slightly polluted, the fish are only slightly polluted." The chain is a multiplier, not a mirror: each step concentrates, so a trace in the water can be a dose in the fish. This is why testing the water is not enough, and why the fishing family's big fish, not the lake sample, is the exposure that matters.

Work in groups of four. Each member takes one rung of the Keenjhar ladder, plankton, small fish, large fish, family, and receives a card showing how many of the rung below they eat and what each carries. Multiply up the ladder, write your rung's total on the board, and the class reads the magnification factor from water to family. Then answer: which single control would cut the family's dose most? Allow 25 minutes.

Distinguish organic from inorganic pollutant behaviour in the body. (Understand) Iron is essential and toxic. Explain the ladder idea using it. (Apply) Why does the route of absorption change the dose that reaches the blood? (Analyze) Distinguish bioaccumulation from bio-magnification with the lake's own rungs. (Understand)

Organic pollutants dissolve in fat and linger; inorganic metals never break down and bind the body's working parts. Essentiality and toxicity sit on one ladder, iron essential at one dose and poisonous at another, arsenic toxic at every rung. The three routes of absorption, lung, gut and skin, each deliver a different dose to the blood. Bioaccumulation builds within one organism and bio-magnification up the chain, so a trace in the water becomes a dose in the top predator, the big fish and the family that eats it. The chain is a multiplier, not a mirror.

I can state the body-behaviour difference of organic and inorganic pollutants. I can place iron, fluoride and arsenic correctly on the essentiality ladder. I can name the three absorption doors and rank them for a given exposure. I can build and explain a magnification ladder with real numbers.

Find out what fish, if any, appears in the school's or the neighbourhood's meals, and from where. Write three sentences: the fish's place in its own food chain, whether it is a top predator, and the one question a family should ask about the water it came from. Do not name the school.

A Class 9 pupil looks up from his textbook and says, "Sir, if the greenhouse effect is natural, why is everyone shouting about it?" The teacher walks to the window. "This glass," he says, "keeps the room warm in winter. That is the natural effect, and we need it. Now imagine someone seals the vents and adds another pane every year. The problem is not the glass. The problem is the extra panes." This topic is the physics of the glass and the extra panes, stated simply enough for a Class 9 pupil to carry home.

The mechanism is short and physical. Sunlight arrives as short-wave energy and warms the Earth's surface. The warm surface radiates the energy back as long-wave heat. Greenhouse gases, water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane and others, let the short-wave sunlight through but absorb part of the outgoing long-wave heat, returning some of it downward. The trapped part warms the lower atmosphere. Without this natural effect the Earth would average far below freezing; the glass keeps the room alive. textbook.com.pk The problem is the enhancement. Burning coal, oil and gas, clearing forests, and raising livestock add carbon dioxide and methane to the atmosphere faster than the natural sinks absorb them, so the gas layer thickens: the extra panes. The observed results NASA summarises: global average surface temperature has risen about one degree Celsius since the late nineteenth century, carbon dioxide has increased about 250 times faster than the natural rises after the last ice age, the ice sheets are losing hundreds of billions of tonnes a year, and the sea has risen about 20 centimetres over the last century (NASA, 2024). textbook.com.pk A worked example. Pakistan's own connection to the gases, in one paragraph. The country's emissions per person are low by world standards, but its energy, still coal-and-gas heavy, its deforestation pressures, and its growing livestock all add to the shared layer; and the floods and heatwaves of Topic 6.6 are what the shared layer, thickened by everyone's extra panes, hands back. The justice question, smallest emitters, heaviest losses, is real, and it belongs in the classroom honestly: it explains the global negotiation of Unit 5.4, and it does not exempt anyone's next kilowatt. Common misconception. "The greenhouse effect is itself a problem." The effect is natural and life-sustaining; the enhancement is the problem. The distinction is not pedantry: it tells the pupil that the remedy is not to remove the glass but to stop adding panes, which is why mitigation means cutting emissions, not banning a natural process.
documents.s: The greenhouse gas effect and global warming: causes and effects

documents.t: Work in pairs. Your teacher gives each pair a lamp, a thermometer, and two glass or clear plastic sheets. Measure the temperature under one pane, then two, at one-minute intervals for five minutes. Record the two curves and answer: what does the second pane change, and what in the real atmosphere plays its role? Allow 20 minutes.

Explain the greenhouse mechanism in three sentences, sunlight, heat, gases. (Understand) Why would the Earth freeze without the natural greenhouse effect? (Understand) What does "250 times faster" mean for the carbon cycle? (Analyze) Pakistan's per-person emissions are low. Give the honest two-sided statement of its position on the shared layer. (Evaluate)

The greenhouse effect is natural and physical: short-wave sunlight in, long-wave heat out, gases returning part of it down, keeping the Earth warm enough for life. The enhancement is the problem: fossil fuels, deforestation and livestock thicken the gas layer, and the observed results include about one degree of warming since the late nineteenth century, rapid carbon-dioxide growth, shrinking ice sheets and rising seas. Pakistan's per-person emissions are low and its losses heavy, which frames the justice of the global negotiation without exempting anyone's next kilowatt.

I can explain the mechanism in three sentences without jargon. I can state the natural-versus-enhanced distinction and why it matters. I can name the main greenhouse gases with one source each. I can give the honest two-sided statement of Pakistan's position.

Find the school's last electricity bill and ask the clerk what powers the grid, the fuel mix in the bill's notes or the local knowledge. Write three sentences: the school's own panes, the national mix, and the one energy change the school could realistically make.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

Explain the greenhouse effect and its enhancement to a Class 9 pupil in your own words, using the pane picture, naming the two gases Pakistan's own activities add most, and ending with the one sentence you want the pupil to remember. In November in Lahore, the morning assembly moves indoors and the announcement says the AQI is "hazardous, again". A Class 7 pupil asks the trainee teacher the question this topic exists for: "Sir, is this fog? My grandmother says it is fog." The trainee looks out at the grey and answers carefully. "Your grandmother's fog was water. This is water with a city in it."

Smog is polluted fog, or, more precisely, a visible mixture of pollutants held near the ground, and it comes in two types. Sulfurous smog, the winter kind, forms when sulfur dioxide and particles from coal and waste burning mix with fog under a temperature inversion, the cold-air lid Unit 3 met. Photochemical smog, the summer kind, forms when traffic and industrial emissions cook in sunlight into ozone and a haze of secondary pollutants, worst on hot, still afternoons. Lahore's winter grey is mostly the first kind with a base of the second's leftovers, and the integrated satellite-and-survey study of Unit 3 found it critical for both environment and public health in the district (Anwar et al., 2026). textbook.com.pk The health effects are Unit 3's air-pollution effects concentrated: the PM2.5 and the ozone inflame airways, worsen asthma and heart disease, and the WHO attributes 4.2 million premature deaths a year to outdoor air pollution, of which smog episodes are the visible peaks (WHO, 2024). The grandmother's fog never did this; the water only made the poison visible. textbook.com.pk The control measures are Unit 3's chain, applied to an episode. At the source: cleaner fuel and upgraded kilns, enforced engine standards, an end to crop-residue and waste burning, the measures that shorten the episode for everyone. At the pathway: little can be done while the inversion lid sits; the honest answer is that the pathway cannot be cleaned. At the receptor: the school's AQI watch, indoor hours, masks that filter PM2.5, and asthma plans ready, the measures that protect the assembly. A worked example. Read the announcement morning through the chain. The AQI is hazardous, so the receptor measures fire at once: assembly indoors, windows shut, sports cancelled. The same reading, published daily, is the evidence for the source measures, kiln upgrades, traffic alternation, burning bans, that the district's winter plans now carry. One number, two ends of the chain; the school acts on one end and votes for the other. Common misconception. "Smog is just fog." Fog is water; smog is water plus pollutants, or sunlight plus pollutants, and the difference is a health effect. The test is the index, not the eye: the AQI reading tells the assembly what to do whatever the grey looks like.
documents.s: Smog: types, causes, human health effects and control measures

documents.t: Work in pairs. Your teacher gives each pair twelve cards, causes, effects and controls mixed. Sort them onto the two panels, sulfurous and photochemical, then swap one card with another pair and defend the placement. Allow 20 minutes.

Define smog and name its two types with their seasons. (Remember) What does a temperature inversion do to a city's winter air? (Understand) Why can nothing be done at the pathway link during an inversion? (Analyze) The AQI reads hazardous on assembly morning. Name the two ends of the chain the school acts on. (Apply)

Smog is polluted fog: sulfurous in winter, sulfur dioxide and particles under an inversion from coal and waste burning, photochemical in summer, traffic emissions cooked by sunlight into ozone. Its health effects are air pollution's effects at their peaks, 4.2 million premature deaths a year worldwide. Controls act at the source, fuel, kilns, engines, burning bans, and at the receptor, the AQI watch, indoor hours, filtration, asthma plans, while the pathway honestly cannot be cleaned. The AQI number serves both ends.

I can define smog and distinguish its two types and seasons. I can explain the inversion's role in the winter kind. I can name the receptor-end measures a school actually takes. I can explain why "just fog" is the wrong reading.

Find out whether the school has an AQI routine, who checks, what threshold moves assembly indoors. If it has none, draft the three-line routine you would propose: who checks, at what threshold, what changes. Do not name the school.

Write the reply a teacher gives a Class 7 pupil: what smog is, the two kinds, what the winter grey over Lahore mostly is, and the two things, one at each end of the chain, that the pupil's own school can do about it. Two photographs hang side by side in the corridor of a Hyderabad college. The first: Karachi in June 2015, the week the morgues ran out of space, more than a thousand lives lost to the heatwave. The second: the same province in August 2022, a third of the country under water. A first-year student asks the question the whole course has been building toward: "What do we actually do about this?" The answer is two words, and this topic is them.

The causes are Topic 6.4's enhancement: fossil-fuel energy, deforestation, industry and agriculture thickening the greenhouse layer. The effects arrive as the extremes the thickened layer feeds, and the WHO reports that 3.6 billion people already live in places highly susceptible to them, with about 250,000 additional deaths a year projected between 2030 and 2050 from undernutrition, malaria, diarrhoea and heat stress alone (WHO, 2023). Pakistan's own decade holds both photographs: the heatwave and the floods, and the review literature describes the country as suffering the disastrous effects of a crisis it did least to cause, examining the floods' environmental, social and economic implications and the policies that answer them (Adnan et al., 2024). textbook.com.pk The two responses answer different questions. Mitigation reduces the causes: cutting emissions, moving to renewable energy, planting and protecting forests, efficient transport and industry. It works on the shared layer, for everyone, over decades. Adaptation reduces the harm of what already arrives: heat-action plans and cool shelters, flood-proof schools and early-warning systems, drought-resistant crops, water storage. It works locally, now, for the exposed. The two are partners, not alternatives: mitigation without adaptation abandons the exposed present; adaptation without mitigation surrenders the future. textbook.com.pk A worked example. Read the two photographs through the responses. The heatwave's answer is adaptation's textbook: Karachi's heat-action plan, drinking points, cool rooms, checked-on neighbours, the measures that cut the 2015 toll in the calmer years since. The floods' answer is both: adaptation in early warning, elevated schools, re-built wells; mitigation in the national and global emissions policy that decides how many such floods the next decade holds. Pakistan's own climate policy carries both, and its plantation drives and renewable programme sit on the mitigation side while its flood plans sit on the other. The course, whole. Every tool returns here. The chain from Unit 2 tells the receptor-end school what to do on a heat day. The hierarchy from Unit 3 orders the adaptations: remove the exposure, relocate the assembly; guard, shade and water points; procedures, the heat drill; protect, the water bottle. The governance stack from Unit 5 names who owns the mitigation, the Paris pledges, the national policy, the provincial plan. And the teacher's own step, Unit 1's fifth, influence others, multiplies through a classroom. The student's question, what do we do, has a two-word answer and a whole-course method behind it. Common misconception. "Mitigation and adaptation are alternatives; choose one." They answer different questions, the future's causes and the present's harms, and every serious plan carries both. The second misconception is quieter: "It is too late for anything." The honest reading is the opposite of paralysis: every fraction of a degree avoided is harm prevented, and every adaptation installed is harm softened, which is why the WHO describes cutting emissions as able to result in very large gains for health (WHO, 2023).
documents.s: Climate change: causes, effects, mitigation strategies and adaptation

documents.t: Work in groups of three. Your teacher gives each group sixteen cards, real climate responses from tree plantation to heat-action plans to solar panels to flood warnings. Sort them into mitigation and adaptation, then flag the four you would present to the district government first, with one sentence of reasoning each. Allow 25 minutes, then each group presents its four.

Define mitigation and adaptation, one sentence each. (Remember) Why are the two responses partners rather than alternatives? (Analyze) Place the heatwave's and the floods' answers on the two sides, and justify any response that sits on both. (Analyze) Apply Unit 3's hierarchy to a school's heat-day plan, one control per level. (Apply)

Climate change's causes are the enhanced greenhouse layer; its effects arrive as extremes, heatwaves and floods, with 3.6 billion people highly susceptible and a quarter-million additional deaths a year projected. Mitigation cuts the causes for the shared future, renewable energy, forests, efficient industry; adaptation softens the harms of the arriving present, heat plans, flood-proofing, early warning. Pakistan's two photographs answer to both sides, and the course's tools, the chain, the hierarchy, the governance stack, the teacher's multiplication, are the method. The student's question has a two-word answer: both, now.

I can define mitigation and adaptation and give two examples of each. I can explain why both are needed, future and present. I can place the heatwave's and the floods' answers on the right sides. I can carry the course's tools into one school-scale climate response.

Write the school's one-page climate page: two hazards the school already faces, one adaptation the school could install this term, one mitigation the school community could join this year, and the two names, who leads each. This is the course's last practicum task; make it the one you would actually hand over.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: Write 170 to 200 words on the following. The principal asks: "Heat and floods, which should we prepare for?" Write the answer this course supports: what the two responses are, why the school prepares for both, the one adaptation and the one mitigation you would start this term, and the line that says who checks. End with the sentence you want the staffroom to remember. Toxicology asks four questions, the agent, the route, the effect and the dose, with dose the founding one and its caveat, the no-safe-level agents. Substances classify by origin, anthropogenic against natural, by use and by effect; the origin axis decides the control, banning the made and managing the natural. Effects divide by clock, acute against chronic, then by target: genotoxic, mutagenic, teratogenic, carcinogenic and sensitizing, with the dose-response curve rising from a threshold for most effects and no known safe level for the genotoxic class. Organic pollutants linger in fat and inorganic metals never break down; essentiality and toxicity share one ladder; the three absorption doors deliver different doses; bioaccumulation builds within one organism and bio-magnification up the chain, the multiplier that makes a trace in the water a dose in the family. The greenhouse effect is natural and life-sustaining; its enhancement, fossil fuels, deforestation, livestock, is the problem, with about one degree of warming observed. Smog is polluted fog, sulfurous in winter and photochemical in summer, and its controls act at the source and the receptor. Mitigation cuts the causes for the shared future; adaptation softens the arriving present's harms; the two are partners, and the course's tools, the chain, the hierarchy, the governance stack, are how a school answers.

The founding question of toxicology is: (Remember) a) where was it made b) how much reaches the site c) who sells it d) what colour is it Arsenic in Sindh's groundwater is a poison that is: (Understand) a) anthropogenic and bannable b) natural and only manageable c) synthetic and replaceable d) biological and treatable Cutting emissions and installing cool shelters are, respectively: (Understand) a) adaptation and mitigation b) mitigation and adaptation c) both mitigation d) both adaptation A teratogen's harm depends on: (Understand) a) dose only b) timing as well as dose c) the season only d) nothing measurable Genotoxic carcinogens are regulated with no safe level because: (Analyze) a) they are always immediately fatal b) their dose-response shows no known threshold c) they cannot be measured d) they only harm workers Iron is essential at one dose and toxic at another. This illustrates: (Apply) a) the origin axis b) the essentiality ladder c) bio-magnification d) sensitization A farm worker takes in the same pesticide by skin, breath and hand-to-mouth. What changes across the three? (Apply) a) the substance's chemistry b) the dose reaching the blood c) the effect class d) nothing at all The natural greenhouse effect: (Understand) a) is the problem to remove b) keeps the Earth warm enough for life c) began with industry d) exists only in cities Lahore's winter grey is mostly: (Understand) a) photochemical smog b) ordinary fog c) sulfurous smog under an inversion d) desert dust alone Heat-action plans and flood-proof schools are examples of: (Apply) a) mitigation b) adaptation c) bioactivation d) source control

Name toxicology's four questions, in any order. (Remember) Why do controls differ for anthropogenic and natural poisons? (Analyze) Distinguish acute from chronic effects with the ward's two patients. (Understand) Why does a sensitizer's harm appear only after years of safe use? (Analyze) Name the three absorption doors and rank them for a spray drift exposure. (Apply) Distinguish bioaccumulation from bio-magnification in one sentence each. (Understand) Explain the greenhouse mechanism in three sentences. (Understand) Name one mitigation and one adaptation a school could adopt this term, and say which protects the present and which the future. (Apply) Why can nothing be done at the pathway link during a smog episode? (Analyze) Mitigation and adaptation answer different questions. State both questions. (Understand)

A parent says the school should "ban every chemical and go natural". Using the classification and the dose idea, write the honest reply with one real example per side. (Analyze) The district health office asks for the two clocks brief: acute and chronic effects, the different plans they need, and the one special class every pregnant staff member must know. (Evaluate) The fisheries office asks why it tests big fish, not only water. Using the ladder and the multiplier idea, write the page, ending with advice for the fishing families. (Evaluate) Warming and the winter grey are one air story. Explain to a Class 9 pupil how the greenhouse effect's enhancement and Lahore's smog grow from the same human activities yet harm by different routes, using the pane picture and the two smog types, and name one control at the source they share. (Analyze) Course capstone: the principal asks, "Heat and floods, which should we prepare for?" Write the answer: both responses, why both, one adaptation and one mitigation to start this term, who checks, and the sentence the staffroom should remember. (Create)

b - the dose makes the poison is the discipline's first law. b - arsenic dissolves naturally from rock; it can only be managed, tested, treated. b - mitigation cuts the causes for the shared future; adaptation softens the arriving present's harms. b - the unborn child's stage of development decides the teratogen's harm. b - the no-threshold dose-response is the reason for no-level strictness. b - the essentiality ladder: required at one rung, poisonous higher up. b - the route changes the dose that reaches the blood; the substance is the same. b - without it the Earth would average far below freezing. c - coal and waste burning under an inversion, with photochemical leftovers. b - adaptation softens the arriving present's harms.

Model: what is the agent; how does it enter (route); what does it do (effect); how much does it take (dose). Marks (4): 1 per question. Model: anthropogenic poisons are made or concentrated by people, so they can be banned or replaced; natural poisons cannot be banned, only managed, tested, treated, avoided. Marks (2): 1 per half. Model: the sprayer's collapse an hour after exposure is acute, the antidote clock; the thirty-year well drinker's biopsy is chronic, the testing clock. Marks (2): 1 per patient correctly classed. Model: the first exposure teaches the immune system; later exposures trigger the trained overreaction, so the harm appears only after the lesson is given. Marks (2): 1 for the teaching; 1 for the later attack. Model: lung, gut, skin; for spray drift, skin first (the wet spray on the body), lung second (the mist breathed), gut third (hand-to-mouth). Marks (3): 1 for the doors; 2 for a defensible ranking. Model: bioaccumulation is the build-up within one organism, entry faster than exit; bio-magnification is the rise in concentration up the food chain as each predator eats many prey. Marks (2): 1 per sentence. Model: short-wave sunlight in and warms the surface; the surface radiates long-wave heat out; greenhouse gases absorb part of the heat and return some downward, warming the lower atmosphere. Marks (3): 1 per sentence. Model: any real pair, for example mitigation, joining a tree-planting drive or shifting a generator's load hours, which protects the future by cutting emissions; adaptation, shade shelters or a heat-day plan, which protects the present by softening the arriving harms. Marks (2): 1 for a correct mitigation-adaptation pair; 1 for the present-versus-future placement. Model: the pathway is the air under the lid; dispersion cannot be increased while the inversion sits, so the only honest action is at the source and the receptor. Marks (2): 1 for the physics; 1 for the consequence. Model: mitigation answers how we stop feeding the future crisis (cut the causes); adaptation answers how we soften the harms already arriving (protect the exposed). Marks (2): 1 per question.

Six topics, one arc: the microscope half first (6.1 substances, 6.2 effects, 6.3 the body), then the atmospheric half (6.4 greenhouse, 6.5 smog, 6.6 the capstone). The two-bottles hook of 6.1 and the two photographs of 6.6 are the unit's bookends; the ladder activity in 6.3 and the pane model in 6.4 are its two hands-on anchors. Teach 6.6 with the whole course open: it is the integration, not an appendix.

The guide names interactive lectures, seminars, group work, case studies, presentations, guided reading, home study and individual tutorials. This unit leans on case study (the ward, the lake, the photographs) and on the two measurement activities, the pane model and the AQI routine. The home-study element is the school's climate page in 6.6, the course's last practicum task and the one most worth collecting.

"Natural means safe." Probe with arsenic and snake venom against a life-saving synthetic: what is the honest axis? "A small dose of anything is harmless." Probe with the no-threshold class and the sensitizer: which two classes break the rule, and how? "The greenhouse effect is the problem." Probe with the frozen-Earth question: what would we lose if the glass came out? "Smog is just fog." Probe with the index: what does the AQI read on a foggy clean morning and on a smog morning? "Mitigation and adaptation are alternatives." Probe with the two photographs: which single response answers both?

6.1, Two bottles, four questions (20 minutes, pairs). The "rather have spilled" choice forces the dose argument; accept any defensible answer. 6.2, Class the case (25 minutes, groups of three). The case cards should mix clocks and classes; the most instructive card read aloud is usually the sensitizer, which defeats the intuition. 6.3, Build the ladder (25 minutes, groups of four). The board arithmetic of the magnification factor is the moment; keep the numbers simple enough to multiply in public. 6.4, The pane model (20 minutes, pairs). A desk lamp, a thermometer, two clear sheets: the second pane's curve is the whole mechanism. If kit is short, run it as one demonstration with a pupil recording. 6.5, The two-panel sort (20 minutes, pairs). The one-card swap and defend is the learning; a wrong placement defended is worth more than a right one unexplained. 6.6, Sort the responses (25 minutes, groups of three). The four cards presented to "the district government" teach prioritisation; require the one-sentence reasoning.

The pane model and the climate page are the unit's practicals. The AQI routine draft (6.5) and the climate page (6.6) both run at the practicum school and both are handover artefacts, written to be used. Debrief the course's full set of practicum tasks together in the last session: the waste log, the risk register, the near-miss book, the plan, the climate page, that stack is the trainee's portfolio and the course's real assessment.

This course equips prospective teachers with a grounded understanding of critical thinking and reflective practice as professional capabilities - the nature of thinking, the barriers to it, and the habits of mind that make reflection a disciplined professional act rather than an occasional one.
documents.s: Critical Thinking and Reflective Practices - Course Overview

documents.t: Assessment follows the GECE default: 60% summative / 40% formative (Constitution Art. III.7). This course's guide does not specify a course-wide breakdown of teaching strategies or practical work beyond what each unit's own topics cover - see each unit's Teacher Notes for the strategies used to teach it.
Recommended sources from the course guide are listed for scope and further reading only; they are never reproduced as content.

Before you can teach pupils to think critically, it helps to be clear about what critical thinking actually is - and, just as importantly, what it is not. In everyday staffroom talk the phrase is sometimes used to mean "being sceptical about everything" or "finding fault with what other people say". This unit uses a different meaning, the one the course guide follows: critical thinking is the habit of judging a piece of reasoning against a set of clear standards. It is a skill you can train, not a personality you either have or lack.

By the end of this unit you will be able to: Explain what critical thinking is and distinguish it from merely criticising or from general scepticism. Name and apply the recognised standards used to judge a piece of reasoning. Identify the common barriers that stop people - including teachers - from thinking critically. Distinguish a statement, a claim, an issue and an argument, and recognise when a piece of text is making an argument. Analyse a described teacher's reasoning against the standards and name the barrier it shows.

None beyond HSC-level general study skills. This is the opening unit of the course. No prior logic or philosophy is assumed, and none is needed. If you have ever had to decide whether a colleague's argument was convincing and why, you already have the experience this unit builds on.

What thinking is, and what makes it critical - the functions of thought and the idea of critical thinking. The standards, and what they are for - the standards applied to reasoning and why they matter. What gets in the way - the barriers that stop critical thinking. Statements, claims, issues and arguments - the basic units reasoning is built from. The critical thinker, and the teacher as one - the characteristics of a critical thinker, applied to teachers.

Each topic is one learning cycle. Start with the classroom situation, work through the explanation, and try the activity before you move on. The "Check your understanding" items are there to help you retrieve what you have learned - have a go at them without looking back, then check your answer. The unit ends with a summative assessment that draws the five topics together.
